in writing. in the 2007 green paper, the commission draws attention to the validity of the debate on the need for its involvement in the problem of increasing mobility in eu cities, based on the principle of subsidiarity. in accordance with the principle of subsidiarity, the union shall act within its competences only when it is necessary and when it adds value to the action of the member states. the purpose of the subsidiarity principle is to ensure that decisions are taken as closely as possible to the citizen by continuously checking whether action to be taken at community level is justified in the light of the possibilities that exist at national, regional or local level. the lisbon treaty, which is in the process of ratification, further strengthens the role of the member states in determining whether the eu institutions should also be involved at local level. the package of measures to be taken to increase mobility in urban areas discussed often treats innovative technologies and intelligent transport systems separately. these two areas should be synergistically integrated to achieve the effect of increasing street capacity, improving travel comfort and traffic conditions, reducing travel time and energy consumption, reducing emissions, reducing the costs of road fleet management and maintenance and renewal, and ultimately improving road safety. in view of the above, the commission's action plan on urban mobility will be underpinned by the completion of the ratification of the lisbon treaty and the implementation of the czech presidency's programme, which prioritises strengthening the functionality of the eu's internal transport market.
the rapporteur. - mr president, commissioner, i have to ask you to leave. we're changing the subject: we're going to talk about the connections between the institutions of the european union and its citizens, the connections that are broken, the connections that have a big gap between them. and jean monnet said in the past: 'we are not creating a union for states and governments, we are creating it for citizens'. the european union is expanding, citizens are coming, and the european institutions, the institutions of the european union, have a problem with contacting citizens. this has been demonstrated by the painful experience of the french and dutch rejection of the european constitution and the irish rejection of the treaty of lisbon. it is true that the eu institutions are trying to improve contact with citizens, they are opening up to them, they are clearly recognising the role of civil society. the range of eu communication policies in this area is growing, and has even been given the special name of citizens' dialogue, but this is not enough. and that is why the european parliament is taking up this challenge, trying to create this kind of mechanism and to propose this kind of contacts between the institutions of the european union and its citizens, which will eliminate the lack of democracy, will show that citizens also play an important role in the decision-making process within the european union. article 10 of the lisbon treaty states: 'every citizen has the right to participate in the democratic life of the union. decisions are taken as openly and as closely as possible to the citizen. this is accompanied by an additional provision which also refers to the legislative initiative of one million citizens of the european union, who, after the entry into force of the treaty of lisbon, will be able to approach the european commission and urge it to prepare a legislative proposal on a matter of importance to citizens. that is why i am talking about civil dialogue in this report, a dialogue which is not defined by law, but a dialogue which is necessary and which i would like to see guided or guided by the following principles: firstly, i have introduced the principle of the representativeness of civil society in this report. i would like to see civil society well represented at eu level, well represented by partners who properly and appropriately reflect and represent the interests. i want the citizens' dialogue to be reciprocal, bilateral - that is, not just the european union speaking to the citizen and the citizen of the union responding, but the eu institutions informing the citizen when that voice has been taken into account and what the consequences of the citizen's opinions have been. this is why we need feedback from the union to the citizens. i want the citizens' dialogue to be based on the principle of transparency, that we follow clear rules when inviting representatives of society to the dialogue, that we have a systematic publication of the lists of organisations that have joined the consultation. it would be good if the union had a person in charge of this aspect, namely dialogue. the rules for civil dialogue are difficult to define, and i therefore expect that the european commission, which has already prepared specific rules for a strengthened culture of consultation and dialogue (i.e. in 2002), will want to prepare such rules which will become common to all the institutions. and i just want to point out that member states should also be obliged to promote civil dialogue. i want everything that is in this report, and that i have not had time to say, to be tested in the first possible situation, namely the european parliament elections, in the election campaign, and that we take this first step in contacting european citizens, communicating what the union has best to offer them and taking from them the lessons that we should include here.
member of the commission. − mr president, first of all the commission would like to thank the rapporteur, ms grabowska, as well as the committee on constitutional affairs for their excellent report. we agree that civil society plays an important role in european integration. it is one of the key tools for communication between european institutions, eu society and eu citizens. it helps citizens to exercise their right to participate in the democratic life of the union. the commission has a long and healthy tradition of interaction with civil society organisations. this cooperation between the commission and civil society has grown, covering a wide variety of issues from policy dialogue to project management, both within the eu and in our partner countries. the treaty of lisbon would put our existing practices on a more formal footing and provide a fresh impetus to further enhance them. it would also open the door to another option for civil society to operationalise its views through the citizens’ initiative. involving interested parties in an active dialogue requires the provision of appropriate instruments for civil society to express its opinions and be heard. the eu institutions also need equally appropriate instruments to ensure that what we hear from civil society and citizens is properly picked up and put into the system. the commission welcomes the fact that the current report supports many of the ideas the commission is already putting into effect. through its mandate, the current commission has taken a series of initiatives to involve civil society organisations and individual citizens in a public debate on eu issues. one of the more innovative examples of these efforts has been the citizens’ consultations, experimenting with deliberative polling and face-to-face consultations. to understand people’s needs and expectations, over the past 35 years the eurobarometer has been developed into a very valuable tool for monitoring public opinion in europe. neither the commission nor parliament can, however, single-handedly organise a europe-wide public debate. this will only be possible if eu institutions and member states work together. that is the purpose of the political declaration on ‘communicating europe in partnership’ signed by parliament, the council and the commission on 22 october 2008. in this context, the commission and parliament are already coordinating efforts with the member states via the management partnerships, which include regional and local campaigns on specific issues, linking up with action by local authorities and ngos. eleven new management partnerships in 2009 will make this approach even more effective. the commission shares the view that fruitful dialogue depends on the active participation of all sides: the eu institutions, the member states and civil society. the commission hopes that the lisbon treaty will come into force and stands ready to take the necessary action to put its provisions into practice and to continue developing civil dialogue.
in writing. a democratic and citizen-friendly european union requires the eu institutions and the member states to work closely with civil society at national, regional and local levels. civil society, representing the many non-governmental and non-profit organisations set up by citizens of their own free will, plays a very important role in the european integration process by presenting the positions and demands of union citizens to the european institutions. effective and reliable information to citizens and the promotion of civil dialogue are therefore of paramount importance, in particular in promoting and disseminating the actions and intentions of the european union, in building a network of european cooperation and in strengthening european identity among civil society. the european union needs a wider public debate, more effective civic dialogue and greater political awareness to achieve its political aims and objectives. the lisbon treaty strengthens citizens' rights vis-à-vis the union by facilitating their participation and that of associations representing civil society in the debate on a 'citizens' europe'. the european union institutions should work more closely together to build a european citizens' dialogue and promote a pro-european attitude among eu citizens. it is necessary to encourage citizens to take a greater part in european debates and discussions, and to participate actively in the forthcoming elections to the european parliament, because, as jean monnet said, 'we are not creating a union for states and governments, we are creating a union for citizens'.
in writing. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the report by ms grabowska on the prospects for developing civil dialogue under the lisbon treaty is a waste of time and resources. so the question is, is it really a fundamental question? what is this debate really about? after all, the treaty is dead - ireland rejected it in a national referendum. this means that the document has no legal force. to build anything on it is to build in a vacuum, without a foundation. building on a treaty that doesn't really exist because it was rejected is a violation of democracy and the equal rights of free peoples. so once again, the encyclopedic knowledge of the term "democracy" is being bowed. in my view, democracy is a conscious choice, not a forced and unconscionable disregard for the will of the people. in a democracy, the sovereign is the people, not a group of interests, and the ultimate form of sovereignty is a referendum, not a decision by a ruling clique that is contrary to the will of the people. is that so hard to understand?

in writing. in the debate on the euro, i would like to highlight three negative aspects of its operation. 1.the three non-euro area member states (england, sweden and denmark) have grown faster than the euro area since the introduction of the euro, i.e. from 2002 to 2007 inclusive. gnp in these countries grew almost twice as fast as the euro area average, and unemployment was lower. 2.the fight against the effects of the current financial and, consequently, economic crisis is clearly more effective in these countries than in the euro area. the central banks of england, sweden and denmark have very quickly and significantly reduced interest rates, while providing liquidity to commercial banks. it also appears that fiscal policies in these countries will be more effective than fiscal policies in the euro area. 3.new member states preparing to join the euro area are required to meet a number of monetary and fiscal criteria for two years before joining the euro area. some of these criteria are contradictory, such as the need to be in erm 2 and thus to maintain the deviations of the national currency against the euro within a fluctuation band of +/- 15% while keeping inflation low. countering the pressure to devalue the national currency means that central banks have to intervene, and therefore put more national money into circulation, which obviously increases inflationary pressure. in order to encourage new member states, the commission should consider how to eliminate this apparent contradiction.

in writing. − the unfair commercial practices directive and the directive on misleading and comparative advertising are of great importance for increasing consumer confidence and providing businesses with greater legal certainty in the internal market. this is particularly important in relation to cross-border transactions, which are becoming more common on the european market. in the case of such transactions, national consumer protection authorities continue to face difficulties in taking appropriate action in the country of destination. the correct transposition, implementation and enforcement of those directives are essential to achieve the objectives of those directives. unfortunately, a number of member states have not yet complied with this obligation, which does not contribute to building the right relationships between businesses and consumers. in 2007, the european commission introduced the so-called systematic checks mechanism for the first time as a tool to monitor and enforce the implementation of consumer protection legislation on airline websites. the irregularities were confirmed on as many as 43,6% of the websites checked, which only confirms the need for more controls over the enforcement of the already existing rules. i welcome the commission's initiative to create a publicly accessible database of national measures transposing these directives.
in writing. - i strongly support the report by mrs barbara weiler on the transposition and enforcement of the directive on unfair commercial practices in the internal market and the directive on misleading and comparative advertising. the problem of misleading and comparative advertising limited to business-to-business transactions has been addressed by the introduction of a single consolidated directive. the issue of unfair commercial practices in consumer-to-business relations is addressed by directive 2005/29/ec. the directives were designed to increase consumer confidence (their protection has been enhanced by the establishment of a blacklist of commercial practices that should be prohibited and by better harmonising consumer protection against unfair practices) and to provide businesses with greater legal certainty. a higher degree of protection could be achieved if the provisions of the directives were accompanied by effective legal enforcement measures. member states must therefore control their legal systems and increase the transparency of the transposition process. the changes introduced must be supported by accessible implementation procedures and effective remedies that give consumers the right to bring actions for damages for losses suffered as a result of unfair commercial practices, such as the consumer protection control mechanism for airline websites, which was first applied in 2007. at member state level, awareness and education campaigns on means of exercising consumer rights should also be considered.
in writing. - ucits are undertakings for collective investment in transferable securities. they are the product of harmonised investment funds which allocate funds in accordance with investment strategies. the ucits framework directive, which is the subject of the klinz report, ensures cost transparency and, which is particularly important in times of economic and financial crisis in the eu member states a high degree of investor protection. the directive lays down the basic requirements for the organisation, management and supervision of the funds. it is true that european investment funds are small compared to the us market, which results in high costs for investors. there is therefore a need to review the ucits package, to adapt it to the needs of investors and to ensure the competitiveness of the eu funds sector. the amendments proposed by the rapporteur are mainly to introduce new rules on the merger of funds (so that it would be treated as a domestic merger with tax neutrality), to introduce a key investor information document (replacing the simplified prospectus) and to simplify the current notification procedure by means of a direct exchange of information between supervisors.
vice-president of the commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i should first like to thank the chairman of the libe committee, and i should also like to thank the rapporteur, mr carlos coelho, for his excellent report and also for the excellent cooperation he has had with the commission on a sensitive and sensitive subject. the commission proposal was to introduce harmonised exceptions to the requirement to take fingerprints so that all european citizens are treated equally. the commission also wanted to protect children from trafficking in human beings by making the internationally recognised principle of one person, one passport legally binding. i would like to welcome the efforts of the european parliament to secure agreement on this proposal at first reading, as fingerprints must be introduced in member states' passports by 28 june 2009. if no agreement had been reached, everyone would have been obliged to give their fingerprints, even newborn babies, as soon as they travel abroad with a passport. so i really want to express the commission's satisfaction with the proposed negotiated compromise. the commission will now proceed with the report requested by the european parliament in the most efficient way possible. i think it is not worthwhile to dwell on it, and i shall now listen with interest to the speeches of the members of the european parliament, and i would like to thank your rapporteur, mr carlos coelho, who has done an excellent job.
on behalf of the ppe-de group. – mr president, i am happy to support the proposals presented today. i believe there is an urgent need to create a common set of standards for the verification of biometric data. colleagues may not be aware that at present there are wide discrepancies between countries as to how rigorously, for example, they verify passport photographs. many countries require that the citizen applying for a passport actually present him or herself in person, together with their documents and photographs, and in these cases the officials at the passport-issuing office can see if that person bears a resemblance to the photo presented. however, in some countries – maybe most notably in the united kingdom – applications by post are the norm, and the authenticity of the photo is only confirmed by a so-called ‘professional person’ who has known the applicant for at least two years. the list of persons eligible to do this in the united kingdom makes for fairly interesting reading. this verification can be made by your optician or your dentist, but also by a professional photographer or a fire service official – no disrespect to members of these professions. it is also interesting that fairly lax rules on verification exist in the united states. verifications of photos for passports for first-time applicants can be carried out at so-called ‘acceptable facilities’. in fact, this means the staff at the local post office. it seems incredible for such a security-conscious country, whose citizens enjoy visa-free travel to europe, to have such a system of verification. so, in order to make passports secure, we really need to bring in much more reliable biometric data, namely fingerprints. we also need to ensure that the agency responsible for their collection and verification complies with the same standards, not only within the eu but also in those nations whose citizens do enjoy visa-free travel to europe, to assure us that they too are meeting the same stringent requirements as are our citizens here in europe.
the introduction of passports containing biometric elements to identify the document holder is a response to calls to combat counterfeiting, terrorism and illegal immigration. it is therefore essential to ensure a high level of trust in the collection of biometric data and to establish common basic standards for the collection of data in a way that ensures their security and reliability. i support the rapporteur's proposal to analyse the differences between member states in the compulsory documents required for the issuing of a passport. the security of these documents is usually lower than that of biometric passports. therefore, there is a risk that they will be more easily falsified or counterfeited.
mr. chairman, please! the harmonisation of the rules on security standards, combined with the introduction of biometric identification elements, should have a positive impact on the credibility of documents during their control and thus constitute an element in the fight against counterfeiting. these factors in turn guarantee a more effective fight against crime, terrorism and illegal immigration. in the absence of appropriate tests related to the use of new technologies, member states should introduce their own requirements for the protection of citizens' rights. it is necessary to set an age limit for children as passport holders and to eliminate the cases where one passport can be issued to a holder and his children without biometric data. such situations may facilitate trafficking in children, as the control of the child's identity is made more difficult. in order to prevent such procedures, each person should hold his or her own passport. finally, i would like to stress that in order to ensure the security of the holders of passports and other identity documents, a high level of discretion should be introduced in the process of collecting biometric data.
mr. chairman, please! i would like to begin by congratulating the rapporteur and saying that i support this report. i think they're not only important, they're good. i shall begin by saying that it has been stated that a passport is a document issued by each member state in accordance with its national legislation. we have different passports. except for the covers. but it is important to strike a balance between the security features of these passports, so that they identify the european union citizen, or any other person entering the european union, and at the same time counter the crimes that passports are notorious for, such as illegal immigration, terrorism, child trafficking and forgery. in this report, i believe, that balance has been struck. there is no indication that the restrictions we put on the report in any way affect or restrict member states in issuing passports. i would also like to draw attention to one principle which i fully support - one person, one passport. it's a good rule for children, and i wish there were no financial barriers for parents who want to get their children a passport, and they may have little money. i would also like to draw attention to one weak point in this report, but which the rapporteur does point out, namely that modern, untested technologies require revision, and it is fortunate that in three years' time we will be able to do so. i also call for the role of the european data protection supervisor to be taken into account. this eu institution must be more closely involved in the whole procedure, and i call for this.

in writing. mr president, as you know, many dangerous chemicals are allowed to be used in the public domain despite the harmful ingredients that go into them. one such substance is dichloromethane, which is used primarily in the manufacture of pharmaceuticals, solvents, and other products. it is particularly harmful to human health because it is classified as carcinogenic. it damages the nervous system and causes severe damage to internal organs, which is associated with a direct threat to human life. because of the faster rate of ventilation of the lungs, children are more susceptible to poisoning, as are those at risk of cardiovascular disease. alarmingly, deaths have been reported from dichloromethane poisoning. in view of the existence on the market of products which can be considered as alternatives to those containing dichloromethane and in view of the fact that some member states have prohibited the use of that substance, it appears necessary to introduce an absolute prohibition of its use. another argument for removing dcm should be that, as the experts point out, it is impossible to ensure that consumers can use dcm safely. the commission's proposal to introduce training on the professional use of dcm products would cost around eur 1.9 million in the first year of implementation. therefore, the withdrawal of dcm from general circulation seems to be the most sensible and responsible solution.

in writing. i would like to thank prime minister mirko topolánek for presenting the priorities of the czech presidency. the three e's: economy, energy, europe in the world, which are to form the backbone of the community's presidency, are experiencing additional, unplanned external actions: gas and gas. the problem of the conflict in the gaza strip is political. but it has become so military that humanitarian causes have come to the fore. people are dying out there! not just the hamas fighters who initiated the armed clashes, but innocent children, women, men. the union, together with the un, must do everything possible to find a solution to this bloody conflict. jews and palestinians can live side by side in peace. i ask that you continue to work towards this goal. the gas problem is felt in many european countries. the dispute between the two companies russian and ukrainian has turned into a dispute between these countries. this is a major problem for many people in countries where the energy supply is limited in the middle of a freezing winter. this also results in significant economic losses, as the gas is also used for industrial purposes. it is therefore high time to create a common eu oil and gas system that uses diversified sources of supply. we must also look for new sources of energy and return to modern methods of gasification. poland is taking such steps. i wish our czech friends every success in achieving the eu's objectives.

in writing. - mr president! - what are you doing? i am voting in favour of the report on the regulation of the european parliament and of the council amending council regulation (ec) no 2252/2004 on standards for security features and biometric data in passports and travel documents issued by member states (a6-0500/2008). i agree with the rapporteur's proposal to introduce the 'one person, one passport' principle, so that each person has his own passport with his biometric data. the situation where one passport can be issued for the holder and his children with their names but containing only the biometric data of the parent-passport holder may significantly facilitate trafficking in children. i also support mr coelho's initiative to allow two exemptions from the fingerprinting requirement, exempting children under the age of six and all persons whose fingerprints cannot be taken for various reasons.
in writing. − the european arms market is fragmented, with negative economic consequences. the main objective of the adopted directive is to counteract this fragmentation and to create a single arms market within the european union, while taking into account the specificities of the defence market and the protection of the security interests of the member states. the member states have taken the view that the existing public procurement directive does not sufficiently take account of the specific nature of public procurement in the field of defence. hence the numerous measures adopted in the directive concerning the award procedure, the selection of tenderers and the contractual requirements applied by contracting entities. the control procedure provided for in the directive is also intended to ensure effective legal protection for tenderers and to promote transparency and non-discrimination in the award of contracts. i believe that the rules adopted will contribute to a real opening of the market while taking into account the issue of national security. the directive should also lead to cost optimisation, both in national budgets and on the industrial side, and to the supply of the armed forces with the best equipment available on the market.

in writing. − the report on the state of fundamental rights in the european union 2004-2008 recognises effective protection and promotion of fundamental rights as one of the most important foundations of democracy in europe. at the same time, the committee rightly notes that the member states often evade control at eu level by considering the protection of human rights to be a purely internal matter, thus undermining the community's authority to defend fundamental rights at international level. the european commission should therefore focus on encouraging member states to cooperate more closely with it by offering to include in future human rights reports not only analyses of the situation in the world but also in individual member states. it is also worth noting a number of proposals to combat discrimination policies in the union effectively, stressing that equal opportunities are a fundamental right of every citizen, not a privilege. it is extremely worrying that some 20% of children in the european union live below the poverty line, often from single-parent families or with parents born outside the community. in this regard, it is necessary to adopt appropriate access to rights measures, focusing on the needs of children, and to take effective measures by member states to combat poverty.
in writing. - i voted against the report on the situation of fundamental rights in the european union (2004-2008), by italian mep giusto catania, because the author of this report did not so much describe the situation in this area over the past four years as expressed opinions on subjects suggesting or even attempting to impose on the member states legal solutions that fall within their exclusive competence. i believe that the countries of the union cannot be forced to legislate in ways that are not acceptable to their own citizens. the very term "marriage" should be reserved for the union of a man and a woman. the proposals of the member for catania do not lead to tolerance of homosexual behaviour (which i support), but directly to discrimination against biologically valid relationships, i.e. heterosexual ones. the question is whether the aim is not to restrict the rights of the family in its traditional sense, which consists of the mother, the father and the children. very personal matters related to sex life become politicized activities, for example by publicly demonstrating one's homosexual orientation, including in so-called "love parades". this report, in my view, by using phrases such as 'reproductive rights', which in the current understanding of international law means, among other things, free access to abortion, opens wide the door to such practices.
in writing. - i voted against the report by mr giust catania on the situation of fundamental rights in the european union (2004-2008). i voted against it because i'm against the fundamental rights. on the contrary, i'm not. i believe that fundamental rights are of particular importance for the union and for the world. the problem is that the report by mr catania is detrimental to the implementation of fundamental rights. why would you do that? well, because the demand for the establishment of eu law to combat homophobia or the recognition of homosexual unions are not fundamental rights. if anything, those demands should be in a completely different report. the european parliament's extension of the definition of fundamental rights cannot be effective because it has no power to legislate on international law. in addition, some member states do not agree with such an expansive interpretation. so this is just a political gesture and wishful thinking. the danger is that this is a sphere for member states to decide and should decide. the european union is not a single market. i don't like homophobia, but to establish a community law to combat it is absurd. if the union is to combat homophobia, it can be said that it should also combat anti-polishness, anti-russianism, anti-germanism, anti-frenchness, anti-islamophobia, anti-papism, anti-clericalism, anti-catholicism and many other attitudes and behaviours. forcing the acceptance of legal homosexual unions by member states can be even more dangerous.
in writing. - in today's vote i voted in favour of the report by mr catania on the situation of fundamental rights in the european union. unfortunately, fundamental rights are frequently violated in the european union, particularly in cases of discrimination against minorities and violations of privacy. the problem is also the respect of equal opportunities, especially the right to equality for women. the rapporteur calls on the member states to reject the arguments based on tradition and religion that justify violence and discrimination against women. in many countries of the community, citizens, especially the most vulnerable, children, are affected by discrimination and poverty. the report rightly condemns all forms of violence against children, such as domestic violence, sexual violence and corporal punishment in schools. member states are evading scrutiny of human rights practices, undermining the credibility of the union's external policy in the world. i believe that the communities cannot apply 'double standards' in their internal and external policies.

in writing. − the report on fundamental rights in the eu 2004-2008, adopted today by the european parliament, calls for the mutual recognition of same-sex unions in all eu countries and the mainstreaming of such arrangements in the law of the member states. in another part of the report, the report defends so-called reproductive rights, which in the language of international law mean, among other things, free access to abortion. parliament has broadened its criticism of so-called discriminatory remarks by adding religious leaders to the list of those who have made such remarks. the eu fundamental rights report has been used by the european left to promote abortion and homosexual demands that have nothing to do with fundamental rights. there is no document of international or european law that would confirm the existence of such rights. despite its non-binding nature, this is the most damaging document adopted by the european parliament in this term of office. this is another attempt to redefine the concept of fundamental rights in order to change their meaning without having to take action to amend the treaties in the un or eu. another aspect of the report is the call for a specific eu directive to provide for penalties for so-called homophobic behaviour. given the capacity and vagueness of the wording, it is an attempt to exclude homosexual communities from the democratic right to free criticism. its application could have consequences of a censorship nature. the final vote (401 in favour, 220 against, 67 abstentions) showed that meps were deeply divided in their assessment. this is a failure for the rapporteur, because fundamental rights should unite parliament, not divide it.
in writing. −on 15 march 2006, the un general assembly adopted a resolution replacing the un commission on human rights with the human rights council, an international subsidiary body for the promotion and protection of human rights. the change of name was accompanied by the introduction of new mechanisms and procedures that increased the human rights council's capacity. the purpose of the report is to assess the council's achievements and to compare the expectations it sets with the tasks it has carried out. in addition, the report aims to identify possible improvements in the functioning of the council. it must not be forgotten that democracy and human rights are the foundations of the european union's international functioning. the union has established a very prominent role for itself, it is active in international human rights bodies, it has been active in setting up the human rights council, it is a co-author of texts such as conventions and resolutions setting standards for the protection of human rights. unfortunately, in many cases the union lacks foresight and speed (mainly because of the sometimes time-consuming procedures for developing a common position) and leadership in human rights initiatives.
in writing. − in accordance with the treaty on european union, the union is putting the concept of transparency and the creation of an ever closer union between the peoples of europe first, in which decisions are taken as openly as possible and as closely as possible to the citizen. transparency allows citizens to participate more closely in the decision-making process and ensures that the administration is more legitimate, more efficient and more accountable to the citizens in a democratic system. the european court of justice's judgment in turco has far-reaching implications for transparency and access to documents of the european institutions relating to legislative matters. that judgment confirms that the principle in question should be applied as a matter of priority and applies to all community institutions and (very importantly) that the possibility of derogating from it should be interpreted restrictively and weighed in each case against the overriding public interest of openness. the public increases trust in the institutions by providing the opportunity for public debate. ets concluded that in this case the refusal of access to documents could not be justified by the general need to protect the confidentiality of legal opinions on legislative matters.

president-in-office of the council. − mr president, the council would like to thank the european parliament for placing this item on the agenda of its first part-session this year. you will probably agree with me that the czech presidency displayed remarkable foresight when it placed security of energy supply as one of the cornerstones or priorities of our presidency this year. the european union is undoubtedly facing a major gas supply disruption as a result of the dispute between the russians and the ukrainians and between the gazprom and naftogaz organisations. the extent of this supply cut now covers about 30% of the community’s total gas imports. so this is a situation that not even the cold war years have seen us exposed to – the total cut-off that we are facing today. the council and the commission were aware of the potential problem. as you know, we faced a similar situation three years ago, in 2006, and this is more or less a recurring annual problem, as each year russia increases the prices of the gas it exports to its neighbouring countries towards market levels. therefore, we were extremely vigilant, in view of the community’s large degree of dependence on russian gas. indeed, for some member states, dependence on the gas supplied by russia reaches about 100%. i would like to stress in particular the difficult situation of countries like bulgaria or slovakia. it also gives us an explanation as to why, for example, in the central and eastern european countries, this is problem number one – the people are freezing and it is on the front page of the newspapers. i know that in some other countries, which are not facing the problem with that kind of intensity, the situation is probably different, at least in pr terms. this time, we already received a formal warning from the russian side on 18 december 2008 through the eu-russia early warning mechanism that a problem might occur if the ongoing negotiations between ukraine and russia did not result in an agreement on prices, transit fees and payment of the debts. so we were not that surprised by what has happened, but we were surprised by the magnitude and the intensity of the cut. contacts, therefore, took place at the highest level prior to 1 january 2009 in order to avert the disruption of supply. the czech presidency had been monitoring the situation well before the beginning of the year. i personally already met russian officials in prague two days before christmas eve. the commission took adequate precautions in order to follow the development throughout the holiday period and shared its information with the gas coordination group in early january. both prior to and after 1 january 2009, the presidency and the commission – working very closely with andris piebalgs – received assurances from both actors that gas deliveries to the eu would not be affected. as you know, the czech presidency, together with the commission and with the aid of some member states, has been in contact with both the ukrainians and the russian gas companies and travelled several times in order to meet with both sides. in these contacts we have not sought to blame either side, or take sides, or even act as a mediator, since this is a commercial dispute. rather, we have emphasised to both parties the gravity of the situation, stressing the fact that the credibility and dependability of russia as a supplying country and of ukraine as a transit country are both clearly damaged. as the gravity of the situation has increased, we have also acted as a ‘facilitator’ as far as deliveries of gas to the community were concerned – a role that was very much appreciated by both parties, because they were not talking to each other at all. let me give a brief synopsis of what has happened since the early morning of 1 january 2009 – new year’s day. on 1 january 2009, russia announced it had stopped deliveries of gas to ukraine, whilst keeping deliveries to the eu at full level. that same day, the czech presidency and the commission issued a statement calling on both sides to look for a prompt solution and honour their contractual obligations towards eu consumers. on 2 january 2009, as it became clear that deliveries to the eu were beginning to be affected, a formal declaration by the czech presidency on behalf of the eu was issued and early in the morning on the same day in prague, we received a ukrainian delegation led by the minister of energy, yuriy prodan. this was made up of all parts of the ukrainian political spectrum, such as the adviser to president yushchenko, representatives of naftogaz and the representative of the mfa. on 3 january 2009, we had a lunch in prague with the director of gazexport alexander medvedev, and i personally took part in both meetings. both meetings revealed a flagrant lack of transparency as regards contracts between gazprom and naftogaz and especially a lack of confidence which prevents progress in reaching an agreement. the stories given by both sides were totally different on certain issues, so that was the moment when we started to push the monitoring issue. in an effort to tackle this problem of divergent views, the idea of a joint fact-finding mission by the presidency and the commission, led by the czech minister of industry and trade, martin říman, and by matthias ruete, the director-general of dg tran, emerged, and it obtained the mandate to do this from an extraordinary coreper i session, which we called on 5 january 2009, the first working day after the holidays. the mission went to kiev. they also visited the dispatching centre and then the next day they travelled to berlin to meet the gazprom representative on 6 january 2009. also on 6 january 2009, as the gas supplies were severely reduced to several eu member states, leading to a major supply disruption, an extremely strong statement by the presidency and the commission was issued, calling on both sides to immediately and unconditionally resume gas supplies to the eu. the presidency and the commission then sought to accelerate the conclusion of a prompt political agreement between the russian federation and ukraine so that gas supplies could be restored without further delay. gas supplies were also the number one topic of the european commission’s meeting with the czech government, traditionally the strategic session, which took place on 7 january 2009 in prague and also dominated the first informal council which we organised in the czech republic – the general affairs informal meeting held in prague last thursday. again, we were planning to discuss energy security in advance, but, of course, we had to react promptly and thus adopted a strong declaration by the presidency on behalf of the eu, which was approved by all. following the complete standstill reached by gas supply transiting through ukraine on 7 january 2009, with severe consequences for those member states with little possibility to mitigate the cut, we stepped up pressure and after lengthy and difficulty negotiations got both sides to agree on sending a monitoring team composed of independent eu experts, accompanied by observers from both sides. this team was tasked with providing an independent monitoring of gas flow transiting through ukraine to the eu and is deployed in both countries. monitoring was defined by russia as a precondition for the resumption of gas supplies. deployment of this mission was not easy to achieve, as you probably observed. first, the resistance of the ukrainians to include a russian expert in the monitoring mission had to be overcome, then an annex added unilaterally by ukraine to the agreement painfully brokered by our presidency was refused by russia. after several trips by prime minister topolánek to kiev and moscow and difficult negotiations with president yushchenko and prime minister tymoshenko and also prime minister putin in moscow, the agreement was eventually signed on 12 january and created a legal basis for the deployment of the monitors, and asked for the resumption of russian gas supplies to the eu. russia then announced that the supply would be resumed on 13 january at 08.00 in the morning, but then – i do not know whether it was 13 january – the progress did not take place as expected. on monday 12 january we, the czech presidency, convened a special council of energy ministers in order to press for further transparency on transit-related issues, identify short-term mitigating measures to be taken until supplies are fully restored and identify medium- to long-term measures that are needed to prevent the consequences of such major disruption in future. the council also adopted the conclusions reflected in document 5165 which urged both sides to resume gas deliveries to the eu immediately and to develop solutions that prevent recurrence. furthermore, in these conclusions, council agreed to urgently develop the strengthened medium- and long-term measures relating inter alia to transparency regarding the physical flow of gas, demand and storage volumes, regional or bilateral solidarity arrangements, to address the issue of missing energy infrastructure interconnections (which is a huge problem), to continue to diversify the transport route and sources, and to address the financing aspects of this, also by speeding up the revision of the security of gas supply directive. a further meeting of the gas coordination group on monday 19 january now looks likely. the energy council, the tte, will revisit the issue at its scheduled 19 february meeting through the conclusions it will adopt on the commission’s communication on the second strategic energy review. these conclusions and the commission communication will be discussed at the march european council meeting which will no doubt devote adequate attention to the events of the past weeks. allow me also to make a couple of final remarks in that introductory statement. first, the key objective of the presidency in the recent dispute has been an immediate resumption of gas supplies in the contracted amounts. the dispute is not over yet, as we all know. therefore it is essential that the eu does not become entangled in the bilateral quarrels between gazprom and naftogaz. second, both the presidency and the commission keep urging both parties to dialogue in order to reach a compromise under which gas supplies to the eu could be restored. the failure to respect the agreement of 12 january by either russia or the ukraine would, in the view of the presidency and the commission, be unacceptable. the conditions for the resumption of supply – as stipulated in the agreement – have been fulfilled and there is no reason therefore not to restore the supply fully. the presidency is well aware of the number of problems which persist. these need to be addressed, otherwise the insecurity concerning russian gas via the ukraine will linger on. first, there is this issue of the technical gas that the ukraine needs to keep its transit system running. it is necessary that both sides reach a transparent agreement defining who is responsible for the technical gas supply and who pays for it. second, it is crucial that the russia-ukraine contracts on gas prices and transit fees set clear and legally binding conditions preventing similar disruption from recurring. the presidency, together with the commission, have repeatedly called on both sides to sign such a contract. however, neither we nor the commission intend to intervene in the negotiations on the contractual conditions between the two commercial subjects. the presidency is also aware of the widely-shared consensus among the member states that short-, medium- and long-term solutions be adopted without delay that would prevent similar situations from recurring in the future. energy security is one of the top presidency priorities. the presidency has taken the lead in chairing the discussion on possible solutions for our energy dependency trap: be it the informal council, as i mentioned, or the tte-energy session. of the issues mentioned in the energy council conclusions, i would like to mention the following. firstly, the member states agree that the creation of a functional and efficient solidarity mechanism is one of the cornerstones of future eu energy security. secondly, solidarity presupposes interconnections of european energy networks, as well as improvements in energy infrastructure. thirdly, increased gas storage capacity is crucial for the operability of the solidarity mechanism. fourthly, in the light of the current crisis, the presidency also urges agreement on the review of the directive concerning measures to safeguard the security of natural gas supplies by the end of 2009. furthermore the eu needs to diversify its gas resources and supply routes. to this end, the presidency will organise the southern corridor summit in may 2009, expecting tangible results as regards the diversification of resources and supply routes and as regards closer cooperation with the countries of the southern caucasus and central asia. eu energy security is not feasible unless internal energy security market is completed and functional. therefore the presidency is looking forward to close cooperation with the european parliament to compromise on the third energy package at second reading. the presidency is also ready to continue discussions of the second strategic review with the aim of reflecting its outcomes in the spring council conclusions. finally, in order to boost energy security the eu should strengthen the transparency mechanism and so on. i think the community is prepared for the situation both politically and technically. politically, the presidency, together with the commission and other member states, has invested, and will continue to invest, considerable effort in order to solve the situation. technically, during these recent weeks, we have acted in accordance with the directive concerning measures to safeguard the security of natural gas supply. this directive established the gas coordination group, which now proves its value. it requires member states to prepare national emergency measures for this type of situation, sets minimum standards for the security of the gas supply to household consumers, and it prescribes that the gas coordination group should ensure the community coordination. this mechanism has had a considerable effect in mitigating the effects of the crisis. to give you an idea, gas from storage was used and sold to neighbouring countries and even to members of the energy community, alternative fuels were used for electricity production, gas production was increased – including from algerian, norwegian and other russian sources – extra deliveries of gas were made to neighbouring countries. i stop here. i assure you that everything is being done, both at the political level and at the technical level, to incite the ukrainian and russian negotiators to re-install full contractual gas supplies to europe and to minimise the negative consequences to our citizens and economies until that is the case. as you know, we are on the hotlines all day in parliament because time is expiring and we need to have results. if we do not have results, it will inevitably have political consequences in our relations with both countries.
member of the commission. − mr president, we are currently living through one of the most severe energy crises in european history, comparable with the oil crises that we had in the 1970s and 1980s. the difference is that those oil crises were global while this is very clearly an eu crisis. where are we today? well, in spite of promises made and the protocol signed on monday 12 january 2008 between russian and ukrainian ministers, myself and the two companies involved, russian gas is not yet flowing through ukraine to eu consumers. the commission has fulfilled its part of the deal: providing a european team of monitors to be spread over key places in russia and ukraine to observe the operations and report on their accuracy. we were able to mobilise a team composed of commission officials and industry experts in 24 hours and they were already in russia and ukraine last saturday to enable the flow of gas to resume as soon as the protocol was signed. yesterday russia resumed gas deliveries to ukraine in relatively small quantities that meet less than one third of the normal flow, but decided to use an entry point which, according to the ukrainian company, is difficult to use, and this led ukraine to stop transport. the report of our monitors confirms that it was technically difficult (though not impossible) to ensure the transport under these conditions. today, unfortunately, the same situation occurred and the only solution is for the two parties to ensure full coordination of their technical operations, so that volumes and entry points match the requirements of the gas transport system. if there is no further coordination, there will be no gas supply, and eu monitors and the commission on the spot are trying to encourage both sides to find this technical agreement. at the same time, i do not take sides. i do not want to blame one or the other party. but it is very clear that both parties have lost their reputation as reliable energy partners of the european union. (applause) returning to the history of the last month, i wish to say that the eu reacted promptly, voiced its concerns, and both parties have been constantly urged by the highest-ranking political leaders to restore immediate supplies and to fulfil their obligations. in normal contacts with both parties earlier in the years, knowing from previous experiences that deals are usually struck in the night from 31 december to 1 january, we always reminded them: ‘please find a solution to your bilateral gas issues because it is affecting our transit’. well, unfortunately this was not the case. we know where we are today in spite of all these efforts, and i strongly believe that the solution is in the hands of the two parties. but do they want a solution? the presidency and the commission have called and are still calling on russia and ukraine to resume gas flows immediately. we have done our part. we are genuinely able to provide a full response about where the gas goes: not one cubic metre of gas goes in a different direction without us noticing. i believe that the measures that we have taken are sufficient. but if both parties say that some other measures are necessary, we are ready to consider that, because i also see the lack of coordination and contacts between the two sides. this is the immediate crisis. what next? i know that whatever solution we will find now is temporary, so to restore the credibility of this transport route we will need a long-lasting solution; so the contacts between those parties will definitely be continued during the czech presidency, but will also, unfortunately, have to continue under the swedish presidency. but i believe that we have provided answers for security of supply in the second strategic energy review, in the work parliament and the council have done on the energy and climate change package. these are the solutions provided, and we cannot rely on external suppliers which unfortunately do not honour their contractual obligations and do not take into account consumer interests. but i would like to stress particularly two issues that should be addressed immediately: one is the lack of interconnection. yes, there has been solidarity, but in a lot of cases it was hampered by the lack of sufficient infrastructure to deliver gas from the storage facilities that are there to the places where there is an acute need of gas supply. i believe that the debate on the recovery plan, where infrastructure is also mentioned, is really a good instrument to address these places, because there is not always enough commercial interest to really provide for this type of intervention. second, we definitely missed an opportunity in 2004 when we discussed the gas supply security directive. the instrument which was prepared was weak and did not meet the current needs. we have prepared, and we will shortly be submitting, the new draft proposal on the security of gas supply directive; an impact assessment is being made and in the coming weeks it will be here in parliament. i believe we should react immediately and really find coordinated community mechanisms to respond to this type of crisis. the presidency has really worked very hard and i would like to congratulate the presidency for always taking the lead, with the full support of the commission. i believe that in these difficult times the european union has proved that it is speaking with one voice. the european union is led by the presidency and supported by the commission. but i also very much welcome all the activities that the european parliament carries out, because parliament provides the basis for an agreement. if two parties do not speak at government level, if the companies are trying to play games, which could provide for political stability? it is the broad political basis in ukraine and russia that speaks together, and i would thank mr saryusz-wolski for his activities in providing this exchange of views, and also president pöttering who took part in conciliating both parties. the solution is so easy if they would just talk to each other. so i believe these were very important activities and i very much hope that after today’s meeting in parliament – because it is followed by both sides – there will be additional encouragement to resolve the issue. the party suffering the most is the party that is not responsible for this crisis, the party that has come in to facilitate matters; and this facilitation costs european taxpayers and european consumers money. so i believe it is high time the gas flowed again towards the european union in stable conditions.
on behalf of the ppe-de group. – mr president, this major disruption in supply is a dramatic one for european citizens, european industries and european jobs and it comes on top of the economic crisis. we parliamentarians of this house, in our coming european elections, will all have to answer questions about what we have done to protect our industries, our jobs and our citizens. contrary to some initial opinions, the problem concerns political and multilateral entities and is not bilateral and commercial in nature. three years ago, when we witnessed the first gas crisis following russia’s cutting of energy supplies, europe realised its vulnerability and its limitations. already then it became obvious that we need a common eu foreign policy on energy. our group, the ppe-de group, has supported this idea from the very beginning. it was our group which took the lead by asking for an own-initiative report towards a common european foreign policy on energy, which i had the honour to present to this house in september 2007 and which was unanimously supported by all the political groups and adopted almost unanimously. it called for a comprehensive strategy with a precise road map towards a common eu external policy on energy, recommending a number of actions to be taken: in the short term, solidarity mechanisms, unity in defending our interests, more efficient energy diplomacy; president-in-office of the council. − mr president, at this late hour i wish to make a few remarks on the council’s position on the horn of africa. the horn of africa of course is a challenging region which deserves our particular and increased attention as it has a major impact on the eu. the eu closely follows developments in this region and prepares to engage even more with the countries of the horn of africa. i know that parliament also keeps abreast of developments. the visit that your delegation made late last year to eritrea and ethiopia and also djibouti was important. i also took note of the motion for a resolution on the horn of africa that has been elaborated partly in the context of this visit. it clearly displayed to the region and to europeans the growing engagement for the horn of africa within the eu. on behalf of the council, i welcome the involvement of parliament in our efforts to address the challenges in the horn of africa. there are several sources of tension in the horn of africa. i will get to them in more detail. however, in the view of the council these tensions are often linked in one way or another within the region. for this reason, the council is particularly looking to discern the regional links between ongoing conflicts. what are these links between conflicts? first, there is a dispute between ethiopia and eritrea, which might be considered as one of the principle causes of instability in the whole region. this is reflected in the following ways: the support of opposing warring factions in somalia; destabilisation efforts in each other’s countries – let me mention ogaden, oromo in ethiopia in particular; it is reflected also in support for the revival of the peace process in sudan; eritrea has suspended its membership in the intergovernmental authority for development (igad). and, last but not least, the conflict in somalia has caused one of the most serious humanitarian situations that we face in the world today. the increase in acts of piracy off the coast of somalia is another serious consequence of this conflict. another serious issue is the competition for natural resources such as water and minerals in the horn of africa. this phenomenon increases pastoralist conflicts in areas populated by different cultural and ethnic groups. it also increases food insecurity and human insecurity in general, which contributes to the conflict and the migration. there are also serious regional interdependencies. let me mention some of them. there are the border conflicts, as mentioned before: the disputes between ethiopia and eritrea, sudan and ethiopia and djibouti and eritrea, which might be considered as sources of instability in the region. i would also stress that improved regional cooperation would contribute to lowering tensions around national boundaries. food security is another interdependency. this is of course a major concern in the region. recurring droughts, as well as floods, have a devastating effect on the population. once again, regional cooperation could mitigate the effects of these natural events. as you know, some argue that this problem is at the origin of the conflicts in darfur, somalia and many other areas of the horn of africa. i am not sure that gives a full explanation, but i do believe that this question must be resolved in each of the countries and within the regional context in a fair and transparent manner. piracy was initially localised to a small part of the somali coast. the pretext of the pirates was to levy a fishing tax on a ship in somali waters. as you are certainly well aware, this activity has expanded significantly and now threatens the delivery of humanitarian aid to somalia and maritime safety in the gulf of aden and well beyond, including ships travelling off the coast of kenya and tanzania. there are also several other interdependencies which have a serious impact on europe and on the countries of the horn of africa, such as terrorism and migration. so what are the actions which the european union undertakes? what is our engagement or involvement? the main political instrument at the disposal of the council – which i have the honour to represent here today – is a political dialogue, not only with the individual countries but also with other regional stakeholders, such as the african union, the intergovernmental authority on development, the league of arab states, and the united states and china as important countries. political dialogue is a mutual commitment in the cotonou agreement between the eu and each of the countries in that particular region. this dialogue is principally pursued through the heads of the eu missions in the countries concerned. it is a very important instrument to the council, as it gives us a direct contact with the authorities of those countries. it provides an opportunity to hear their point of view, but also to clearly explain our perceptions and raise concerns that we have on certain issues. this particularly concerns matters of governance and human rights. those are the main issues. on top of this, the council disposes of the instruments of the european security and defence policy (esdp). since september 2008, the council has deployed this instrument to fight piracy off the somali coast, first through the coordination cell eu navco, based in brussels and then since december 2008 through the maritime operation called eu navfor atalanta. finally, the eu acts through the financial instruments of the european commission such as the african peace facility and instrument of stability. i will let commissioner ferrero-waldner elaborate further on that because that is the commission’s responsibility. of course the council is always looking, together with the european commission, for ways to enhance the effectiveness and the visibility of eu action. i look forward to hearing your proposals and recommendations on this particular issue.

member of the commission. − mr president, it is a great pleasure for me to speak to you about belarus because positive progress has been made, which we were very happy to see. belarus is very high on our agenda, but not solely because it is one of the countries hit hard by the current financial crisis in the region. there is also a unique opportunity for us to really begin a new chapter in our relationship with belarus. we are now half-way through the six-month suspension of sanctions against belarus that was the decided at the meeting of eu foreign ministers on 13 october 2008. as this suspension will end on 13 april 2009, now is the time to make the first assessment of whether belarus is moving in the right direction and whether we can therefore extend the suspension and take further positive action towards belarus. the 13 october general affairs and external relations council was very clear that the positive progress which began with the release of the remaining political prisoners in august would have to continue for the suspension to be extended. the areas in which we need to see further and sustained progress are: no further political arrests or imprisonments; cooperation with the osce/odihr on reforms to electoral legislation; progress on media freedom; better operational conditions for ngos and no harassment of civil society; and serious progress on the freedom of assembly. we have seen some progress in the last three months. for example, the ban on two major independent newspapers has been lifted and they have now even resumed printing and distribution. secondly, ‘for freedom’, mr milinkievich’s organisation, has been allowed registration and, thirdly, there will be consultations between belarus and the odihr on 22 january on electoral reform. this progress has been in direct response to requests made by the commission in early november and we find it encouraging. however, we still need more progress if we are to begin a new era in our relationship and if we are also to confirm the suspension. we need to see progress on media freedom, including internet freedom and the accreditation of foreign journalists. we also need to see easier registration procedures and working conditions for ngos and the lifting of the restrictions on the freedom of ngo activists – like, for example, mr barazenka – and we need to see further evidence that peaceful demonstrations can take place freely and without participants fearing arrest. progress is, however, a two-way street. if belarus can make this serious progress, then i think it is also essential that we reciprocate with a significant package of measures. the commission has been working on proposals for such a package, which could include the following: an extension of the technical dialogues which began a year ago, on energy, transport and environment to other areas; a symbolic increase in the enpi allocation for belarus to back these talks; helping belarus to adjust to the new economic challenges it is currently facing and extending eligibility for eib and ebrd loans to belarus; intensifying contacts: on 26 january the troika will meet with foreign minister martynov on the margins of the gaerc, where i intend to say clearly to mr martynov what exactly the eu expects from belarus and what we have on offer; and, naturally, intensification of civil society dialogue. at this juncture, i believe all efforts should be pooled and meetings that meps could have in minsk with belarusian parliamentarians, for example, would also be most useful. a further issue for reflection is the potential to open negotiations on visa facilitation and a readmission agreement. on this issue, the ball is in the council’s court, and it is clear that belarus still has further progress to make. but we, the commission, stand ready to kick-start work and contribute to negotiations as soon as the ministers acknowledge that sufficient progress has been made. finally, we stand ready to develop the full range of our enp and eastern partnership offer for belarus. this would comprise the unblocking of the pca and a significant increase in our assistance. after 13 april, should ministers assess that sufficient progress has been made, the decision will be made as to whether to confirm the suspension of sanctions. should belarus’s progress be great enough to warrant this, we are indeed ready to reciprocate and i hope that we could then really open up a new chapter in relations with belarus.

madam president, commissioner, i would like to thank you for your report. i want to draw attention to three points in this debate. first, russia is increasingly clearly using the supply of energy resources, mainly gas, to exert a strong political influence. the recent gas conflict between russia and ukraine has not only caused huge economic losses to many eu countries, but also, with the eu's approval, pushed ukraine back into a clear economic dependence on russia. it is hard to imagine that the ukrainian economy could function at a gas price of over $400 per 1,000 cubic meters. secondly, a new eu-russia partnership agreement must be negotiated, including energy issues, but with the explicit stipulation that supplies of energy resources will not be used by russia for political influence and that any losses resulting from non-supply will be borne entirely by russian suppliers. thirdly, the european union, through its own financial resources and the european investment bank, should support, first and foremost, those gas investments which actually diversify gas supplies to the european union and thus provide real opportunities for importing gas from countries other than russia, such as the nabucco pipeline.
madam president! the gas and financial crisis forces us to act quickly and pragmatically over individual interests and economically unjustified ideas like the nord stream pipeline. the second strategic energy review does not provide the desired added value. a number of the themes listed in the review encounter significant implementation difficulties. the citizens and economies of the union need quick and concrete decisions and actions that will secure relatively low and stable energy costs over the next 15 years. they will lead to potentially significant savings in industry, transport and households. they will significantly reduce the union's dependence on imports of hydrocarbons and ensure the correctness of their supply. they will lead to the development of a programme and plan of specific projects and their investment implementation as soon as possible, using the research results. these economic activities will reduce co2 emissions and eliminate the need for bureaucratic emissions trading, which is good for traders but not for the economy.
madam president! last but not least, the gas supply crisis is making the issue of the security of supply of this very important raw material come up again and again. in europe, we're not in a bad situation in terms of our location. we're almost surrounded by gas resources: north africa, the middle east, central asia, russia. the problem is that there is no single market for gas in europe. there is therefore no more or less uniform price. i would like to point out that in the united states there is such a market and the price for 1,000 cubic meters of gas is below 200 dollars. in europe, we pay about $400. this is because we don't have the infrastructure to make it possible for gas to be transported between countries. and finally, the nabucco pipeline. it's time we put this pipeline on the right priority and put our financial resources into making it happen.

in writing. the energy crisis of january is slowly becoming an annual ritual. the harsher the winter, the more certain it is that the russian federation will turn the gas hooks on the european countries. it is all the more surprising that, in the face of another gas conflict, which has affected the citizens of the european union, chancellor angela merkel continues to push for proposals to implement the northern gas pipeline with community funds. what the european commission should be doing now is preparing a plan for the diversification of energy sources. investments should be made in the construction of new transmission networks that would bypass uncertain energy exporters such as the russian federation. in one of my amendments to the report by mrs anne laperrouze, we emphasize the importance of supporting 'the nabucco pipeline, the only project in existence to diversify energy sources and gas transport routes' without russia's participation. the establishment of gas interconnectors to enable interconnections and the rapid transfer of gas reserves in case of future crises should also be a priority. our trade agreements should be based on a special "energy security clause" which would be the business ethic for this sector. it is important for europe and the rest of the world that is doing business in a civilized way that the russian federation ratifies the energy charter treaty. i believe that only a united and uncompromising european position can persuade the kremlin to take such a decision.
on paper. wise poles after the damage! an old saying, not very flattering to my countrymen, can be extended to the whole of the european union. it took the bitter experience of the russian-ukrainian gas war in january 2009 for energy security to become a priority for the european community as a whole. we cannot hide behind the absence of the treaty of lisbon, which includes provisions on energy solidarity. it is only through political will, backed by a cold analysis of the recent crisis, that future scenarios can be outlined and the european union freed from similar troubles caused by the blockade of gas supplies via ukraine. both the commission's communication and the anne laperrouze report highlight the ways to deal with emergencies - increasing reserves and creating a transmission network that ensures technical availability. these are uncontested matters. it will be more difficult to agree on a long-term strategy, which must take account of a realistic stance towards russia as europe's main supplier of oil and gas. interdependence, as we have seen, does not guarantee continuity of supply and relationships based on rational economic considerations. the interference of political motives is too obvious to be naive. the most difficult thing in relations with our eastern neighbours will be to root out the tendency to conclude bilateral agreements, and this is the real measure of success or failure of the community's policy of energy security and solidarity!
