the commission's vice-president - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, mr tabajdi, respect for minorities is an essential principle which is one of the preconditions for the accession of a new country to the union. the copenhagen criteria are specifically aimed at the countries applying for membership of the union. respect for the rights of persons belonging to minorities, including respect for the principle of non-discrimination, is a principle on which the union is founded. but the union has no general competence in the field of the protection of minority rights. it is up to the national authorities to ensure such protection, in accordance with their constitutional order and their international commitments. the question of the institutional organisation or autonomy of minorities is therefore a matter for the member states. similarly, it is up to each member state to decide whether to sign or ratify the framework convention for the protection of national minorities and the european charter for regional or minority languages, which are the two major instruments put in place by the council of europe. the union therefore does not have the competence to adopt, as suggested in the question, general legislation setting standards for the protection of minorities and control mechanisms. but the union can adopt measures on certain matters within its competence which have a positive impact on the situation of persons belonging to minorities. for example, as regards the commission's policy against discrimination on grounds of race, ethnic origin or religion, it is necessary to ensure that community legislation in this field is implemented and that the directive supplementing this legislation is implemented. the adoption on 28 november of the framework decision against racism and xenophobia is another example. through this framework decision, the union is contributing to improving the situation of persons belonging to minorities in relation to certain behaviour to which they are subject. the union also focused on the situation of the roma minority. the integration of immigrants is a topic of increasing importance for the member states and the european union. in 2005, the commission presented a common programme for integration, which provides the framework for a common approach to integration in the european union. and the union has allocated a budget of €825 million for 2007-2013 to implement the european integration fund. three new commission initiatives will be launched in 2009: the third edition of the handbook on integration, the european integration forum to further involve civil society in our work, and an integration website, a one-stop shop to bring together information on integration and facilitate the exchange of good practice among all those involved in integration. the role of the european union in the field of multilingualism is not to replace the action of the member states but to support and complement this action. the european commission's policy on multilingualism includes regional languages as well as languages spoken by minorities. respect for linguistic and cultural diversity is one of the cornerstones of the european union. and this respect for linguistic and cultural diversity is now part of the european charter of fundamental rights, which states in article 22: 'the union shall respect cultural, religious and linguistic diversity'. the latest commission communication, adopted in september 2008, also states that each of the many languages, whether national, regional or spoken by minorities or immigrants, adds to our common culture. the main tools available to the union in this area are its funding programmes, and in particular the lifelong learning programme 2007-2013. finally, the european union agency for fundamental rights is a very valuable tool for us in collecting data for the development and implementation of all these community instruments and policies. following the european parliament's request to the fundamental rights agency, which is based in vienna, the agency's work programme for 2009 provides for a comparative report on the situation of ethnic and racial discrimination in the european union, which will allow us to update the 2007 report on racism. that's all i could say. in other words, we have no legal basis for organising the protection of minorities. this is really a matter for the member states. but, on the other hand, the union must of course avoid any discrimination against a citizen belonging to a minority.

in writing. - climate change has been the subject of 13 european parliament resolutions in different legislative periods. despite the efforts of both the commission and parliament, the issue has remained controversial. the report by karl-heinz florenz does not improve the situation of those who are not convinced that human activities are the decisive factor in climate change, which has been governed by the laws of nature alone for millions of years. the idea of an integrated european policy is another matter. given that the report does not refer to the specific situation of the new member states, let alone acknowledge their efforts to reduce pollution and greenhouse gas emissions since 1989, there can be no question of an integrated approach. the goals of different countries are entitled to differ. countries must have the right to choose their energy technology. in the context of the recommendation to the commission to set a binding target of 20% increase in energy efficiency, there seems to be a reasonable suspicion of a disguised promotion of expensive foreign technologies for this purpose.
in writing. - i voted in favour of the florence report entitled 2050: the future starts today - a recommendation for the eu's future integrated climate policy. the report was prepared by the interim commission on climate change, which was set up in june 2007. the report is a list of recommendations for reducing carbon emissions that should be implemented by the community institutions (mainly the european commission) and the member states. action at local level will also be necessary to achieve the objectives. climate change is rapid and has serious negative effects. the eu and the group of industrialised countries should adopt a target of reducing greenhouse gases by 25% to 40% by 2020 and, in the longer term, aim to reduce emissions by 80% by 2050 compared to 1999. other recommendations included in the report include partnership with third countries in the mediterranean on solar energy production, achieving net zero energy consumption in new residential buildings by 2015 and in new buildings by 2020, with the possibility of extending this target in the longer term to include renovated buildings. it also includes the creation of a european renewable energy community to support research and development into breakthrough technologies.
in writing. - i supported a resolution on improving energy efficiency through the use of information and communication technologies. itcs should become the future solution in virtually all energy-using appliances, enabling huge savings in energy consumption. failure to do so could lead to a significant increase in energy demand in the coming years (around 25% in 4 years). the biggest savings are possible in the electricity generation and transmission sector. the efficiency of the generation of this energy should be improved by about 40% and its distribution by about 10%. itcs will contribute both to better management of the energy grid and to facilitate the integration of renewable energy sources. ict will also bring significant savings in heating, air-conditioning and lighting in buildings. all of this will contribute to a significant reduction in co2 emissions both per unit of energy and on a global scale. these technologies, including micro- and nanoelectronic components and systems themselves, as well as many advanced techniques (e.g. photonics), will increase competitiveness and create new opportunities for business and the labour market. taking into account that energy efficiency improvements are reductions in energy consumption in the generation, transmission, distribution and final consumption phases of energy, due to technological changes, behavioural changes and economic changes, providing the same level of comfort and services, modern itcs should be used as widely as possible.

vice-president of the commission. − mr president, the treaties do not confer any power of initiative on the commission in the field of consular protection. within its limited powers, the commission is trying to boost, as much as it can, the effectiveness of the citizenship rights european citizens are entitled to – see, for example, the commission action plan 2007-2009. i repeat that the adoption of the lisbon treaty would certainly very much improve this situation. i hope that mrs sinnott, who shared her experience with us, will use the fact that the lisbon treaty would change the situation and her experience to help to organise support for the lisbon treaty in ireland. the deplorable events in mumbai show that, already today, there is a clearly a huge margin for improvement if we are to fulfil the legitimate expectations of eu citizens.
on the tape. the increasing mobility of eu citizens requires the adaptation of the existing consular protection rules to the new situation. eu citizens must be granted protection and assistance by their own country, through its diplomatic missions and consular posts (article 3 of the vienna convention on diplomatic relations and article 1 of the vienna convention on consular relations) and, under the maastricht treaty, additional diplomatic and consular protection for eu citizens outside the community, as a result of their european union citizenship. in practice, this means that every citizen of the union enjoys, in the territory of a third country where the member state of which he is a national is not represented, the diplomatic and consular protection of each of the other member states on the same conditions as the nationals of that state. unfortunately, the crisis in bombay last year, caused by the bombings, has demonstrated the inadequacy of many diplomatic missions in the practical application of the common provisions on the security of union citizens. the procedural problems encountered by dozens of europeans, including the european parliament delegation on the spot, and the disproportionately long waiting times for duplicates of lost documents have shown that the idea of european solidarity is not easy to achieve! the right to consular protection in third countries is one of the main determinants of european citizenship. member states should make every effort to implement it properly, ensuring equal treatment and care for all community citizens.

madam president! after world war ii ended in europe, many nazi criminals fled to south america to escape justice. attempts to bring them back and bring them to justice have proved to be extremely difficult. and that led to desperate steps like the israeli intelligence services who simply abducted eichmann from south america to bring him to justice. it is clear that the tradition of fleeing to south america in the belief that there is a place of refuge and that one can live out one's days with impunity despite the crimes committed is not going away. actions like the brazilian government's are fueling this belief and making the feeling of impunity, unfortunately, very widespread. it is therefore of the utmost importance that this extradition request be granted.
in writing. for the eu-middle east agreement, the priority today should be to try to restore stability and help implement the peace programme in the gaza strip. the european union should do everything it can to help bring an end to this conflict, which is killing innocent people. in addition, efforts should focus on helping the population, guaranteeing basic livelihoods. the daily food needs of the people of the gaza strip are only met by 60%, making them even more vulnerable to disease and harsh conditions. lack of drinking water is as dangerous to health as lack of food. needless to say, the lack of medical care and the destruction of schools and government buildings are making it very difficult to restore order and return to normalcy. we must remember that it is only by solving many of the basic problems of our daily lives that we can focus on the economic development of the middle east and close trade cooperation with that region. the european union has the chance to help the arab world, all the countries of the middle east, to become a prosperous region, which in turn will create a framework for closer cooperation between the middle east and the union.
(parliament adopted the resolution) mr president, thank you. i think that the union's foreign policy deserves some attention. mr president, we have a special debate today on three major reports on foreign policy, on security and defence, and on eu-nato relations. our annual report on the common foreign and security policy (cfsp) has become a main vehicle through which parliament expresses its strategic view on eu foreign policy. in this year's report we have decided to focus on policy-making and policy-shaping. we have focused on the need to establish a genuine dialogue with the council on the main objectives of the eu's common foreign and security policy. we have recognised that it is in progress, namely that for the first time the council's report systematically refers to the resolutions adopted by the european parliament. we are grateful: this is a real achievement. however, we have also expressed our regret that the council does not engage in a full dialogue with the views advanced by parliament, nor does it refer to those resolutions in operational documents as joint actions or common positions. we expect that the council's annual report will provide opportunities to establish a dialogue with parliament aimed at developing a more strategic approach to the common foreign and security policy. we have reiterated the most important principles in our report which should underline our foreign policy. in our view, the cfsp must be underpinned and guided by the values which the european union and its member states cherish, notably democracy, the rule of law, respect for the dignity of the human person, for human rights and for fundamental freedoms, and the promotion of peace and effective multilateralism. we believe that the european union can make an impact, but only if it speaks with one voice and if it is equipped with appropriate instruments like those stemming from the lisbon treaty and a more generous budget. we can undertake effective action only when it is legitimised by both the european and national parliaments acting at their respective levels and in accordance with their own mandates. in order to be credible and to respond to the expectations of eu citizens - and i say this on the eve of new parliamentary elections coming soon - the cfsp must be allocated resources commensurate with the objectives and specific targets. we therefore regret that as in previous years the cfsp budget is seriously under-funded. we address horizontal and geographical issues in our report. on horizontal issues let me just enumerate the most important ones we touched on: first, upholding human rights and promoting peace and security in europe's neighbourhood and at global level; second, support for effective multilateralism and respect for international law; third, the fight against terrorism; fourth, non-proliferation of weapons of mass destruction and disarmament; fifth, climate change, energy security and issues like cyber security. in this report we are intentionally selective. we are therefore concentrating on some strategic and geographical priority areas such as the western balkans, the middle east and the wider middle east, the south caucasus, africa and asia and obviously relations with our strategic partner, the usa, as well as relations with russia. this report should be seen in conjunction with and complementary to parliament's more detailed reports. it shouldn't be trying to duplicate them. i want to thank my colleagues in the house from the different political groups for their understanding and excellent cooperation. we have tried to take most of the concerns on board, and i hope that the report will be endorsed by a handsome majority of our house. finally, to our partners from the council and the commission, i would like to say that we hope that this occasion can help us to develop a deeper strategic dialogue between parliament, the council and the commission, which will bring more democratic legitimacy to the hard work you are doing, mr solana and mrs ferrero-waldner, in order to have more cooperation in our triangle. i hope that you will treat this as a possibility for developing more synergy, a possibility for strengthening our common voice the voice of all three actors and give more democratic and parliamentary legitimacy to our common goal which is: foreign policy; one voice; european union.
on behalf of the uen group. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. the liberal end of history predicted in the 1990s has turned out to be a pipe dream. we have every right to feel more and more alone. there is therefore no alternative to cooperation between the european union and nato. there is no alternative to greater engagement by europe and the united states in international security matters. otherwise, the rules of the international order will be de facto set by korea, iran or hamas terrorists. energy, raw materials, piracy, cyber security are all things that need to be addressed. we've seen in poland recently how difficult it is to coordinate the rescue of hostages. the common nature of decisions does not, however, prejudge their quality. that is why i would not overestimate the role of the treaty of lisbon. the limitations of our efficiency lie in the european capitals. it is there that the political will to pursue a common world policy is to be sought, not in procedures.

mr president, the citizens of europe need a strong union with a competitive foreign, security and defence policy. this will not happen if our union keeps idle in one place. china and india are growing not only in economic power but also in military might. europe’s competitive advantage should be based on knowledge and innovation. this should be nurtured and supported by all of us. in an effective security strategy, our european forces should have access to equipment and resources of the highest quality. while the united states spends trillions of dollars on security, we in europe are slow or idle in developing our own strategy. in a time of crisis, we are closing firearms factories, like the factory in radom, poland. we should instead be investing in advanced technologies, such as the recoilless technologies being developed in poland as we speak. innovation creates new business and jobs. we cannot build european capabilities by shutting down our own factories.

madam president! the european union must act in the interests of the security of the citizens of all member states. it should first of all take up some of the responsibility for combating terrorism and react strongly to its manifestations. recently, the murder of a polish engineer by the pakistani taliban has received widespread attention. the so-called european diplomacy did not participate in the previous negotiations for his release. this disturbing case, which is part of a wider security problem, should be the subject of a separate debate in the european parliament and lead to concrete action, which i call for. the priority right now is to get the body of the polish man killed and help his family. the necessary emergency measures cannot, however, replace a comprehensive approach to terrorism and increased diplomatic pressure on countries such as pakistan.
madam president! nato, as an international security organization, has proven itself in a time of relative peace in europe. of course, the sense of security it gives us is largely limited by the pace of decision-making by the investigative bodies or the decisions of the covenant. after all, nato is the stabilizer of world security. attempts to 'soften' the north atlantic alliance by weakening its position by expanding the eu's military structures are a mistake. the european union today has a problem with agreeing on tough political decisions, let alone military ones. the union should focus on strengthening its internal security and enhancing the defence capabilities of its members, in particular against states bordering countries with a high level of instability, states with extreme nationalist ideologies or states in the interest of terrorist groups. the union should not become too involved in efforts to build up large expeditionary forces for operations outside europe.
madam president! the european parliament agrees with the common foreign and security policy of the european union. there is a consensus among the main political forces on this. the problem, the real political problem, is how to achieve this fundamental goal. firstly, the ratification of the treaty of lisbon as soon as possible. these political leaders, who are delaying the ratification process of the treaty, are undermining the shaping of the european union's common foreign and security policy. it is difficult to talk seriously about a common security policy for the european union without the lisbon treaty. secondly, i would like to emphasise the issue of human rights in the formulation of the union's external policy. this policy should support international law: international humanitarian law, liberal democracy and the rule of law. thirdly, this policy requires a serious development of the european defence policy, the development of the european union's military structures and the european defence industry.
member of the commission. − madam president, let me just make a few remarks, and one in particular: i think this debate has shown that there is a growing acceptance of the approach europe follows in crisis management and conflict prevention. the munich conference on security confirmed the comprehensive approach, because security and development go together – you cannot have one without the other. i believe this european approach is a core element of our strategy to promote peace and security in our neighbourhood, but also beyond. it works, but it must be adequately resourced, so we have to work on building our capacities and capabilities in both the civilian and military fields, and we will try at least to play our part as much as we can. but i would also like answer your questions, in poverty eradication there will be no sustainable peace. therefore, this is very important, and the promotion of human rights is also a part of this equation. finally, let me say a word on early in writing. international security is one of the greatest values for all actors in international relations. today, we are witnessing a redefinition of this concept and a shift in focus to non-military factors that threaten international stability and security. examples of such threats include organised crime, cyber terrorism, piracy (which we are witnessing off the coast of somalia), climate change and the threats posed by the global economic crisis. the european union, while devoting its attention to the building of common military instruments such as the eurocorps, the european air transport fleet and the eu's permanent headquarters, cannot forget other, no less important threats. more attention should be paid to building bodies and institutions that would enable us to overcome the financial difficulties caused by the global economic crisis and to protect the environment and biodiversity. the internal risks, such as drugs, social deprivation and cybercrime, must also be considered. all these elements are important factors in international security, in the security of the european union and in the security of every nation. without addressing these fundamental issues, it is impossible to create a stable european security strategy.

member of the commission. − mr president, first and foremost, i wish to express my gratitude to the committee on industry, research and energy (itre) and particularly to the rapporteur, ms riera madurell, for supporting our proposal for the community legal framework for a european research infrastructure. listening to you was music to my ears! let me also thank the itre shadow rapporteurs for their constructive support. together, we are coming an important step closer to a legal framework which will allow member states to collaborate for the construction of new large research infrastructures, which are becoming increasingly complex and expensive and can only be built if several european countries work together. you have discussed the new legal instrument in depth, and you have made many amendments which will help to clarify the text and give it a better structure, notably regarding definition, scope and status, and by introducing references to the european strategy forum on research infrastructures (esfri). the commission will make all possible efforts to support the implementation of these amendments by the council. we are especially glad to see that we agree on the most vital aspect of the discussions taking place right now in council, and which risks blocking adoption – i mean the vat issue. as you know, all member states agree that it is necessary to exempt research infrastructures set up by several countries from taxes in the host country. many times, for working purposes, it is addressed as a tax exemption issue, which creates some confusion. in reality, it concerns only the implementation of the existing vat directive, which has already been agreed and adopted by the council. the real question is whether european research infrastructure should be given the status of international organisations, as defined in the vat directive, and, as such, be exempt from the vat payment. therefore, we are not talking about fiscal harmonisation but about setting up the legal entities related to research infrastructures. both the legal services of the commission and of the council have clearly stated that this is the right place. this is consequently purely a political decision on how important member states consider the setting-up of new world-class research facilities in europe to be. your unwavering support in this issue could be of great importance!
on behalf of the pse group. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. the idea of the european research infrastructure (eri) is to create unique research workshops run by leading experts in specific methodologies. i think it should be characterized by a concentration of expensive, unique equipment and its scientific support. it is intended to serve as an experimental way of learning, mainly by induction, about the phenomena in the world around us, and as a result to solve practical problems. the eri should also serve the training of young scientists. i believe that the esfri european forum is not about replicating the existing centres of excellence, but about creating, on the basis of the structural and national funds, different and complementary units to those centres, which will create an infrastructure of specialised research units covering a uniform network throughout the union. young, ambitious european scientists will then not have to look for their ideas overseas. i believe that the eri's smooth functioning is therefore dependent on a high degree of specialisation on the one hand and facilitated mobility of the scientific community on the other. this will ensure that research organisations are more efficient by concentrating their activities over time and distributing them locally, i.e. by carrying out the basic research tasks simultaneously in different specialised international eri units which, as non-economic structures, would be exempt from taxation. i thank mrs madurell for her attention and congratulate her, and i wish the commission a speedy implementation of this interesting, but still needing to be clarified, concept for a regulation.
mr. chairman, please! i would like to congratulate the rapporteur on her work. i'm going to quote mrs doyle here. at a time when we're experiencing an economic collapse, we cannot afford to make the mistake of neglecting science and research, the people who work in this field. i therefore support the action to give legal force to the european research infrastructure (eri). we must be aware that the eic requires both a legislative framework and adequate money, which individual regions or even countries cannot provide. the question of proper taxation is also important. i also believe that there is a need for better cooperation between academia and the economy, including small and medium-sized enterprises. i am convinced that the era will also help to improve the situation of scientists, especially young people, if there is a proper correlation with the framework programmes, as mr gierek has said. it may also prevent the brain drain from europe. the lisbon strategy calls for a 3% share of gdp for research and development. today, for the european union, the figure for 2007 is 1.84. so i trust that the eri will make this better.

madam president! the union is facing its greatest economic challenge since its inception. the crisis requires, first, a thorough analysis of the errors in the economic strategy pursued so far. second, to indicate solutions that will work in the future. in this context, the tax system and vat should be analysed in terms of efficiency and effectiveness. however, there is no doubt that the principle should be that the member states have the freedom, liberty and sovereignty to determine the tax system and the amount of vat. we say a firm 'no!' to the unification of the tax system. newly joined countries, often backward, with specific demographic structures, with a large number of young citizens, require a completely different indirect tax policy than the countries of the old union. wherever possible, therefore, in newly admitted countries, vat should be as low as possible. on the other hand, throughout the union - and i have called for this myself - we should try to reduce vat where cultural goods are concerned, such as cds. on the other hand, it is necessary to propose taxation of financial and speculative transactions. what is happening today with capital transferred from the newly admitted countries is a denial of the possibility of control and a denial of the ideological foundations of the union.
madam president! in taking part in the debate on the commission's proposal for reduced vat rates, i would like to draw attention to the importance of this proposal in combating the effects of the current crisis. member states now need effective instruments to protect jobs and prevent recessions. the reduction of vat rates on labour-intensive services fulfils this objective. it reduces the burden on small and medium-sized enterprises, facilitates access to basic services and protects jobs. at the same time, it does not distort competition in the single market, as it supports local service activities, and at the same time it does not threaten budget revenues, as the principle of voluntary operation of reduced rates is preserved. parliament should support the commission's proposal and i hope that commissioner kovacs will succeed in convincing the whole council to accept it.
madam president! the so-called grey area is one of the most serious problems affecting every economy to a greater or lesser extent. the main reason for this is excessive tax burdens on the part of the state, which encourage entrepreneurs to carry out clandestine economic activities, bypassing the fiscal system. as a result, there is a huge loss to the budget and an increase in undeclared employment. in this context, the initiative to reduce vat rates on labour-intensive and locally supplied services on a permanent basis deserves particular support. it creates an incentive for economic operators to operate in the formal economy. it also promotes productivity and employment. at the same time, however, it is also necessary to take into account the possible negative consequences: the introduction of reduced rates for free competition in the european common market or the reduction of budget revenues. a balanced and transparent approach is therefore necessary, as the success of this project will depend on the confidence of the entrepreneurs.
madam president! in poland, the housing sector is already seeing the effects of the crisis, despite the huge demand for housing. poland has not yet rebuilt all the housing destroyed during world war ii. i support a substantial reduction in vat rates, particularly in housing, also for thermal insulation and repair work, not only but above all for the protection of jobs and social cohesion. the ageing of europe makes it necessary to pay particular attention to care services, and here again i would point out the need to reduce vat rates.
member of the commission. − madam president, i am fully aware of the shortcomings of the commission proposals: i know that they are modest and limited in scope. however, i am also aware of the reluctance of certain member states vis-à-vis reduced vat rates in general and the extension of reduced vat rates in particular. this reluctance certainly sets limits on our ambitions, as we need unanimity in the council. for the commission, there were two options. the first was to table an ambitious proposal, which is fully justified, and to run the risk that it might not be approved by the council. in that case, 18 member states that currently apply reduced vat rates on locally supplied, labour-intensive services should return to the standard rate. an increase in vat rates from 5-6% to 20-25% would certainly result in the bankruptcy of thousands of small and medium-sized enterprises and in the loss of tens of thousands of jobs at a time of serious economic crisis. therefore, the commission has chosen the other option, which hopefully will receive unanimous support in the council: saving jobs, giving support to the smes and boosting the building sector. as many speakers mentioned the issue of energy efficiency, i want to repeat what i already said in my introductory remarks: in april we will come forward with a proposal that will be focused on climate change and energy efficiency issues, a review of the energy taxation directive, and the green tax package proposing reduced vat rates for green services that are aimed at increasing energy efficiency. i have been encouraged by the understanding and support expressed in this plenary debate. i thank parliament for its support and understanding, and in particular the committee on economic and monetary affairs and ms van den burg for their work.

in writing. ensuring a level playing field for all member states and increasing transparency and consistency within them is of the utmost importance as it affects the smooth functioning of the internal market in the field of reduced vat rates. member states should be able to apply a reduced rate of vat, inter alia, to services provided locally. the application of the reduced vat rate should be left entirely to the member states, and the tax system should promote employment, increase efficiency and reduce the 'grey area' in the economy. harmonisation of vat exemptions is also necessary as this will help to ensure a balanced and uniform approach by the member states and to avoid adverse effects of the application of these vat rates. the reduction of vat rates on locally supplied labour services should have a positive impact, as it will reduce the scope of undeclared work, thereby reducing its attractiveness and increasing demand in the formal economy. however, in order not to prejudice the smooth functioning of the internal market, reduced rates should be applied with caution. the policy objective of reducing vat rates is to reduce undeclared work and to reduce possible administrative burdens.

in writing. - rationalizing energy consumption is a very important activity. the public should know that this is the most cost-effective way to combat climate change. but the positive effects will not be limited to the environment. the better we use energy, the less we need it, and therefore the less dependent we are on importing it. in the current situation where energy is used as a policy element, this is a fact that cannot be overestimated. we're using energy more and more rationally. the effects of such a policy are measurable. since 1990, eu output has increased by 40%, per capita income by a third, and energy demand by only 11%. a more rational energy management therefore contributes to the economic growth of each member state. energy efficiency and energy saving should play a key role both in reducing the growing demand for energy and in reducing the amount of fuel burned. reducing greenhouse gas emissions, more green energy, a more energy efficient economy is an opportunity to reduce our dependence on imported gas and oil. the european economy must become less vulnerable to energy price fluctuations, inflation and the risks associated with the geopolitical location of these resources.

on behalf of the uen group. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. i would like to draw attention to four points in this debate. firstly, i would like to express the hope that the report by mr lehne will be a strong stimulus for the european commission to prepare appropriate legal solutions which, in accordance with the freedom of establishment guaranteed by the treaty of the european communities, will allow companies to move their headquarters within the european union without unnecessary red tape. secondly, such transfers should, however, allow existing shareholder and creditor rights and, above all, workers' rights to be protected. i would also like to express the hope that the solutions proposed by the rapporteur, namely the drawing up of a transfer plan and in particular an explanatory report on the legal aspects, and in particular the economic aspects and consequences of the transfer for shareholders and employees, will not be an additional obstacle to the transfer of companies. finally, fourthly, the specific incentive to propose such solutions seems to have been the perception of the positive impact of tax competition, and also wage competition, on the acceleration of economic growth in individual member states and, consequently, in the european union as a whole.
madam president! the financial crisis and the resulting economic crisis have prompted employers to try to change the legal status of their establishments in order to reduce operating costs, including those related to the implementation of workers' rights and social obligations. they therefore seek to establish their companies in countries where the laws and economic conditions offer a chance to reduce costs because legal obligations, such as the minimum wage or pension contributions, are lower. the report notes that cross-border relocation of company headquarters should not lead to circumvention of legal, social and tax rules. the workers' rights cannot be violated. we must not allow this to spiral downward in social standards. small and medium-sized enterprises should be supported in a different way, for example by means of loans.
madam president! the adoption of the statute of the european private company will make it possible to create such companies operating in all member states on a uniform basis. the main objective is to counter the current burdensome obligations imposed on smes operating in a multinational environment. in order to do so, they are in fact forced to set up a home company in the country of destination, which obviously entails enormous costs in the 27 different legal systems. the european private company will enable them to register their activities in the same form, whether they are operating in their home country or in any other member state. the savings in time and money on legal advice, management and administrative procedures are undoubtedly a significant facilitation and convenience for entrepreneurs wishing to invest. one of the main concerns of the sceptics is that the capital requirement is not sufficient to cover the creditors. nothing could be more wrong. the most popular form of limited company in the world is the limited company. in our day and age, share capital has been stripped of its most important function, namely, the protection of creditors. in the sep, this protection is taken over by other mechanisms, based mainly on increased transparency of the company's activities and closer cooperation with creditors. the trading partners themselves no longer pay as much attention to the share capital as to the cash flows, which tell much more about the solvency of the company than the capital itself. the issue of workers' rights remains - here, in particular, trade unions are concerned about the abandonment of the standards achieved. i'm calling this a false alarm. the proposed statute contains a clear provision that the participation of employees is to be in accordance with the provisions of national law. a certain danger to the attractiveness of the european private company could be that the employee participation threshold is set too low. i think that the minimum of 500 employees should be maintained so as not to impose additional costs on smaller companies.
madam president! this legislative proposal largely reflects the european parliament's resolution of two years ago, which contained recommendations to the commission on the statute for a european private company. the aim of the proposal is to create a uniform form of company under community law, attractive to small and medium-sized enterprises, created under simplified conditions, with minimal bureaucratic burdens. the commission proposes that the amount of eur 10 000 may be a good threshold for the company's image, but on the other hand, this amount is more difficult to raise in some member states than in others. the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the draft directive on the protection of the environment and the protection of the health of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos. the law of the state in which the company has its registered office should govern employee participation in the company. however, an exception to that rule should be made where the right of participation of a certain part of the employees of a company which they would enjoy in the member state where they actually work would be restricted by the law in force in the country where the european company is established. in such a case, the management of the company is obliged to create a single system of participation for the company as part of a solution negotiated with the employees' representatives. finally, i would like to add that this new company form does not replace the existing national company forms but offers an alternative to them, and only if certain conditions for the establishment of such an undertaking are met.

mr. chairman, please! the draft legislative resolution on industrial missions shows a strong tendency to limit the important environmental aspects of this directive in attempts to introduce increasingly extensive references to the greenhouse effect. many of the amendment proposals drastically tighten the emission standards for compounds emitted by combustion plants which are not directly toxic, while other draft amendments liberalize or only slightly tighten the rules on the incineration or co-incineration of waste. carbon dioxide emissions are not toxic, but emissions of dioxins, furans, hydrochlorides, hydrofluorocarbons, heavy metals and other highly harmful compounds are a real and immediate threat to human health and the environment. the strict monitoring of both the type of waste burned and the hazardous substances generated by the combustion is an important safety condition for the thermal disposal of waste. the introduction of loose thresholds requiring appropriate prevention measures in the event of emissions exceeding those thresholds may result in environmental pollution and health risks. the overall approach proposed shows unequal treatment of different classes of installations, with a particularly restrictive approach to conventional-fuel-fired solar energy installations.

member of the commission. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, business and workers are beginning to feel the effects of the financial and economic crisis. although the situation varies from one member state to another, the employment situation in europe is generally deteriorating. in 2009, total employment could decrease by 1,6%, representing a loss of 3,5 million jobs. the unemployment rate in the european union could be around 10% in 2010. every day, businesses announce that they will be restructured or relocated, often with the loss of many jobs. unfortunately, the situation of qimonda, which announced the closure of its plants in germany and portugal, is not unique. the commission is aware of the negative effects that restructuring can have on workers, their families and the economic and social fabric of the region. however, i would like to stress that the commission has no power to reverse or delay a decision of an undertaking and that undertakings are not obliged to inform the commission of their decisions. i have to say that neither qimonda's management nor their employee representatives contacted the commission. in this context, the commission would like to recall a number of points. in particular, it is necessary to better anticipate and manage restructuring through intensive dialogue with employee representatives and other stakeholders. i think that the newly adopted directive or the amended directive on works councils is one of the great contributions of the eu in this matter. in this context, it is all the more important that the undertakings concerned take care to comply with the obligations arising from the community directives on informing and consulting employees. the commission also calls on businesses to put in place measures to maximise the retention of workers through flexible working arrangements and the use of temporary redundancy for economic reasons. most member states have introduced targeted measures to promote employment and limit the impact of the crisis on citizens. these measures cover four broad areas: keeping workers in employment, rapid reintegration of workers into work, support for the most vulnerable groups through income support, extension of the period of unemployment benefits or increase of family benefits, and strengthening of social protection and investment in social and health infrastructures. to help member states cope with the crisis and its social consequences, the commission has strengthened financial instruments at european level. the european social fund, which helps 9 million workers every year, was simplified, allowing €1.8 billion in project advances to be released. i hope that the european parliament and the council will reach a swift agreement on this issue. the commission will also support those member states wishing to reprogram the european social fund. member states may also request assistance from the european globalisation adjustment fund for the benefit of workers made redundant. in the european economic recovery plan, the commission proposed to broaden the eligibility criteria in order to better respond to the current economic crisis. i hope that parliament and the council will reach a compromise quickly here too. the commission is prepared to assess, together with the german or portuguese authorities, any possible application for support from the european funds. the commission also promotes social dialogue at european level, as the social partners play a crucial role in crisis management. the european social partners are also expected to present a joint contribution to the crisis management at the tripartite meeting on 19 march. it is important for the commission to act together to combat the short-term effects of the crisis and to work towards a future economic recovery. the commission had this objective in mind when it launched the european employment initiative as part of the european economic recovery plan. on 4 march, the commission also adopted a contribution to the european council of 19 and 20 march, which will focus, inter alia, on the need and means of supporting workers affected by the crisis and those who are vulnerable on the labour market. the commission also welcomes the czech presidency's initiative to organise an employment and social affairs summit in may 2009. the aim of this meeting will be to in writing. how to counter the financial crisis? (european recovery plan) the financial crisis can be prevented in the short term and in the long term. the temporary approach is to remove the pathologies that have developed over the last few decades, leading to: banks losing liquidity; trading in 'infected' securities; lack of coherence between the financial and real policy spheres. by helping countries financially, banks are not eliminating the causes of this crisis. the fundamental cause of the crisis is, in my opinion, the neoliberal mechanism of the economy, i.e. its focus on immediate profit, overlooking long-term interests. the long-term approach should therefore adjust the mechanism of the economy to break with the dogmas of the so-called free market. member states and the european commission should not replace healthy competitive market mechanisms, but they have a duty to prevent pathologies. first, the short-term profit should not obscure the long-term interests involved in developing infrastructure, social services, environmental protection, the search for new, sometimes less profitable, sources of energy, etc. secondly, all forms of ownership should be treated equally and their choice should be determined by the efficiency of the management. thirdly, the member states and the european commission should take on the role of coordinator in both the financial and the real spheres. fourthly, the member states and the european commission must develop methods of coordinating the international monetary and financial market, which is inherently prone to speculation.

madam president! for most of us, free access to water is a given. we use a lot of water every day. it is worth noting, however, that according to estimates by the world health organization, one sixth of the earth's population - more than a billion people - do not have access to basic, minimum standards of clean water. this means that in the 21st century, millions of people suffer from thirst and die from diseases caused by drinking contaminated water. i was recently in the largest city in africa, lagos, where only one percent of the population has access to running water. these kinds of data are frightening, but they're not making the front pages of the newspapers, they're not making the mainstream media pay attention to them, and they're not making them the subject of debates and controversies, like aids, malaria, global warming. this is probably because only 2 percent of europeans suffer from it, but 27 percent of africans do. in africa alone, it is estimated that more people die each year from diseases caused by drinking contaminated water than from aids and malaria combined. so it's fair to say that the lack of access to drinking water doesn't kill in a media-specific, spectacular way, and doesn't generate as much publicity as disasters like earthquakes, tsunamis, floods, or armed conflicts. but the fact is, as mr ribeiro e castro said, that on average, 6,000 children die every day from water-related diseases. that means a child dies every 15 seconds. can you imagine the world's reaction, the response, the level of mobilization and determination if this were happening in europe, and not in sub-saharan africa or asia? so access to water is not just a problem for developing countries, it's a problem for developed countries as well. universal access to drinking water is a prerequisite for the development of countries and the effective fight against poverty. without meeting this need, there is no way to improve health care or education. without water for agriculture or simple industry, entire societies are condemned to struggle for daily existence, and the result of this struggle is armed conflict, migration, destabilization, which is to say, development blockades and the widening of development disparities. the forum we're talking about will also include politicians and will discuss current affairs. one of the current issues is the situation in darfur, where president bashir is kicking out organizations that, among other things, are working to ensure that the people of darfur have access to water. so this will be an opportunity to persuade president bashir, among others, to allow international organizations to provide water to the people of darfur.
madam president! the fifth world water forum is an event that should become an opportunity to work on public water management systems that are effective, transparent, regulated and sustainable to meet the needs of society. the special role and tasks here are those of local authorities. in addition, the food crisis has revealed the need to develop new techniques, such as irrigation of agricultural areas. at the same time, in agriculture, we should make sure that we use natural fertilizers or fertilizers that will quickly decompose in the soil and not leach into groundwater. finally, how does the commission intend to implement the european parliament's wishes, as expressed in its resolution of 15 march on the fourth world water forum, concerning the promotion and financing of water management in a spirit of solidarity? water is the most important challenge facing the world and europe.

its strategic rationale is clear: more security, more stability and more prosperity in our eastern neighbourhood. the conflict in georgia and also the gas crisis in ukraine are just two examples of the periodic crises and the instability affecting this region. these have had a direct impact on the union and its citizens. to these two crises we now have to add the financial crisis, which hits our eastern neighbourhood particularly hard. while each crisis requires its own immediate response, we also have to provide medium- and long-term action to prevent new problems from arising and, in addition to these immediate issues, our eastern neighbours all want stronger links with the european union, albeit to varying degrees. they also need reinforced help to consolidate their democratic institutions, statehood and rule of law. the european union can and must respond to these challenges and the eastern partnership is, so to say, our political answer. increasing our support for reforms my initiative. it built on prior ideas by our czech, polish and swedish friends, and it built on many of the european parliament’s suggestions, including deep free trade agreements, more mobility of people and greater funding. as part of the eastern partnership, we also proposed upgrading our political relationships through association agreements with each partner – but only once they have mr. chairman, please! the eastern partnership is a comprehensive set of proposals that should strengthen our eastern neighbours on their path to democratic transformation. each of these countries has an alternative: the russian model or the european model. surely the community has more to offer them. the eastern partnership is not a quest for subordination or a zone of influence, but an arrangement that will bring tangible benefits to both sides. partner countries will be given the opportunity and support to develop their economic and social development. the community will have greater security, both in terms of energy and political security. efforts should be made to facilitate visa regimes. if we make it easier for eastern partnership citizens to come to the community, they will see how much cooperation with the union can benefit them. the intensification of contacts between citizens, especially young people, will also undoubtedly contribute to the rapprochement between the partner countries and the union. we should enable young people to learn, to travel, we should promote scientific and cultural exchanges. a conscious, educated youth is the future of our continent.
mr president, catch-the-eye is a good opportunity for polemics. i disagree with my colleague mr severin. he would admit a droit de regard in zones of influence for russia. if we want stability on our eastern frontiers we need more democracy and more market economy. russia is less democratic and less a market economy than those neighbours, so no joint policy will bring us closer to that goal. symmetry with russia in this policy will not provide us with more progress in the region. we were not invited by russia when the cis was constructed, and a mix of our and russia’s policies would be totally counterproductive.
in writing. – in a time of economic crisis, one could ask the question: should europe focus on looking after its own rather than assisting its eastern neighbours? europe should decidedly continue supporting them. firstly, economic instability in the eastern neighbourhood, mostly notably in ukraine, which is suffering major problems, poses a threat to security in europe. conversely, a stabilised ukrainian economy, increasingly integrated with the eu, is an enormous potential market for eu member states. secondly, bringing our eastern neighbours into the european family, even if the prospect of actual membership of the eu is probably still a not a realistic option in the immediate future, is a long-term project. dealing with the current crisis is something we will have hopefully resolved in the next year to 18 months. the eastern partnership is a project for many years. thirdly, even if the leaders of some of our eastern neighbours, such as the belarusian president, and, to a lesser degree, bickering leaders in the ukraine, may discourage us from tightening these ties, we must remember that our eastern neighbours are more than their current leaders and, in the light of their internal political problems, they need our support, example and encouragement.
in writing. it is welcome that the european union is opening up new areas in its relations with its eastern neighbours. the adoption by the ec in december 2008 of a polish-swedish proposal to strengthen the community's cooperation with the six eastern neighbours is hopeful. i hope that this project will not be a wish on paper, but that it can be implemented for ukraine, moldova, georgia, armenia, azerbaijan and belarus. the eastern partnership envisages a significant increase in political cooperation, including new types of association agreements, far-reaching integration with the eu economy, simplified travel within the eu for citizens of the eastern partnership countries (provided security requirements are met), arrangements to improve energy security for all stakeholders, and increased financial assistance. it is important to be aware that the eastern partnership requires commitment from both the union and the countries involved. this effort can bring significant political and economic benefits. this will lead to an increase in trust and, consequently, stability and security for all. particular hopes can be placed on the proposed main framework of the partnership, and in particular on the establishment of four policy platforms: democracy, good governance and stability; economic integration and convergence with eu policies; energy security; people-to-people contacts. naturally, there are many doubts, such as the real intentions of the belarusian authorities, as well as the question of relations with russia.

member of the commission. − madam president, i am very pleased that this discussion is taking place today, on an issue which has preoccupied many of us for a long time and especially since the sad events a year ago in tibet. therefore i think that it is very good that we are having this open discussion to again see what can be done. before i come to the many issues you raised in the tabled joint resolution, let me also have a quick word on our bilateral relations with china. the eu policy vis-à-vis china is one of engagement. our strategic partnership is strong, and this permits us to tackle all issues, including the most sensitive ones. we have constructed an impressive framework of high-level interaction where we regularly address all the global changes that our citizens are facing, without neglecting the issues where we may disagree. tibet is one of them. let me be very clear – we do not see eye to eye with china on tibet, and we still have a very real and legitimate concern about the human rights situation in tibet, as you have both just outlined; about the fact that tibet has remained largely closed for the international media, for diplomats and for humanitarian organisations for almost a year now; and about the stalemate in talks between the representatives of the dalai lama and the chinese authorities, despite the three rounds of talks last year. these issues were also at the top of the agenda for several eu leaders in bilateral meetings held with the chinese leadership last year. we have endeavoured to find common understanding with china on this delicate subject, and we have been very clear whenever we have addressed the situation in tibet with them. let me again mention the eu’s position, which does not leave any room for misinterpretation. firstly, we support the sovereignty and territorial integrity of china, including tibet. secondly, we have always supported a peaceful reconciliation through dialogue between the chinese authorities and the dalai lama’s representatives. i remember, when i went there with the commission, president barroso and other colleagues, i had specific dialogues with many of my interlocutors on this issue. we have always maintained that there should be a reconciliation dialogue and that the dialogue should go on. this dialogue has to be constructive and substantive, and of course we therefore regret that, up to now, this dialogue has not brought really substantive results. we have always said that the dialogues should address the core issues, such as the preservation of tibet’s unique culture, religion and traditions as well as the need to achieve a system of meaningful autonomy for tibet within a chinese constitution. we have always said that this dialogue should address the participation of all tibetans in decision-making. therefore we would welcome it if these issues were to be addressed in china’s future national human rights action plan. for us, tibet is a human rights issue and has therefore invariably been approached as such. we have also consistently passed this message to our chinese counterparts and listened very carefully to their views. we have made every effort to understand the position in a spirit of mutual respect, but human rights are universal, and the situation in tibet is therefore – rightly – of international legitimate concern to the whole international community, particularly the european union. this fact is, of course, emphasised by the existence of instruments of international law for the protection of human rights over half a century. in your resolution you stipulate the future of a sino-tibetan dialogue. as you all know, at the last round of talks, following the request of the chinese government, the tibetan side submitted a memorandum on genuine autonomy for the future of tibet. in my opinion the paper contains some elements that could provide the basis for future talks. i am thinking of a paragraph on culture, education and religion. i am also encouraged by the fact that, for the first time in a written document, the tibetan side has expressed its firm commitment not to seek separation or independence. i think this is important in order to bring this dialogue further. i am also pleased that the dalai reaffirmed before this house last december his devotion to the middle-way approach and to dialogue as the only means for achieving a mutually acceptable and lasting solution. let me conclude by sharing with you a personal conviction. throughout my political and personal career, i have always strongly believed that, through engagement and dialogue, even the most difficult issues can be addressed and hopefully, when the time is right, can also be solved. therefore i wish to appeal to china and to the dalai lama’s representative to resume this dialogue at the earliest possible opportunity with an open spirit and a view to achieving a durable solution in tibet. i can guarantee, from our side, our wholehearted support for such a process. this is our position and this is the position that we bring to the chinese side.

in writing. - mr president! - what are you doing? is there a link between a scientific career and mobility? to some extent, yes; it can be argued that mobility, especially for young researchers, can have a major impact on their future achievements. it gives them access to new information and allows them to break free from the constraints of their environment. but that's not all. a scientific career begins at an early age, in secondary school, when young people are consolidating their general knowledge, especially in the natural and social sciences. the next stage is the first, second and doctoral degrees. this is, i say this from my own experience, the basic stage of a young person's scientific career, when mobility, easy access to research workshops and an interesting, promising topic pursued under the guidance of eminent scientists is more important to these people than their future retirement. therefore, the creation of the right conditions, e.g. in the european institute of technology and the european research infrastructure, for conducting such studies on the basis of generally available scholarships for doctoral students from the eu and third countries, and their widespread publicity is the most important step in the recruitment of scientific staff. whether young people, as phds, will power industry or scientific institutions, whether they will return to their countries or go further, will depend on the conditions created for them to stabilise their families and careers.

the president-in-office of the council. - thank you, mr president, and thank you in particular to the members of the european parliament for a constructive and interesting debate. let me respond to two points from what has been said. the first is the question of flexibility, and i have heard from the speeches of members that there is a call for the necessary flexibility in the negotiation of those economic cooperation agreements. i would like to stress that the council is very much aware of flexibility in two important areas. firstly, flexibility, making the most of asymmetrical arrangements, timetables, safeguards in line with wto rules. i cannot therefore agree with the view, or the general condemnation, that 40 years of aid to developing countries is a disaster. i think the situation would have been much worse without the help of the european union and other countries. at the same time, i think that having rules that allow for this perceived flexibility allows each of these countries - and i trust the european commission and the commissioner - to be able to find a solution that suits their needs and their interests. and secondly, there is the flexibility that we offer in moving from those transitional provisions of the epas to those full regional agreements in order to promote regional cooperation. the second point i would like to make in the debate is the question of the development dimension of the epa agreements. i am convinced that the agreements are not conventional trade agreements, but that they have a really strong development dimension. the agreements establish long transitional measures of up to 25 years, and also contain derogations. up to 20% of goods originating in acp countries may be exempted from liberalisation. the agreements the next item is the joint debate on:- report by mrs octavia sârbu on behalf of the committee on the environment, public health and food safety on the proposal for a directive of the european parliament and of the council amending directive 98/8/ec concerning the placing of biocidal products on the market, as regards the extension of certain time limits (com ((2008) 0618 - c6-0346/2008 - 2008/0188co ((d)) (a6-0076/2009) and - statement by the commission on the new proposal for a review of biocidal products.
the commission notes that the commission has not provided any information on the number of companies that have been granted the aid. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. the need for harmonisation of legislation on biocidal products in the european union is all the more apparent given the wide variation in national regulations. the absence of common rules is dangerous for human health and life and for the environment, especially in a free market. however, the 10-year period proposed in the original version of the document for the implementation of the legislation is unrealistic due to the extremely complex and costly registration procedures for the compounds used in these preparations. paradoxically, procedures which were intended to be highly safe may contribute to a reduction in the level of controls, which is all the more problematic given that in some cases national regulations have allowed controls on biocidal products placed on the market. however, the elimination of these mechanisms and the introduction of inefficient and costly evaluation procedures may limit the scope of the marketing of biocidal products. nor will a european central list of active substances in biocidal products ensure safety, especially as biological agents are highly variable and resistant to active substances. a limited selection of effective compounds will only promote increased resistance. in addition, the high costs and complexity of the procedures will eliminate small companies from the market, leading to its monopolization by the big players in the industry. therefore, the proposed extended transitional period of 14 years, with the possibility of a further extension of two years, is all the more necessary as the registration of active substances and the transposition of the provisions into national law is not possible before 2014.
mr. chairman, please! due to their specific nature and the potential risk of misinterpretation of the legal provisions, biocidal products are a subject to which particular attention should be paid. i agree with the rapporteur that the extension of the transitional period until 2014 for the evaluation of active substances in biocidal products is necessary to regulate the market with eu legislation. otherwise, would the national legislation, which expires in 2010, make the marketing of a significant proportion of biocidal products illegal, which could lead to a number of paradoxical situations? during the transitional period, this specific market should be closely monitored by national rules. it is worth adding that any regulation on biocidal products should be treated with particular caution, bearing in mind that these are means of destroying and deterring harmful organisms and that they have a chemical action. any disregard for caution can lead to irreversible consequences.

the rapporteur. - madam president! - what are you doing? the reform of the european union's structural policy for 2007-13 has brought about changes in the structure of the funds and the rules for the distribution of aid. one of the major changes was the creation of a new european agricultural fund for rural development linked to the common agricultural policy. while rural development measures were linked to the structural funds and cohesion policy in the 2000-06 financial perspective, thereby separating them from the cap, they became part of a cap-related heading in the new financial framework. however, following the introduction of these changes, the question arises whether this chapter has led to an improvement in the efficiency of the use of the available funds. however, linking the cap funds to rural development measures is only an apparent simplification of the budgetary scheme. in fact, it contributes to the separation of non-agricultural appropriations from cohesion policy and, as a consequence, to the duplication or omission of certain objectives in both chapters. there is a risk that the resources available under regional policy will be used to a large extent for the development of economic competitiveness concentrated in larger urban centres or the most active regions, while the rural fund concentrates its resources on improving non-agricultural areas, on improving the competitiveness of agriculture. in this situation, expenditure to support non-agricultural activities and the development of smes in rural areas would be at the interface between the two funds and would not be covered by either of them. there may also be a lack of resources for the provision of basic public services and infrastructure investments in rural areas, to which the cohesion fund should also contribute. in this context, it is of particular importance to develop a clear, long-term rural development strategy at member state and regional level in order to be able to clearly define priorities and objectives in rural development and to align aid measures accordingly. however, linking the second pillar to cohesion policies would require close coordination of actions at national level. the concept of rural areas has not yet been precisely defined. traditionally, they have been distinguished from urban areas by their lower population density, different employment structure, lower income levels and poorer access to public roads. from the point of view of territorial cohesion, which is also not sufficiently defined, the lower population density should not, however, be the decisive differentiator. one of the union's development objectives is to modernise the social fabric, including the employment structure. territorial cohesion can therefore be enhanced by matching the employment structure of rural and urban areas. however, income levels and access to public goods remain the main challenges for territorial cohesion, and these objectives can be most effectively achieved by promoting non-agricultural activities in rural areas. however, measures for this purpose should not in any way reduce the appropriations for direct payments to agriculture. the difficulty in implementing rural policy stems from the intersection of sectoral policies with territorial cohesion policy, as well as the intersection of the economic and social dimensions, hence the emphasis in the actions so far on the demarcation of competences rather than on the synergy of actions. however, the aim of coordination should be to achieve synergies in the use of the funds. there are many models of coordination of these activities in different countries and it is difficult to say at this stage that any national solution should be a model. however, it seems that it is the political will rather than some organizational solution that will determine success. therefore, the application of the open method of coordination at union level to this aspect of cooperation could be a favourable solution. it should be stressed that rural development policy has a major impact on territorial cohesion. it therefore does not seem appropriate to decouple the tasks of this policy from cohesion policy for regional development. this policy can better than the cap support the solution of non-agricultural rural development problems, such as helping to re-qualify human resources to work in other sectors of the economy. however, integration of rural development policy into cohesion policy can only take place if the octs receive an adequate allocation of funds.

madam president! the two recent enlargements of the european union have considerably widened the regional disparities in the community. as a consequence, we are increasingly seeing the phenomenon of so-called spatial segregation, which leads to the emergence of isolated regional enclaves, particularly in areas far from the poles of development, mainly rural areas. environmentally sustainable economic development and the reduction of regional disparities are the main objectives of the european union's regional policy. in october 2006, the council adopted the strategic guidelines for cohesion as an indicative framework to help member states prepare their national strategic reference frameworks and operational programmes for the period 2007-13. the priorities set out in the document are to make europe and its regions more attractive for investment and jobs, to improve knowledge and innovation for growth, and to increase the number and quality of jobs. the transposition of these priorities into operational programmes should enable regions to meet the challenges of globalisation, structural, demographic and climate change and to enhance the harmonious, sustainable and sustainable development of the regions. it is commendable that all member states have already made efforts to incorporate in their operational programmes priorities corresponding to the objectives of the lisbon strategy. however, the slow absorption of the new programming period in many member states may jeopardise the effective use of the funds. it is of the utmost importance, especially in the new member states, that they consolidate actions to support the capacity to absorb effectively the funds available, including through the use of measures such as the exchange of best practices, information campaigns, the exchange of new technologies and the development of different types of partnerships, so that programme objectives can be translated into real and high-quality projects to effectively address development gaps, particularly in the poorest regions of the union.
madam president! today, with the emergence of national protectionist tendencies in europe, a rationally-led policy of cohesion and rural development is of particular importance. the current system of support from the various rural development funds only sustains, rather than undermines, the level of development of the different parts of the european union. there is a large disparity in agricultural subsidies in the new member states compared to the old ones, and this will continue beyond 2013. farmers all have similar production costs and agricultural services in the new member states are growing, often approaching prices in the old countries. so where is the chance of leveling the playing field in rural areas in the next few decades? only by providing stable, long-term support to local communities in poor regions, with the greatest possible simplification of procedures, can we close the gap and talk about genuine competition in the european union in the next few years.
