madam president! the creation of the european agricultural fund for rural development is of major importance from the structural policy point of view. however, to make full use of the opportunities available, it is necessary to develop a clear, long-term strategy for rural and regional development and to provide for the possibility of continuous coordination of actions at national level. we all know that the debate on territorial cohesion policy is based on different views on the concept of using funds for agricultural subsidies and rural development. there is also a concern that, once the relocations have taken place, some of these funds will be used to develop the most active urban centres and regions, of course at the expense of those that are historically lagging behind and less actively managed. we cannot accept such solutions and consequences.
madam president! cohesion policy is the main pillar of the integration process. a well-functioning cohesion policy is an essential prerequisite for achieving the social, economic and territorial cohesion of the european union. our key challenge today is to reform policy rules quickly, simplify and make more flexible the complex procedures for implementing projects and the rules for funding. the development of an interregional approach and the exchange of best practices are part of and complement the cohesion policy reform agenda. the european commission should therefore make a concrete proposal as soon as possible for the exchange of experience between project promoters. i do not think that any of you here need be convinced that, in the face of the financial and economic crisis, structural measures are a key instrument to stimulate the economy at regional level. it is therefore important to simplify procedures and to speed up the impact of measures on member states' economies. european projects are a way of creating new, sustainable jobs and an opportunity for the poorest, most deprived regions of the european union. cohesion policy should also be an instrument to meet new challenges such as the common energy policy and climate change.
madam president! cohesion policy is often considered to be the most perfect example of the principle of solidarity within the union. it is in the interest of the union as a whole to compensate for the disparities in development between the various countries and regions of the community. in my view, the green paper is a commission document that provides a good diagnosis of the current challenges facing cohesion policy in the union. the commission also sees a particular need to support regions with a specific geographical character, such as mountain areas and rural areas with economic disadvantages, which should be strongly supported. coordination and appropriate planning of support to rural areas is of paramount importance. these are areas characterised by lower economic development, lower population density, insufficient access to all types of public services, limited opportunities to find work other than in agriculture. of course, there is also a great variation in these areas between member states. if we compare rural areas with urban areas, these disparities are even more profound. we have repeatedly criticised the increase in the funds foreseen for rural development in the current financial perspective. i would like to remind you that rural development policy and the funds allocated to it help to keep these areas alive and make life easier for the people who live there. in conclusion, the commission document, the reports produced and today's discussion point in the right direction.
mr. chairman, please! territorial and social cohesion prevents conflict by eliminating its causes. this is why action to level the playing field between urban and rural living standards and to level the infrastructure between regions is so important. a good cohesion policy approach is to promote the use of microcredit. today, in the midst of the financial and economic crisis, when we are all trying to find solutions to protect jobs, we must be aware of the dangers to cohesion policy posed by protectionism and discrimination against poorer regions.
mr. chairman, please! cohesion policy is of additional importance in the context of the current economic crisis, as the structural measures available under it can serve as effective instruments to stimulate the economy at regional level. a focus on pro-growth activities such as research and development spending, innovation and active employment instruments should boost the european economy and ensure a return to growth. i also welcome the allocation of additional funds to improve internet access in rural areas.
member of the commission. − mr president, i saved two minutes from my introductory remarks in order to have more time to respond now to the questions. whilst i regret that i cannot respond to all the questions, i very much appreciate all the bilateral exchanges we have had over the last years in brussels or during my visits on the ground in your constituencies. you are welcome to continue this dialogue with us in the commission. i should like to thank you for this really good and genuine debate today. we need to fully and wisely exploit the potential of all european and national policies to ensure that the european union as an economy and a society comes out of the crisis stronger economically, socially and politically, with solid foundations for long-term sustainable development. i feel that today’s debate confirms that european cohesion policy must play its role in this process both today and tomorrow. it is our common task today to ensure that the potential of cohesion policy – its capacity to deliver sustainable development and jobs – will be used fully and wisely in this new global context. i am not only thinking of the crisis, but also of all those well-known challenges that we identified years ago as important challenges for european development. supporting sustainable competitiveness is the most effective way to achieve cohesion in the european union. in this context, we must use the cohesion policy to target factors such as access by small and medium-sized enterprises to finance. we must also address issues such as better access to public services that aim to improve employability and productivity and thus contribute to more equal opportunities. as some of you have stressed, over the last years it has become common sense that addressing the new challenges clearly requires an integrated and place-based approach – an approach that optimises the use of resources and also mobilises all partners at regional and local level, as well as national and european level, so that we are active at all levels of european governance. concerning the partnership principle, i would like to stress that this has been a very important objective from day one of my term in office, and the commission has invested a lot in making the partnership principle and the cohesion policy a real one – one which is really used on the ground. soon after the negotiations, we conducted a full assessment of how the partnership principle and the process of designing policy programmes were implemented by the member states and the regions. we did not want just the formal presence of partnership principles, so we also worked with partners, helping them to build their capacity to be real partners in the policy management system, and we react quite efficiently to any signals we get from the ground that this principle is not being respected in the individual member states. i have just had a meeting on this very issue with ngos from one of the central european member states. i also fully agree with all of you who say that cohesion policy does not, and must not, work in isolation; that we need to reinforce the synergies and coordination between the cohesion policy and all other sectoral, national or european policies. this is not just to avoid overlap or duplication, but is also about using the synergy that comes from good coordination between the policies. certainly, the rural development and regional policies are an extreme example of the need to have very good coordination and the use of synergies between policies. another example could be competitiveness and the need to take into account the constraints coming from a low-carbon economy and climate change regarding infrastructure investment. i would like to underline very strongly that we have invested a lot in greening the european cohesion policy. we established the objectives relating to climate change, energy efficiency and renewable energy before the major debate exploded on climate change in the european union. today we have one third of cohesion policy funding going directly into green investment in all areas of our life. recently added to the policy is the additional 4% to be used in the area of housing for energy efficiency and the use of renewable energy that allows us to put more emphasis on this challenge. what also clearly emerges from the debate is that we need both continuity and reform in policy delivery. on the continuity side, i would very strongly stress that this multiannual programming, financial additionality, shared management and partnership principles represent a great european value that we should continue to care about. but there is also this need for change to strike a better balance between the demands of financial management and control and the tasks of achieving good results and good implementation of the policy. there is no doubt that we need to put in place a simpler, more efficient and more effective implementing mechanism and reduce administrative complexity and the administrative burden. we have been working with your great support over the last months on this challenge. we already had the first amendment of article 55 back in december and we will be voting on the main chunk of simplification proposals a week from now. the task force that we set up with member states for the simplification of the policies is continuing its work, and at the end of may we will have another proposal, hopefully still related to this period. i agree with you that for the policy to be more effective we also need a stronger focus on results, stronger monitoring and an evaluation culture. we are continuing to work on this. i very much appreciate your support for financial engineering. we are on track, but much more can certainly be done. please also take note with respect to financial engineering, which is today one of the major instruments helping small and medium-sized companies access credit through jeremie and now also through jasmine for micro-credit, that we started this process long before the crisis hit, so the policy has also been relatively well prepared for these difficult times. some of you mentioned the question of transparency. i would just like to remind all of us here that we have new rules for this new period 2007-2013. we have the obligation to inform the public on all the beneficiaries, so we hope that with these transparency obligations we will also see major change with regard to public awareness and the integrity of the whole process. very briefly, on culture, because it was raised as an important element, we are fully aware – and i also see it during my travels – that both regions and cities are major actors in the cultural field in europe. culture also plays an important economic role in the development of regional development. we have recognised this in the framework of the european cohesion policy. we have many regional and local urban strategies that have successfully integrated culture into our policy. let me also inform you that the commission will soon launch an independent study on the contribution of culture to local and regional development, hopefully to be finalised by the beginning of next year. through this we will have a better-informed basis for the further inclusion of culture in european policies. finally, i very much appreciate all your comments not just on the report, but also what you have presented here as your concerns and ideas for the future. i shall include most of those messages in my orientation paper which i will present to council at the end of may. we are also completing the independent study by a group of researchers and experts chaired by professor fabrizio barca. this will be presented publicly at the end of april. the final official assessment of the consultation on the green paper on territorial cohesion will be presented in our sixth interim cohesion report which will be adopted by the commission towards the end of june.
the rapporteur. - mr president! - what are you doing? i'm not going to let you down. my report dealt with a rather specific issue, but one which is very important for optimising the use of eu funds from the point of view of cohesion, whether it is understood in the traditional sense or in terms of territorial cohesion. sustainable growth is a tremendously complex task. any attempt to facilitate this task should therefore be welcomed. however, the concept of territorial cohesion has not yet been sufficiently defined. the green paper is therefore the beginning, not the end, of the debate on this subject. i am pleased that the commissioner has stressed the need to reduce disparities in development and the importance of synergy in the implementation of eu policies. different regions have very different problems related to income levels, geographical location, population movements, etc. however, we must remember what my polish colleagues, mrs staniszewska and mr podkański and mr zapałowski, have said here, namely that the regional centres tend to accumulate funds in their own hands. it should also be borne in mind that the objectives of rural development policy need not be at odds with the lisbon objectives if the relative competitiveness mechanism, i.e. productivity gains at low cost, is used. the agriculture committee has not commented on my report, so i take your silence as consent. i think that deputy baco's voice is more of a misunderstanding. i have made it clear in my report that rural development measures cannot be used to reduce direct payments, but it is also true that rural development measures can help agricultural regions to overcome their economic difficulties by promoting non-agricultural activities. i am pleased with the support i have received from mr nicholson on this matter. finally, i would like to thank the advisers of the committee on regional development and my political group for their help in drafting this report, and all those who have taken part in this debate.
in writing. the rural population is particularly disadvantaged in terms of labour market competition. in the eu, and particularly in poland, there are significant differences in living standards between urban and rural areas. this is mainly about access to the service sector. access to modern technologies such as broadband internet is half as low in rural poland as in the city. the aim of cohesion policy should be to take concrete initiatives to level the living standards of the regions. support for small and medium-sized enterprises in obtaining co-financing from the european agricultural fund for rural development (eafrd) is particularly relevant here. it is the responsibility of national governments to support small and medium-sized enterprises by removing administrative and legal barriers and providing the necessary infrastructure. these are the basic conditions for the development of remote areas.
in writing. i thank mr becsey for his report, which is so important to me and my countrymen. many people are not aware of the impact that microcredit has on the economic and social development of a country. low-cost loans, which do not require adequate collateral, are not only a tool for the poorest people in the third world. this idea has also proved successful for the unemployed, those wishing to start their first business and existing micro-entrepreneurs. offering the possibility of financing projects to people without credit is one of the most important elements of the 'think small first' principle. by offering these loans, we promote entrepreneurship and increase employment, which prevents and reduces social exclusion. so microcredit has a very positive effect, which is particularly important for my country, on the unemployment rate. however, there are a few important considerations to keep in mind when introducing this type of loan service. first, the institutional and legal framework for microcredit must be adapted to the degree of development of the loan fund market. secondly, it is necessary to examine the procedures which cover this service. unfortunately, due to their complex nature, micro-entrepreneurs and start-ups are more likely to apply for consumer credit. third, to promote microcredit, entrepreneurs should be made aware of the possibility of obtaining non-bank credit. with these reservations, i welcome the microcredit service in poland with open arms.
in writing. in the debate on cohesion policy, i would like to draw attention to the issues raised in the report by mr roszkowski on cohesion policy. 1.in the financial perspective for 2007-13, the european agricultural fund for rural development (eafrd) became pillar ii of the cap and was therefore separated from cohesion policy. this has the consequence, particularly in the light of the tight budgetary allocations, that cohesion policy, mainly the european regional development fund (erdf), focuses on developing economic competitiveness, concentrated in larger urban centres or the most active regions, while the eafrd concentrates its resources on improving the competitiveness of agriculture. this approach may result in either duplication of some objectives or omission of some objectives in both sections (e.g. environmental protection, education, culture). 2.it is therefore necessary to assess whether the rural development funds for 2007-13 will be used more to support agriculture or whether they will also be used more to support rural beneficiaries outside the agricultural sector or beneficiaries who, while remaining in rural areas, will switch from the agricultural sector to other types of occupational activity. if it turns out that support for agriculture is preferred under pillar ii, it would seem that it would be more advantageous in the long term to link these measures to cohesion policy. 3.the financial resources for the financing of pillar ii of the cap must also be increased, for example by reducing the direct payments for large-scale farms and gradually increasing the rate of modulation, as called for by the ep.
in writing. regional policy, in the form of the structural funds and cohesion, is rightly considered to be the community policy most visible and tangible to the people of europe. no other policy provides comparable visibility to the european union and better illustrates the benefits of integration. that is why we attach such importance to the debate on the future of cohesion. cohesion has never been more necessary than now, when the two parts of europe, divided by the iron curtain since the war, have come together. for the countries that have lagged behind the yalta decision, this is the most important issue. and the particular circumstance is the crisis and the potential value of the structural funds as an anti-crisis package. we cannot allow a repeat of the 2008 situation, when 4.5 billion euros of unused funds were returned, which was our collective failure. the most important thing today is to make this section of the union budget more attractive. in the short term, other things take precedence. in the longer term, cohesion policy must be defended as a community policy that creates opportunities for all regions. as such, cohesion policy should draw on regional and local wisdom in how resources are used. the multiplication of project evaluation criteria increases the credibility of the evaluation and thus complicates the process of using the funds. it doesn't make sense today, in the face of the crisis, or in the long run.
in writing. poland will receive over €67 billion from the eu budget in 2007-13. in 2008 alone, the european commission granted poland a total of pln 19.3 billion in financial transfers. however, the specific nature of the implementation of the programmes means that most payments will be made in the last years, i.e. 2013-15. unfortunately, there are already fundamental constraints on the effective implementation of the structural funds in poland. from the start of the 2007-13 programmes to the beginning of march 2009, almost 8,400 co-financing agreements were signed for a total expenditure of pln 15,4 billion. the eu's contribution is pln 11.4 billion. unfortunately, the total value of the payment requests is pln 1.75 billion. excessively long procurement procedures can delay the implementation of the structural funds and thus contribute to a low absorption rate. the structural funds are public funds subject to national legislation on public procurement. legislation in the field of public procurement must simplify the effective procedure for selecting the contractor. too long tendering procedures can delay the implementation of the structural funds. eu measures should be part of mitigating one of the most serious effects of the financial crisis. accelerating spending will allow the economy to be fuelled in 2009 by investment in infrastructure, human capital and enterprises estimated to be equivalent to at least around 1.3% of gdp. to do this, the government must make it easier to access eu funds and simplify procedures.

in writing. - it is true that art subjects are taught in schools all over europe. it is also true that europe, or societies, are changing rapidly, and with it, information and communication technologies. europe is also uniting, and cultural education can serve this process no less well than, for example, the common market. this can be done through arts education at all levels of education, i.e. deepening theoretical and practical knowledge of europe's diversity and multiculturalism. there is a lot of it, and it is constantly being added, but the fact that it is taught in different countries does not make it possible, for example, to train an artist whose knowledge and potential will be recognised and used in another member state. the question of coordination therefore arises, and here the badii and cutchet reports propose an interesting solution, namely the open method of coordination, i.e. 'bringing the issue to practical ground' and 'learning from each other by looking at the examples of those countries which have best solved the problems. this method is therefore practically entirely in the hands of the member states. this approach is flexible, allows for coordination of complex issues and allows for a rapid response to today's challenges. the issue of training artists is complex: their creativity must be stimulated through a special individualised master-learner approach, equipped with knowledge of europe's constantly evolving culture and with creative tools, and given the freedom to pursue a career. a sensible and constructive reflection on art education is an investment in the future and identity of a europe united in its diversity.
in writing. - dialogue with citizens is a serious and difficult matter, but those in power must master this art well. that's the essence of their work: dialogue, compromise. in this context, the background of the report seems to be somewhat contradictory. it calls for the ratification of the lisbon treaty to be completed as soon as possible, as one of the important conditions for the dialogue on europe. the report concludes that the treaty will increase transparency and involve citizens in decision-making. it may seem that those who dislike the treaty will be ignored and their voices will not be heard. so it's hard to talk about dialogue and compromise. the idea of creating a 'common european knowledge' through the study of european history and european integration is also controversial. this would be the aim of a programme agreed at community level and adopted on a voluntary basis by the member states, paid for by the community budget. in short, this is a historic compromise which will serve as a tool for building common european values. i think we should not go so far. historical compromise is a vague notion, if such a compromise is necessary at all. besides, the instrumental use of history is objectionable, even if the intentions are sincere. the key to effective dialogue lies in the present, which presents us with enough problems as it is. we need to talk! in short, yes to dialogue, no to reporting.
in writing. - the debate on the issue of dialogue between the union and its citizens is very much needed. the way in which europe is perceived by its citizens, and the way in which the community works, remains a key issue. people accept what they know, but what's distant, unknown, makes them anxious. the examples of the irish referendum and earlier in france and the netherlands show that the voices of our citizens cannot be ignored. decisions should not be made in the privacy of the offices without the public's input. nihil novi - nothing new about us without us. it is necessary to reach the poorest and least educated citizens. we need a clear and readable message to the public about what we are doing, what we want to achieve and finally what benefits this activity will bring to our citizens. real integration is impossible without full acceptance of the union's actions by our electorate. surveys show that only just over 50% of eu citizens are satisfied with their country's membership of the community. of course, this varies from country to country. success will be achieved when the rate is 80%. the responsibility to bring the eu closer to its citizens lies not only with the eu institutions in the broad sense, but, in my view, primarily with us, the members of the european parliament. i myself organize hundreds of meetings every year with youth, farmers, entrepreneurs. let us teach our citizens to benefit from the eu. the first test of our effectiveness will be the june election.
in writing. − the rapporteur notes that active dialogue with citizens on europe is poorly developed. i'm afraid he's right, though. often, information about the union reaches only the well-educated and wealthy, which contributes to the skepticism and antipathy of the rest of the citizens of european countries. the education of european citizens is therefore an essential element in the further development of the european community. the rapporteur is seeking to find ways of reaching a wider audience, which will allow citizens to have a better knowledge of the european union. it is based on the following pragmatic and popular methods to reach the widest possible audience: introducing a year-long education programme on the european union since 1945 in schools, creating a television news channel modelled on cnn in the us, or creating websites in a form that is as accessible to young people as possible. i agree and support the importance of the information campaign on the european union as a method of raising public awareness and i also think that the rapporteur has very good ideas for implementing it.

in writing. −the multilingualism of the eu is an asset in its contacts with third countries. this can give us a significant competitive advantage, which is why education programmes and language exchanges should be encouraged, but not only within urban areas where access is already easier. in pursuing this policy, we must also remember that united europeans are first and foremost citizens of their own countries. we have to make sure that they can identify with their own language. this aspect is also dealt with in mr moore's report.
in writing. - the issue of multilingualism and its preservation is one of the most difficult challenges facing the community. the effects of a multilingual policy are far-reaching and, of course, if misunderstood, can be lamentable. europe's strength is its multiculturalism, which is also expressed in the multiplicity of its languages. it is also a shared commitment, based on the need and the challenge of turning multiculturalism into a force that unites the community, acts externally and gives europe its rightful place in the world. so the stakes are high. the wrong policy of multilingualism is to favour one or more languages and condemn the rest to be marginalized in all public activities. the european union, through its legislation and institutions, has a huge potential to implement a good language policy. the greater the responsibility, the greater the responsibility. the vasco graçy moura report does not solve all the problems of the right of coexistence and the privileges that this gives to the various european languages. besides the official languages, there are a great many other languages spoken in europe that are more or less in danger of disappearing. a good multilingualism policy is one that defends these languages. the report focuses on learning official languages rather than on the implementation of the idea of multilingualism. but these issues require sensible policies of an evolutionary nature, and i think the report on this path is acceptable.
in writing. - multilingualism is undoubtedly a great asset of a united europe. the language skills acquired should help to improve qualifications, to get a better job or to acquire new interpersonal contacts. according to annual surveys by linguists, multilinguals have greater abilities, more fluency, and a more developed imagination than monolinguals. they're also more creative and have a broader mindset. i will not mention the obvious benefits of being able to communicate with a larger number of people, often of a completely different mentality, often from different cultures or nations. the benefits of multilingualism that i mentioned are a sign that we should all make learning languages a priority. that is why it is so important that every citizen of the community should have the same access to learning foreign languages on an equal footing. i therefore support all the commission's efforts to study and evaluate foreign language teaching, teaching methods and curricula. i believe that these measures are intended to standardize the system of teaching foreign languages throughout the union in the future, which will lead to an increase in language competences and will be reflected in the number of highly qualified community citizens.
in writing. - i am strongly in favour of multilingualism in the european union. the multilingualism of europe is underlined by its cultural plurality, which is a testament to its uniqueness. the linguistic competences of the citizens of a united europe should be constantly developed. multilingualism is an essential element of european integration, allowing eu citizens to freely choose where to live and find work. at the same time, the importance of the mother tongue as a means of acquiring appropriate education and vocational qualifications should be emphasised. we should pay particular attention to the need to continuously improve the competence of foreign language teachers and to introduce modern teaching techniques. the rapporteur stresses the importance of enabling citizens who wish to pursue their education privately to learn foreign languages, while stressing the importance of language learning also for older people. like the rapporteur, i believe that it is important to continue to encourage citizens to learn foreign languages and that special attention should be paid to citizens with fewer opportunities. i believe that language learning will counteract discrimination and promote the integration of the countries of a united europe. i fully support the european parliament's demands for a multilingual europe.
in writing. - i voted in favour of the report by mr vlasak on the urban dimension of cohesion policy in the new programming period. i live in the city of poznań, which is the capital of greater poland. almost every day i experience the positive impact of the development of the city on the development of the whole region. i would even venture to say that there is a much-awaited synergy between urban development and regional development. urban development has nothing to do with local centralization. those who attack the promotion of large cities often fail to understand the importance of these cities to the regions in which they are located. some of the functions of urban centres cannot be transferred to rural areas. city managers have a special responsibility. the challenges they face in planning, spatial planning, social dialogue, culture and education, and in supporting the creation of new, sustainable, knowledge-based jobs are very difficult. some of these tasks require close cooperation with local authorities at other levels. it is also important that the urban dimension of cohesion policy is not competitive with, but complementary to, rural development. both rural and urban areas can and should develop, and both processes are supported by the european union.

in writing. − the success of microcredit in reducing poverty in developing countries, particularly in south asia and latin america, has not yet been transferred to the eu. however, demand for microcredit is high, especially from people who cannot obtain loans in the traditional banking sector. the microcredit business is different from traditional banking. it is not only for economic reasons and not only for profit, but it also serves the purpose of cohesion by trying to integrate disadvantaged people who want to start a micro-enterprise. the success of the european microfinance initiative could contribute to achieving the objectives of the renewed lisbon strategy for growth and jobs and to creating an innovative, creative and dynamic european economy. in particular, they may serve the priority of unlocking economic potential by promoting the social and economic integration or reintegration of persons through self-employment. i therefore support the conclusions of the report which calls for the adoption of the appropriate national institutional, legal and commercial frameworks necessary to promote a more favourable environment for the development of microcredit and the establishment of a harmonised european framework for non-bank microfinance institutions.

first, the context of the financial and economic crisis renders any encouragement of greater cooperation between ebrd and eib more relevant than ever. yet the crisis also means that cooperation between public international financial institutions is no longer just a policy-driven aspiration but a vital necessity. faced with the dramatic decline in private flows of credit, we came together last month with the world bank group to launch the joint ifi action plan in support of banking systems and lending to the real economy in central and eastern europe. this is a eur 24.5 billion package over 2009 and 2010 of which the ebrd will contribute eur 6 billion. the action plan recognises that an effective crisis response in europe’s integrated financial markets requires fast and coordinated action by all stakeholders: parent banks which own a large part of the region’s financial sectors; important local banks; home and host country authorities of cross-border banking groups; european institutions and the ifis. with this wide range of stakeholders we are working together to implement the plan and are developing the coordination and cooperation mechanisms to do so. and we see – as we saw last august when faced with the conflict-driven banking crisis in georgia – that this kind of ifi cooperation, born of need, is the kind that works best. second, under the aegis of the european union, new structures of cooperation between ebrd and eib offer great new opportunities for us to work together. i refer in particular to the western balkans investment framework, now being launched, as well as to the eastern partnership announced by the european council in recent days which will build on the good cooperation we have already established through our memorandum of understanding and the neighbourhood investment facility. these initiatives, facilitated by ec funds, bring us together to work concretely on specific projects and programmes combining the strength of each institution and, as such, offer an excellent crucible in which to forge the development of our joint work. i believe it is in this context that we may find divisions of labour, applications of joint expertise and the necessary mechanisms of cooperation, including common standards, which you have called for. third, i take the european parliament’s views as welcome input to the early stages of the ebrd’s fourth capital resources review which we will conclude at our annual meeting in zagreb in may 2010. the ebrd has taken a proactive stance in response to the crisis: supporting our clients in countries of operations, we are expanding our instruments, and aim to invest eur 7 billion in 2009 – an increase of more than 20%. at the same time, we have to acknowledge that our risk exposure is also increasing. the full implications of the current situation on our portfolio and on the development of our business cannot yet be clearly seen. yet the importance of our partnership with the eib and with the european union in meeting our commitments, both to our shareholders and to our countries of operations, is clearer than ever.
president of the eib. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, let me begin by thanking you for giving us the opportunity once again to continue the constructive dialogue which has been established between the eib and parliament over the past few years. i am particularly pleased to have the opportunity to discuss the two reports before us today, because they are both interesting and raise very relevant questions, questions which i hope we will have the opportunity to return to later. today, of course, we are facing a crisis of a particular magnitude, probably the most serious crisis since the end of the second world war, and it is therefore quite normal that in this context the member states should call on our two institutions to try to contribute to the european union's response to this crisis. you know that in this context the member states, our shareholders, have asked the european investment bank to substantially increase the volume of its lending in 2009, an increase of some 30% compared with the initial forecasts, and to direct this additional effort mainly in three directions: firstly, loans to banks for small and medium-sized enterprises; secondly, energy and, in particular, the fight against climate change; thirdly, the fight against climate change; and fourthly, the fight against climate change. and thirdly, a special effort for the countries most affected by the crisis. where are we today? i'm going to give you figures that actually cover the last three months of 2008, so from the time the first calls were made to the eib and the first two months of 2009. over the five months, we signed loans for more than 31 billion, an increase of 38% compared to the same period in late 2007/early 2008. in the first direction, loans for small and mediumsized enterprises, 5.6 billion were signed during this short period. many of you have stressed the importance of supporting small and mediumsized enterprises in the current context. we are making a very special effort in this direction and i can already tell you that the target which we had set for ourselves of 15 billion of these loans for the years 2008/2009 will be exceeded. as regards the second objective, energy and the fight against climate change, we have also made a special effort here and it is in this context that we must place the financing for the automobile industry because it must be clear: what we are financing in this sector are research, development and production projects for clean cars, that is to say cars which will meet the new european union standards for reducing co2 emissions. and finally, as regards the third priority, support for the countries most affected by the crisis: during the same five-month period, we signed loans worth 910 million in hungary, 600 million in latvia, 1 billion in romania and 1.1 billion in lithuania. i think i can say that we are trying to respond to the call of the member states and to implement what has been agreed quickly. and president mirow himself has already referred to the joint action plan with the sfi and the ebrd in support of the banking sector in central and eastern europe. of course, this increase in the volume of our loans is only possible thanks to the capital increase which was decided by our shareholders - it costs nothing to the budget of the member states - but we needed the authorization of our shareholders to convert our reserves into capital, that is what was decided. many of you asked questions about the control and supervision of the european investment bank, and i personally think that the question is quite legitimate. when a financial institution develops in this way, it is natural to worry about how it is actually controlled. there is what already exists, which is not negligible: it is a number of internal controls, it is also and above all an external control by an independent audit committee and which reports directly to our governors. the lisbon treaty also provides for the strengthening of the audit committee by adding persons with proven experience in banking supervision. can we go any further? i would remind you that the court of auditors already controls all the eib's activities as soon as they involve the use of funds from the european budget. should we go further to formal banking supervision? that is what mrs stauner wanted. mr bullmann indicated that things might not be so simple. it's worth discussing. i can simply confirm today that the european investment bank is fully prepared to submit to formal banking supervision if it is deemed necessary. for the time being, we have organized, with the financial sector supervisory committee in luxembourg, a form of informal supervision. in reply to mr audy, i would say that the approach he had wanted to be taken last year with the cebs has been achieved. we therefore asked the committee of european banking supervisors, but they told us that they themselves had no authority in this matter and could not even act as an adviser. we are therefore still in the hands of those who wish to take the initiative in this respect. i'll call you back when we're ready. a word to conclude on the cooperation between our two institutions. president mirow has already indicated that it is developing well, particularly in the western balkans and in our eastern neighbours, more recently in turkey. i simply want to say, in respect of speaking time, that we fully agree with the recommendations contained in mr mitchell's report. we believe that it would be in the common interest of our institutions, but also of our borrowers, if we moved towards a more rational, more functional division of labour. i would like to conclude by saying a few words about mr seppänen's report. i would like to say how much we appreciated mr seppänen's constructive approach, which proposes a temporary solution, which allows the eib to continue its activities, but which sets a date for a substantive debate on the role of the european investment bank outside the european union. i have no doubt that this is a debate that will hold us back and which i think is timely.

in writing. the review of the current financial framework provides a good opportunity to reflect not only on how the available funds are allocated, but also on the future shape of the eu budget. the main focus of the changes to the current financial perspective and the next one should be to deepen integration and to achieve specific objectives. recently, we have seen far-reaching changes in the structure of the eu budget. cap spending is no longer the largest part of the community's budget. at present, it is cohesion policy and actions related to the implementation of the lisbon strategy that can count on the most support. there is no doubt that this evolution is beneficial for the future of a europe with an innovation-oriented, knowledge-based economy and a high level of employment. however, this change cannot come at the expense of undermining europe's food security and reducing farmers' incomes. equally worrying is the progressive reduction in the level of the eu budget relative to the gni of the eu member states. statistics show that if the budget were to be maintained at the level of 1993-1999 (calculated as the same ratio to gdp) in the current perspective, an additional eur 200 billion would be available for the implementation of european policies. the pressure to reduce the community budget is harmful, since it limits its flexibility and ability to adapt to changing needs. i therefore call for the eu budget to be adapted to the new challenges not by shifting resources from the cap, but by increasing the union's budgetary resources accordingly.

in writing. − the automotive industry is in a particularly difficult situation in the current economic crisis. the forecasts for this year are not optimistic either. they indicate that there will be a further decline in new car sales. the european commission and the european parliament consider that industry has the main responsibility for dealing with the crisis. but it is the industry in particular that should respond to the structural problems of production efficiency and capacity utilisation in a way that improves competitiveness and sustainability in the long term. action at eu and member state level can only support actions undertaken by producers themselves. in particular, these are actions to restore access to finance on reasonable terms, stimulate demand for new vehicles, protect skill and employment levels and minimise social costs. a number of countries have adopted plans to help the automotive sector, but as the european commission notes, these must be in line with eu law and the applicable competition rules, and in particular the rules on state aid, in order not to disrupt the functioning of the european internal market. any financial, tax or scrapping measures must also support and accelerate the necessary technological transformation of the sector, in particular in the field of energy efficiency of engines and emission reductions.

president-in-office of the council. − mr president, i am grateful to the members of this parliament for the opportunity to provide an update on developments in belarus, and in particular to report on the outcome of last monday’s discussion on this issue in council. as many of you will be aware, following the council’s decision last october to suspend temporarily and partially the visa-ban list, we have seen a number of positive developments in belarus. i would point in particular to the registration of the ‘for freedom’ movement and of the centre for chernobyl initiatives, the printing and distribution of independent newspapers such as narodnaya volya and nasha niva, the round table on regulation of the internet with the osce representative on the freedom of the media, the ongoing expert consultations with osce/odihr on improving electoral legislation, and the establishment of consultative councils, including one on human rights issues, which brings together representatives of civil society and even the opposition. these steps, whilst they might appear relatively minor to some, are significant in the belarusian context. this has been acknowledged by some representatives of civil society in belarus. however, there have also been incidents which are a cause for our concern. the important human rights ngo, viasna, has been denied registration, there are problems with the accreditation of some of the independent media, and, while there is less harassment against civil society and opposition activists than earlier, short-term detentions continue to take place. we are also following closely complaints from the opposition over ‘forcible conscription’ to the army. se we cannot deny that the picture is mixed. nevertheless, we are convinced that there is a need to continue with a policy of engagement and to support the positive developments. this should be the way forward in our relations with belarus. we must keep in mind our wider strategic interests in the region as well as the impact of the financial crisis when we consider our future policy direction. these were the considerations which lay behind our decision on 16 march. this decision, while extending for one year the restrictive measures, maintains the suspension of the application of the travel restrictions imposed on certain officials of belarus for nine months. the in-depth review foreseen by the end of this nine-month period will concentrate on the five areas set out in the council’s conclusions of october 2008. these are electoral reform and other concrete actions towards respect for democratic values, the rule of law, human rights and fundamental freedoms, including freedom of expression and of the media, and freedom of assembly and political association. we firmly believe that the continuation of the suspension agreed last week will enable us to pursue our policy objectives. it will provide us with the opportunity to continue to raise with our belarusian partners developments which concern us in the field of human rights. the launching, in the coming month, of a human rights dialogue will be particularly important. following the lifting of the ban on bilateral political contacts, a number of high-level visits have taken place, including a ministerial troika at the end of january. the aim of these various contacts has been to encourage belarus, and to create understanding over differences in expectations. we hope that the dialogue will continue over the coming months. we are convinced that we need to be constructive with minsk. we remain realistic and do not expect any dramatic changes. transformation takes time, and it is in our shared interest to take every opportunity to encourage further positive developments. it is important that our policy of engagement has been openly supported by representatives of civil society in belarus, who took part recently in a very helpful discussion with members of this parliament. we also maintain regular contacts with the representatives of belarusian civic society and we intend to continue this dialogue as well as our support to civic society and the independent media in belarus. let me close with a few words on the eastern partnership, which was endorsed last week by the european council, and will be launched at a summit-level meeting in may. belarus is one of the six eastern partnership countries. we strongly believe that belarus should be involved in this new initiative from the outset. but the extent of its participation in the bilateral track will depend on a number of factors, in particular progress in some of the areas to which i have just referred. i am grateful to the public support which parliament has given to the outcome of the council last monday. clearly the in-depth review to be conducted in nine months’ time will be a key to any further decisions, and will have an important bearing on our future relations with belarus more generally. the council is very ready to continue to keep this parliament informed of developments, and welcomes the opportunity for you to continue to contribute to this debate.
member of the commission. - mr president, belarus is at a crossroads. we are in fact on the eve of a council decision confirming the temporary suspension of the stay ban until the end of the year and we are on the eve of the adoption of a resolution by the european parliament. it is time to take an initial stocktaking of our policy towards belarus after six months of sanctions suspension since october 2008 and to reflect on the prospects for the next nine months. i am personally convinced that the decision taken by the european union last october to suspend sanctions was the right one and that this suspension has indeed triggered a positive process. belarus has taken steps which are undeniably in the direction of more democracy. i am thinking in particular of the return of two independent newspapers to the newsstands, the fact that mr milinkevich's own organisation has finally been legalised, the cooperation with the osce/odihr on electoral legislation, the various congresses of opposition parties or ngos - such as the union of poles in belarus - that have been able to take place. the commission has already made some progress in this area, but it is not yet clear whether it will be able to take action in the future. that is why the european union's response to this mixed assessment was mixed, with the balanced decision taken at the last cagre. the extension of the suspension of sanctions allows us to maintain dialogue, as civil society itself has expressly asked us to do, including at the forum held in the european parliament no later than 4 march. at the same time, we retain our leverage as sanctions can be reintroduced at the end of the year if we consider that the progress made by then is insufficient, and we will continue our review civil society forum. the text of the commission proposal is unambiguous as regards belarus' participation in the bilateral part of the eastern partnership. the development of bilateral relations also affecting all our neighbours to the east, i am personally in favour of economic support measures for belarus. a first significant step has been taken by the imf, with the active support of its european members, namely a loan of 2 billion us dollars to deal with the immediate effects of the crisis, precisely to put an end to the balance of payments. and the next step should allow belarus to access eib loans and broader ebrd loans to finance projects related to trans-european networks, while helping to diversify the country's economic ties. in parallel, the commission is strengthening its of the situation in the coming months and in our dialogue with belarus, its authorities and civil society, and i hope that this first step will lead us to a deeper mutual commitment based on concrete progress.

the rapporteur. - madam president, commissioner, i have to ask you to leave. we are debating today the extremely important issue of the food distribution programme to the most needy in the community. it is important because it affects many millions of people who live in poverty and need special support. we support the european commission's proposal to increase funding by 2⁄3, i.e. from eur 305 million to almost half a billion per year, and to expand the range of products delivered under this programme. of course, this programme will not solve the problem of malnutrition and poverty among the community's citizens, but it will certainly help to reduce it. we are opposed to the proposal to introduce, and i repeat it now, cofinancing from national budgets, because this could limit or even context of the ongoing economic crisis. i believe we can work out a compromise in the council. we also want the food products distributed under this programme to come from the european union. if member of the commission. − mr president, i would like to thank everyone for all the comments. in general, i hear a very positive approach to the proposal for the most needy. mr president, could i just be allowed to focus on some of the comments that have been raised here today? first of all, i think that we have to keep in mind that poverty is not confined to certain areas or regions within the member states. unfortunately, it is an issue that all member states have to face. it is true that the extent of the problem and the means available to remedy it are not identical throughout the whole european community. the allocation of the budget to the member states, as well as the differentiated rates for cofinancing for cohesion and non-cohesion countries, does of course already take into account the financial capacity of every country. this means that the bottom line will be that there will more money available for the so-called ‘new’ member states than is the case today. regarding the budget, i would just remind you that we have actually increased the budget available for the programme for the most needy by two thirds – up to eur 0.5 billion – and i think this, together with the newly introduced cofinancing, will help alleviate some of the problems. i think we also have to keep in mind that this scheme is a voluntary one. member states that have a social system in place in their own country certainly need not use this scheme. we do not seek to replace social policies that are already implemented in member states and, to a certain extent, also managed by ngos. our intention is to underpin them by the provision of food, which i still consider the central aim of the agricultural policy. i believe that the changes that we have proposed go in the right direction. i think the provisions are reasonable and well balanced. the programme –when hopefully voted through this parliament as well – will be able to meet the challenges of the future. it will be difficult to be against or to oppose this programme in a situation where unemployment is currently increasing dramatically all over europe, thereby heavily increasing the number of people at risk of poverty. so i look forward to the votes of this extremely responsible parliament.
the rapporteur. - i'll address some of the issues raised. first of all, i said that i was against co-financing, noting that we are now in a period of economic crisis, when the number of poor and unemployed people is increasing. we will evaluate the programme in 2011 or 2012 and then we will consider what to do with the co-financing. let's give ourselves time. let's not do this in a crisis. secondly, i share the commissioner's view that it will be difficult to limit the food distributed to food from the union, because this will increase costs and increase the administrative part of the programme. third, take the example of the us, how much money under the farm bill was allocated to support agriculture by funding free food stamps. fourthly, and finally, i encourage countries not participating in the programme to apply. the program is open. fifthly, the funds allocated to this programme do not restrict farmers' access to the cap, because we have savings under the cap. i want to go back to the source. as we know, the objectives of the cap were already formulated in the treaties of rome. they talk about the need to provide affordable food to the public and to guarantee farmers a fair level of income. it can be concluded that these are, firstly, production tasks, which determine the necessary production volume. second, social tasks, social, because we're talking about the right prices so that consumers can afford to buy food. so the rome statute sets out certain social goals. and finally, thirdly, economic objectives, related to ensuring adequate income for farmers. when we talk about affordable food for the poor, often unemployed consumer, it should be available to him at much lower prices, or even provided free of charge, of course, under special programmes and under certain conditions. in conclusion, the common agricultural policy also includes some social policy elements.

madam president! the beauty of culture comes from its regional, local diversity, changing with the development of societies. regional cultures, deeply rooted in tradition, provide a strong foundation for national cultures and their various currents. they also attract with their colour and expression, stimulate artistically, convey experience and emotion, and strengthen the bonds of local communities. regional cultures are pushed forward by the inspired community of professional creators. it is often thought that regional culture must be an amateur movement and a professionally supported one. this is probably the reason why the european union is also tending to finance large and expensive projects, including international ones involving professional creators from different countries. regional and local cultures are gradually dying, with many of their expressions, disciplines and creative skills disappearing. today, we can speak of traditional and folk culture in regions that are historically backward and only to a small extent in others that are developing. there is therefore an urgent need to develop a programme of scientific research, documentation, protection and development of regional culture in all its spiritual and artistic manifestations. these are the features of my amendment to the resolution under discussion. i hope it will have the support of the members of parliament.
madam president! you have to eat, move, and hide from the cold and rain. these are the elements of production and trade that serve to satisfy basic needs. but the kind of fork he eats, the shape of his bike, the roof of his house, it's not an economy anymore, it's an expression of culture. man has a spiritual need to create, simply for the sake of creating. and glory to god when others can see it with their eyes or touch it and feel better. what is important is the cultural diversity that is often associated with the regions. we must not unify these regions and cultures, but rather encourage their diversity. culture is the expression of the soul of a region. the union would be very uninteresting without the cultural wealth it now has. it's costly to maintain a culture, and it's our job to support it. without it, there will be no economy and no happy people in the european union.
madam president! europe's cultural wealth is the result of the great diversity of its regions. it is this diversity that needs to be protected. cognac lace is very different from brabante lace. the mixture created by the superficial extraction and reproduction of the culture leads to impoverishment. we must preserve this diversity in all its forms and manifestations, including multilingualism and material culture, because it is the basis of our identity, the source of creative development, the source of enriching borrowing. it also gives cultural tourism a sense of place. regional culture needs to be supported and protected. i'm asking the european commission for a program like this.
madam president! the motto of the european union is unity in diversity. and this diversity is what makes the european union so attractive, and it's also what makes us so different from the united states, for example. cultural diversity is also, in fact, based on the enormous diversity of our regional cultures, the diversity that makes these regions and entire countries so incredibly attractive to tourists. they are a tourist attraction for us europeans, and they are also a tremendous tourist attraction for others who in this europe can see, can experience and appreciate such unprecedented diversity. so, for this reason, for example, regional culture needs to be promoted. but it is also important to remember that regional culture is a bridge that also allows the presence of people in regions that are inhabited by so-called high culture. without this, it would be difficult to speak of the standardization and dissemination of certain patterns and cultural perceptions.
madam president! the unity of europe, while preserving its diversity, identity and cultural heritage, is a great value for our community. individual peoples, regions and different local communities cultivate and develop their own culture and traditions, bring this heritage to a united europe, share it with other regions and in turn learn about their achievements and achievements in this field. so they share something with others, and they take something from others. it is also important that the union budget should be used to support cultural heritage in the regions and, even more importantly, in the small countries. those who feared that after integration they would lose their culture, their identity, find that the opposite is true - that the union promotes regional, folk and local culture.
the rapporteur. - mr president! - what are you doing? the report identifies the european union's relations with russia as being of key importance to the economic and political interests of the union. it underlines the role that russia can and should play in the international arena, and in particular in our common neighbourhood, contributing to the economic and political stability of the region. on the other hand, however, the report draws attention to russia's disproportionately strong reaction to georgia's military intervention in south ossetia and to the unprovoked and large-scale russian military action in abkhazia, and stresses the need for meaningful security dialogue a dialogue that must be based on respect for international law and the territorial integrity of states. notes that the events in the caucasus and the recognition of the independence of both enclaves ossetia and abkhazia call into question russia's willingness and ability to build a common security area in europe with the european union; the report calls for the conclusion of talks on russia's full implementation of the agreements ending the conflict in georgia, including the status of abkhazia and south ossetia, before any negotiated agreement is adopted, and for russia to make firm commitments not to use force against its neighbours. the report draws attention to the fact that recent events related to russia's violation of georgia's territorial integrity and the gas supply crisis threaten eu-russia relations. the report provides an opinion on the need to replace the current agreement with a new comprehensive agreement, which will cover all aspects of our cooperation and will be legally binding. it should also contain clear dispute resolution procedures. the report also raises the issue of energy security and the inclusion in the negotiated agreement of the basic provisions of the energy treaty, as well as the transit protocol, irrespective of whether the treaty is legally binding today also binding on russia, but which russia may terminate. the report draws attention to the great potential of possible mutual economic links based on full equality between the two sides, which can create a situation of beneficial interdependence. the report stresses the importance of the member states, especially in their relations with russia, and of the european union as a whole, speaking with one voice and consulting each other in accordance with the provisions of the eu treaties, with sufficient time in advance, on any bilateral initiatives with russia, especially those which may have implications for other countries of the european union or for the european union as a whole. the report focuses on human rights and freedoms in russia. recalls that russia, as a member of the council of europe, is obliged to respect the principles on which the council is founded and notes that compliance with these principles will be essential for the success of the negotiations on cooperation between the european union and russia; it also regrets that russia is resisting the introduction of effective measures to prevent the human rights abuses of the authorities so frequently condemned by the european court of justice from taking place. among the recommendations in the report, it is worth noting the european union's continued support for russia's membership of the world trade organisation, recognising the importance of russia implementing the obligations of membership by the time it is formally granted, in particular by not withdrawing from practices that have already been introduced. in this context, it is worth mentioning the strong emphasis on the effective protection of intellectual, commercial and industrial property. in addition to numerous recommendations on human rights, media freedom, judicial independence and the shrinking space for ngos in russia, the report raises the issue of visa facilitation and makes numerous references to economic issues such as shipping problems in the baltic and along the northern coast of russia, the issue of flights over siberia and reciprocity in relation to the possibility of free investment.
on behalf of the uen group. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. by using energy supplies as a tool of political pressure and applying the principle of 'divide and rule', the kremlin is corrupting europe from country to country, from cyprus to the netherlands. and he does it with amazing efficiency. the european union has shown astonishing passivity in its attack on sovereign georgia. the union leaders suddenly became invisible. where was javier solana or commissioner ferrero-waldner at the time? meanwhile, nicolas sarkozy, the president of france, has been humiliated by the russians' complete disregard for the peace agreement he negotiated. europe's weakness in its relations with russia is therefore due to its own naivety and shortsightedness. energy companies from austria, germany and italy are doing bilateral business with the kremlin. this directly translates into political pressure being exerted by moscow on individual member states. germany is building a gas pipeline under the baltic sea to bypass poland, and russia has already cut off energy supplies to lithuania, the czech republic and other european union countries. if nord stream is built, the same thing could happen to my country, poland. the union's policy towards russia must be based on unity and solidarity. therefore, consultation with other member states on bilateral agreements with russia that might affect them is absolutely essential if we are to be effective in our relations with russia.
madam president! the report gives a fairly detailed account of the human rights violations that have recently occurred in the russian federation. their example clearly shows that russia disregards all the standards that apply throughout the free world. i therefore call on the council and the european commission to start enforcing the human rights treaties in which russia has committed itself and to make the further negotiations on the agreement dependent on this. very often, in joint meetings with the russian side, i hear duma deputies say: 'let's leave these human rights behind and get to the specifics, namely trade'. we can't accept that approach. there is nothing more important than freedom, health and life. these are the values that are often forgotten in russia, but the values of money are always remembered.
madam president! it is common knowledge that any agreements with russia have a more desirable meaning than as legally binding documents over a longer period of time. however, further efforts are needed to improve relations with that country. of course, this cannot happen on the current basis, when the european union's almost 500 million people, who produce more than 20% of the world's gross domestic product, are the party vying for the favour of a much weaker and smaller partner. i say this because it is not uncommon for the interests of some members of the european union to trump european solidarity, and russia is ruthlessly exploiting this. of course we should deepen economic cooperation with russia, but we must demand from our partner the same standards as from all the member states of the european union and there can be no question of accepting human rights violations.
madam president, russia is our greatest neighbour, a great country which has lived through imperial mirages in the last century, but has also lived through terrible experiences. it takes time and persistence to recover from this trauma, and it also takes patience on our part. the negotiations on a new agreement will therefore be difficult and arduous. the report is demanding, but fair. the greatest challenge in european policy is to ensure that there is a coherence between an effective partnership with our six eastern neighbours and good mutual cooperation with russia. progress will depend on a true convergence of our ways of life, and an understanding of the fundamental values, which should not be betrayed.
madam president! the use of gas supplies for political blackmail, the threat to georgia's independence, the genocide in chechnya, the lack of a fair trial in the murder of anna politkovskaya and litvinenko are the main obstacles to contacts with russia. unfortunately, russia has not taken a single step towards democratization and respect for human rights. this does not bode well for negotiations and further cooperation. if we are to be effective in negotiations, we must pursue a common, uniform and united policy. this is important for such a significant neighbour of the european union.
president-in-office of the council. − madam president, i would like to thank you all for this interesting debate. i think it is very necessary regarding our future relations with russia, and a number of important points have been covered in the debate. i can support much of what has been said here. for those who speak of the need for engagement, i think it is clear that a new agreement is of great importance for the further development and intensification of cooperation between the eu and russia. it is also clear that the new agreement must continue to improve on the current partnership and cooperation agreement (pca). it has to reflect the realities of today’s cooperation with russia. our relations now are a lot deeper and more wide-ranging than they were only a decade ago. for those who speak of energy, we must clearly state that the eu wishes to strengthen cooperation with russia through the instruments we have – the meetings of the energy dialogue and the permanent partnership council on energy. there will be a meeting of the permanent partnership council on energy during this presidency. the objective is to promote trust and transparency in eu-russia energy relations. we cannot afford another disruption of the energy supply. we should also strengthen the early warning mechanism and make it more operative. to those who speak of human rights, i think that the application of the rule of law, an independent judiciary and full respect for human rights – including free and independent media – are necessary to promote stability and prosperity in russia. the eu follows the human rights situation in russia with concern and we raise – and will continue to raise – those concerns at our eu-russia meetings. for example, the conduct of cases such as the resumption of the khodorkovsky trial will be a kind of litmus paper for us regarding the rule of law in russia. for those who speak of leverage, i agree very much that we have to speak with one voice when talking with russia, and we need this kind of debate to shape the form of this one voice. unity and solidarity are essential, and we will work very hard to achieve this. it is important that the member states inform and consult each other as much as possible about bilateral issues with russia which could have repercussions on other member states and the eu as a whole. parliament’s suggestions in this regard are worth considering, although, given the existing council structures, i am not entirely sure that the creation of a formal consultation mechanism is the most practical way forward. i strongly feel, however, that some kind of mechanism or common approach is needed to complement the existing framework of eu-russia relations. there is definitely some room for improvement in our policy towards russia, and unity and solidarity are indeed the key words in this context. we already have quite intensive political consultation in the council when it comes to showing solidarity, but this is also a question of political will. i agree that we need greater trust and understanding between the eu and russia. we need to overcome the suspicions of the past and build on the real and substantial relationship which has evolved over the years, but this is certainly a two-way process and we need two to tango. the new agreement is one way to do this. the other is through a better dialogue. parliament has an important role to play here and i can, therefore, agree with the suggestion that the role of the parliamentary cooperation committee should be strengthened under the new agreement. the parliamentary dimension – like civil society contacts – has much to offer in terms of communicating and promoting the fundamental democratic principles and values on which the eu is founded. we therefore look forward to remaining in a dialogue with you as the negotiations progress.
member of the commission. − madam president, debates on russia are never easy. russia, on the one hand, is an important global partner, but, on the other hand, it is also a big neighbour, and there i for us, but it is also true for russia and for many other global partners. therefore i think we have to see this very clearly, but at the same time we also have to see russia as a great neighbour, where sometimes we do not see eye to eye in the common neighbourhood. and we have a common neighbourhood – some of you have mentioned that, be it moldova or nagorno-karabakh or, of course, georgia. want to come much more into line with the european union on certain key issues like standards of governments, freer trade and others. in these activities, i think it is important that we have these countries as partners. but at the same time we have also said, on the multilateral platform, that we are, in principle, open to third countries like russia on an ad hoc basis, as appropriate; certainly russia is also a full member in the black sea synergy, where regional matters are handled. so there is also a chance to work together in order to overcome some difficulties that exist. on
