increase efficiency and diversify supplies. the new agreement with russia should therefore lay down, as we always say, legally binding reciprocal commitments. and, in parallel to the new agreement and for the short term, we are working with russia to make the early warning mechanism more efficient, as i said before. we should also foresee monitoring and conflict prevention and resolution, and this should also involve belarus and ukraine. we know that russia is a very important energy partner for us, contributing 40% of the gas we import and 20% of the gas we consume. this is, as i said before, a relationship of interdependence. since we represent over two thirds of their export revenue – which has made a very significant contribution to russia’s economic development – it is essential that there should be no repeat of the events of last january, and therefore we are working with both the ukrainians and the russians to prevent that. on human rights we do not always see eye to eye. on the one hand, the eu and russia share common international commitments, as i said, through the instruments that we have signed together at the un, at the oecd and at the council of europe. these commitments reflect values and include the obligation to respect the decisions of the bodies they set up. that is particularly true for the european court of human rights, but it is also evident that the eu and russia interpret commitments differently. the european union and russia have chosen the path of dialogue on these issues, and this is the right way. this means that we must also listen to the concerns the russian side expresses sometimes with regard to some developments inside the european union including, for instance, the issue of russian-speaking minorities. but it is also true, as the president-in-office of the council said, that there are clear concerns about the failure to respect human rights in the russian federation, and continuing cases of attacks on human rights defenders, journalists and others reflect badly on russia. we raise these issues regularly with the high authorities: myself with sergey lavrov, and president barroso with his interlocutors. we also use our twice-yearly human rights consultations to do so as well. the discussions in the bilateral meeting between president barroso and president medvedev on 6 february also included an exchange on ponomarev last night is the latest reminder of how difficult the situation for human rights defenders is in russia. but let me say that the two strands have clearly been reflected in the mandate that the council has given the commission to negotiate. both are there, and this is the content of our mandate. therefore, i think the right way is to follow up on this mandate and, as i said, we are always ready to report on the follow up of our negotiations, as we have just been doing.

in writing. russia is an important partner of the european union. the union expects its partners to cooperate in a fair and honest manner. interdependence can be mutually beneficial, but it doesn't have to be. on the contrary, it can be a source of anxiety and conflict. we should do everything possible to make economic cooperation, security, energy security, respect for human rights and democracy a constructive and positive element in our relations. whether that happens depends largely on the russian side. russia can take the side of western values and standards. no one is forcing russia to choose one way or the other. that is a choice russia must make. one thing seems certain: i have no doubt that europe will not change its values at the behest of russia or any other country. we are so consistent, or even stubborn, not because it would mean giving up our values. europe, if it were to abandon its basic principles, would cease to be europe. that is why, for example, we will always respect the territorial integrity of georgia. we don't do this because we like georgians in any particular way. the reason for this attitude is loyalty to the principles that constitute our world. destroying this world would be suicide. this is not the scenario that the union wants, nor, i believe, that russia wants.
in writing. the conclusion of a new eu-russia agreement is one of the most important challenges facing eu diplomacy. the european parliament has an active role to play in shaping the shape and content of this agreement. the report provides a comprehensive analysis of the most relevant aspects of the eu's relations with russia, with a particular focus on the current relationship. i believe that the adoption of the report will be a significant step in shaping the new partnership agreement between the european union and russia. the main points of the agreement should be the subject of not only thorough consultation but also tough negotiations between the parties to the future agreement. the report presents a variety of problems, the solution of which is of particular importance for each country. i would like to remind you of the difficulties in trade between poland and the russian federation. only a unified eu position can solve these problems. the report provides an exhaustive list of issues that need to be addressed, but it is not likely that all of them will be resolved in the short term, for example because of cultural and social differences.

in writing. discrimination is a serious problem in europe and beyond. in a special eurobarometer survey in 2008, 15% of europeans said they had experienced discrimination in the past year. the proposed directive, which the european parliament has been waiting for for over four years, is an attempt to put into practice the principle of equal treatment of persons irrespective of religion, belief, disability, age or sexual orientation, not only in terms of access to employment but also to goods, facilities or services such as banking, housing, education, transport and healthcare. the document also defines minimum framework standards to ensure protection against discrimination. member states can always increase the level of protection, but they cannot invoke the new directive to reduce existing standards. the directive gives injured persons the right to compensation and states unequivocally that member states not only have a duty to express their will but also an obligation to combat discrimination. a significant number of eu countries have already introduced legislation to a greater or lesser extent to protect people outside the labour market from discrimination on grounds of religion, belief, disability, age or sexual orientation. this draft directive will allow for the introduction of coherent european legislation in this area and will make it clear that europe as a whole does not allow for discrimination. freedom from discrimination is a fundamental right and should apply to everyone in the european union!

in writing. in the debate on the european funds, i would like to draw attention to four proposals from the european commission to speed up the use of structural funds funds by beneficiaries. 1.increased support from the european investment bank (eib) and the european investment fund (eif) for projects co-financed by the structural funds 2.simplification of procedures relating to the eligibility of expenditure, retroactively from 1 august 2006 (e.g. inclusion of non-monetary contributions of the beneficiary in eligible expenditure) 3.increase payments due from the structural funds by 2%, allowing for an additional advance payment of eur 6.25 billion in 2009. 4. accelerating expenditure on large projects, inter alia by enabling beneficiaries to submit payment applications before the project is approved by the european commission. all the above-mentioned changes to increase the liquidity of beneficiaries as well as simplifying the rules deserve strong support and should be implemented as soon as possible.

madam president! according to the eu debate 2009 portal, only 52% of europeans trust the european parliament as an institution in 2008. that's a three percent drop from last year's results. one in two voters is not sure whether he will take part in this year's european parliament elections. only 30% of those surveyed said they would take part. and 68% of voters will not go to the polls because they believe their vote doesn't matter. so i would like to ask: is the european parliament planning some spectacular last minute initiative to get people to vote? will we be able to expand the information channels for europe in any way? in my country, there is not the slightest european debate. the prime minister is doing absolutely nothing about it. so, then, is the rest of us to stand by and watch?
madam president! at the last meeting of the committee on agriculture, commissioner fischer boel said that one of the major successes of the common agricultural policy was the reform of the sugar sector. i would like to state that, following this reform, poland now has to import about 20% of its sugar from the sugar-exporting country. and sugar prices have gone up 60 percent in just two years. it is important to consider whether the commissioner and her colleagues were wrong or whether this was a planned strategy to make some countries more profitable. i would like to emphasize unequivocally that the entire agricultural policy is, in the opinion of polish voters, a policy that is extremely asymmetrical and directed at the countries of the old union.

mr. chairman, please! we're discussing the working hours and rest periods of motor transport drivers in a time of economic crisis. thousands of cars are parked, unable to find employment. and so, like drivers, many, many companies are increasingly on the verge of economic disaster. the authors of this question - mr jarzembowski, mrs wortmann-kool, etc. - rightly raise the issue of: 1. the complexity of the system, 2. its reliability or unreliability, 3. the practice of applying the restrictions we have been using so far. there is no scientific evidence that more flexible use, which would even allow for an extension of the working week in a given situation, would have a negative impact on traffic safety, especially when traffic is decreasing. it is not difficult to foresee that the rigorous application of these restrictions, accompanied by the introduction of new charges for road transport - let me mention the euro-vinna and the internalisation of external costs - could jeopardise the future of this sector. the subject is certainly worth debating and i would very much like to hear the commission's position on this.
rapporteur. − mr president, it is my pleasure to present the report on the problems and perspectives concerning european citizenship, which was adopted unanimously by the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs (libe) last month. european citizenship does not replace national citizenship. it is an added bonus, giving eu citizens unique rights, notably the right to the freedom of movement, the right to consular protection and the right to petition parliament and the european ombudsman. parliament’s report takes into consideration the commission’s fifth report on european citizenship, covering the period from 1 may 2004 to 30 june 2007. this is a unique period. five years ago, on 1 may 2004, 10 new member states joined the european union. the result of that accession, especially of states from central and eastern europe, was a hitherto unseen scale of inter-union migration. the new citizens of the union embraced the rights granted to them, especially the right to free movement. they benefited from the opportunity to be educated abroad and, in those countries which opened their labour markets, they undertook legal work. the scale of migration, however, poses many challenges for the host countries. these are challenges for both the central and local authorities. local authorities, particularly, where they are responsible for the provision of services such as housing, health care and primary and secondary education, are often confronted with the day-to-day problems of the new immigrants. much has been done to aid integration, as well as to help newcomers benefit from the same rights as citizens of their host countries. nevertheless, instances of discrimination remain. sometimes these are the result of legal loopholes and sometimes the result of a lack of knowledge of how to apply the law. the libe committee took a very constructive and practical approach in its work. there was cross-party agreement that our priority was to highlight the problem areas and undertake steps to remedy them by providing central and local government in member states with the necessary resources and support. our primary concern was that the individual citizen should not be hindered in any way from benefiting from his or her rights. the second right i mentioned, that of consular protection, is still, unfortunately, poorly applied. this fact was brought starkly to our attention when our own colleagues found themselves in a dramatic situation during the terrorist attacks in mumbai. if meps had problems exercising their right to consular protection in such an extreme situation, what chance does the average citizen have in more mundane circumstances? increasing citizens’ awareness of their rights was a key issue raised throughout the report and a number of measures are suggested for greater awareness building. if only 31% of citizens consider themselves to be well-informed about their rights, we still have a lot to do. i trust the commission will take into account parliament’s recommendations and will report back in its sixth report on the concrete progress made. finally, i would like to thank my shadow rapporteurs, the staff of the political groups and the libe committee secretariat for their hard work. a special word of thanks goes to all those who participated in the public hearing on the report, especially the representatives of the ngos. it is fitting that, in a report on citizenship, the citizen’s voice, via the ngos, was heeded in drawing up the final report.
madam president! the current task of eu legislation is to simplify it and make the law transparent and understandable to every citizen. ecolabelling is information for consumers about environmental issues, including information about the product, which facilitates the decision to buy it. the introduction of this system will contribute to improving the environment and combating climate change, and will also contribute to reducing water consumption. the information on organic products quantitative and other should be clear and legible. consuming more organic, natural, regional food will help improve the health of our society.

mr. chairman, please! i could not support mrs vălean's report. it allows a situation of conflict of laws, in breach of the principle of subsidiarity, by promoting the reunion of families from third countries with a different culture, including those which allow polygamy. he's creating legal confusion. as you know, the definitions of 'family' and 'family member' differ in our countries. there are also different rights, such as inheritance rights, family rights and social assistance rights. the creation of rights to social benefits without consent and without taking into account the economic situation of the host country can lead to serious social conflicts. i object to the continuing violation of the principle of subsidiarity in this house.
mr. chairman, please! given the difficulties related to visa procedures, it is necessary to simplify them, inter alia, by reducing the costs incurred by applicants. this will help to improve the union's cultural exchange and cooperation with third countries. i think it is important to simplify the visa procedures for people who have family in the member states. i will take the example of poland, whose history has been interwoven for hundreds of years with the history of countries such as ukraine and belarus, where a significant polish minority lives, who do not have polish citizenship, but who often cross the borders of the union to visit their relatives. it is therefore necessary to simplify visa procedures to the maximum extent possible for people who have gained the trust of the issuing authority by not breaking any visa laws. i consider it important that the introduction of biometric identifiers will facilitate the exchange of data and help the future integration of the visa system, thereby facilitating the visa process as well as improving security across the union. this report is important for the development of the union's relations with third countries.

in writing. - i vote in favour of the report on the proposal for a council decision on the conclusion of the agreement between the european community and the swiss confederation amending annex 11 to the agreement between the european community and the swiss confederation on trade in agricultural products. i agree with the rapporteur's observations on the further integration of the two markets. indeed, the agreement would help to increase the productivity of the agricultural sector of both parties and to keep food prices fair and relatively stable from the point of view of the citizens. however, i agree with the belief that both sides should carefully negotiate full trade liberalization. the value of bilateral trade is significant and the removal of barriers would have a very significant impact, in particular on the agricultural economy of the eu countries neighbouring switzerland and on swiss farmers.

in writing. − in the light of article 18 of the treaty establishing the european community, every citizen has the right to move and reside freely within the territory of the member states. directive 2004/38/ec lays down in detail the legal possibilities for the movement within the union of union citizens, their immediate family members or a partner as defined by a legal act. however, freedom of movement should be considered together with the provisions relating to the free movement of workers and the freedom to provide services. as we know, four of the eu countries have still not opened their labour markets to workers from the countries that joined in 2004. as many as 11 european union countries continue to apply restrictions on their labour markets for citizens of romania and bulgaria. i think that this phenomenon is not only a negative influence on the integration process. we should aim to remove the existing barriers as soon as possible. in accordance with article 20 of the treaty, any citizen shall, in the territory of a third country where the member state of which he is a national has no representative, enjoy the diplomatic and consular protection of any other member state on the same conditions as nationals of that state. the announced measures to strengthen consular protection in third countries should be implemented as soon as possible and the negotiations with third countries on visa-free travel should be continued.
in writing. - i supported mr angelakas' report because it emphasises the use of specific amounts of money to co-finance regional and local renewable energy programmes in housing. it is also very good that it is the member states who will set the criteria and decide which residential buildings are eligible for funding under national rules. this is a sign that this money will be directed to the facilities that need it most in each of the member states.
in writing. − the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs has prepared a proposal on the basis of the hague programme. it aims to simplify visa policy by establishing a community code on visas. it aims to facilitate the process of applying for, extending, revoking, withdrawing and limiting the period of validity of visas. the code will unify and specify the precise rules for issuing visas, their type and period of validity. in addition, the documents needed to obtain the appropriate type of visa will be specified. the european union's unified visa law will remove the legal provisions that have made the visa process more difficult. the community visa code will facilitate the movement not only of union citizens but above all of non-eu citizens. this will facilitate both civil and professional communication between the community and non-community countries. in the light of this change, particular attention should be paid to the continuous training of customs officers, in particular those working at the european union's borders. the eu's visa policy should reflect the main priorities of its foreign policy. i think that the creation of a community visa code is a good idea to harmonize the legislation of the member states.
in writing. - discrimination is a problem that is of the utmost relevance in the era of european unification and that we cannot ignore. although we have already raised this issue on several occasions, its effects are still unsatisfactory. the diversity of discrimination is a significant problem. discrimination on grounds of ethnic or racial origin is prohibited both in and outside the labour market. discrimination on grounds of religion, belief, disability, age or sexual orientation is now prohibited only in the workplace. i believe that attention should be paid to combating discrimination not only within working life but also outside it. discrimination should be defined in the same way regardless of gender. prevention of inequality is the most important issue, but we cannot forget about the people who are discriminated against. we must ensure that the law is enforced and that those who discriminate are punished consistently. discrimination is a very serious issue both in the context of private life and the process of european integration. i fully agree with the rapporteur, ms kathalijne maria buitenweg, and thank her for her very good and comprehensive report.

the rapporteur. - mr president, commissioner kallas, i have to tell you something. we are talking about the european development fund, which covers the countries of africa, the caribbean and the pacific. from our point of view, these countries are a nonstandard region, nonstandard countries, nonstandard problems. in 2007, we have increased payments and increased commitments in terms of the implementation of the fund, which also means an increase in efficiency, and this is certainly a positive point. and that's where i'd like to start. the fund consisted of two parts: one part managed by the european commission and the other part managed by the european investment bank. the part that was managed by the european commission is the part that is the subject of the discharge debate, while the part that is managed by the european investment bank is still beyond our scope. i'll be back to that. the basis of our debate is the court of auditors' position. the court of auditors clearly stated that the turnover, liabilities and revenue for 2007 as a whole were legal and regular, but that there was a high fiduciary risk associated with budget support, including because of the commission's so-called 'dynamic interpretation' of the eligibility criterion. however, the audit revealed a significant level of error and indicated, we agree that rapid improvement in supervision and control is necessary. the possibilities are there, and we share that view. the sample selected for the verification was composed of 6 countries, representing 250 transactions. one very important point is that the commission is still not in a position to provide complete accounting information. we welcomed the declaration that the new system would be operational from february 2009. i hope commissioner kallas will confirm that fact. another very important thing is to distinguish in contracts between words and actions. the drafting and signing of the document is very confusing. the commission has to explain this, especially since the countries of the region also have different approaches. it is very important for us as parliament not only to assess the correctness of the report after the fact but also to give it a control and audit nature so that we can prevent any possible deviations. avoiding deviations also helps to assess the benefits we derive from the allocation of funds. it is not just a question of accounting for the correctness of the accounts, but also of the degree to which the objective has been achieved, and from this point of view we point out the need to cooperate with the national parliaments, which should have a good understanding of this issue. it's about working with the authorities, the governments, and also with civil society. the aspect which seems particularly important is the question of the control of the funds managed by the european investment bank. the european investment bank remains, in our view, an institution that cannot be controlled. we very clearly state in the report that the european investment bank had €2.2 billion at its disposal. these were public funds, not funds from the financial markets. the european investment bank therefore appears to be the least democratic institution with public funds. in closing, i would like to thank commissioner kallass for his cooperation during this term. i would like to thank the court of auditors, in the name of mr jacques luczkiewicz, member of the court of auditors. i thank my colleagues on the committee on development and the committee on budgetary control, which mr bosch has led with efficiency and substance.
the next speaker is mr christofer fjellner. i would like to inform you that the rapporteur, mr søren bo søndergaard, will be arriving later because of a delayed flight, and i will therefore give him the floor later.
vice-president of the commission. − mr president, this is the fifth time i have stood before you as you prepare to vote on a commission discharge resolution. and, for the fifth time, i must admit that – despite unquestionable progress in budget execution – we still do not have a positive das. in the draft resolution before you (paragraph 58), the rapporteur…"demande, sans délai, à la commission de livrer ses propositions pour atteindre l'objectif d'une das positive". so i will do this, ‘sans délai’. i will give the three main reasons why, in my view, we did not achieve a positive das, although this was the objective set at the beginning of the current commission mandate. we probably relied too much at the beginning on member states sharing our concern about the negative public and political impact of the negative das when, in fact, our call for action only really became effective when backed up by the policy of ‘warn, solve or suspend payments’. so there was too much carrot and too little stick initially. we have also pursued evolution rather than revolution. we put aside more radical solutions, for instance on simplification, in our pioneering attempt to fix the das. obviously, five years for our action plan was not enough. some results of our action plan are only now starting to show their impact. the next commission will reap the benefits, which without the action plan could not be expected. but your question is, ‘how and when can you guarantee a positive das?’ first, i should remind honourable members what the so-called ‘negative das’ is. article 248 of the treaty gives the court of auditors the task of providing a statement of assurance ‘as to the reliability of the accounts and the legality and regularity of the underlying transactions’. it was inserted into the maastricht treaty at the last moment without any real discussion about the implications. this has proven highly problematic since. the so-called negative das is part of the court of auditors’ opinion. it says that certain areas of expenditure are still materially affected by errors, although to different levels. the court also states that our annual accounts are reliable and gives many positive and adequate comments about our financial management. as such, the das does not sound at all special, compared to how audit opinions are generally phrased. but we face a highly politicised and often deliberate misinterpretation of this sentence. so i must confess that it has surprised me how difficult it is to convince elected politicians and public opinion that budget management in the european union is much better than what is reflected in this sentence. so we must do something to end this damaging political assessment of the use of european funds. for urgent, more guaranteed results, one could imagine three options: option one: change the treaty. the way the current treaty is phrased, the reasonable public expectation for sound financial management has been undermined – automatically and almost inevitably – every year since the maastricht treaty entered into force. during the intergovernmental conference on the lisbon treaty, i looked at whether one could fix article 248 of the treaty. together with the court, we looked at what could be a more realistic task for the court, perhaps covering the budget over a three-year cycle, rather than annually, and asking the court to take into account that most commission control systems are multi-annual, ensuring that errors are corrected over time. we contacted several national delegations: they all agreed; nobody acted. option two: i now come to the second option and the most radical short cut to the positive das. under the current treaty we should perhaps stop allocating funds to management schemes so complex that we cannot meet the current low thresholds for error. if we cannot collectively handle the current sophistication, then we must simplify. ‘simplify’ is a nice word which everybody likes. there are millions of transactions to check. how could 480 auditors, based in luxembourg, however competent, working with a very complex legislative environment, in 27 member states with 23 official languages, possibly have the basis for issuing a statement each year on the legality and regularity of all underlying transactions in all spending areas? if you wish simplification to have a quick and effective impact on the error rate, my view is that it means abandoning shared management in some areas. it means reducing the number of transactions from millions to a few thousand. taking the example of the structural funds, it would mean clearly defining the responsibilities that are currently shared. to achieve that, the structural funds could be turned into budget support to the poorer regions. an eligible region or member state would see eu funds channelled into the state budget, to be spent via national systems, under the exclusive accountability of the minister of finance, and audited by the supreme audit institutions of member states. a member state would get one annual tranche from the eu budget, and would be accountable to its own citizens and other member states based on results. eligibility rules, procurement procedures and absorption rates would no longer be a european problem. in this radical scenario, we would drop the millions of projects too small and sophisticated to be under arms-length oversight from brussels. no more small, creative projects ending up being ridiculed in the euro-sceptic press! option three: if you cannot change the treaty or its interpretation, we could perhaps discuss what it means for a given type of transaction to be ‘ok’. we could set realistic and cost-effective thresholds for what ‘legal and regular’ is. this is the discussion about tolerable risk. for the moment, the court applies a uniform 2% materiality threshold across the board. the court itself has asked for better risk analysis and political agreement on the tolerable risk in various budget areas. to move this discussion forward, you now have a communication from the commission on the table. your rapporteur is suggesting welcoming this communication as a ‘solid methodological basis’ and calls for further analysis, data collection, dialogue and concrete proposals. i would be grateful for this support and suggest we move ahead as quickly as possible. the council also now seems ready to engage. based on your overall political support, the commission would like to proceed with proposals to set specific tolerable risk levels, budget heading by budget heading. for each future spending proposal, you would be asked to ‘tolerate’ a carefully calculated level of risk, so that the court – hopefully – would adjust its materiality threshold on that basis. we must start now. if we wait for a revised financial regulation, or indeed the next financial perspectives after 2013, this would not be reflected in the discharge procedure for the next five years. ladies and gentlemen, today you are preparing to vote on whether to grant discharge for 2007, a year for which the auditors now say that for all budget areas except that the structural funds, as much as 95% or more of the payments are free from serious financial error. this is the best das ever, an improvement over last year, for a year with higher payment levels, in an increased number of member states, the eu-27. our financial management is steadily improving and it is certainly good enough to deserve discharge. but it cannot stand the test of perfection. the eu was created to bring peace and prosperity. it has delivered so far. obviously, looking at the eu’s institutional set-up, it is possible that no auditor was present at its creation and so it is not perfect. but audit perfection is a rare phenomenon anywhere in the world. thank you for your attention and please vote in favour of discharge. you will see no complacency from the commission.

the rapporteur. − in july 2006, the commission presented a strategy to reduce the overall risk and negative impact of pesticides on human health and the environment. the last element of this strategy is the proposed pesticide application machinery directive amending the machinery directive 2006/42/ec. the directive lays down requirements that must be met by machinery and application equipment in order to limit the adverse effects of pesticides on the environment, the operator and the surrounding area. the establishment of these requirements will reduce the differences between the rules and procedures adopted for the application of pesticides in certain community countries, ensure a uniform level of environmental protection in the community, and allow the free movement of these machines on the union market, which is of particular importance for small and medium-sized enterprises, which are the most frequent producers of these machines. the draft directive and amendments were discussed at workshops, meetings with representatives of the council, the commission, the shadow rapporteurs, stakeholders and during tripartite talks. due to the considerable technical differences between the various types of machinery ranging from straight, hand-operated to self-propelled, operated by qualified operators , parts of the amendments were omitted and it was decided that they would be included in the standards in question, which were commissioned by the commission to the european committee for standardisation. this has led to a consensus, amendment no 39 has been adopted and the council has confirmed this position. i am particularly grateful for the assistance and cooperation of the shadow rapporteurs, the commission and council representatives, the imco commission administration and the institutions concerned. i am calling for a directive to help protect the environment, operators and the surrounding area when pesticides are applied.
in writing. − member states cooperate in the field of public protection within the framework of national legislation and on the basis of international agreements. the council decision (2002/956/jha) provides for the protection of public persons in accordance with the national provisions of the member state concerned or on the basis of the rules of an organisation or institution of an international or transnational character. protection of public persons is a responsibility of the host member state in view of the threats to public figures in recent years, i fully support the decision taken to amend the existing council decision establishing a european public protection network. its main objective is to extend the scope of article 2 to include the definition of 'public person' as any person, whether in public office or not, who is considered to be at risk because of his or her voice or influence in public debate. i believe that this decision will increase the safety of the public and will have a positive impact on the development of democracy.
in writing. − the european parliament's pesticide application machinery directive amending directive 2006/42/ec of 17 may 2006 on machinery makes a very important improvement to the legal provisions. it is designed to harmonise environmental and human health standards in the european union. at the same time, the harmonisation of rules will allow for a smooth flow of machinery and thus increase competitiveness on the european market. the directive will require member states to carry out regular inspections of professional pesticide application equipment and to establish a system of regular maintenance and periodic inspection of the equipment. as a result, the directive will reduce the use of pesticides (thus reducing their negative impact on the environment) and will have a positive impact on the health of consumers and citizens who come into direct contact with pesticides at work.

member of the commission. − firstly, i would like to mention that it is important to clarify that the efta states that are parties to the eea agreement – that is, norway, iceland and liechtenstein – are subject to strict state aid discipline based on the eu model. article 61 of the eea agreement is closely modelled on article 87 of the ec treaty. the efta surveillance authority (esa) is in charge of its implementation. under protocol 26 of the eea agreement, it is entrusted with equivalent powers to those of the european commission in the field of state aid. those states must notify any new state aid measure to the esa and get its approval before putting it into effect. the esa may also investigate alleged incompatible aid granted by these efta countries. switzerland is a different case, because it has not ratified the eea agreement. with switzerland, the state aid rules are those laid down in the 1972 agreement between the european economic community and the swiss confederation. under article 23 thereof, state aid which affects trade between the community and switzerland and distorts or threatens to distort competition is incompatible with the agreement. procedurally, in case of incompatible aid, the affected party can refer the matter to the joint committee established by the agreement and it can take safeguard measures if the granting party fails to put an end to the practice in question. while remedies for incompatible aid are harder to obtain in swiss cases, the commission still endeavours to apply the provisions of the 1972 free trade agreement whenever possible and necessary. for example, on 13 february 2007, it took a decision concluding that three swiss cantonal tax regimes were incompatible with the 1972 agreement, and it is currently negotiating with the swiss authorities in order to find a satisfactory solution to this issue. the commission is aware that provisions on state aid found in existing trade agreements, such as the 1972 agreement with switzerland, need to be improved and that is why, in line with the conclusions of its 2006 communication ‘global europe: competing in the world’, the objective of the commission is to try and negotiate stronger rules on state aid and better remedies, such as the application of a dispute settlement mechanism, in future free trade agreements.

vice-president of the commission. - madam president, i represent president barroso today in this discussion on our 2007 annual report on monitoring the application of community law. the president asked me to convey his disappointment that he was unable to participate in this debate. the commission welcomes the support given by parliament to the approach it adopted in its 2007 communication 'towards a europe of results application of community law'. the commission attaches great importance to the correct application of community law. this is one of the priorities of the barroso commission. this is why the commission has made a particular effort to improve its working methods, for the benefit of citizens and businesses, as explained in the 2007 communication. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos at work is based on the principle of equal treatment for men and women. first, there was the introduction in january last year of more frequent decision-making in infringement proceedings in order to facilitate the advancement of cases; secondly, the introduction of the european union pilot project in april last year with 15 member states is testing a new method to improve problem solving and the availability of information. thirdly, the main objective of this initiative, which is close to parliament's interests, is to better serve the interests of citizens and businesses with regard to the issues and problems they have identified in the application of community law, including breaches of community law; fourthly, however, the commission will continue to decide to pursue infringements in the event of non-compliance in the context of the european union pilot project, in particular through infringement procedures; fifth, president barroso provided the chair of the parliament's legal affairs committee, mr gargani, with factual information on the operation of the pilot project in december 2008. the letter also confirmed the commission's intention to send parliament a detailed report on the first year of operation of the project. preparatory work has begun. the commission also adopted, following the communication, a more political annual report. while it continues to report on the work done in the previous year, it also seeks to identify priorities for the application of community law and a programme to implement these priorities. the report constitutes an important strategic statement by the commission on a key aspect of the better regulation programme. one of the aims of this initiative is to provide more useful information to parliament to better guide the interinstitutional discussions to follow. parliament welcomes the identification of priorities in the 2008 annual report, in particular those concerning fundamental rights and quality of life. for the first time, the commission sets out in its annual report more precise priorities in the various sectors. the objective remains to work more focused on actions that will produce more effective results in the interests of all citizens and businesses. the actions taken on the priorities identified last year and the progress made will be reported in this year's annual report, as will the new priorities for 2009-2010. thank you. i look forward with great interest to hearing the contributions of the various members of this debate and i will give some answers to mrs frassoni at the end of this debate.

in writing. - materials with particle sizes below 10-9 meters are nanomaterials. they may occur as loose or nanoparticle secretions in the casing of other materials, e.g. composites. these are nanomaterials obtained by a 'top-down' technology, i.e. by high-energy milling. due to their large surface area and high surface energy, nanoparticles are characterised by:- the ability to catalyze chemical reactions;- considerable reactivity (potential);- ease of penetration into living cells. loose nanoparticles released uncontrolled into the environment may pose a health hazard. it is not known whether loose nanoparticles of various materials can enter living cells and cause cancer-causing chemical reactions. the source of nanoparticles released into the environment are:- products intentionally produced by the 'top-down' method, e.g. zinc oxide molecules in uv filter creams, or bactericidal additives, e.g. nanosilver;- unintended by-products in the form of nanoparticles, e.g. as a result of combustion, tyre friction and other processes that uncontrollably rise through brownian motion to form nanoaerosols. so, if you deliberately add nanoparticles to, say, filter creams that are designed to block ultraviolet rays, are they not going to cause health side effects? it can and should be investigated. do the nanoaerosols around us not cause health hazards by their catalytic action? this also requires urgent scientific research, which is difficult to carry out for physicochemical reasons.

the rapporteur. - mr president! - what are you doing? our civilization is a civilization of animal exploitation. for meat, for skins, for various economic needs, we kill billions of animals. we also kill them occasionally for non-economic reasons, for sport, like hunting, for entertainment, like in the corridor. for me, killing animals is not a sport or a pastime or a culture, but let's leave it at that, because the subject of our discussion is killing animals for economic purposes. protection of animals during slaughter. is that possible? can you protect an animal you want to kill? yes, you can, by sparing him unnecessary suffering. by protecting animals from inhuman treatment, we also protect our own humanity. the proposed regulation advances the standards of animal protection at the time of slaughter, introduces higher, better technical standards and promotes better control of their implementation. it introduces greater personal responsibility for the proper treatment of animals, and it introduces the need to appoint a special official responsible for the protection of animals in slaughterhouses. the new regulation replacing the old 1993 directive is a clear step forward in the implementation of the animal welfare idea, and that is why i, as rapporteur, support this regulation. several issues have been controversial. the issue of ritual slaughter comes to the fore. the principle is to kill the animals after stunning and rendering them unconscious, but for religious reasons an exception is allowed killing without stunning if religious reasons require it. and as you know, we're talking about people in islam and judaism who kill animals without being stunned. the amendments to the committee on agriculture aimed at a total ban on ritual slaughter in the european union have been dropped. the members agreed that such a ban would be unenforceable. the commission also rejected the proposal that each member state should have the right to prohibit ritual slaughter by its own legislation. that's the issue in the 28th amendment. i would point out that voting for this amendment means that member states will not be able to prohibit ritual slaughter on their territory. voting against this amendment would mean returning to the european commission's position that ritual slaughter should be banned in national law. the question of the establishment of national reference centres, which should be established at national level, is controversial. the agriculture committee rejected that idea in amendment 64. i personally believe that such reference centres should be set up and that they could also perform control functions in relation to the treatment of animals at the time of slaughter. i would like to draw attention to the suggestions made by the committee on agriculture in my report. first, that the efforts to introduce higher standards of animal slaughter receive financial support from the european union. the high ideals of animal welfare cannot be achieved without financial investment, without creating material incentives to introduce higher standards. and the second thing. the report proposes that the increased standards apply not only to producers in the european union but also to importers of meat products into europe. we want to make sure that animal products are only placed on the eu market from animals that have been slaughtered in the manner required by eu law. ladies and gentlemen! the latest session of the european parliament is largely devoted to animal protection. today we have passed a ban on the import of products from cruelly killed seals, we have passed higher standards for the protection of experimental animals, and now we are debating higher standards for the protection of animals during slaughter. i am glad that parliament is doing so much for the protection of animals, and i am glad that i can be a part of it. the spirit of st francis of assisi is present in this house and may it be present in the next term.

rapporteur. − madam president, i have two or three short technical, but important, points. firstly, we have a block of amendments proposed by the agriculture committee, among others amendment 64. this amendment should be voted separately. it focuses on the issue of creating the national reference centre, which is a very important part of the whole regulation. the agriculture committee has proposed to remove the obligation to create the reference centre at a national level. my opinion, as the rapporteur, is that this is against the general logic of the whole regulation. i suggest voting on amendment 64 separately. secondly, please note amendment 28, which focuses on the controversial and emotional question of ritual slaughter. voting in favour of this amendment will eliminate the possibility of a total ban on ritual slaughter at national level. voting against amendment 28 will preserve the possibility of this ban. the third point concerns amendment 85. the commission has proposed to reduce the time of transport of animals from farms and waiting in slaughterhouses to 24 hours. voting in favour of amendment 85 will eliminate this reduction of transport time. voting against amendment 85 will support the commission proposal to reduce the transport time.

the rapporteur. - mr president, commissioner, i have to ask you to leave. i would like to begin by expressing my warm thanks to mr gérard deprez, rapporteur for the libe committee, to all the shadow rapporteurs, to the representatives of the czech presidency and to the european commission for their successful cooperation. despite the rather distant negotiating positions at the beginning, we have managed to reach a compromise which i hope will allow us to reach an agreement with the council at the first reading. the draft regulation establishes a mechanism under which member states will be able to renegotiate, negotiate and conclude bilateral agreements with third countries on judicial cooperation in civil and commercial matters. a similar mechanism is provided for in respect of bilateral agreements on jurisdiction, recognition and enforcement of judgments and decisions in matrimonial matters, on parental responsibility and on maintenance obligations. this is a response to the practical problem raised by opinion 1/03 of the court of justice on the new lugano convention, according to which, in so far as the communities have exercised their powers under article 61 (c) of the treaty to adopt legal measures in the field of judicial cooperation in civil matters, they also exercise their competence to conclude external agreements. the proposed instrument lays down the detailed procedure. for this reason, the legal framework of the proposed mechanism must be strictly limited in terms of subject matter and time. the first condition is that the project is limited to bilateral agreements on jurisdiction and the recognition and enforcement of judgments in civil and commercial matters. the second condition is implemented by the so-called 'sunset clause', according to which an agreement concluded under this procedure automatically ceases to be valid when the community concludes an agreement with the third country concerned. i certainly see the need to include in the legal framework the question of the exercise of external powers in the area of the law applicable to contractual and non-contractual obligations, as well as in matrimonial matters. however, it seems appropriate to clarify that the proposed mechanism will be applicable not only to sectoral agreements defined by the limited scope of this project, but also to other agreements such as bilateral agreements and regional agreements between a limited number of member states and neighbouring third countries. of course, only in very limited cases, on specific issues, to solve local problems. i was sceptical about the need to set the 'sunset clause' at 31 december 2014 if the draft regulation requires the european commission to report on the application of the regulations by 1 january 2014. moreover, the process of negotiating agreements with third countries is often complex and very time-consuming, leaving member states little time to use this new procedure. therefore, the compromise proposal to end the regulation on 31 december 2019 allows for a fuller and more effective use of this procedure by member states. despite the european commission's differing view, i believe that the commission should take account of the regulations in its report on their application in the context of other legislative instruments such as brussels i. the proposed mechanism, which includes two-stage control by the commission, will undoubtedly serve to ensure the coherence of the acquis. however, i have tried to make the proposed procedure as flexible as possible, to reduce the time needed for the commission to react and to reduce the bureaucratic burden. the democratic legitimacy and role of the european parliament are beyond doubt, and that is why i insist that the european parliament, together with the member states, should be able to receive information at every stage, from the intention of a member state to enter into negotiations with a third country to the conclusion of an agreement. i would like to stress that the procedure for concluding bilateral agreements with third countries gives us a unique opportunity to demonstrate that the european union is able to solve the problems of its citizens in their interests, which is particularly important in the context of the economic crisis and the growing euroscepticism in many member states. i would like to conclude, mr president, by saying that despite some differences in the strict legal approach, we must be pragmatic, and of course respect the community's legal acquis.
mr. chairman, please! in the area of civil justice, in addition to the acquis communautaire, there are numerous bilateral agreements which member states have concluded with third countries. in accordance with article 307 of the treaty, member states are required to eliminate any possible incompatibilities with the acquis which may exist in such agreements. in its opinion of february 2006, the court of justice upheld the finding that the community had been granted exclusive competence to conclude international agreements with third countries in the fields of jurisdiction and the recognition and enforcement of judgments in civil and commercial matters. the question therefore arises whether all existing or proposed bilateral agreements with these countries should be replaced by community agreements to a certain extent. or, rather, in the absence of a community interest, leave the power to conclude them to the member states? however, this derogating procedure must be subject to very specific conditions relating to the scope and duration of the mechanism. it is therefore important that the commission establishes a strategy and sets priorities for the development of the community's external relations policy in the field of judicial cooperation in civil and commercial matters.

acting president of the council. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your reply. first of all, let me congratulate you on the election of your new president. i look forward to working with jerzy buzek during the swedish presidency and, of course, also in the period afterwards. it is an honour for me to address the european parliament as president of the european council. i know that more than half of you are elected to this house for the first time. together you all give a voice to 500 million europeans. there are high expectations for you. i speak to you in times of challenge. rarely has eu cooperation faced such severe and varied challenges. in the short term, we have the ambition to ensure a smooth transition to a new treaty the treaty of lisbon. we must continue to deal with the economic and financial crisis now and in the longer term. beneath the surface, a growing climate crisis threatens to be the greatest of our long-term challenges. one thing is clear. to succeed in the many challenges facing the swedish presidency, we must work side by side with you - you who are at the heart of european democracy. we hope for your support and cooperation, and that you are ready to take up the challenges with us. when we talk about the history of the eu, we often say that cooperation has laid the foundations for peace in a europe that has so often been marked by the opposite. i want to tell you that my grandfather was a swedish soldier on the norwegian border during the second world war, a war that sweden was not involved in. the closest my grandfather came to war was to occasionally catch a glimpse of it from a safe distance. this was sweden's longstanding relationship with europe: a distant observer. when europe was in ruins after world war ii, sweden was untouched. we were economically richer but poor in the european community. 20 years ago, the barbed wire between austria and hungary was cut. the berlin wall was torn down, and europe was changed almost overnight. then several countries began the journey that has led to the presence of representatives from 27 countries in this hall today. sweden was one of these countries. a late starter needs time to catch up. in the late 1980s, our political commitment in sweden to europe began to mature. the awareness of sweden's proximity to and dependence on europe is slowly growing. in bringing sweden into european cooperation, i.e. in upholding openness, globalisation and free trade, foreign minister carl bildt played a decisive role, driven by a firm conviction that sweden belonged in europe. eighteen years ago, we submitted our application for membership of the european union. finally, we had matured in the conviction that people's everyday lives and our future were best shaped by cooperation and community with others, that we had something to contribute and that we had much to learn. now we were no longer afraid of cooperation. we dared to be part of europe. these turbulent years for sweden, from the mid-1980s onwards, ran in parallel with my own deepening of political involvement. the desire for europe was strong in me and in many of my generation of swedish politicians. i remember how i was welcomed to visit the european parliament as a young member of parliament. it was a sign of the openness and accessibility of the parliament, despite the fact that sweden was outside the union at the time. a few years later, in 1997, after sweden became a member, i helped to set up the epp group's youth organisation, youth of the epp, and i became its first president. in this way i got to see how european cooperation worked in practice. together we sought european solutions to european problems. we not only got to know each other, but also each other's history and culture. it gave me a chance to get to know the capitals of europe and the number of churches i visited in europe is not easy to count. in 20 years, sweden has gone from being a distant observer to being an active participant in european cooperation. this, in turn, has affected the swedish people. ten years ago, one in three swedes thought that membership of the eu was good for our country, but the same number thought the opposite. today, it's the other way around. almost two out of three swedes think that eu membership is good for sweden. in the european parliament elections in june, over 45 percent of swedes went to the polls. this is eight percentage points more than in 2004, and it is more than the european average. today sweden is a country that appreciates and celebrates its membership of the eu. we woke up late, but we've been working hard to catch up. it is a victory for all of us who believe in european cooperation. (applause from the centre) ) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your report. we are facing the fate of our generation, a social problem that unlike many others is growing slowly and only in the wrong direction. our world has a fever. the fever is rising and it's up to us to respond. the greenland ice sheet is shrinking by more than 100 cubic kilometers every year. the west antarctic ice sheet is melting faster and faster. we know that the greenland ice sheet alone can lead to a rise in sea level of up to two meters. the effects will be dramatic. if sea levels rise just one meter worldwide, a hundred million people would have to move in asia alone. the people most affected are those in bangladesh, eastern china, and vietnam. however, we also face other serious consequences. climate change will threaten the survival of many plant and animal species. this is despite the fact that we are sticking to the two-degree target set by the un, which was endorsed last week by the g8 and the major economies forum in l'aquila. our climate is threatened by our use and dependence on fossil fuels. that's the bad news. so who are the good guys? though time is short, it is still on our side. but we must act now. we already have the conditions for the development of renewable energy and energy efficiency technologies. according to the international energy agency, more than half of the measures needed to keep the 2c target can be achieved with the technology we already have. in addition, action on climate change is accompanied by very valuable side effects, effects which in themselves justify the action. when we use less energy, we save money. we are improving public finances while giving households more resources. when we invest in renewable energy and improve energy efficiency, we improve our energy security. we become less dependent on imports from countries that are sometimes both politically and economically unstable. investments in the green economy will create new jobs and drive growth in the coming decades. let me give you a concrete example. many eu countries were affected by the gas crisis in ukraine in january. last week, i spoke with president yushchenko about how we should try to avoid a similar incident. at the same time, it is important to be able to turn the prospects. if ukraine invested in energy efficiency to the same level as the czech republic or slovenia, this would translate into energy savings equivalent to all of its gas imports for own use from russia. ukraine could become completely independent of gas imports from russia and also save a lot of money just by increasing its own energy efficiency. that's how we have to search for the climate killer. (applause) i would like to thank you. twelve years ago, a coalition of volunteers was built in kyoto. volunteering alone is not enough, however. if we are to succeed in getting a global climate agreement in place, then the journey from kyoto to copenhagen must go from a coalition of volunteers to a shared responsibility. how are we gonna get there? europe must act together and united. we must show leadership and stand by our promises. europe is crucial to bringing others into a global agreement. we need to put a price on emissions around the world. we need to start using national carbon taxes and emissions trading. then the green alternatives emerge. if fossil fuel use is priced out of the climate equation, global warming will continue. the alternatives are not emerging. measures to increase energy efficiency will not be economically viable. however, this is not enough. we need a broader answer to the question 'how'. it is not enough to limit emissions in a circle of countries that voluntarily undertake reductions, but which together account for only 30 percent of emissions. nor are solutions based solely on the constraints of the most developed countries sufficient. because even if the so-called annex i countries were to reduce their emissions to zero, the rapidly growing emissions of the developing countries would still take us beyond the two-degree target. that is why we must discuss the financing of investment in developing countries. we need to ensure rapid technology transfer and we need to ensure that developing countries also make commitments to break the development they have now in front of them. we will also be demanding clear commitments in the medium term, including for non-european countries. the responsibility of a few must now become the responsibility of all. i know that the european parliament will take its responsibility. the swedish presidency sees you as our allies. now we want to write the story of how the climate threat was averted, and we want to write it with you. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your report. the economic and financial crisis spread like wildfire over the world in a matter of weeks. some had warned, but for the vast majority it came as a surprise, especially its scope and depth. in a globalized world, problems also spread quickly to others. the power of the downturn is such that no one has a miracle cure to get out of it quickly. coordinated action by the eu is the best tool we have to meet the challenges of the crisis. besides, there's still a lot that can go wrong. given the circumstances, the eu was able to show leadership through the trials. we agreed on guarantees and traffic rules to support the banks. we agreed on a joint recovery plan to stimulate the economy. president sarkozy and the french presidency played an important role in this process, but i would also like to stress that the european parliament was a driving force. we now need to spend the autumn discussing further measures to get us through the crisis. the economic situation remains difficult and public finances are now strained in all member states. the commission forecasts that the eu deficits will exceed 80% of gdp next year. you can't just close your eyes and pretend it's not a problem. in the midst of all this, we must not forget that behind these figures are people who are worried about their jobs, and who wonder how they will manage to pay their rent and maintain their standard of living. it's our job to answer. when millions of europeans lose their jobs and are excluded, our entire well-being is threatened. this at a time when the pressure on our well-being is already great. we live longer, while working shorter hours and having fewer children. in 50 years' time, there will be twice as many elderly people as children in europe if this trend continues. so what can we do? we must restore confidence in the financial markets. we must quickly put in place effective supervision to prevent similar crises from occurring in the future. the swedish presidency is working to ensure that the council can reach agreement on this before the end of the year. we hope you'll help us bring it to a speedy and final conclusion. our citizens will not accept that taxpayers' money is used again and again to bail out financial institutions that have acted irresponsibly. we must quickly get out of the growing public deficits through a coordinated exit strategy and a gradual return to the rules of the stability pact. otherwise, short-term imbalances are followed by chronic deficits. that means that we are going to have to make big cuts, which are already a reality in parts of the eu, and which we have had experience of in sweden. then there's mass unemployment, social unrest and rising taxation. we must ensure a social dimension in european policy based on sound public finances and on bringing more people into the labour market. it's the absolute best way to protect our welfare systems. i know that this is a very important issue, especially here in the european parliament. it is not sustainable that three out of ten europeans of working age are outside the labour market. the aim must be an active labour market policy which, together with well-functioning social security systems, can effectively manage transitions. we must strengthen the employability of the individual and his or her ability to establish himself or herself on the labour market. we must also activate and reactivate the unemployed. with more in the work, there will be more to support those who are left out. we must also focus on reform, modernisation and adaptation to a new reality. the world outside the eu is not standing still. it's moving forward at an incredible speed. it's something we should embrace and embrace. a review of the eu's lisbon strategy can contribute to a much needed reform agenda. we will begin that discussion in the autumn. in the wake of the economic crisis, we can see ideas of increased protectionism. the wto confirms that the number of trade restrictive measures has increased significantly over the past three months. that is why i welcome the l'aquila agreement to relaunch the doha round to ensure that the countries of the world return to the free trade-friendly path that we know will benefit us all in the long run. the objective must be to bring europe out of the crisis stronger. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your report. when i transparent, more effective and more influential on the international stage. most importantly, however, the lisbon treaty sets the stage for an inward-looking phase in eu cooperation. it is now time boundaries for their activities. we see the spread of drug trafficking and human trafficking. it threatens our democratic values, and it threatens our citizens. at the same time, freedom of movement across our borders is fundamental to our community to study, work and live in another eu country. but a new age calls for new answers. that is why we will be drawing up a new programme in this area in president of the commission. − mr president, these are no ordinary times and this will be no ordinary presidency. in addition to the usual legislative work, the swedish presidency will have other kinds of highly political challenges to deal with, and no one better to tackle these challenges than prime minister reinfeldt and the swedish presidency team. today i want to highlight two of the biggest policy challenges facing the european union in the next six months: dealing with the economic crisis and negotiating an ambitious international agreement on climate change in copenhagen. the worst financial and economic crisis in living memory continues to have devastating effects within our communities and families, with unemployment in particular continuing to rise. getting the economy back on track remains the top priority. the european union’s collective action has led to an unprecedented fiscal effort that is producing concrete results. we have also shown solidarity amongst member states, for instance by doubling the ceiling for balance of payments support for non-eurozone member states to eur 50 billion. we now need to fully implement the recovery package in all its aspects and make sure it translates into the creation of jobs and the promotion of economic activity on the ground. i believe it is essential to prioritise measures that limit unemployment and get people back to work. here we can build on the results of the employment summit held in may as part of a commission initiative with the czech, swedish and spanish presidencies. we need to put into practice the shared commitment to youth and to employment. of course, responsibility for labour market policies lies with member states, but we can and should use existing european instruments to help member states keep people in employment and train them for the jobs of the future. that is why the european commission is about to make a proposal to simplify structural fund procedures and waive the need for national cofinancing from the european social fund for 2009 and 2010. we will also redeploy resources in order to fund a new microcredit facility for employment and social inclusion. i hope this parliament will support these proposals. the commission proposals building on the de larosière report i commissioned last october will form the basis for strengthened financial market supervision and regulation. with the proposals already made – many of them already approved by this parliament and by the council, some still in our decision-making process – we are indeed taking the lead globally in the reform of the financial international system. we will continue to do so, i am sure, at the g20 in pittsburgh in september. moving all these dossiers forward over the next six months is essential to build a new economy, because – let us make no mistake – the post-crisis economy cannot and will not be the same as the pre-crisis economy. we need to rebuild our economic model and put the values back at the heart of our social market economy, where they belong. we need to build an economy and a society based on opportunity, responsibility and solidarity, an economy which will have to reinvent new sources of growth because we cannot rely for ever on monetary and fiscal stimulus; a europe of open and well-performing markets; a europe of smart, green growth; a europe with more effective regulation and supervision of financial markets; a europe that deepens its single market and uses its potential to the full; a europe that resists the trends for fragmentation or protectionism. concerning climate change, europe is already the first region in the world to implement far-reaching, legally binding climate and energy targets. i am proud of the way the commission worked with the last parliament and the council to put this legislation in place, and i want to work closely with you and the presidency in the run-up to copenhagen. our leadership role was very much appreciated in the meetings last week in l’aquila in the g8, and in the major economies forum. you will have heard about the progress made at these meetings. for the first time, all participants committed to capping the temperature increase at 2°c to respect climate science. this is certainly a welcome step forward, but we should not delude ourselves: our ambition and our commitment are not yet matched by others. europe is far ahead of the curve in relation to the rest of the world and, frankly, 145 days from copenhagen, that worries me. in the coming weeks we will step up our work with international partners to secure clear commitments in copenhagen. we also need to make progress on the necessary means to support developing countries and boost technology transfer. in september the commission will put its proposals for financing on the table so that we can build a european consensus and negotiate with others. the climate change agenda is, of course, closely linked with another priority: energy security. today, the commission will adopt proposals to strengthen our rules governing the security of gas supply and reinforcing solidarity between member states, which i trust the swedish presidency will take forward with your support. these are the headline priorities – and rightly so. but there is plenty of other important work to be done over the next six months. let me just flag the stockholm programme, where the commission has recently tabled an ambitious vision putting the citizen at the heart of our justice, freedom and security policy, balancing security with the protection of civil liberties and fundamental rights. for most of this decade the european union has been engaged in internal institutional debates. changes to our governing treaty are absolutely necessary to equip the enlarged european union to work democratically and effectively. i hope that we will see the ratification of the lisbon treaty in the coming months so that we can put its provisions to work and so that we can move on with the policy agenda i have just outlined. it is important to discuss procedure, but i believe it is even more important to discuss substance. the swedish presidency, as well as the next spanish presidency, will have to oversee – hopefully – a complex transition to the new treaty in which the commission and parliament will have to play their full part. the european union has constantly reinvented itself, from the initial vocation of healing a war-torn continent to the building of the internal market and then on to the reunification of europe. during these last 50 years europe has consistently exceeded expectations, confounding doubts. i am sure that we will also rise to the new challenge we face: laying the foundations for the smart, green economy of the future. we will succeed if we respect the key lesson from half a century of european integration: the european union advances when all its parts cooperate in a spirit of openness, trust and partnership. the swedish presidency programme recognises this; the european commission stands ready to play its part and so, i am sure, does this parliament.
