president-in-office of the council. − mr president, it is an honour to be able to stand here for the first time. i expect to be here numerous times during the coming six months to address different issues. the issue on our agenda at this time is iran. before going into the substance of that issue, let me just express our heartfelt condolences to iran on the occasion of the tragic accident earlier today. we sincerely regret the loss of life and express our sympathy with all of those affected by this tragedy. the issue of iran is obviously very high up on the swedish presidency’s agenda. that has to do with the outcome of the election and the question marks – to put it very mildly – that were raised after that election, as well as the political developments that we have seen since then. i think you are all aware of the fact that the european union has taken a very strong and a very principled stand when it comes to these events. we have reiterated that questions over the conduct of elections are issues for the iranian authorities to truly investigate and clarify. we have also been very clear in our response to what we have seen happening on the streets of tehran. we have condemned the crackdown, the violence and the use of force that we have seen against peaceful demonstrations; we condemn the crackdown against journalists, media outlets, communications and protestors. those are contrary not only to the norms and values that we represent but also, obviously, to the wishes for a more open and more reform-oriented society expressed by so many iranians. that being said, we remain in our principled policy of wishing another, a better, a new relationship with the nation of iran. it is a rich nation that has much to contribute to the development of the world and the development of its own region, and we would hope that at some point in time – hopefully not too distant – there will be that possibility for a truly new relationship. before concluding, let me just note one issue that has been occupying us quite a lot, and that is that the iranian authorities did detain a number of personalities who are staff members of european missions, as well as some european nationals. we have been in constant touch with the iranian authorities over these issues. we consider possible accusations levelled against them to be baseless, and i can assure you that we will continue to engage with the iranian authorities in all the ways we can until these issues are resolved in a satisfactory manner – that is, that the persons in question are released.

mr. chairman, please! the death of innocent people is always tragic. but if they die defending values like freedom or truth, then we can say that their suffering is not in vain - as is the case with the recent victims in iran. what's wrong is when a regime shoots at protesters, jails opponents, tortures and kills them. the only source of hope and optimism is that these events may bring to the attention of politicians and the world public the true nature of the iranian regime, which is capable of actions far removed from the minimal standards of the modern world. this regime has blood on its hands. we should remember that and we should act to change a state of affairs that we cannot accept. in such situations, the question is always the same: what can we do? we can support the demands and proposals that have already been made. first, the iranian authorities must stop using violence against those who hold different views from the regime. in the case of countries like iran, the observance of fundamental human rights should be monitored and guaranteed by the international community. second, iran should have free and fair elections, in which all candidates are allowed to stand, not just those who are allowed to stand. incidentally, those who decide on the active electoral law do not have a democratic mandate themselves. the fairness of the elections should be verified by independent external observers otherwise the elections have no meaning. third, we should do everything we can to make the solution to iran peaceful, political, and that means we should support those iranians who want fundamental change in their country, which will result in iran being governed by those who win fair elections, and iran itself ceasing to be a threat to global security. the leader of the iranian opposition in exile told mrs. rajavi that what happened in iran was the beginning of the end of the regime. i sincerely hope mrs. rajavi is right.
mr president, as the situation in iran escalates and the violation of democracy also presents a danger to the stability of the whole region, we have to express our concern and condemnation – but declarations must not only be symbolic and empty. some european leaders are talking about new sanctions to be imposed on iran, but a discussion is needed right now on the promotion of democracy at grass-root level in this country. i am polish, and we in eastern europe know how important these types of actions are for the establishment of democracy. a promotion should be adapted to the political and economic situation in a given country, but previous eu experience in the promotion of democracy in north africa, the middle east and eastern europe has to be reviewed and evaluated in order to see what should be done in iran, what can be done in iran and what is effective under given circumstances in this country. i also want to remind you that, if the eu wants to be credible, it also has to undertake some measures in moldova. soon we will face a new test – on 29 july – with the elections in moldova. the eu has to do everything it can to ensure free and fair democratic elections in this country. it is not enough to talk about support for democracy: we in the european parliament and european institutions have to be more active in that respect.
mr. chairman, please! certainly, the electoral process in iran needs to be brought under control, but the beginning of the conflict should be a declaration by the iranian authorities to refrain from the use of force and to release imprisoned opposition activists, human rights defenders, journalists, protesters, as well as citizens of other countries who are blamed for the situation in iran. the eu has also been active in the fight against terrorism, and has been involved in the development of a number of international conventions, including the international covenant on civil and political rights. i also want to express my concern about iran's nuclear program. tehran has the right to a peaceful programme, but it also has the duty to restore the confidence of the international community that iran's nuclear activities are exclusively peaceful.
mr. chairman, please! the repression of the protests in xinjiang province has once again shown us the authoritarian nature of the communist government in beijing. at least 180 people were killed and 1,600 injured in the worst ethnic clashes in china in decades. it is the duty of the european parliament to condemn violence which has its roots in discrimination on the grounds of ethnicity and religion. this is also how it should be in this case, where the authoritarian force of the state has been directed against the uighur minority. but she is not the only victim of totalitarian regimes. the citizens of a europe based on christian values have a special duty to christian minorities persecuted in other parts of the world. in china, this minority is estimated to number over 30 million people, according to unofficial sources. in this way, people of the size of a large european country are harassed, followed, denied employment, tortured and murdered by the chinese communist authorities. the chinese regime realizes that the christian faith brings with it a desire for freedom and the rule of law, and that is why it is trying to limit its development. but the church's fight against it has not produced the desired results, for the number of believers is steadily increasing year by year. the chinese authorities must understand that the middle kingdom will only become a fully modern country if it respects the basic principles of democracy and religious freedom.
mr. chairman, please! the situation in honduras requires the european union to continue to take concrete and decisive action to stabilise and restore constitutional order and to prevent the escalation of the conflict between supporters and opponents of the ousted president zelaya. i therefore support the initiative of my colleague, mr salafranca, to formulate as soon as possible the possibility of a mission to honduras to be signed by the european parliament. the parties to the conflict must negotiate as soon as possible to reach an agreement that would allow president zelaya to return to office and complete his current term, but without the possibility of changing the constitution to allow his re-election. that would be a solution that would hopefully stabilize the situation, perhaps be acceptable to both... back on track, and obviously this will take more time than it will take in the developed world because the mechanisms to produce new economic growth are much less developed in those countries. one of the remarks that have been made by several members is about the fact that a lot of member states are in fact backtracking on their official development assistance (oda) engagements. the eu member states agreed in 2005 individual minimum aid targets of 0.51% for eu-15 and 0.17% for eu-12, for the new member states to be reached by 2010 and respectively 0.7% and 0.33% by 2015. the countries that had already achieved aid levels higher than these targets promised to maintain. based on these confirmations and higher national pledges of some member states, the eu should collectively reach 0.56% of oda by 2010. i believe that the crisis should not be an excuse to water down donors’ aid promises, and i will insist on remaining committed to delivering the promised aid levels both for eu member states as well as other donors. in 2008 the eu oda has increased by around eur 4 billion to a level of 0.40% of oda and the collective eu oda is forecast to continue increasing. on the basis of the acting president of the council. - mr president! - what is it? it is a great privilege for me to be here today. i am very humbled by this and it will be an exciting time to present the council's draft budget to you. europe is facing significant challenges. the economic situation looked much more worrying six months ago. the situation seems to have stabilized. the risk picture is more balanced and the risks of being drawn into a continuing deep spiral have been reduced. but we are facing significant problems: rising unemployment, growing budget deficits and growing debt. against this background, there is a strong need to maintain long-term sustainable public finances. many countries have a long way to go to achieve fiscal balance. demographics will put a great deal of pressure on public finances. the climate challenge will require the reallocation and allocation of resources. in our view, the budget we are about to agree on should be characterised by great restraint in order to leave room for future needs, emphasis on european added value and investments which can in the short term take us out of the economic crisis and in the long term also strengthen our competitiveness. the council's proposal, which was adopted unanimously, addresses and helps to meet these challenges. it's a disciplined budget. it's a sound government. it stimulates research, education, infrastructure, competitiveness and innovation and it stimulates cohesion. the council proposal also includes margins to deal with unforeseen events. the logic behind our proposal is simple. if we want to stimulate growth, employment and prosperity, the textbook says that we must pursue a policy that is resilient, credible and prudent, but with investments in education, research, infrastructure and in the elimination of income disparities across the union. that's exactly what we've been trying to do. the council's proposal is balanced but still ambitious. compared with the 2009 budget, commitments increase by 1.1% and payment appropriations by just under 4%. our proposal and the agreement we want to reach must meet the following basic requirements, which were also applied at the council's first reading: the budget must ensure that there is sufficient funding for the various eu policy priorities in 2010. the eu must be able to react swiftly to the challenges ahead. the focus must be on adding european value. budgetary discipline and sound financial management are required. otherwise we will not be able to return to a balanced public finances in stages. it's important to respect the ceiling. the eu must have sufficient flexibility to cope with additional needs and unforeseen events. it is crucial that the eu budget has sufficient margins. the budget proposal we are presenting amounts to eur 138 billion in commitment appropriations and eur 121 billion in payment appropriations. the reductions made by the council compared with the preliminary draft budget by the commission are based on a detailed analysis of the implementation of the budget, the budget forecasts and the declarations of activities, and we look at the capacity to implement programmes and measures. the implementation rate and absorption capacity have been the key criteria in our analysis. i thought i'd just get into the headlines a little bit. subheading 1a, research and innovation, is the most important element and adequate funding has been secured in our draft budget. projects in the energy and infrastructure sectors are another area where more resources are being added. adjusting for the accounting effects of the economic recovery plan, the increase in this area amounts to approximately 8%. eight percent of the time. that's a lot. as you all know, the financing of the european recovery plan will be one of the subjects we will have to discuss in the autumn. under 1b, the council accepted the commitment appropriations proposed by the commission. as regards payments, the council considers that some cuts can be made in relation to the preliminary draft budget, but i would like to stress that our proposal nevertheless implies an increase in payment appropriations of 3,2% compared with 2009. title 2: the council proposes strong increases in both commitment and payment appropriations compared with 2009, of 4.5% and 9.5% respectively, after accounting for the recovery plan. title 3: the council made only a few minor adjustments to the commission's preliminary budget. there will be adequate resources for migration policy, including frontex. title 4: it is extremely important to leave a substantial margin for the ceiling under this heading in order to deal with unforeseen needs in the best possible way. the council is therefore securing a margin of approximately eur 310 million at its first reading. this is particularly justified in the light of the letter of amendment which covers additional needs in this area. as regards the reserve for disaster aid, the council accepted the commission's proposal for commitment appropriations. in the context of the common foreign and security policy, its importance is growing and the council is therefore ensuring that adequate resources are available for this purpose. how to administer: given the economic situation and the specific characteristics of each institution, the council made certain targeted reductions. the ambition is that the administration should not grow faster than inflation. the institutions' requests for additional services for new activities were not accepted, except for the new authorities planned for 2010 and for frontex. at our conciliation meeting in july, the importance of the recruitment linked to the 2004 and 2007 enlargements was re-emphasised and a joint statement was agreed between us. at the same time, your representatives indicated their willingness to try to find a common approach to the real estate policy of the eu institutions and bodies. i am sure that we will be pleased to find such a statement later in the autumn. before i close, i would like to recall and highlight the positive atmosphere that prevailed in our meetings with the european parliament. i think that constructive cooperation is the only way to arrive at a good budget.
member of the commission. − mr president, it is a great pleasure for me to have an opportunity to speak to you this morning. i know that the first stages of this budgetary procedure – in particular the july conciliation – took place in a very positive atmosphere, and i hope we can build on this cooperation in the coming weeks. we still have some way to go in the 2010 budget procedures, and there situation following the council’s first reading and the establishment of the draft budget for 2010, the commission acknowledges that the cuts proposed by the council are less severe than in previous years. however, there are some particular concerns which i would like to highlight. the commission regrets the council’s cut of eur 1.8 billion in payment appropriations. these cuts are mr president of the european parliament! ministers, please! dear presidents and representatives of the european institutions! dear colleagues, and above all, dear friends! i stand before you today as the 13th directly elected speaker of this house. i am pleased to have with us the former presidents of this house: mr emilio colombo, mr enrique barón crespo, mr egon klepsch, mr klaus hänsch, mr josé maría gil-robles, mrs nicole fontaine, mr pat cox and mr hans-gert pöttering. (laughter) it's a great honor for all of us that you've come to us. as many of you have said, my election is also a symbol of the fulfilled dreams of the citizens of our part of europe about the unity of the continent. the european union is committed to the development of a common european defence policy and to the promotion of the european defence industry. i know and understand the concerns, needs and expectations of those who have recently joined the union. i know, because in my country they're similar. but now we are all taking responsibility for the future of our continent. there is no longer an old and a new europe. there is our europe! europe as a whole! we want it to be modern and strong. and to make sure our citizens see it. it takes energy and work. this is a goal worth striving for, because it is the dream of generations of europeans. i'm ready for this work and this effort, because these dreams were my dreams too. (applause) ladies and gentlemen, ladies and gentlemen, i have a very special guest. as we enter this term, europe and we ourselves - its representatives - are faced with many challenges. we have to face them. and we must remember that the european parliament has a special role to play in this quest for a better europe, not only institutional but also social - a deeply symbolic role. the european parliament is the heart of the european democratic system. it's the foundation of the sustainability and stability of this system, the guardian of the ideas and values that materialize not only in our decisions and their consequences, but in our debates. but the european parliament also has another task, and that is to create a vision of a new europe, a vision that goes beyond the present, beyond what is, to what should be. to create and co-create this vision, it takes imagination, knowledge, wisdom, and above all, courage. hannah arendt, a german philosopher of jewish origin, argued that politics is the only domain, next to religion, where miracles happen. we in europe saw this miracle exactly 20 years ago, and that's why we believe in the power of courage, imagination and wisdom. i think everyone in this room believes that. (laughter) i am optimistic about the challenges ahead. in my view, these are the following important challenges: first, the economic crisis and european solidarity; second, energy and the environment; third, foreign policy; fourth, human rights and the value system; fifth, our parliament and its reform. the most difficult and painful is the economic crisis. we have to beat him, and we will. europe has taken the lead, proposing solutions in the g8 and g20 -- solutions that, while preserving our social model, help the world to repair its economy. in the face of globalisation, europe must speak with one voice. it is now, in times of crisis, that we must take special care of growth and combat unemployment, revive the ideas of the lisbon strategy and find ways to invest in new technologies, innovation, education and human capital. the role of the community budget is important in ensuring that european research programmes have clear priorities and procedures. under the new treaty, parliament and the council will have the same budgetary powers. the codecision procedure will cover agriculture, fisheries, foreign trade, justice and home affairs, giving us equal powers also in the field of agricultural expenditure. we must guard against the temptation to protectionism and the renationalisation of common policy areas. cohesion policy must remain a priority in the next community budget if we are to achieve full integration of the re-united continent. the single market is our great achievement. we must defend and consolidate it if europe is to remain a competitive continent. this means strengthening, not weakening, european integration. have the courage to speak up for your beliefs. the community we are building cannot be animated, understood and lived without two elements: solidarity and social cohesion, because there is no true community without concern for all, especially the most vulnerable: the unemployed, the uneducated, those living far away in the provinces. the swedish presidency's main objective is to combat unemployment. we'll be vigorously assisting her in that. on the other side of the iron curtain, we once shouted in the streets: there is no freedom without solidarity. we can now say that without solidarity there is no community. nor will there be a modern, strong europe. (applause) we will not overcome the economic crisis without the powerful intellectual, economic, creative potential of women. the demographic crisis requires strengthening the family and childhood. we also need to ensure that women do not have to sacrifice their careers for family and child-rearing. (applause) to overcome the demographic crisis, and at the same time to continue democratic principles, we also need to be an open community. immigration has always been good for europe. we need to propose solutions that allow us to invite immigrants, create the conditions for integration, but also expect them to be open to integration themselves. we are facing an energy crisis. europeans may not understand geopolitics, but they do understand that their heating has been turned off. we must continue to diversify our energy sources by increasing investment in renewable energy and fossil fuels. nuclear energy remains at the disposal and decision of the member states. we need to expand the external pipeline network so that we are not dependent on any state. we need to increase the interconnections between our gas and electricity networks and consider the possibility of joint gas purchases, so that a genuine european energy solidarity market can be created. i think it is time for a real common energy policy for the union. i'll make sure of it. president-designate of the commission. - the mr president, ladies and gentlemen, we are living in unprecedented times. i am personally convinced that in the history books of the future, we will be talking about one before the financial crisis and one after. this crisis is not just financial, economic and social. it's also a crisis of values. that is why i think we must put at the heart of our response to this crisis our european model of society, our social market economy. at the same time, the crisis has shown how interdependent we have all become in this globalisation. there is the financial crisis, but also the energy crisis. there are food security issues and climate change, where europe is now leading the way. that is why i believe that we can say that this is the moment of truth for europe. do we want to shape globalization with our values, by standing up for our interests, or do we want to suffer globalization, by following the initiative of others? the choice is clear to me. we must rise to this challenge together because if we do not do so together, europe risks being marginalized. we have experience. i believe that there is no other region in the world which has had the same experience as we have in establishing an internal market, common rules, common institutions, even a single currency and policies of solidarity and cohesion. we have this unique experience. so i believe that instead of suffering globalization, we can shape it, because we are naturally a laboratory of globalization, we are champions of global governance. this is not the time for the status quo, nor for routine. we need to have an agenda for transformation. we need a strong europe more than ever. with the lisbon treaty, we will be stronger tomorrow, we will have more capacity to act. when i say a stronger europe, let us be clear! this does not necessarily mean more centralisation of power. i am committed to the democratic principle of subsidiarity, which is of course linked to solidarity, while taking decisions at the most appropriate level. when i speak of a stronger europe, i am also speaking of the european spirit, the european decision-making culture, the community method and the will to act together - not only the capacity to act but also the will to act, the political will. we need a europe which defends its values and interests with uncompromising determination, which rejects all protectionism but is not naive and which is able to show that spirit of voluntarism. it is this spirit of voluntary service that has guided the drafting of the document which i sent to all of you before this meeting. the mandate of the commission which i now chair was the first commission of the enlarged europe, of the greater europe of 27. i believe that now that we have consolidated this europe, we have the conditions for a new ambition: a new social ambition, because there is a crisis and unemployment is the first problem of europeans; a new ambition in the fight against climate change, where we already play a leading role; and a new ambition in the response to globalisation. last week i had the opportunity to discuss these political guidelines with all the political groups that invited me. i think it was a very useful, constructive and open discussion. i received many points of view. i believe that the time has now come for us to reach a broad consensus and to reach some level of agreement on the way forward. before you all today i pledge that if i am confirmed by this parliament i will apply those political guidelines during my second term and i will, together with incoming commissioners, translate them into the next commission's legislative and work programme. i am not going to repeat those guidelines now but i think, after discussions with all of you, it will be useful to make some of the elements in the guidelines more concrete and also to take on board a number of your suggestions. in the interests of transparency, i would like to highlight those areas with all of you now. first of all, the basic line: as we fully implement our recovery plan in order to move out of this economic and financial crisis, we must keep an eye on the future. we must reinvigorate our inclusive social market economy. we will invest in new sources of sustainable growth, in smart green growth, in the networks of the future from digital infrastructure to the european super grids for electricity and gas all this to promote high levels of employment and social provision and to reinforce the european model of society, while succeeding in an increasingly competitive world. solidarity must remain key. that is why, apart from all the decisions already taken and proposed in terms of structural funds and in terms of doubling our balance of payments support for some countries in difficulty, i want to commit myself to using all the instruments at my disposal to help those member states with serious budgetary constraints - namely the new member states - back onto the road to recovery. but we cannot return to the previous growth model. it has clearly proved unsustainable. we have to create the conditions where the transition to a low-carbon economy is a source of competitive advantage for our businesses, a source of jobs for our workers and a source of hope for future generations. yes, i agree with those of you who said that coordination is not enough. yes, we need to map out a genuine european agenda. yes, we need an integrated vision for a coherent european strategy, a european union 2020 strategy that builds on open markets by combining new sources of sustainable growth, employment and social cohesion, our climate and energy security agenda, a fresh approach to industrial policy and a move to a knowledge society. i stand for a particular emphasis on innovation and support measures for smes. yes, this means overhauling the lisbon strategy after 2010. yes, we need a much more integrated approach to the economic, social and environmental strands of the different strategies. as president of the commission, i commit myself to doing my best to convince member states also to accept this coherence and coordination approach. i said in the guidelines that the economy needs a financial system that is more ethical, robust and responsible. regulation and supervision have not kept pace with the integration and innovation of financial markets not in europe; not at global level. let me say that i have been shocked by the scale of unethical behavior that we have seen. we cannot allow a return to 'business as usual'. the issue of bonuses, for example, requires urgent action. we are now in a leading position in the g20 - a process which, by the way, was started in europe - but it is true that more needs to be done. next week, on the eve of the g20 meeting in pittsburgh, the commission will adopt proposals to build a true european system of supervision - a system that reflects the integrated nature of our single market. a review of our action in three years will provide an opportunity to see what further action is needed. it is crucial that we get regulation that ensures the responsibility and the legitimacy of the financial sector without stifling innovation. i want europe to keep its world leadership in financial services. in my guidelines i also explained why the crisis calls for a much stronger focus on the social dimension in europe at all levels of decision-making in europe, but also at national level. the financial sector and the economy may be showing signs of recovery but let's be clear the crisis is not over for those who have lost their jobs and we cannot say the crisis is over before we come back to the creation of employment instead of rising unemployment. i would like to make my commitment to a high level of employment and social cohesion through a number of actions that i have discussed with some of you. i have clearly stated my attachment to the respect of fundamental social rights and to the principle of the movement of workers. the interpretation and the implementation of the posted workers directive fall short in both respects. that is why i am committed to proposing, as soon as possible, a regulation to resolve the problems that have arisen. this regulation will be co-decided by the european parliament and the council. a regulation has the advantage of giving much more legal certainty than the revision of the directive itself, which would still leave too much room for divergent national transpositions and take longer to produce real effects on the ground. but if we discover during the preparation of the regulation that there are areas where we need to revise the directive itself, i will not hesitate to do so. let me be clear i am committed to fighting social dumping in europe whatever form it takes. the issue of social impact assessments for all future proposals was also raised and i agree that this is needed. the first test case for such a social impact assessment should be the revision of the working time directive. on the basis of this impact assessment, the next commission will consult social partners and will come with a comprehensive legislative proposal. in the guidelines, i emphasize the importance of services of general interest for our european model of society. the lisbon treaty makes this point very clear and i am ready to work with you to develop a quality framework for services of general interest. i also highlighted gender equality and the need to eliminate the gender pay gap, so i now commit myself to working with you on a women's charter, also as a way of commemorating the 15th anniversary of the beijing conference in 2010. in my guidelines i express my determination to make the lisbon treaty innovations in international relations, including the european external action service and the post of high representative and vice-president of the commission, work effectively. i believe it is one of the greatest innovations of our lisbon treaty and i am committed to reinforcing cooperation with the european parliament in the field of external affairs in general. but europe needs the means to match its ambitions. as i said in the guidelines, this requires a root-and-branch reform of the european union budget covering the expenditure and revenue side. we need to move away from a narrow focus on net balances and move towards an approach based on solidarity, burden-sharing and equity. the european union must have a more transparent and efficient way of financing its policies and i am ready i hope with the support of this parliament to take this battle to the member states as we reshape the union's budget. i also want to work more closely with the european investment bank to look at innovative forms of financing. i am also committed to smart regulation, and i want to reiterate that simplification of procedures and the reduction of administrative burdens on businesses, particularly smes, will remain a priority in the next commission. this task just like the impact assessment board and ex post evaluation will be placed directly under my authority to fully reflect the priority i give it to it. i will also defend - as we have done over the years and sometimes in difficult circumstances - the integrity of the single market because, without a single market and without a cohesion policy, we will never have a european union. but why stop there? why only defend the internal market? i want to complete the missing links to unleash its full benefits for businesses and consumers. the commission has already taken a number of decisions. i am committed to translating these priorities into the organization of the next college once i have been confirmed by you. but i can already share with you today some organizational changes that i intend to introduce. i will create the post of commissioner for justice, fundamental rights and civil liberties, including citizens' and minority rights as a reflection that the european union is a community of rights and values. i will also create the post of commissioner for internal affairs and migration, including security. one of the key tasks of this commissioner will be to develop a truly common approach to migration: promoting the integration of legal migrants, fighting illegal migration and related criminal activities, and ensuring solidarity between member states. we need solidarity. we need solidarity when we have to give support to our baltic friends or countries affected by the gas crisis between russia and ukraine, but we also need solidarity when we have to give support to our mediterranean friends when they are facing challenges with which they cannot cope alone. i will also create the post of commissioner for climate action to reflect the fact that climate change is a challenge that needs to be addressed across the whole range of our policies. a dedicated commissioner for climate action will also send an important signal that, regardless of the level of ambition that comes out of copenhagen, europe is serious about maintaining momentum for action. we also need a fundamental review of the way the european institutions access and use scientific advice. in the next commission i want to create the post of chief scientific adviser, with the power to deliver proactive, scientific advice throughout all stages of policy development and delivery. this will reflect the central priority i attach to research and innovation. i think we have a lot to do in this field. if there is one area where the fragmented efforts in europe are not giving the result we want, it is precisely in the field of research and innovation. i believe that, from fighting climate change to energy security, the potential is there if we want to work together in research and innovation for europe. what i propose is no less than a transformational agenda for europe. in order to realise this ambition, i have suggested a special partnership between parliament and the commission. we represent the two european institutions par excellence and this gives us a special responsibility to create a true european public space for debate. i am committed to making my contribution to european parliamentary democracy. i've had the opportunity to discuss this over the last couple of months with president buzek, which led to many of the improvements proposed in my guidelines, like a regular question time. following my meetings with the groups, i am ready to take up the suggestion made by some of you, not only to meet your conference of presidents on a more regular basis, but also to establish an appropriate dialogue with your conference of committee chairs. very concretely, i will invite the conference of committee chairs to meet the whole college of commissioners every year before the adoption of the commission's legislative and work programme. we are indeed living in very exceptional times, times of uncertainty and power shifts. there may be a fundamental change in the relations between the most important powers in the world and there is indeed a great risk in these times of anxiety of the emergence of national egoisms, of naked nationalism, of ugly nationalism and some forms of extremism. there is a real danger that our achievements in european integration are called into question. that is why i believe it is important to have this special relationship between commission and parliament to fight those national egoisms. let me finish with a plea to each and every one of you. now, more than ever, we need a strong europe and a strong european commission a strong commission, let us be frank, has to be a political commission but a political commission must not be a partisan commission. as president of the commission, my party is europe. the next college, like the current one, will contain a significant number of members from a variety of political families. i am committed to having europe's political diversity reflected in the college and in the most important positions. but only with this cross-party support can we in fact have a strong europe and a strong commission. we need a commission that delivers on its promises. we also need a parliament capable of mobilising the effective majorities necessary for a europe of action. if you want a strong commission that sometimes stands up to member states and to national egoisms, you should give the commission the strong support it needs. we all have our different political, ideological positions and we come from very different political families but i believe that, in times like the ones we are living in, in times of crisis, apart from our convictions we also need a strong ethic of european responsibility. it is to this ethic of european responsibility to each of you that i make my appeal my appeal with passion for europe. let us embark on this european journey together. i'd like to inform you that we have a new processing rule. maybe not everyone has heard of it yet. this rule says that if during a speech, someone in the audience raises a blue card, they can ask the person who is speaking a question. the question cannot exceed 30 seconds and the person who is speaking must agree to the question being asked. this is a new rule we haven't had before. it's about keeping our discussions alive.

with respect of community rules. this is very important. if we want to have a real european union, we have to have this internal market respected. let us be frank about it: sometimes some national politicians, when there is a problem, say it is the fault of brussels and when they have success, say it is their merit. so please let us not embark on those accusations that it is because of brussels president of the commission. - madam president, first of all a point of order. i would like to say, particularly to the non-attached members, that i did not go to their group because they did not invite me. it's very simple. of course, i have strong differences with some of these members and also with others, but i have gone to all the groups that have invited me, all the groups that have been members are not here to listen to me, but i will make an effort anyway. first, the question of the bonuses, the last question. i would draw your attention to the fact that at the end of 2004 the commission - my commission - made a recommendation on excessive remuneration, not only in banks but also in the economic system in general. unfortunately, at that time, no one paid attention to our recommendation. i am glad that the issue of bonuses and excessive pay is now a greater priority and i hope that we can find a solution, based on the proposals we have put on the council's table. they are on the table: a recommendation but also a binding part of the directive on the capital of banks. many of the questions were on energy security, from mr saryusz-wolski, mr marinescu and others. commission that europeans look to, not just the europeans of the union. at the time of the russia-ukraine problem, president putin decided to call me, precisely to inform me of this problem, and you know how much time and energy we have spent in the commission, with other partners, trying to find a solution to a problem that concerned russia and ukraine, but which had consequences for european consumers. i'm personally very attached to these files. that is why we have launched the interconnection programme in the baltic states, and why the commission has unblocked the nabucco problem, which was completely blocked, let us be clear. i therefore include these issues among the commission's top priorities, but there is indeed resistance to the implementation of a genuine internal energy market. i hope that during the next term of office, with your support, we will overcome these remaining obstacles, let us be frank and sincere, and establish a genuine integrated energy market in europe. you can count on me in the commission to defend the european interest uncompromisingly. i believe that this issue of energy security is also essential for the fight against climate change. i say again, especially to the greens: we can always be more ambitious, but frankly, i think we should be pleased that the european union, on the basis of a commission proposal, is at the forefront of the fight against climate change. it is obvious that we would not have had the agreement of all the member states afterwards if it had not been for the work, and i would like to say this, of the presidency of mrs merkel, and then of mr sarkozy, because they also worked for this, and it is right to recognise this. all the member states have made an effort, but it was on the basis of an ambitious proposal from the commission that we were able to fight against global warming and i am counting heavily on you to keep europe at the forefront of this fight. i have already given a reply on social questions: i have already given very concrete commitments on the questions of the posting of workers, on the problems of public services. i will be ready to work with you on the principles i have mentioned and have made very clear today: against social dumping, for the social market economy. i know that this is an interesting ideological debate, but i believe that we have the answer in europe. we need an internal market, which is our strength, and at the same time a high level of social cohesion. this is european creation, this is contribution. in the quotation i quoted at the beginning of my paper, i quoted a great contemporary european historian, mr tony judt, who teaches at new york university. he said, "maybe the united states will have the strongest military in the world, maybe china will sell cheaper products, but only europe has a model that can serve as an inspiration to the rest of the world". the 21st century may well be the century of europe. i believe that. i believe we can lead this globalization not with force, but with inspiration. we have a social market economy which is not owned by the christian democrats, the social democrats or the liberals. it was created by europe, especially after the second world war: not only the process of european integration, but also this social market economy which aims to combine free markets, open markets. europe is the world's largest exporting power. we europeans must therefore reject protectionism and at the same time promote the european model of social dialogue, the european model of social security. when i hear some "declinologists", "crisophiles" say that now it is the americans, the chinese, who are running everything, i say to them: what is president obama doing anyway? president obama is trying to -- i wish him luck -- to introduce a national health care system that we have pretty much everywhere in europe, with differences. it is the americans who are taking inspiration from the european model. what are the chinese doing? they're also, to support demand, thinking about starting a social security system, and i think they'll have it, because there's going to be a rise in wealth in this country, and this rise in wealth in china is good for the whole world. what are the united states and other great powers doing now? they're starting to talk to us about member of the commission. - the mr president, on mr kelly's question, it is foreseen that very large sums will be raised by the treasury departments of the member states from the auctioning of greenhouse gas emission allowances and among the measures that governments can take is to use part of this money to support low-wage or energy-poor people. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the new renewable energy directive requires member states to support and implement administrative and infrastructure reforms to facilitate the development of renewable energy sources. each member state has committed to achieving certain targets by 2020 and has to submit by june next year a national renewable energy action plan, which will analyse how the targets will be achieved. with regard to the recast of the energy performance of buildings directive, the commission has also committed to further strengthening community financial instruments and proposing new ones to support the implementation of this directive. the commission already provides direct funding for a variety of energy efficiency and renewable energy projects, such as: - a series of research and development efforts under the framework programme for research and technological development. - eur 727 million for the period 2007-2013 from the 'smart energy - europe' programme, to help remove various obstacles to the development of renewable energy sources and to improve the business environment and public awareness. - over eur 500 million for offshore wind projects under the european economic recovery programme to stimulate private investment in the sector. - the sustainable energy financing initiative, managed jointly by the commission and the european investment bank, with a budget of eur 15 million for 2009 and aimed at mobilising financial resources from the capital markets and the marguerite fund, european energy, climate change and infrastructure fund, managed by the european investment bank. the commission also encourages member states to use a significant part of the funds of the european union's cohesion policy funds to support energy efficiency and renewable energy projects.
member of the commission. − within its field of competence the commission has so far responded rapidly to help prevent disastrous social consequences in developing countries, in particular in the least-developed countries, most of which are acp states. these measures include honouring aid commitments and leveraging new resources, acting counter-cyclically, improving aid effectiveness, sustaining economic activity and employment, revitalising agriculture, investing in green growth, stimulating trade and private investment, working together for economic governance and stability, and protecting the most vulnerable in developing countries. concrete actions and procedures have already been put in place to speed up delivery of aid. an ad hoc ‘vulnerability flex’ instrument will mobilise eur 500 million from the european development fund. this v-flex is complementary to actions taken by the world bank and the imf, and will target the most vulnerable countries with poor resilience capacity, giving rapid grant assistance to help them to maintain priority spending, notably in the social sectors. as the v-flex utilises previously unallocated reserve funds, it represents additional financing for these highly vulnerable countries. eur 80 million has also been mobilised for the funding under the existing edf flex mechanism for countries that suffered significant export losses in 2008. in addition, the mid-term review of cooperation strategies for countries funded from the ec budget is currently under way, and the mid-term review for acp countries funded from the edf has been accelerated in order to re-define and adjust the national strategies and allocations in early 2010. nevertheless it is important to recall that development policy is a shared competence within the eu. the prime responsibility for delivering on the oda commitments lies with the member states themselves. i strongly believe that the crisis should not be an excuse for our member states mr. chairman, please! five years ago, the baltic sea became virtually an internal sea of the european union. today we are debating a draft strategy to make the most of the enormous potential of this region, a project initiated by the european parliament. however, not all the recommendations of our chamber have been accepted by the commission. the most serious is the absence and abandonment of the creation of a separate budget line for the baltic sea region. the commission shall ensure that the funding will come from existing instruments, mainly the structural funds. however, i am afraid that without the funds earmarked for this purpose alone, we will not be able to achieve all the objectives we have set out. the authors of the strategy mention the need for close cooperation with russia. however, the biggest threat to the baltic sea today, the construction of the nord stream pipeline, cannot be ignored. the european parliament adopted a negative position on this issue last year. i hope that the new commission will also bear this resolution in mind when implementing the action plan attached to the strategy.
mr president, it is indeed a unique european regional policy initiative and a pioneering project. innovation-driven prosperity, the environment, accessibility in terms of transport and energy connections, and security and safety are the four major areas for joint work by all partners who are involved in preparation of the strategy: all three european institutions – parliament, the commission, the council – but also national governments, regional and local authorities, business and academic communities and non-governmental organisations. the process of the preparation of the strategy has led to a genuine partnership between all of them. development challenges increasingly do not respect administrative or political borders. the strategy will make it possible to replace the often very fragmented and scattered policy responses with a genuine shared response to shared development problems and opportunities. the european parliament’s committee on regional development, which is the leading committee on this project in parliament, will give high importance to it in its work. we will hold the debate on 6 october with the commission and the council; the own-initiative report will be prepared in the months to come. we will also keep the implementation of the strategy under review and i trust that this action-oriented strategy enhances the union’s chances to build green, modern and competitive economies.
in writing. the baltic sea strategy, announced in june 2009, aims to make the region environmentally friendly, prosperous, easily accessible and attractive, and safe. this is particularly relevant in the context of the increasing challenges facing the baltic sea since the eu enlargement in 2004. it is important to take action to improve the ecological situation in this region, which is currently one of the most polluted marine areas in the world. thousands of tons of toxic warfare agents lie at the bottom of the baltic sea in mines, missiles, bombs, containers and barrels. the quantity of these chemicals ranges from 30 to 60 thousand tonnes, of which the quantity of the mustard gas itself is estimated at 13 thousand tonnes. the chemical weapons were sunk after world war ii, in the late 1940s. it was a weapon found in the german occupation zones, and it was difficult to bury it in the ground, so it was decided that it would be best to sink it in the seas. the breach of the chemical weapons stored on the bottom of the baltic sea by creating any kind of infrastructure can lead to an ecological disaster, and it is the breach during the construction of the baltic gas pipeline of the chemical weapons storage sites from the second world war that is one of the greatest threats to the ecosystem. it is therefore necessary to assess the environmental impact of the construction of the pipeline on the baltic sea basin.

clear signal that we are opening a new chapter in our relations between the european union and tajikistan. tajikistan is an important part of our overall strategy for central asia. it's a hard-to-reach country, one of the poorest countries in the world. it has a poorly guarded border with afghanistan, and is thus a major drug smuggling route and an entry point for radical islamists into the region. we therefore have a great interest in supporting tajikistan, both for its own sake and to try to solve common problems. we're already doing that through a series of contacts. the the eu's eastern neighbourhood with which we have not yet concluded a comprehensive post-cold war agreement. if we are serious about addressing all the issues i have mentioned, we must create an appropriate framework for our future relations. the arrangements for political dialogue and practical cooperation with tajikistan need to be improved to better reflect the common challenges facing the region. a partnership and cooperation agreement would allow for a more structured discussion of issues of common interest: human rights, the rule of law, the fight against drugs and organised crime, as well as terrorism and religious organisation. at the same time, we must make progress on issues of democracy, good governance and human rights in the region. we are well aware that this is not an easy task. it is therefore very welcome that there is a structured dialogue on human rights with tajikistan which gives us the opportunity to have a frank discussion. the second round of this dialogue will take place on 23 september in dushanbe. we must continue to encourage tajikistan to embark on a reform programme. the way things turn out is often very worrying. we would like to see a more democratic approach in the country in terms of freedom of association, freedom of religion, freedom of the media and the development of civil society. we must do our utmost to convince tajikistan that the rule of law must be respected in the fight against illegal activities, drug trafficking and terrorism. we must stress that human rights and fundamental freedoms must be respected as a means of preventing ethnic or cultural conflicts. we are also very concerned about the widespread corruption in the country. it impedes both the development of tajikistan and effective donor contributions. we should use all available channels to appeal to the tajik authorities to address this problem as quickly as possible. we cannot ignore the fact that all - or at least a very large number - of drug trafficking transit routes pass through tajikistan. the country is at risk of exposure to radical movements and international organised crime. we must increase our support for tajikistan to counter this activity, but at the same time consider alternative sources of revenue. this strategy is also very much in line with our commitment to afghanistan and the efforts to stabilise that country. we welcome tajikistan's interest in cooperating and contributing to these efforts. tajikistan has shown an open and constructive attitude to discussions on our common challenges. that's good. this dialogue is an important element in assisting tajikistan in promoting cooperation with its neighbours and in finding solutions to pressing and complex regional problems, such as climate change, water and border management. given our strong interest in addressing many of these problems more effectively and efficiently, i welcome the opportunity to create a new basis for our relations with tajikistan. the partnership and cooperation agreement provides us with a framework within which to further develop bilateral relations and thereby contribute to the overall objectives of our strategy throughout central asia. i therefore call on this parliament to give its consent to the conclusion of the agreement so that it can enter into force as soon as possible.

central asia strategy any more, nor does it serve to support the kind of relationship we now seek with tajikistan. your assent to the new eu-tajikistan partnership and cooperation agreement, which is before you for debate today, would therefore represent a major step forward, allowing us to widen and deepen our cooperation with this country. today’s tajikistan is confronted as has been said already by major economic and social challenges. it is important – and in europeans’ own interests – that tajikistan should succeed in tackling its difficulties. this is a country which shares a nearly 1 500 km border with afghanistan, and which lies close to the swat valley in pakistan. it is a territory vulnerable to spill-over from these conflict areas and to infiltration by islamic militants. tajikistan is also key to efforts to stem the flow of illegal drugs to europe from afghanistan. greater cooperation with the european union can therefore play a part in helping to prevent the spread of instability. a key element in tajikistan’s vulnerabilities is its weak economy. the poorest of the central asian republics has been badly hit by a substantial decrease in prices for aluminium and cotton due to the global downturn. this, taken together with a 34% drop in remittances in the first half of 2009, gives rise to concern that poverty levels may be rising, and that a precarious socioeconomic situation could provoke social unrest. i believe that we are now on the right track with tajikistan, supporting and encouraging indispensable reforms. this has also been the focus of eu special representative morel’s frequent visits and of my own visit in spring 2008. there is progress but clearly more needs to be done. the government has made clear that, in addition to greater trade and cooperation, it is willing to implement measures to improve social welfare, health, education, tackle corruption and improve human rights. it is to be welcomed that president rahmon reform is still making slow progress, but we hope the recommendations of a recent human rights civil society seminar in dushanbe will be taken into account by the government, particularly in reform of the legal profession and the new criminal procedure code in tajikistan. i am of course very well aware of your concerns on democracy and human rights in tajikistan and i can therefore assure you that the commission will take these concerns fully into account in our dialogues with this country. as to the economic reforms, we see progress for example on the drafting of a cotton debt resolution mechanism, which hopefully will pave the way for wider agricultural reforms and the implementation of ‘freedom to farm’, crucial to tackling poverty in the country. the european parliament’s assent to the pca today will help us to continue to work with tajikistan on a whole range of political and economic reforms, with a special focus on democracy and human rights, and also to ensure their thorough implementation. the reform effort is already underpinned by a relatively large amount of bilateral assistance from the commission. indeed it is eur 66 million for the period 2007 to 2010 which will even rise to eur 70 million over the three years 2011 and 2013. our aid will focus on sector support for social protection and health, public finance management reform and technical assistance for private sector development. this process will be supported by our delegation in dushanbe. it is my intention that, before the end of this year, our regionalised office there should become a fully-fledged delegation to encourage the reform process and facilitate full implementation of the pca. in particular, i hope it will help us to maintain a thorough assessment of progress in the key areas as i have mentioned, which we will then measure against clear benchmarks.

mr president, madam minister, madam chairman of the commission! instead of using big words - and i think there's an inflation of big words in the european parliament - it's worth asking why the irish said yes, when last year they said no. i think it is an oversimplification to say that the crisis has pushed the irish into the arms of the lisbon treaty. it seems that the main reason the irish, the citizens of the green island, supported the treaty is what they got from the european union in the meantime. ireland has guaranteed itself and all the member states its own national commissioner. that's what we have ireland to thank for. the union also guaranteed that it would not interfere with taxation in ireland. and for that, we thank dublin. it is hoped that this will be the final withdrawal of germany and france from plans to unify taxes within the union. finally, brussels promised not to interfere with the republic of ireland's legislation on moral and civil matters, including the protection of the life of the unborn. the irish government and the irish people should be congratulated on this success in the negotiations. and funny, in a way, is the joy of those who are celebrating the result of the referendum in ireland. in many cases, these same people were against holding referendums in their member states.
mr. chairman, please! the adoption of the treaty of lisbon marks the end of a historic process of major enlargement of the european union with ten new member states. this process began in the 1990s and culminates in the acceptance of institutional changes that adapt the union to the new reality. the adoption of the treaty is a new stage and an opportunity for the union to take a step forward. the institutions that we will be able to create are only an opportunity, and it is up to us to make the most of that opportunity. it is also a good moment to prove to citizens who are sceptical of the european project that the union is alive, changing and, above all, responding to people's problems. the most important thing is to propose a new policy to meet the challenges we face. but there is a fear that instead of focusing on this, we will be dominated by discussions about formal and personal solutions: who to choose for what positions? the european union must not allow national egoism, which can grow stronger in times of crisis, to undermine the opportunity that the union now has. the first thing to do is to convince citizens that the union is not just about elites, posts and red tape, but also about new and more effective ways of solving their problems.
mr. chairman, please! the lisbon treaty has enabled europe to tackle challenges that go far beyond the internal problems of its member states. will she be willing to do that? it's hard to say. the european citizens will certainly have a lot to say about this. but beyond the treaty, the union must also have the will to act, a presence in the world, a sense of responsibility for the world, its stability and development. its security and development also depend on it. we must confront the often-repeated metaphor of europe as a country that is safe, prosperous, democratic, human rights-loving, but that is introverted, that turns its back on the world. the lisbon treaty forces us to better understand the challenges we face. in irish, "so" is a way of saying that a united europe is now looking at poland and the czech republic. i have no doubt that the treaty of lisbon will soon enter into force. but while we wait for the signatures of presidents kaczyński and klaus, let's think about how the discussion during the current reform went, let's draw conclusions from what happened. let's prepare for the future! let's prepare for the next reform, because the great project we are creating - the european union - is an unfinished idea. and i just want to say one last thing: thank you, ireland!
in writing. president lech kaczyński, contrary to a public promise, has not yet signed the treaty of lisbon. the delay has been over a year and a half. it is unjustified, reprehensible, even illegal. on 1 april 2008, the president was authorised by the sejm to ratify the treaty of lisbon. according to the constitution of the republic, the president has to sign it. it's not a question of his good will or his willingness, but his duty. if he doesn't do it, he's breaking the law. by making the signing of the treaty dependent on the decision of citizens of another country, president kaczyński has made poland a country incapable of taking a sovereign decision and has offended the patriotic feelings of poles. in ireland, the supporters of a strong, united union have won. in poland, a president who has almost no support in the public is on the verge of victory. was he holding back for personal reasons, afraid of losing a hard-line anti-union electorate, including one associated with radio maria? if so, it's high time we started impeachment proceedings. according to the constitution of the republic of poland, there are two possible ways. the state court or the application of article 131 (4) of the polish constitution (recognition by the national assembly of the permanent incapacity of the president of the republic to perform his duties on grounds of ill-health). the poles don't want to hold back the development of the european union. no, it's the opposite. they want to initiate beneficial changes in europe. president kaczynski has no right to interfere.
in writing. although the union and its institutions function well without the lisbon treaty, its non-adoption would create the image of a community unable to agree and take important decisions. this treaty introduces new voting rules, where the strength of the states' vote is explicitly dependent on the number of inhabitants. compared to the current nice voting system, large countries, including germany, gain and medium countries, including poland, which benefited from the nice vote, lose. the creation of a new institution, the president of the european council, commonly referred to as the eu president, raises some concerns about the division of powers. let us remember that there are already: the president of the european commission and the president of the parliament, and the head of state who holds the presidency of the union - the so-called presidency - and the high representative for foreign affairs. in addition to introducing the position of high representative, popularly known as the union minister for foreign affairs, the treaty strengthens the union's foreign policy by establishing common diplomacy. it also sets out the possibility of withdrawal from the union, the possibility of a citizens' initiative and the need to create a european energy policy, which is very important for the future of europe. we look forward to the final ratification of the treaty!
in writing. – irish 'yes' to the lisbon treaty is a good news for europe. there is no doubt that the treaty will serve for the benefit of the european union by simplifying its decision making process and creating a better field for its effectiveness. in contrary to what its opponents say the treaty does not bring any major revolution. never before however so much has depended on the process of implementation. the devil is in the detail. with its innovations the treaty can increase for instance visibility of the eu on the international scene. much depends however on the final arrangements that will determine the character of the new instruments, like the european external action service. it is therefore essential that the european parliament takes its due role in the process of creating new institutional setting foreseen by the lisbon treaty, wherever possible. it will make this process more transparent, increase its legitimacy and finally it will serve, i believe,for its better outcome.

agenda. on monday 28 september more than 100 people were killed in conakry, guinea, when members of the guinean security forces shot into crowds of demonstrators. guinean citizens had gathered in a stadium in the capital to demonstrate against the presumed intention of the guinean military interim leader, captain moussa dadis camara, to run for president. the final death toll is still unknown, as the soldiers also collected the bodies rather than allow them to be counted at public morgues. at this stage we do not know the real dimension of these tragic events. the number of injured people is said to be at least 1 200, and eye witnesses have reported that soldiers raped women on the streets of conakry. during the violent repression, several opposition leaders were wounded and temporarily arrested. the number of protestors still under detention is also unknown; the houses of opposition leaders were ransacked and shops looted by uniformed men. in a tv statement the following day, captain camara expressed his condolences with the families of those killed and visited some of the injured. he proclaimed two days of national mourning and pledged to investigate the violence. he distanced himself from the killings by saying that he was not in control of the elements of the military responsible for the atrocities. the european union immediately and forcefully condemned these brutal and shocking events. a presidency declaration, a statement by high representative solana and a statement by eu commissioner de gucht were issued the following day. we will have to insist on the liberation of the arrested prisoners and a thorough investigation of the events. the violence in guinea received worldwide condemnation. the un security council was briefed last wednesday on the situation in the country. the african union condemned the events and decided to prepare a report on possible measures to be taken. the economic community of west african states (ecowas) called for a full international inquiry into the matter. parliament, as you know, condemned the unconstitutional change of power, and in its resolution of 15 january 2009 called for respect for human rights and a rapid return to constitutional order. the eu decided to open consultations under article 96 of the cotonou agreement, and eu development aid – apart from humanitarian aid and support for democratic transition – was frozen. we have not been alone; our international partners have acted in line with us. the african union and ecowas decided to suspend guinea until it established a democratically elected parliament or government. an international contact group on guinea co-chaired by the african union and ecowas, and with participation by the european union, was put into place. in march, the military junta agreed with the opposition to have elections before the end of 2009, which gave reasonable hope for a peaceful and democratic transition. captain camara gave his assurances that none of the coup leaders would stand for political office. a national transitional council was to guide the transition process and prepare the necessary modification of the constitution in order to help elections. what can we do, then, to prevent further violence, and how can we help the people of guinea in their legitimate desire for democracy, the rule of law, peace and development? well, there are three main areas of action. first of all we should maintain and reinforce political pressure on the regime in conakry, notably in the context of the international group. captain camara’s decision not to run could allow calm to return. the nomination of the president of burkina faso, mr blaise compaoré, as facilitator in the crisis on behalf of ecowas and the international contact group is a very positive sign, and the european union has welcomed this appointment via the presidency. we hope that his mediation will contribute to a secure, peaceful and lasting solution to the situation in guinea. secondly, the option of targeted sanctions against individuals responsible for violence could be further explored. we will need to coordinate this approach with the african union and other international and bilateral partners. the upcoming eu-african ministerial troika in addis ababa and the meeting on guinea on 12 october in abuja will be important in this respect. thirdly, we should continue to provide humanitarian aid to the civilian population and support the democratic transition process. the latter will nevertheless depend on the credible willingness of the transitional authorities of guinea to re-engage in a peaceful and constructive dialogue with a clear commitment to refraining from further violence and to respecting the human rights and political freedoms of its citizens. we will spare no efforts to help the people of guinea in this critical moment and we are determined to support a return to civilian, constitutional and democratic government through free and transparent elections. we encourage all stakeholders in guinea to refrain from violence and to make a peaceful and democratic transition.

madam president! the word "schengen" has been changed in this room by all the cases. most of us would agree that this is a great success, for the people of the new countries, the new members of the european union, this is a measurable success of integration. but at the same time, it's a huge commitment that these countries, the baltic countries, poland, slovakia, romania and bulgaria, have made. the new member states are responsible for the eastern land border of the european union and are fulfilling that responsibility to the full. but i'd like to say something that wasn't discussed in this room. the schengen agreement, which we are proud of and which we admire, is a nightmare and a source of great difficulty for all those who have been granted a visa policy, the so-called schengen visas. i am talking about the people of ukraine, moldova and other eastern countries who want to come to the european union. schengen visas are very expensive, and the people in these countries have to pay about what they earn in a month. they're subjected to the humiliating process of getting these visas, standing in gigantic queues. this is schengen, too, for them schengen means shame, wall and problem. i would like to see the schengen evaluation system at least mention what is related to the visa policy, evaluate it, evaluate how, perhaps in some way justified, but we do not know for how long, we have introduced such instruments that separate us from the many people who naturally want to come to our area, this schengen area. and while that's not the subject of this report, i wanted those words to be heard here in the debate today.
madam president! it is fortunate that the discussion we are having today on the schengen acquis comes at a time when the european union, including the european parliament, is beginning a major debate on the so-called stockholm programme, a major project concerning areas of vital importance to the citizens of the european union, such as justice, freedom and security. the two elements of this programme, namely the freedom and security of the citizens of the european union, are perfectly in line with the assessment of the schengen project. we must ask ourselves why the european union was created and why we are so concerned about the success of this great project. after all, it was not made for politicians, international organizations, or individual nations. it was actually created for the good of the citizens. the welfare of citizens, their freedom and liberty, but also the highest standards of security that should be guaranteed to them, are therefore among the main elements of the work that the institutions of the european union should be concerned with. it is therefore not right that we are discussing the excluded schengen area without linking this discussion to the evaluation of the community programme on migration, the community visa programme and the community programme on cooperation with the so-called neighbouring countries. only a joint discussion and assessment of the situation can lead to the right conclusions. that is why parliament needs to be involved in these decisions, and i hope that it will be. therefore, i am convinced that the schengen acquis, which
