possible, in cooperation with the european parliament, of course. i therefore have great respect for carlos coelho and i fully support his report.
madam president! due to delays and problems in completing sis ii and the forecasts that it will not be fully operational until the end of 2011, or even as some claim in 2015, it was decided to carry out tests of sis ii to check its functionality by the end of this year. if sis ii is found to be defective, an alternative plan is supposedly in place to improve sis i. the questions therefore arise: is the european commission prepared to implement the alternative plan, how will the issue of the investments made by the member states that incurred the costs associated with the purchase of equipment to operate the new system be resolved and whether it will be used in the alternative plan, and how does the commission intend to enforce contractual penalties on the project promoters?
the next item on the agenda is the statements by the council and the commission on climate change and developing countries in the context of the un conference on climate change in copenhagen.
mr. chairman, please! i was very concerned to hear reports of the meeting of the ministers of finance and the ministers of the environment, and in particular the draft outcome document, which fails to address the key question: how does the european union intend to support the world's poorest countries in their efforts to reduce carbon emissions and adapt to climate change? this is indeed a crucial matter. the draft document does not even repeat the amounts proposed by the european commission: that the needs of developing countries in this area are estimated at 100 billion euros per year until 2020, and what would the european union's possible contribution be in this amount? moreover, there is no decision on what cofinancing mechanism the member states should introduce, and we know that the proposals in this area are very different. of course, it is understandable that some people argue that we should be careful with specific declarations, and wait for proposals from other countries, especially economically strong ones. but if the union is to be a leader in the fight against climate change, it must try to put forward concrete proposals and concrete solutions, especially since some of this is our internal affair, like the co-financing mechanism. it is our duty to negotiate a fair deal with the developing countries. the world's poorest countries have contributed the least to climate change, yet they are the ones suffering the most from its consequences. the heavy dependence of many of the poor countries on agriculture and fisheries, as well as their poor infrastructure, puts them in a very difficult situation when it comes to climate change. so far in the last four years, africa alone, the poorest of the continents and one of the most vulnerable to the consequences of climate change, has received less than 12 percent of the funds that are available to fight climate change. that way we don't get those countries to get involved in this process.
mr. chairman, please! parliament's position on the global distribution of co2 reduction commitments is unfortunately unbalanced in terms of the cost of this reduction. the resolution calls into question the hard-won climate package, the costs of which are now being borne unevenly by the central european member states. adopting the solutions proposed today will only further increase these inequalities. we are trying to impose economically lethal standards on member states, while not requiring anything specific from the countries most responsible for co2 emissions in the world. it's unfair and ineffective. and without global scale, we're only deepening the competitive advantage of china, india, brazil. the resolution goes even further. it proposes that we pay extra to the poorest countries. 330 billion euros by 2020 means between 16.5 billion and even 40 billion from a country like poland. this is political madness that undermines the economic sense of being a member of the european union. moreover, this method is ineffective, as demonstrated by the preparations for the start-up of export power plants in the kaliningrad region bordering poland. copenhagen is not worth signing an agreement that will not share the burden of reducing co2 emissions in the world proportionately.
madam president! the european union is a leader internationally in promoting dialogue on climate change and in setting policy priorities for reducing co2 emissions. in the ongoing preparations for the copenhagen conference, the european union has made more commitments than any other region in the world. none of the industrialized powers, nor the united states, japan or australia, has so far come up with a concrete proposal, with concrete numbers to help developing countries in their efforts to reduce co2 emissions and support the development of energy-efficient renewable energy technologies. europe will only be a credible partner in the negotiations if it presents realistic, achievable and common sense proposals that will be the starting point for achieving international consensus and agreement. europe now needs allies and support for its current proposals. therefore, it is prudent to raise the reduction commitments from 20% to 30% if other industrialized countries are not willing to set themselves such ambitious targets. financial support for developing countries should also be a real commitment. it can't just be a wish list. it should be an aid scheme that takes account of the principles of sustainable development and should allow beneficiaries to plan their actions. another point, which is important from the point of view of the citizens of europe, is that we should not forget that the copenhagen summit, our resolutions and the preparations of parliament for that summit should be accompanied by a clearly defined system of communication with the citizens, with society. the commission's proposal is to set up a european network of experts to help the eu institutions and citizens to develop their own climate action plans.
madam president! in the context of our debate, i would like to draw attention to two aspects. firstly, when we propose to reduce co2 emissions and to allocate funds to developing countries, we cannot forget the current economic and financial situation caused by the global crisis, because setting ambitious targets is very important, but i think the most important thing is to achieve them. secondly, we should focus on the issue of public awareness and the need for change in environmental issues. a study conducted at last year's poznan climate conference shows that the public sees climate change as a serious problem, but believes that it is only up to the government to solve it. this is why we need an appeal, an information campaign, to change attitudes and promote behavioural patterns to increase efficiency or reduce energy consumption in households and to make people aware that the way we live, the way we work has an economic and ecological cost.
in writing. for the past five years, i have witnessed an unprecedented climate hysteria being unleashed here in the european parliament by a select group of recruits from all political factions, mainly the greens and the socialists. this hysteria is skillfully fuelled by speeches by the president of the commission and the former president of parliament, who are threatening unimaginable disasters from climate change. people who think rationally about this issue are accused of having no moral code and are simply - as in my case today - not given a 'democratic' voice. the economic decisions contained in the climate and energy package, based on the unreliable hypothesis of the causes of climate change, are not only a cynical mockery of common sense, but also a harbinger of future economic and civilizational disaster. we must demand an honest discussion, based on the views of the whole objective world of science, on the causes of climate change and, above all, on how to prevent it.
in writing. a month and a half before the copenhagen summit, the world is looking to us to take concrete action, to be responsible and to think in terms of working together for people and their safety, in the face of the inevitability of climate change. you all know the reports of the intergovernmental panel on climate change, which clearly state that most of the warming observed over the last 50 years is due to human activities. climate change has become the geopolitical and economic priority of the 21st century, which requires bold and long-term action. we need to define, through global consensus, climate treaties that will build new models for reducing emissions after 2012. the kyoto protocol was the first step in breaking the minds of world governments about environmental protection. we should continue to think this way. but the point is, you can't just stop at reducing emissions through developed countries like the united states or china. support is needed for smaller, poorer countries that are struggling to implement alternative, green energy sources. it's not just about funding, it's about education and sharing experiences in building green economies. when we make decisions, let us also remember the citizens. they're the ones we should be informing, educating and encouraging to invest in the environment. as with any security policy, citizen support and cooperation is essential.
mr. chairman, please! the schengen treaty has given a new quality to the territory of most of the countries of the european union. despite the fact that it has been so short a time, we often forget what europe looked like with its border crossings and the difficulties of moving people between the member states. the schengen agreement is another success of our integration, but it also brings with it a great responsibility. the new member states have taken responsibility for a large part of the land borders. in addition to the positives, there are also negatives, as too many restrictions have been introduced on the movement of residents of neighbouring countries bordering mainly on the new countries of the union, such as poland and latvia. these difficulties have resulted, among other things, in severe restrictions on movement along our eastern borders. a new division is being created, a kind of barrier between countries that have had and have close relations due to history, family ties and, above all, neighbourly ties. in accordance with the schengen provisions, a common internal control system has been introduced for the relevant services in the european union countries that are signatories to this system. however, it seems that this system of controls is being used excessively, which does not serve to build a positive image of the unity of the european union.
in writing. - i voted with great pleasure in favour of the resolution on the regulation repealing certain acts in the field of the cap, because we keep hearing that we have too many regulations in the eu that restrict the functioning of the market economy. this is particularly true of the cap, where many existing acts are no longer needed, despite the introduction of many simplifications and the abolition of a number of provisions. a number of acts no longer have legal effect and the contents of subsequent acts have been incorporated into other documents. this creates a huge time and financial burden on our farmers and requires extensive administration. i therefore believe that it is necessary to further update, consolidate, simplify union law and repeal a number of unnecessary acts so that the existing rules are simple, transparent and understandable. it will bring the union closer to its citizens.

president of the commission. - first of all, mr rangel, thank you very much for your greetings. it is with great pleasure that i now find in the european parliament the same procedure that we have in portugal and that i have followed, both as leader of the opposition and as prime minister, and i therefore hope to have a good opportunity to debate with the honourable members. as regards the specific question you are asking, the question is clear to me: all the countries have already approved the treaty of lisbon from a democratic point of view. ireland by referendum, the other countries by parliamentary procedure. the ratification process in the czech republic has yet to be completed. we are waiting for the conclusion of the procedure before the constitutional court, but when that procedure is completed we will certainly have completed the ratification process because there is a general principle of law, european law and international law, which is the principle of loyalty in cooperation between the member states and the institutions and also the principle of good faith in the negotiation of international agreements.
president of the commission. - the european council decided that it could only appoint new commissioners when there was legal clarity on the treaty and at the moment we have not yet completed this process. the commission will therefore be in a current affairs situation as from 1 november. we obviously want this process to be as rapid as possible and we are preparing everything, everything we can prepare for the next commission and that is what we will do. now, there is one point here, and i have to be honest with the members: we are not in control of the exact timing, it obviously depends on the completion of the ratification process in the czech republic.

president of the commission. − thank you very much, mr kamiński. in fact i said in my political guidelines, which i believe were endorsed by the european parliament with the strong support you gave for my re-election, that the internal market is a priority and we should fight all kinds of economic nationalism. i have good news for all of you. just today i entrusted mario monti with a mission to prepare a report on the future of the single market, containing options and recommendations for an initiative to relaunch the single market. i am delighted that he has accepted this mission, as it is a way of having some outside expertise, to build support, hopefully together with the european parliament, so that we can give a new impetus to the internal market, and to see how we can make the internal market fit for the 21st century. i believe that this is particularly important for consumers and also for small and medium-sized companies, which sometimes feel the pressure and suffer from distorting behaviour in the common market.

mr. chairman, please! i hope the dairy farmers are over the worst of it. this hope is reinforced by the decision to support milk producers with eur 280 million next year. but the key question remains: what about production and milk producers in the long term? the most important issue in this case is the future of milk quotas. we have two trends today. the first is the result of the review of the common agricultural policy, which gradually increases production quotas and aims to abolish quotas in 2015. and the second trend is contained in the current proposal of the european commission, which aims to reduce milk supply by means of a new method of calculating the surplus levy. these two tendencies are contradictory. i am personally in favour of maintaining the quotas, but only if the allocation of quotas between the countries of the european union and the producers is based on objective and fair criteria. to develop and adopt such fair and objective criteria would be very difficult, but it might be worth a try. as regards the extension of article 186, yes, but i think that this should be accompanied by a definition of the tasks and instruments that the commission will be able to use.

acting president of the council. - mr president! - what is it? we are facing a meeting of the european council next week. it is a wide-ranging agenda and many issues affect the welfare of all of us. we will discuss issues such as combating climate change, finding ways to lead the eu out of the financial and economic crisis, promoting energy security and tackling the problem of irregular migration. the european union will be best prepared to deal with all these issues if we get clarity on the treaty issue. it is important that the treaty of lisbon can enter into force as soon as interest to the european parliament. at the end of next week, the heads of state or government will try to clarify the ratification of the lisbon treaty and the progress of that process. the address the issue of deciding on the eu's bid in the negotiations on emission reductions for international aviation and shipping, develop the eu's strategy for action in developing countries in terms former president of the czech republic. - mr president, madam member, ladies and gentlemen, thank you for the invitation and for the opportunity to speak to you on the twentieth anniversary of the dramatic breaking down of border barriers, the cutting of barbed wire, the demolition of the wall between european nations and, in the case of germany, the wall between two parts of the same nation. it was the end of the bipolar divide, not just in europe, but in much of the world. it was a moment so historically important that many felt that from this moment on, there would be peace and the world would only flourish. it didn't happen, the story didn't end, of course. it is all the more important to see this anniversary not only as a call to reflect on the present but, above all, as a call to reflect on the future. i shall add five comments on the subject of european integration. for such a surprisingly rapid fall of the iron curtain, none of us were and could have been completely prepared. it would be against nature. and so there was a phase of certain embarrassment, of exploring different alternatives, of uncertainty. later, nato boldly expanded to include new members, anchoring them securely and helping them focus on preparing to join the european union. later, the union really began to open up to the new democracies of central and eastern europe. he has had some trouble with these countries from time to time. it's more than understandable. a democratic political culture cannot be created or restored overnight. it takes a long time, and there are a lot of unexpected problems to solve. communism was in power for the first and hopefully the last time in modern history, and so for the first time we were also faced with the phenomenon of post-communism. we had to face the consequences of a long reign of fear and all the dangers associated with a historically unprecedented redistribution of property. there are many obstacles, and the experience of such a state of affairs is still in its infancy. still, i think the west did the right thing. any other alternative would have been more troublesome and costly, not only for him but for everyone. not only could a new struggle for spheres of influence or even dominance over each other develop in earnest, but the states that remained outside the western gates would most likely become the breeding grounds of various nationalists and populists, as well as their armed militias, and perhaps the site of dangerous local conflicts, all the more dangerous since, for obvious reasons, no real peace conference has ever been held since the second world war to bindingly, precisely and permanently adjust post-war conditions in europe. i think many of those who have been brandishing flags with sickles and hammers in their hands until recently would be able to grab the national flag very quickly. we could see where this path leads in the former yugoslavia. but demons, as we know, always awaken other demons. so no one knows if the disease will spread to western europe. we live in a time when any local conflict - thanks to globalisation - can easily escalate into a global one. the procedure chosen was therefore the most natural and practical one in history. moreover, it was a move that could also be interpreted as an expression of reflected shared responsibility for recent developments, the origins of which included some short-sighted concessions by the democratic world. i would therefore like to conclude by saying that whatever concerns the european union has today are worth accepting, because any alternative to the present course of events would be much worse and more dangerous. the only thing we can ask of europe in this respect is for understanding and patience. the question is, of course, what can we offer europe? i have long believed that after what we have undergone in the totalitarian system, we should or we are directly obliged to explain this experience convincingly to others and to turn everything that follows from it into concrete impulses. it's not easy, and i'm not sure we've succeeded so far. for totalitarian or authoritarian forms of government have very subtle beginnings and very sophisticated ways of controlling society. only now, with the passage of time, are many of us realizing how sophisticatedly we have sometimes been entangled in totalitarian networks. all of which requires us to exercise extreme caution. it should be our contribution to ensuring that what we've been through can never happen again. what does it require? first of all, a clear and unequivocal solidarity with all those who today face totalitarian or authoritarian regimes anywhere in the world. no economic or other particular interests should prevent such solidarity. even a small, subtle and well-intentioned compromise can even after a long time and indirectly have its fatal consequences. evil cannot be given a chance, for by its very nature, it will exploit any opportunity to give it a chance. europe has had its share of bad experiences with appeasement policies. to free-thinking people or to outspoken witnesses of conditions in north korea, burma, iran, tibet, belarus, cuba, or elsewhere, our support may help more than we think. but it will help us too. it will help us to prepare a better world and at the same time to be better ourselves, that is, to better embody the concrete content of the values we profess in general. the european parliament recently awarded the sakharov memorial prize to the russian community monitoring human rights in russia. i think it was an important act. i remember what it meant in my country when the president of france invited us to a working breakfast during his state visit, against the will of the leadership of the state. it's all about the surface. in totalitarian conditions, it's just that one breakfast or one suppressed student demonstration can, under certain circumstances, set history in motion. each of us, beyond our own unique identity as a being, is also made up of several layers of our shared identity. to a greater or lesser degree, each of us is also shaped by our family, community, country, company, church, association or political party, our nation, our civilization, and finally the inhabitants of this planet. all of this points to some type of home, whether geographic, ideological, linguistic, ethnic or otherwise, all of which we are co-created with. and to all of this, we must also add our different types of patriotism, our goals, our affinities, our inclinations, our pride, our characters, our traditions, our customs, our habits, our peculiarities. the world is diverse, the human race is diverse, and each of us is diverse. of course, this shared responsibility also gives rise to shared sovereignty. we have some sovereignty on all levels of our identity, but we don't have, and we can't have, complete sovereignty on any. the only thing that is going on is that these sovereignties should complement each other and, as far as possible, not contradict each other. you can imagine why i am making this point here: the debate on the european constitution and the treaty of lisbon is largely centred on the question of the relationship between national and european sovereignty. the answer is clear: they should complement each other. just because i feel european doesn't mean i'm not czech. on the contrary, as a czech, i am also a european. i am saying in a rather poetic way that europe is the homeland of our homelands. i am convinced that european sovereignty will gradually be strengthened in the future. i don't know if it's faster or slower, i don't know what turns and twists it's going to take, but i know that the integration process has to continue. it is in the vital, even existential, interest not only of europeans but of all. the reasons are obvious: we live in a single global civilization, where it doesn't matter whether the owner of a greenland fishing business lives in taiwan and owns a piece of a bank in brazil or the owner of a czech mine runs his business from a computer in iceland. in such an area, the various transnational, supranational and continental communities play and will play an increasingly important role. there is not and will not be an end to nation states, only these states are coming together and will continue to come together and act in many ways together. technological and economic development will simply force it. on the other hand, at a time when the world is moving towards a dangerous unification, the formation of various smaller communities of states and peoples, which are in some way close to each other, can be one of the instruments for better defending their national or regional identities. the free and non-violent association of states also enhances peaceful coexistence. or were most of the wars of recent centuries wars between nation-states? what better way to tame the various national rages than by the practical cooperation of nations? however, the principle of multi-layered sovereignty can only be accepted against the background of civil and political identification with it. i have noticed that in our country - and probably in many other countries - we often talk about the czechs and the czechs, and that they are some kind of evil foreigners in brussels. but aren't we in brussels too? this division between us as a priori good people and as evil people who want to harm us at any cost reveals only one thing: a poor understanding of the very principle of integration. so, too, we must face it patiently. we're on the same ship, and that ship has a good heading. and it will be as long as all its passengers share responsibility and do not play their own game and play for themselves. we do not gain significance or uniqueness in a community by shouting about our unspecified national interests, masking only a lack of inner confidence, but by a meaningful way of being among others and participating in a common work. europe has been the main center of civilization on this planet for many centuries, and if it wasn't, it certainly thought it was. so she felt entitled to export her culture, her religion, and her inventions to the world, regardless of whether anyone wanted it. moreover, the export of these values has often been accompanied by violence. it is even possible to say that the whole of modern civilization - not only with all its greatness, but also with its present short-sightedness - has its origins in europe. europe should learn from this and build on it in new ways. that is, he will no longer impose anything on the world, but will only try to inspire it. just offer him an example that others can take from, or not take from. it is hard to find a place on this earth where so many nations or ethnic groups, so many minorities and minorities in minorities, are concentrated in different states. yet, in recent decades, europe has managed to create perhaps the strongest transnational alliance that we can see in the world today. and, most importantly, this union did not come about as it has always been throughout history, as the product of the rape of the weak by the strong. on the contrary, it was the product of a substantive agreement. so integration has moved from the battlefield to the conference rooms. if nothing else, this alone can serve as a great challenge to the rest of the world. i mentioned the increased importance of transnational agencies in today's world. i see the optimal political order for the coming decades in the creative partnership of these larger transnational or continental entities, based on a certain common moral rather than political minimum. but for these relationships to be meaningful, they must be based on two basic principles: complete equality between the parties and maximum honesty. a relationship where for some practical reason - for example, the fear that the oil or gas supply might be interrupted - someone puts on blinders and forgets all the murdered free-thinking journalists and all the other nasty things that they would have liked to talk about under other circumstances is not a partnership. because it's based on a lie. true partners must be able to tell each other everything they think, the whole truth, and they must also be able to listen to it in its entirety. european integration, which has allowed the greater part of our continent to live in peace for so long, is indeed a unique attempt at democratic cohesion. it's not, and it's not going to be, a pure federation, or even a traditional confederation. it's just something new. may this experience be instructive to others! but that's not the point. i believe that the european union has a chance to inspire the rest of the world with something much deeper than just its model of cooperation between nations. this possibility is the consistent attempt to rectify all the issues, which has predetermined or influenced the whole character of contemporary civilization. it's a movement that may be starting a little bit. i mean a shift away from the cult of profit at any cost and regardless of its long-term and irreversible consequences, a shift away from the cult of quantitative growth and growth growth, a shift away from the primitive ideal of catching up and outdoing america or china or anyone else, as well as a shift away from dangerously unconceptual colonization of the earth and mindless plundering of the planet with no regard for the environment and the interests of future generations. i am, of course, referring to the ingenious conservation of energy, where the success of a state is measured not by the growth of its consumption, but by its decline. but all this is possible only if something begins to change in the very soul of the modern european. he should be a little more humble in the face of the latest discoveries in cosmology, and think about what he will be when he dies, and bow before the mystery of the universe and of being alone, and in short, relate more to eternity and infinity, as he did in the early stages of european development. we should seriously consider that nothing that has happened can ever be forgotten, that everything is remembered somewhere, even if only in the form of a passing light, and that therefore nothing is forgiven forever. but back to europe as a partner of others: the vast majority of wars in the observable history of the human race have been wars over borders, or territories. the important lesson here is that not only nation states but also the transnational community should always be clear about where they start and where they end. blurred or disputed borders are a common source of misfortune. the european union should also bear this in mind. therefore, it should also be clear about its external boundaries. if he wants to tear down the border, he's got to know where it is first. the idea of geographical self-identification would therefore be promoted on a broader, that is, planetary scale. it should thus make a significant and very tangible contribution to what we all desire: peace among the peoples and nations of this planet. the issue of shared sovereignty is the one most frequently raised in european debates as a matter of the union's institutional set-up. i respect the energy and the achievements of the union in recent years. that is why i dare to look into the distant future. this parliament, which you sit in, is directly elected, and the number of seats each state seeks to match its size. i think that the european parliament should have a little more power than it does today, as the only body directly elected by all europeans. legislative work should therefore move more clearly from the executive to the legislature. the european parliament must not be seen as a mere ornament of the union. however, i believe that in time there could be another, smaller body alongside it, elected from among the representatives of the national parliaments, with all the member states represented by an equal number of their members. in this or similar way, two things could be solved at once: first, the feeling that the various national parliaments feel that they are excluded from european decision-making would be eliminated. secondly, there would be only one body of the union, guaranteeing the complete equality of all the member states. of course, such a body would meet only very rarely, only when a certain number of members request it, and only on matters requiring consensus. moreover, this solution would make it possible to avoid the complexity of the commission's composition according to the national key and the complexity of the european council's vote counting. i must confess that it would be more important for me personally that the commissioners were indeed the best experts in their field than that they were at all costs my countrymen or even fellow countrymen. as for the european council, it is today a peculiar combination of executive and representative power. her status should be clearer, too. it seems to me that it would be closer to the specific position of the heads of state in a parliamentary democracy, that is to say, a kind of semi-concealed and positional collective head of the state, whose visible and understandable representative would, of course, be an individual, namely the president, whose existence is already envisaged by the treaty of lisbon and who is very important: note that where a collective leadership of the state appears, it is usually threatened with disintegration. i'm not saying that this is the case with the transnational community, but i feel that somewhere at the very top there should be a single human face that represents the whole complex complexity and that helps us understand it better. i have said many times that i would like to see a european constitution that is thin, clear and readable, that even schoolchildren can understand, and that everything else - which is now thousands of pages - is just an annex. the charter of fundamental rights, as a text which formulates the values or ideals to which the union is committed, with which it seeks to be in harmony, which it has in mind in its decisions, would naturally have to be an organic part, or even the first part, of such a constitution. ladies and gentlemen, allow me one last remark, which will kind of bring me back to where i started. from a distance, the european union looks like a very technocratic body, concerned only with economics and money. the eternal speculation about budgets, quotas, tariffs, taxes, trade rules and regulations of all kinds are probably necessary and i do not disdain them at all. i even think that the famous guidelines or standards for making goulash - the usual reason for the eurosceptic mockery - are meant to protect something czech or hungarian rather than an attack on the member state and its identity. however, i think that the union should place an ever stronger or more visible emphasis on what is really most important. i mean, on my spiritual and value foundations. it is an unprecedented attempt to build a great and original transnational community based on respect for human freedom, human dignity, on the basis of real democracy, not just a sham or formal democracy, on the basis of trust in common sense, decency, the ability to have a dialogue on equal terms within this community and with anyone else. and of course, respect for the peoples, their traditions, their achievements, the countries they inhabit, their homes, including the landscape in which these homes are located. and of course, respect for human rights and human solidarity. europe's rich spiritual and cultural history - based on a combination of elements from the ancient world, judaism, christianity, islam and, later, the renaissance and the enlightenment - has formed a set of unquestionable values that the european union professes, but which it often sees only as a pretty veneer of what is really going on. but are not these the values that they pursue first and that guide everything else? i'm not advocating anything revolutionary, anything revolutionary, anything radical, but i'm not advocating anything revolutionary. i am only advocating a deeper reflection on the very origins of european unification, a more vigorous cultivation of our european identity, an articulated attitude to a moral order that goes beyond the world of our immediate benefits or a world that is simply aimless and determined by quantitative indicators of prosperity. for 20 years, europe has not been cut in half. i firmly believe that it will never again allow itself to be divided, but will instead be the space and the initiator of ever deeper solidarity and cooperation. may the schiller ode to joy for us and our descendants cease to be a poem celebrating friendship between people and grow into a suggestive sign of our common effort to make the world more human. (the delegates stood and applauded the speaker.)
former president of the czech republic. − mr president, members of parliament, thank you for your invitation and the opportunity to speak to you as we mark the twentieth anniversary of the dramatic breaking down of the closed borders, the cutting of the barbed wire, the demolishing of walls between the european nations and, in the case of germany, of the wall dividing two parts of the same nation. it was the end of the bipolar division not only of europe but, to a large measure, of the world as a whole. it was such a historically important moment that quite a few people had the impression that henceforth calm would reign and the world would thrive and prosper. that did not happen. history did not stop there, of course. and that makes it even more important to view the present anniversary not only as an invitation to reflect on the present, but above all as a challenge to consider what the future holds. i would like to contribute to that reflection five remarks on the theme of european unification. no one was fully prepared for such an astonishingly rapid collapse of the iron curtain. nor could they have been. it would have been unnatural. and so there ensued a phase of perplexity, a search for various alternatives, and uncertainty. then nato took the bold step of taking in new members, thereby affording them security and enabling them to concentrate on preparing to join the european union. subsequently the eu did indeed start to open its doors to the new democracies of central and eastern europe. from time to time those countries cause it headaches of various kinds. but that is perfectly understandable. a democratic political culture cannot be created or renewed overnight. it takes a long time and throws up all sorts of unanticipated problems in the meantime. communism ruled just once in modern times (and, hopefully, it was the last time), but that meant that the phenomenon of post-communism was also a new experience for us. we had to confront the consequences of the rule of fear that lasted for so many years, as well as all the risks relating to a redistribution of property without precedent in our history. so there were and still are many obstacles and we are only now acquiring the experience we need to deal with such a state of affairs. i believe, nonetheless, that the west went about things in the right way. any other approach would have given rise to even more anxieties for the west and for everyone, and would also have been more costly. not only was there a real risk of a new struggle being triggered over spheres of influence, or the actual domination of one group by another, but the states that remained outside the western gates would most likely have turned into a stamping ground for various nationalists and populists, along with their armed militias, and also possibly a place of dangerous local conflicts, which would have been all the more dangerous in that, for well-known reasons, no real peace conference took place after world war ii to decide on a binding, precise and lasting post-war settlement in europe. i think that many a hand that until recently had held up a flag with the hammer and sickle would have been capable, without much ado, of reaching for a national flag instead. we were able to see where that path could lead in the former yugoslavia. demons, as is well known, always awaken other demons. so no one can tell whether that contagion would not soon have infected the western half of europe. and we live in a period of history when, as a result of globalisation, any local conflict could easily develop into a global one. so the approach adopted was the most natural in historical terms, and the most advantageous in practical terms. moreover, it was an approach that could also be interpreted as an expression of thoughtful shared responsibility for the way things had evolved in the recent past, which were partly due, in their origins, to short-sighted concessions on the part of the democratic world. to sum up then: however bothersome we might have been to the european union up to the present, it is worth putting up with it, because any alternative to the course of events to date would most likely have been much worse and much more dangerous. in the circumstances, all one can ask of europe is patience and understanding. however, the real question is what we can offer europe. it has long been my opinion that after what we endured under the totalitarian system, we need – we are duty-bound, even – to convincingly convey this experience to others and to make specific suggestions based on its various implications. it is not an easy task and i am not sure we have made a good job of it to date. the point is that totalitarian or authoritarian forms of government tend to have very inconspicuous beginnings and employ very ingenious means of controlling society. only now, with hindsight, do many of us realise how deviously we were entangled in the totalitarian web. that all obliges us to be particularly circumspect. this should be our contribution to guaranteeing that what we went through will never be repeated. what does it require? above all, clear and unequivocal solidarity with anyone anywhere in the world who is confronted by totalitarian or authoritarian regimes. no economic or other particular interests should stand in the way of such solidarity. even a minor, discreet and well-intentioned compromise can have fatal consequences – even if only in the long term, or indirectly. one must not retreat in the face of evil, because it is in the nature of evil to take advantage of every concession. besides, europe has already had its own unfortunate experience of appeasement policies. our support can help liberal-minded people or outspoken witnesses to the situation in north korea, burma, iran, tibet, belarus, cuba or anywhere else, much more than we think. but it will help us too. it will help us build a better world and also to be more true to ourselves; in other words, to put into practice the values that we proclaim in general terms. recently, the european parliament awarded the sakharov prize to memorial, the russian association that monitors how human rights are respected in russia. i think that was a significant act. i recall how important it once was in my country when, against the will of the government, the french president invited us – the opposition – to a working breakfast during his state visit. these things might seem superficial; but that is how it is in totalitarian regimes: a single breakfast or a single suppressed student demonstration can – in certain circumstances – set history moving our identity is created not only by what is unique to us as individuals, but also by certain so-called shared layers of identity. the identity of each of us is moulded, to a greater or lesser extent, by our membership of family, community, region, firm, church, association, political party, nation, sphere of civilisation, and, last but not least, of the planetary community. all this has to do with various sorts of homes we can have: based on geographical location, or on opinion, language and ethnic or other grouping. these all help create us. it is also connected with our various types of patriotism, our goals, affinities, inclinations, sources of pride, our emblems, traditions, customs, habits and peculiarities. in short, the world is full of diversity, and that is equally true of humankind at large and each and every one of us. these shared affiliations are also the origin of shared sovereignty, of course. at each level of our identities we have a certain measure of sovereignty, but at none of them do we have absolute sovereignty, nor can we have. the only thing that matters is that these sovereignties should be mutually complementary and that, as far as possible, they should not contradict each other. i am sure you have an inkling of why i am following this train of thought at this particular time: after all, the debates about the european constitution and the lisbon treaty centre to a large extent on the issue of what the relationship should be between national and european sovereignty. the answer is obvious: the two should complement each other. after all, the fact that i feel myself to be a european does not mean that i stop being a czech. on the contrary: as a czech i am also a european. i tend to say somewhat poetically that europe is the “homeland of our homelands”. at the same time i am convinced that european sovereignty will gradually grow stronger in the future. how quickly this will happen i cannot say. nor do i know what sort of circuitous route it will take. but i do know that the process of integration must continue, because it is in the fundamental, nay existential, interest of everyone, not just the europeans. the reasons are obvious: we are part of a single global civilisation in which it matters little whether the owner of a fishing business in greenland lives in taiwan and owns part of a bank in brazil, or that the owner of mines in the czech republic runs his operations from a computer in iceland. in such a context various supranational or continental associations are playing and will play increasingly important roles. this is not the end of nation states, neither now nor in the future. they will simply continue to come together and act jointly in many areas. technological and economic developments will quite simply demand it. on the other hand, at a time when the world is heading towards an unhealthy unification, the establishment of various smaller associations of states and nations, sharing certain affinities, can be one of the instruments for ensuring better protection of their national or regional identities. the gradual and non-coercive grouping of states naturally strengthens peaceful coexistence as well. or were the majority of wars in recent centuries perhaps not wars between nation states? how better to restrain various national demons than by practical co-operation among nations? however, the only way the principle of multilayered sovereignty can be accepted is if there is civic and political identification with it. i have observed that in my country, and most likely in many other countries too, people often talk about 'sus' – in my case, the czechs – and 'them', meaning those nasty foreigners in brussels – as if we weren’t in brussels too! this division into 'us', the good guys by definition, and 'them', the bad guys intent on doing us harm at all costs, is evidence of just one thing: a lack of understanding of the very principle of integration. so that too is something that needs to be tackled with patience. we are all in the same boat and that boat is steering a good course. and it will continue to do so as long as all its passengers share the responsibility and do not each play their own game and make their own interests paramount. making a lot of noise about not very clearly specified national interests, which simply serves to disguise a lack of self-confidence, is not the way to acquire prestige or a unique position in the existing community. that can be achieved only by purposeful interaction with others and involvement in the common cause. for many centuries, europe was the centre of civilisation on this planet, and even when it was not, it definitely thought it was. it therefore felt entitled to export its culture, its religion and its inventions to the entire world regardless of whether or not anyone wanted them. furthermore, on numerous occasions, these values were exported by force. in fact one can go so far as to say that the entire civilisation of modern times – with all the splendid things this means for the world, but also and equally with its present short-sightedness – originated in europe. that should all be a lesson for europe, which should find a new way to draw inspiration therefrom, no longer imposing things on the world but simply seeking to be a source of inspiration for it. it can offer an example that others can choose to follow, but are not obliged to. it would be hard to find on this planet a region where so many nations or ethnic groups are concentrated, not to mention all the minorities and minorities within minorities. nevertheless, over recent decades europe has managed to create maybe the firmest supranational union in the world today. and yet – and this is the most important thing – this union did not come into being, as invariably in the past, as a result of the subjugation of the weaker by the stronger. on the contrary it was the product of pragmatic agreement. thus integration has shifted from the battlefield to the conference hall. if nothing else, then this alone can serve as a challenge to the rest of the world. i have mentioned the increased significance of supranational entities in today’s world. what i see as the optimal political order in the coming decades is the creative co-operation and partnership of these larger supranational or continental entities based on a certain common minimum, one that is more moral than political. however, if these relationships are to be meaningful, they must be based on two fundamental principles: total mutual equality and maximum sincerity. a relationship in which, for practical reasons – such as fear that deliveries of crude oil or gas might be disrupted – people place blinkers on their eyes and forget about all the murders of independently minded journalists or all sorts of other unacceptable things – even though in other circumstances they would readily speak of them – is not a relationship of partnership, because it is based on duplicity. real partners must be capable of speaking their mind fully to each other, speaking the whole truth, in other words, and they must also be capable of listening to the whole truth. european integration, thanks to which the greater part of our continent has lived at peace for so long, is truly a unique attempt at the democratic union of states. it is not a pure federation, nor even a traditional confederation, nor will it be soon. it is simply something new. i hope it is an experiment that will prove instructive for others too! but that is not the main point. it is my belief that the european union has a chance to inspire the rest of the world with something much more profound than its model of international co-operation. i refer to the opportunity to consistently strive to remedy all the questionable things with which europe has predetermined or influenced the entire character of contemporary civilisation. this is something which may already have started. what i have in mind is the shift away from the cult of profit at all costs and regardless of its long-term and irreversible consequences, a shift away from the cult of quantitative growth and 'growth of growth', a shift away from the primitive ideal of catching up with or outstripping america or china or anyone else, as well as a shift away from the perilously haphazard settlement of the earth and the mindless plunder of the planet without regard for the environment or the interests of future generations. i am thinking here of course of the ingenious ways we are finding of saving energy, at a time when the success of a state is not measured by the growth, but by the fall, in its consumption. this is only conceivable, however, if something starts to change in the very soul of present-day europeans. in the light of the latest cosmological discoveries they really ought to show a bit more humility, and give some thought to what will happen after their deaths. they ought to show deference to the mystery of the universe and of being per se – in short, they ought to renew a greater relationship with eternity and infinity, as was once the case in the initial phases of european development. we should give serious thought to the fact that nothing that has happened can unhappen, that the memory of everything is retained somewhere, even if only in the form of flying light – and therefore nothing is forgiven for ever. but to return to the question of europe as a partner of others: the overwhelming majority of wars in recorded human history were wars over frontiers or rather territories. this is an important lesson: not only nation states but also supranational communities need to know where they start and where they end. fuzzy or disputed boundaries are often the source of misfortune. that is something the european union should bear in mind too. that is why it, too, should be clear about its external borders. if it wants to break down borders then it must first realise where it lies. the idea of geographical self-identification should therefore be supported on a broader, i.e. a planetary, scale. that would also constitute an important and very specific contribution towards what we all yearn for: peace among the peoples and nations of this planet. in debates on europe, the topic of shared sovereignty is most frequently raised in connection with the institutional organisation of the european union. i respect the energy devoted by the eu to this issue in recent years, as well as the successes it has achieved. for that very reason i will make so bold as to view this question, too, from a longer-term perspective. this parliament in which you sit is directly elected and the number of seats held by the individual states is intended to correspond to their size. i think the european parliament should have somewhat greater powers than it does at present, since it is the only body elected directly by all europeans. thus legislative activity should shift more distinctly away from the executive authority to the legislative authority. the european parliament must not be allowed to appear to anyone as just some costly embellishment of the eu. however, it is my belief that in the future another, smaller body could come into existence, to which national parliaments would elect representatives from amongst their number, with each member state being represented by the same number of members. in this or a similar fashion it would be possible to solve two issues at once: firstly, it would eliminate the feeling that various national parliaments have that they are excluded from european decision-making. secondly, it would ensure that there was one eu body in which the absolute equality of all member countries would be guaranteed. a body such as this would meet only on the rarest of occasions, of course, only when a certain number of members requested it, and only in respect of matters requiring a consensus. moreover, such a solution would mean that the commission would not have to be composed on the basis of such a complicated national ratio, and the european council would not have to count up its votes in such a complex fashion. as i far i personally am concerned, it is more important to me for the commissioners to be truly the best in their fields than for them to be my compatriots at all costs, let alone fellow party members. as far as the european council is concerned, it is currently an odd amalgam of executive and representative authority. its status should also be clarified. it seems to me that it ought to be something like the specific status of heads of state in a parliamentary democracy, in other words, it should be a sort of semi-concealed and semi-overt collective head of the union of states, whose visible representative, intelligible to all, would naturally be an individual, the president, whose existence is already provided for in the lisbon treaty, and who is of great importance: we should bear in mind that wherever some sort of collective state leadership emerges, there is generally a risk of its collapse. i do not suggest that this necessarily applies to supranational communities, but i feel nonetheless that somewhere there should be just one single human face representing that entire complex machinery, one that would ensure that it is all more readily understandable. on numerous occasions i have indicated that i think it would be splendid if, sometime in the future, there existed a short, intelligible and readable european constitution, that even schoolchildren could understand, while the rest, which already amounts to thousands of pages, would simply be addenda to it. naturally, part and parcel of such a constitution, or even the very first section of it, should be a charter of fundamental rights, in the shape of a text setting out the values and ideals to which the european union subscribes, which it seeks to respect and which it bears in mind when taking its decisions. ladies and gentlemen, allow me a fifth and final remark which will bring me back towards where i started. seen from a distance, the european union looks like a very technocratic body busying itself solely with economics and money. the never-ending quibbling over the budget, quotas, customs duties, taxes, trading rules and all sorts of regulations is probably necessary and i do not disdain it in the least. what is more, i actually think that the proverbial recommendations or standards regarding such traditional targets of eurosceptic scorn as the preparation of goulash are intended more as protection of something distinctively czech or hungarian, rather than as an attack on a given member state and its identity. nevertheless, i believe that the european union should place greater and more evident stress on the things are truly of foremost importance, namely its spiritual foundations and values. after all, this is an unprecedented attempt to build a large and original supranational community on the basis of respect for human freedoms and human dignity, on a foundation of genuine and not simply ostensible or formal democracy, trusting in common sense, decency, and the power of equal dialogue within this community and with anyone else outside. and also based, of course, on respect for individual nations, for their traditions and achievements, for the lands they inhabit, for their homes and the landscape in which they are located. and also, of course, on respect for human rights and on human solidarity. europe’s rich spiritual and cultural history – combining elements of antiquity, judaism, christianity, islam and more recently, the renaissance and the enlightenment – has created an array of indisputable values, to which the european union certainly pays lip service, but which it often regards simply as pretty packaging for the things that really matter. but is it not these values that are of the essence? and is it not they that set the direction for everything else? i am not advocating anything revolutionary or radical here. all i am saying is there could be a deeper reflection about the very foundations of european unification, a more emphatic cultivation of our europeanness, and a better articulated relationship to the moral order that transcends the world of our immediate benefit, or a world of mere prosperity going in no particular direction and determined solely by quantitative indicators. for twenty years now, europe has no longer been severed in half. i firmly believe that it will never again allow itself to be divided, but will, on the contrary, provide scope and initiative for ever deeper solidarity and co-operation. my wish is that schiller’s ode to joy should cease to be for us and our descendants simply a poem celebrating friendship among people and be transformed instead into a powerful symbol of our common striving for a more humane world. (sustained applause.)
former president of the czech republic. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i thank you for your invitation and for the opportunity to address you on the occasion of the 20th anniversary of the day when the border barriers were dramatically torn down, the barbed wire was cut and the walls separating the nations of europe and, in the case of germany, the wall dividing the two halves of a single nation were demolished. it marked the end of the bipolar divide not only in europe but also, in a much broader sense, in the whole planet. it was a moment of such historical significance that many felt that peace and prosperity would reign in the world from then on. but it wasn't like that. history, as it could not be otherwise, continued its course. and so it is all the more important, if possible, that we not only see this anniversary as an invitation to reflect on the present, but above all as an opportunity to reflect on what the future holds. i would like to contribute to this reflection by making five comments on the subject of european unification. no one was really prepared for such an incredibly rapid fall of the iron curtain. no one could be. it would have been illogical to do otherwise. so there was a period of perplexity, of searching for different alternatives, of uncertainty. nato took the courageous decision to accept new members, thus guaranteeing their security, allowing them to concentrate on their preparation for joining the european union. later, the eu really began to open its doors to the new democracies of central and eastern europe. these countries sometimes give you headaches of all kinds, but it is perfectly understandable. the democratic political culture cannot be created or renewed overnight. it's a long process, fraught with all kinds of unforeseen events that have to be overcome as you continue to move forward. communism has only been imposed once in modern history - and hopefully the last time too - so the phenomenon of post-communism was new to us. we had to face the aftermath of the reign of fear that had reigned for so many years, as well as the dangers of a redistribution of property unprecedented in our history. the obstacles were many - and still are - and we are only now beginning to gain the experience needed to deal with a situation of this nature. i think, however, that the west did the right thing. any other alternative would have caused much more complication for himself and the rest of the world, and would have been much more costly. it could have led to a new struggle for spheres of influence or for the direct domination of one group over another, and, moreover, the states that would have remained at the gates of the west would probably have become the playground of nationalists and populists accompanied by their armed militias, and perhaps also the scene of dangerous local conflicts; a danger that could have been multiplied by the fact that, after the second world war, for reasons that are well known, no peace conference was held to fix in a binding, precise and lasting way the terms of the post-war europe. i think that many of those who had recently raised a flag with the hammer and sickle waved the national flag with great haste. we have seen in the former yugoslavia where this path can lead. demons - everyone knows - always wake up other demons. so no one knows for sure whether this epidemic could have even spread to the western half of europe. we live in an age when any local conflict, as a consequence of globalisation, can easily become an international conflict. the approach adopted was therefore the most logical from a historical point of view and the most appropriate in practice. it could also be interpreted as an expression of deliberate co-responsibility, the result of the way things had evolved in the more recent past, an evolution whose origins derived in part from a series of concessions that the democratic world had made with a view to the short term. in short, the many problems we have caused the european union so far have been worth it, because any other alternative to the course of events would have been, in all probability, much more dangerous and simply worse. in these circumstances, all that can be asked of europe is patience and understanding. however, what really counts is what we can offer europe. i have long felt that after what we suffered under totalitarian regimes, we needed - i would even say we were obliged to - to share our experience with others, with conviction and in a simple way, and to make concrete recommendations based on its implications. it's not an easy task, and i'm not sure we've achieved it yet. in reality, totalitarian or authoritarian forms of government often come to power quietly and resort to very ingenious methods of controlling society. only now, thanks to the perspective that the passage of time gives us, do many of us realize how far we had let ourselves be caught in the net of totalitarianism. all of this requires us to act with caution. this prudence will enable us to contribute to the achievement of one objective: to ensure that what we suffered will never happen again. how can i do that? above all, we must be clearly and unequivocally in solidarity with all those who, today, anywhere in the world, are faced with a totalitarian or authoritarian regime. such solidarity should not be subordinated to economic or other interests. even a small, discreet and well-intentioned commitment can have fatal consequences, even if these only manifest themselves in the long term and indirectly. in the face of evil we cannot retreat, because evil, by its nature, takes advantage of even the slightest of our concessions. moreover, europe has already had unfortunate experiences when it has tried to impose its peace policies at any cost. our support can help, more than we think, free spirits or witnesses who echo the situation in north korea, burma, iran, tibet, belarus, cuba, etc. but it will also be a help to us. it will help us to build a better world by being true to ourselves, or, in other words, by putting into practice the values we publicly defend. the european parliament recently awarded the sakharov prize to memorial, a russian association which works to ensure that human rights are respected in russia. i think it's a very significant decision. i remember how important it was on one occasion in my country when, against the will of the government, the french president invited us - the opposition - to a working breakfast during his state visit. these are situations that may seem superficial. but that's how things work in a totalitarian regime: a simple breakfast or the suppression of a petty student demonstration can, under certain circumstances, change the course of history. our identity is not only made up of what is unique and unique to us as individuals, but also of what are called shared layers of identity. our identity is also, to a greater or lesser extent, the result of our membership of a family, community, region, company, church, association, political party, nation or civilization, and, of course, of our membership of humanity. all of this is related to the different types of home we can have, whether they are geographical, of opinion, linguistic, ethnic, etc. each and every one of these aspects contributes to making us who we are. identity is also associated with different types of patriotism and our goals, affinities, inclinations, sources of pride, symbols, traditions, customs, habits and peculiarities. in short, the world is diverse, humanity is diverse, and each of us is diverse. of course, this shared ownership is also the origin of shared sovereignty. all levels of our identity contain a certain degree of sovereignty, but in none of them is such sovereignty absolute; in fact, it cannot be. what really matters is that these sovereignties complement each other and, as far as possible, do not oppose each other. i am sure you can imagine why i am raising this series of points now: after all, the debates on the european constitution and the treaty of lisbon are largely concerned with determining the relationship between national and european sovereignty. the answer is obvious: both must be complementary. the fact that i feel european does not mean that i am no longer czech. on the contrary, since i am czech, i am european. i often say in a rather poetic way that europe is the home of our homelands. at the same time, i am convinced that european sovereignty will gradually be strengthened in the future. i do not know whether it will do so quickly or slowly, or what winding roads it will take, but what i do know is that the process of integration must continue, because it benefits us all substantially, or rather, existentially, not just the europeans. the reasons are clear: we are part of a single, globalised civilization in which it makes little difference whether the owner of a greenland fishing company lives in taiwan and owns part of a bank in brazil, or whether the owner of a mine in the czech republic runs it from a computer in iceland. in this context, supranational or continental partnerships play, and will play, an increasingly important role. it is not a question of the disappearance of the nation states, either now or in the future. they will simply continue to associate and act together in different areas. technical and economic developments leave them no choice. moreover, in an age when the world is heading towards disastrous homogenization, the creation of small associations of states and nations, more or less related, may be one of the most effective means of ensuring the protection of regional or national identities. the progressive and non-coercive association of different states also logically strengthens peaceful coexistence. were not most of the wars of the last few centuries conflicts between nation-states? what better way to control nationalist demons than real collaboration between different nations? however, we can only accept the principle of a multi-layered sovereignty if it is associated with a civic and political identity. i have noticed that in my country - and probably in many others - we tend to speak of 'us', in my case the czechs, and 'them', when referring to those evil foreigners in brussels. this distinction between 'us', the good guys, and 'them', the bad guys who want to harm us at all costs, shows the misunderstanding that hangs over the principle of integration. this is a question which we must also tackle with patience. we are all in the same boat; a boat that is sailing in the right direction. and it will stay that way as long as all its passengers take a shared responsibility and do not set out alone for their own benefit. making a lot of noise around vague national interests will not allow us to achieve a unique or prestigious position in the existing community; it only serves to hide the lack of confidence in ourselves. that position can only be achieved through meaningful interaction with others and our commitment to the common cause. for many centuries, europe was the center of world civilization, and even when it wasn't, at least it thought it was. thus, she felt empowered to export her culture, religion, and inventions to the entire world, no matter if others had asked her to do so. and that is not all, for on numerous occasions these values were exported by the use of force. in fact, we could even say that the whole of modern civilization - in all its splendor, but also, and to an equal extent, in its present shortsightedness - was born in europe. europe should learn from all this and find a new way of using this experience, to stop imposing its criteria on the world and become merely a source of inspiration, proposing an example that others can freely choose to follow, without being obliged to do so. it is difficult to find a region on our planet where so many different nations or ethnic groups are concentrated, not to mention all the minorities and the minorities within the minorities. nevertheless, over the past few decades, europe has succeeded in creating what is probably the strongest supranational union in the world today. and yet - and this is the most important thing - this union was not born, as had always happened in the past, of the subjugation of the weaker by the stronger. on the contrary, it was the fruit of a pragmatic agreement. in this way, integration moved from the battlefield to the conference room. this achievement alone is a challenge for the rest of the world. i have already mentioned the growing importance of supranational entities in today's world. i believe that the best possible political order in the coming decades will be achieved through the creative cooperation and partnership of these great supranational or continental entities, based on a few common minimum principles, of a moral rather than a political order. however, for these relations to have any meaning, they must be based on two fundamental principles: total reciprocal equality and the utmost sincerity. a relationship in which for practical reasons - for example, fear of interruption of gas or oil supply - some prefer to look away and forget all the journalists killed for defending freedom of expression or any other similar event, which, in other circumstances, they would have openly denounced, is not a partnership relationship, as it is based on hypocrisy. true partners must be completely honest with each other: they must not hide the truth and they must also be able to listen to it. european integration, which has enabled most of our continent to live in peace for many years, is the only real attempt at democratic union between states. it is not a true federation, not even a traditional confederation; it is still a long way off. it's just something completely new. i hope this experience can serve as an example to others! but that's not the main thing. i believe that the european union can serve as an inspiration to the rest of the world in relation to something much deeper than its model of international cooperation. i am referring to the opportunity it has to strive to correct systematically all the controversial principles by which europe has predetermined or shaped the character of contemporary civilization. this is a process which may have already begun. what i mean is that we must stop idolizing the making of profits at any cost without regard to their irreversible long-term effects, quantitative growth and the 'growth of growth', the old ideal of catching up with or even surpassing the united states, china or any other country that gives us an advantage, as well as the dangerous and arbitrary colonization of the earth and the unreasonable plundering of the planet with no consideration for the environment or the interests of future generations. i am thinking, of course, of the ingenious ways of saving energy that we have discovered, at a time when the success of a state is measured not by the growth, but by the fall, of its consumption. however, all this is only possible if something begins to change within the european people of today. in the light of recent cosmological discoveries, europeans should be a little more humble and think about what will happen after death. they should bow before the mystery of the universe and of being itself. in short, they should be constantly reminded of eternity and infinity, as was the case in the early stages of european development. we must not forget that nothing that has happened can be undone and that the memory of what has happened never completely disappears, even if it is now only a fleeting reminiscence, so nothing is forgiven forever. but let us return to the question of europe as a partner: the overwhelming majority of the wars that have plagued mankind were fought over the control of a border or a territory. we can draw an important lesson from this: not only nation states but also supranational communities must know where their territories begin and end. diffuse or controversial boundaries are often a source of conflict. the european union should bear this in mind. it must therefore define its external borders more precisely. if you want to tear down the borders, you first have to know where they are. so the idea of geographical self-identification should be understood in a much broader context, on a planetary scale. it would also make an important and concrete contribution to the goal we all want: peace between the peoples and nations of this planet. in the debate on europe, the question of shared sovereignty is often discussed in connection with the institutional organisation of the european union. i respect the efforts and achievements of the eu in this field in recent years. and out of this respect, i dare to look at the matter from a long-term perspective. this parliament of which you are a part is elected by direct suffrage and the distribution of seats among the various countries is made according to their size. i believe that the european parliament should have more powers than it does at present, since it is the only body directly elected by all european citizens. the legislative activity should therefore be transferred more clearly from the executive to the legislative. no one should see the european parliament as a simple but costly adornment of the eu. i am convinced, however, that in the future another body, smaller in size, could be created; the national parliaments would elect their representatives to this new body from among their own members and each member state would have the same number of members. this structure, or another of similar characteristics, would allow two questions to be resolved at the same time: first, national parliaments would no longer feel excluded from the european decision-making process and, secondly, there would be a european body in which the absolute equality of all member states would be guaranteed. the body would meet only on exceptional occasions, only when a certain number of members request it and only on matters requiring consensus. moreover, if this solution is adopted, the composition of the commission would no longer have to be based on such a complicated national weighting and the council would not have to count its votes in such a complex way. in my view, it is more important that the commissioners are really the best in their field than that they are my compatriots at all costs or belong to my party. the european council is now a strange mixture of executive and representative authority. their status should also be clarified. it should be similar to the status of heads of state in a parliamentary democracy; in other words, it should be a form of collective,
