semi-occult and semi-manifest leadership of the union of states, whose visible representative, known to all, is naturally a natural person: the president. this figure, already provided for by the treaty of lisbon, is of great importance: we must not forget that whenever some form of collective leadership emerges, there is generally a risk of collapse. i do not mean that this premise should necessarily apply to supranational communities, but i have the impression, nevertheless, that there should be only one human face representing this complex machinery, which would allow a better understanding of it to be ensured. i have already mentioned more than once that i think it would be great if at some future time there was a short, intelligible and easy-to-read european constitution that even children could understand, and the rest - which already consists of thousands and thousands of pages - would just be annexes to it. of course, part of such a constitution, or even its first section, should be a charter of fundamental rights, which would set out the values and ideals on which the european union is founded, which it advocates and which it takes into account when it makes decisions. ladies and gentlemen, allow me to make one last remark to tie in with the beginning of my speech. from a distance, the european union looks like a highly technocratic body dealing only with economic and monetary matters. the endless discussions on the budget, quotas, customs duties, taxes, trade rules and all kinds of regulations are probably necessary, and i will not be the one to dismiss them in the slightest. moreover, i believe that the well-known recommendations or rules on goulash preparation, which are the traditional targets of eurosceptic sarcasm, are in fact intended to protect something typically czech or hungarian and in no way attack a particular member state or its identity. however, i think that the eu should place more emphasis, and more prominently, on what really matters, namely its spiritual foundations and its values. in the end, it is an unprecedented attempt to build a great and exceptional supranational community based on respect for human dignity and freedoms and on a true democracy, not just formal or figurative, but one that is endowed with common sense, honesty and the ability to maintain a dialogue on an equal footing both within and outside the community itself, and also based on respect for individual nations, their traditions and achievements and the territories they occupy, and their homes and the regions in which they are located, as well as respect for human rights and human solidarity. europe's rich spiritual and cultural history, combining elements of antiquity, judaism, christianity, islam and, more recently, the renaissance and the enlightenment, has shaped a set of unquestionable values, which the european union does not tire of repeating - there is no doubt about it - but which often serve only as the pretty wrapper of what it really cares about. but are not these values the very essence of it? are they not the ones who serve as a guide for everything else? i am not advocating anything really revolutionary or radical. i would simply like to invite you to reflect more deeply on the foundations of european unification, to cultivate more of our european specificity and to establish a more articulated relationship with the moral order that goes beyond our immediate benefit, or a world that drifts forward solely driven by the pursuit of prosperity and determined exclusively by quantitative indicators. it is twenty years since we left europe divided in two halves. i firmly believe that europe will never allow itself to be divided again; on the contrary, it will become the pioneer of greater and deeper solidarity and cooperation. my wish is that schiller's "ode to joy" will no longer be for us and our descendants simply a poem celebrating friendship between peoples and will become a powerful symbol of our common struggle for a more humane world. (the house will then rise to its feet and applaud the speaker)
, former president of the czech republic. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i thank you for inviting me and giving me the opportunity to speak to you on the 20th anniversary of the day when the border barriers were dramatically breached, the barbed wire cut, the walls that separated the nations of europe and, in the case of germany, the two parts of a country, were torn down. it was the end of the bipolar divide not only of europe but also, to a large extent, of the whole world. this moment was so important to history that everyone felt that from this moment on, calm would reign and the world would only prosper. it didn't happen, the story didn't stop, of course. it is all the more important to see this anniversary as an invitation to reflect on the present, but above all as a call to consider the future. i shall contribute five points on the subject of european unification. no one was and could not be fully prepared for such a sudden fall of the iron curtain. it was against nature. then there was a period of some perplexity, of considering several alternatives, of uncertainty. secondly, nato took the courageous decision to expand to new members, thus providing them with security that helped them to focus on preparing for entry into the european union. later, the union really began to open up to the new democracies of central and eastern europe. these countries occasionally cause various worries, which is quite understandable. the democratic political culture cannot be created or renewed overnight. this is a long process in which many unforeseen difficulties have to be resolved. communism reigned for the first time - and hopefully the last - in modern history and we found ourselves confronted for the first time with the phenomenon of post-communism. we have had to face the aftermath of a long reign of fear and all the risks of a redistribution of property unprecedented in history. many obstacles have been and are still present, and we are only just beginning to gain experience in dealing with this situation. however, i think the west has done the right thing. any other alternative would have caused far more trouble, not only for the west but for everyone, and would also have been more expensive. not only could a new struggle for spheres of influence or for direct domination of one another have developed in a worrying way, but the states that would have remained at the door of the west would very likely have become the playground of various nationalists and populists, with their armed militias, and perhaps also the scene of dangerous local conflicts, all the more dangerous since after the second world war, for known reasons, no real peace conference came to regulate in a binding, precise and lasting way, the conditions of the post-war period in europe. i believe that many of those who a short time ago would have held in their hands the flag with the hammer and sickle would very soon learn to hold a national flag. we have seen in the former yugoslavia where this road leads. demons, as we all know, always wake up other demons. thus, no one knows whether the contagion would not have reached western europe. we live in a time when any local conflict, because of globalization, can easily become an international conflict. the approach adopted was therefore the most natural one from a historical point of view and the most appropriate in practice. moreover, it was a move which could be interpreted as an expression of a deliberate shared responsibility for events in the recent past, the origins of which lay in particular in certain short-sighted compromises in the democratic world. so, in summary, whatever problems we are causing the european union today, they are worth taking on because any alternative to the present course of events would be far worse and far more risky. in these circumstances, europe can only be asked to show understanding and patience. the real question is what we can offer europe. i have long held the view that after what we have suffered under totalitarian regimes, we should - we are obliged - to explain this experience convincingly to others and to turn everything that results into concrete initiatives. it's not easy, and i'm not sure we've gotten this far. in reality, a totalitarian or authoritarian power always has very discreet beginnings and very sophisticated means of controlling society. even today, looking back, many of us realize how ingeniously we were once caught in the snares of totalitarianism. all of this requires us to be especially careful. this caution should be our contribution to ensuring that what we have experienced can never happen again. what does it take? firstly, to show clear and unequivocal solidarity with all those who today, everywhere in the world, are confronted by totalitarian or authoritarian regimes. no commercial or other interest should interfere with this solidarity. even a small, insignificant compromise, made with good intentions, can have disastrous consequences, even in the long run and indirectly. you can't back away from evil because it's in its nature to take advantage of every compromise. europe has had its own disastrous experiences in the politics of peace at any cost. our support can help more than we think free minds or witnesses who speak out loud about the situation in north korea, burma, iran, tibet, belarus, cuba or elsewhere. and it will help us too. this will help us to build a better world while being more true to ourselves, giving more substance to the values we generally claim for ourselves. the european parliament recently awarded the sakharov prize to the russian organization memorial, which monitors the human rights situation in russia. i think it is an important act. i remember a very significant event in my country at the time, when the french president on an official visit invited us, the opposition, to a working breakfast, against the wishes of the government. these are seemingly superficial things, but under totalitarian conditions, it turns out that a breakfast or a suppressed student protest can contribute in certain circumstances to the march of history. multiple layers of our identity, called shared, help create the identity of each of us, in addition to what is unique to us as a being. to a greater or lesser extent, each of us is the result of belonging to a family, a locality, a region, a company, a church, an association or political party, a nation, a civilization and finally, the community of the inhabitants of the planet. all of this refers to our home, whether it be geographical, opinion, linguistic, ethnic or otherwise, we are the result of all of this. in addition to this there are the various aspects of our patriotism, our aims, our affinities, our inclinations, our pride, our symbols, our traditions, our habits, our customs and our peculiarities. in short, the world is full of diversity, and so are humanity and each of us. of course, from this shared ownership also comes a shared sovereignty. on all levels of our identity, we have a degree of sovereignty, but we never have and never can have complete sovereignty. it is only a question of these sovereignties complementing each other and, if possible, not opposing each other. you will no doubt guess why i am entering into such considerations at this particular moment: the debates on the european constitution and the treaty of lisbon are largely centred on the question of the reciprocal relations defining the sovereignty of states and that of europe. the answer is clear: they should complement each other. if i feel european, it does not mean that i cease to be czech. on the contrary, as a czech, i am also european. i am used to saying in a rather poetic way that europe is the homeland of our homelands. at the same time, i am convinced that european sovereignty will gradually be consolidated in the future. i do not know whether it will happen quickly or slowly, i do not know which winding roads and detours will lead us there, but i do know that the process of integration must continue. it is in the substantial, even existential, interest not only of europeans, but of all. the reasons are obvious: we live in a single, globalized civilization, where it does not matter whether the owner of a greenland fishing company lives in taiwan and owns shares in a brazilian bank or whether the owner of a czech mine manages his operation from iceland. in this environment, various supranational or continental societies play and will play an increasingly important role. this is not the end of the nation states, these countries are merely coming together, they will continue to associate and act together in many areas. the only thing that forces them to do this is technical and economic progress. on the other hand, in an age when the world is moving towards harmful standardization, the constitution of several small communities of states and nations, more or less close to each other, may be one of the ways of better defending national or regional identities. of course, the gradual and nonviolent association of states also strengthens peaceful coexistence. in recent centuries, have not most wars been between nations? what better way to control the various nationalist demons than by real cooperation between nations? of course, the principle of multi-layered sovereignty can only be accepted if it is backed up by a civil and political identification with this principle. i have noticed that in my country - and probably in many other countries - people often speak of "us" - in my case, the czechs - and "them", referring to some nasty foreigners in brussels. but are we not in brussels too? this distinction between "us" as a priori good people and some evil "them", presented as those who want to harm us at all costs, only indicates an almost total lack of understanding of the integration process itself. this too must be dealt with patiently. we're all in this together, and this ship has taken the right direction. it will continue along this course as long as all its passengers share responsibility and no one rides alone in his own interest. it is not by shouting in favour of vague national interests, by merely masking our lack of self-confidence, that we will gain prestige or a unique position in a constituted community, but by means which give meaning to our existence among others and by our participation in the common work. europe has been for many centuries the principal centre of civilization in the world, or so it thought when it was not. it felt it had the right to export its culture, religion and inventions to the world, without asking whether anyone wanted it or not. on the other hand, the export of these values has been accompanied by violence on more than one occasion. it can even be said that the whole of modern civilization - not only with all its great significance for the world but also, to an equal extent, with its present myopia - has its origins in europe. the continent should learn from all this and relate to this experience in a different way, no longer imposing anything on the world but striving only to be a source of inspiration, to offer an example to which others can refer or not without being obliged to. it is difficult to find on this earth a region where so many nations or ethnic groups, so many minorities and minorities within minorities, are concentrated in several states. yet europe has succeeded, in recent decades, in creating what is perhaps the strongest supranational alliance we can see in the world today. but - and this is the most important - this alliance was not born as it has always been in history, namely that it is not the result of the violent domination of the weak by the strong. it was, on the contrary, the result of a genuine concertation. so integration has moved from the battlefields to the conference rooms. this alone is a major challenge for the rest of the world. i mentioned the growing importance of supranational configurations in the world today. it seems to me that the optimal political order for the next few decades lies in a creative collaboration of partnerships between large supranational or continental entities, based on common minimal concepts, more moral than political. to be meaningful, these relations must of course be based on two basic principles: full equality for both parties and maximum openness. when for practical reasons - for example, the fear of interruption of oil or gas supplies - some close their eyes and forget all the journalists murdered for their freedom of thought or any other similar facts that they would have been happy to report under other circumstances, there is no partnership relationship, because this relationship is based on duplicity. real partners need to be able to tell each other everything they're thinking, which is the whole truth, which they also need to be able to hear. european integration, which has brought peace to most of our continent for so long, is a unique attempt at democratic union between states. it is not a true federation, not even a traditional confederation, we are still far from it. this is something new. if only this experience could serve as an example to others! but that's not the most important thing. i believe that the european union has the opportunity to inspire the rest of the world by something deeper than its single model of cooperation between nations, by systematically seeking to redress all the controversial acts by which europe has predetermined or influenced the whole character of contemporary civilization. that trend may be starting to emerge. what i am saying is that we must turn our backs on the cult of profit at any cost, with no regard for its irreversible and long-term consequences, the cult of quantitative growth and 'growth of growth', the primitive ideals of the united states, china and others to catch up and outpace, the dangerous and disorderly colonization of the earth and the senseless plundering of the planet with no regard for the environment or the interests of future generations. i am thinking of course of ingenious ways of saving energy, when the success of a country is not measured by growth but, on the contrary, by a decrease in its consumption. all this is of course only possible if changes begin to take place in the mind of the contemporary european. in the face of the latest discoveries in cosmology, he should still be a little more modest, he should reflect on what will happen after his death, bow down to the mystery of the universe and of being itself, in other words refer again, as was the case in the early stages of european construction, to eternity and infinity. we should seriously consider that nothing that has happened can be undone, that everything has a memory somewhere, if only in the form of a flying light, and that therefore nothing is forgiven forever. but back to europe as a partner: the vast majority of wars in the known history of the human species were a struggle for a border or territory. the lesson here is that not only nation states but also supranational communities should always know where their territory begins and ends. blurred or disputed borders often lead to disaster. even the european union should remember this. it should therefore also have a clear view of its external borders. if it wants to abolish borders, it must first know where they are. the concept of geographical self-identification should thus be promoted on a larger scale, at the global level. in this way the union would make a significant and very concrete contribution to building what we all aspire to: peace between men and nations on earth. the question of shared sovereignty is most often raised in european debates in connection with the institutional organization of the union, to which i pay tribute for the energy it has deployed in recent years on this subject and for the successes it has achieved. that is why i am risking looking further into the future. this parliament in which you sit is elected by direct suffrage and the number of seats allocated to each state is supposed to correspond to its size. i believe that the european parliament should have more powers than it does now, as the only body directly elected by all europeans. therefore, legislative work should be transferred more clearly from the executive to the legislative. no one has the right to regard the european parliament as a mere expensive ornament of the union. however, i believe that a smaller body could emerge in time, in which the national parliaments would elect representatives from among themselves, so that all the member states would be represented by the same number of members. in this way, or in a similar way, it would be possible to solve two problems at once: first, it would eliminate the feeling that is widespread in several national parliaments, according to which they are excluded from the european decision-making process. secondly, there would be a single body of the union which would guarantee complete equality between all the member states. such a structure would, of course, meet very rarely, only when a number of members request it and only on matters requiring consensus. this solution would also simplify the complicated composition of the commission, which is currently based on a national proportion, and would avoid the european council having to carry out such a complex calculation of its votes. i must say that it seems to me more important that the commissioners are really the best specialists in their field than that they are at all costs my compatriots or even members of my party. the european council is currently a strange amalgam of executive and representative authority. its status should also be clarified. it seems to me that we should approach the specific position of the head of state in parliamentary democracies. in other words, it would be a kind of collective leadership of a group of states, half hidden, half visible, whose visible and comprehensible representative would naturally be a person, namely the president, whose existence is already provided for by the lisbon treaty and whose role is very important. let us remember that when a state is headed by a collective leadership, there is usually a risk of disintegration. i do not say that this can also be the case in a supranational community, but i do feel that it would be better to have a human face representing the whole of this complex machinery and making everything more understandable. i have said on more than one occasion that i would be delighted if there were a european constitution in the future which was concise, understandable and readable, which even schoolchildren could understand, and that all the rest (which today amounts to thousands of pages) were just annexes. of course, this constitution should contain, perhaps even in its first part, a charter of fundamental rights in the form of a text setting out the values or ideals to which the union subscribes, which it strives to conform to and which it takes into account in its decision-making. ladies and gentlemen, allow me to make one final remark, which brings me back to where i started. from a distance, the european union appears to be a highly technocratic body that is only concerned with economics and money. the endless debates on the budget, quotas, customs duties, taxes, trade rules and various regulations are probably necessary and i do not disdain them in the least. i even believe that the famous recommendations or standards for goulash cooking, which are usually the subject of sarcasm by eurosceptics, are supposed to protect a czech or hungarian peculiarity rather than harm a particular member state and its identity. i think, however, that the union should put more emphasis, more strongly and more visibly, on what is really important, namely its spiritual foundations and its values. after all, it is an unprecedented attempt to build a supranational community, large and original, based on respect for the freedom of individuals, human dignity, on the basis of a genuine democracy which is not only apparent and formal, and on faith in common sense, honesty, the capacity for fair dialogue within this community and with all third parties. it is also based on respect for individual nations, their traditions, their achievements, respect for the countries in which they live, their homes, and in particular the regions in which these homes are located. and of course also on respect for human rights and human solidarity. europe has a rich spiritual and cultural history, based on the combination of ancient, jewish, christian, islamic and renaissance and enlightenment elements, which have formed an undeniable set of values that europe claims verbally but often sees only as a beautiful packaging for what is really important. are these not the values that are the foundation? are these not the values that guide the direction we should take? i am not advocating a revolutionary, subversive or radical position here. i only encourage a deeper reflection on the very foundations of european unification, a deeper cultivation of our european character and a deeper articulation of the relationship with the moral order which transcends the world of our immediate profits or the world based on prosperity alone, which leads nowhere and is determined only by quantitative indicators. for 20 years, europe has not been divided in two. i firmly believe that it will never again allow itself to be divided and that it will, on the contrary, be the theatre and the initiator of ever greater solidarity and cooperation. let us hope that for us and our descendants schiller's ode to joy will no longer be a mere poem celebrating friendship between men but will become a evocative symbol of our common efforts for a more humane world. , former president of the czech republic. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i thank you for the invitation and for the opportunity to address you on the 20th anniversary of the dramatic events which broke through the border barricades, cut through the barbed wire and demolished the walls between the peoples of europe, or in the case of germany, between two parts of the same people. this was the end of the bipolar division of europe and, to a large extent, of the world as a whole. this was such a momentous moment in history that some people felt that peace was now coming and that the world would simply flourish. this did not happen, and it certainly did not bring an end to the story. the commission has already taken a number of initiatives to promote the use of the euro, and it is therefore important that the current anniversary should not only be a moment to reflect on the present but also and above all a call to think about the future. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. the iron curtain was brought down so suddenly and unexpectedly, and no one could have been fully prepared. that would have been unnatural. and so, first, there was a phase of a certain disorientation, of the search for different alternatives and of uncertainty. then nato bravely opened up to new members, anchoring them in security policy and helping them to focus on preparing for membership of the european union. later, the eu began to open up to the new democracies of central and eastern europe. these countries have been a bit of a pain in the ass from time to time. but that's more than understandable. a democratic political culture cannot be created or renewed overnight. this takes time and involves overcoming unexpected difficulties. communism was in power for the first time, and hopefully for the last time in modern history, and that is why we also encountered the phenomenon of post-communism for the first time. we had to face the consequences of a long reign of fear and all the risks of a redistribution of property like never before in history. there were and are many obstacles, and the experience of dealing with them is only beginning to mature. i still believe that the west did the right thing. because any other alternative would have caused far more worry, not only to him, but actually to everyone, and would have been more expensive. not only could a new and dangerous struggle for spheres of influence or even for the dominance of some over others have been ignited, but the countries that would have remained at the gates of the west would have most likely become a playground for nationalists and populists of various colours and their armed militias, perhaps even the scene of dangerous local conflicts, all the more dangerous because, for well-known reasons, after the end of the second world war, there was never a real peace conference to settle the post-war order in europe in a binding, precise and lasting way. i think that many of those who were raising the flag with a hammer and sickle a short while ago could have quickly and easily taken up the national flag. and we have seen where this leads in the former yugoslavia. and a demon is known to awaken another demon. who knows if this infection might have spread to the western part of europe. we live in a time when any local conflict can easily escalate into a global conflict because of globalization. the approach chosen was therefore the most natural and the most practical in historical terms. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to carcinogens at work is a step in the right direction. i would like to conclude by saying that, although we are still very concerned about the european union today, it is worth accepting this, because any alternative to the present course of events would clearly have been considerably worse and more dangerous. in this situation, europe can only be asked to be understanding and patient. the question is, of course, what we have to offer europe. i have long held the view that, after what we have experienced in the era of totalitarianism, we should, indeed we have a duty, to pass on this experience to others in a convincing way and that we must transform the resulting experience into concrete initiatives. this is not an easy task, and i doubt whether we have succeeded so far. for totalitarian or authoritarian forms of government often start out very inconspicuously and have very sophisticated methods of keeping society in check. only now, with some time between us, are many of us realizing how cleverly we were then entangled in the totalitarian web. all this requires us to be particularly careful. this should be our contribution to ensuring that what we have experienced will never happen again. what is involved? above all, a clear and unequivocal solidarity with all those who today - wherever they may be in the world - are living under a totalitarian or authoritarian regime. we must not allow economic or other special interests to prevent us from this solidarity. even a small, unobtrusive and well-intentioned compromise can have fatal consequences, albeit after a certain time and indirectly. there is no compromise with evil, for it is the nature of evil to take advantage of every concession. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council and parliament. the people who love freedom and who speak out against the conditions in north korea, burma, iran, tibet, belarus, cuba and elsewhere are being helped by our support far more than we think. but it also helps us. it helps us to create a better world and at the same time it helps us to be more true to ourselves, because it enables us to give concrete content to the values we profess in general. the european parliament recently awarded the sakharov prize to memorial, a russian association which monitors the human rights situation in russia. i think that was an important act. i can still remember the great significance it had in my country when the french president invited us - the opposition - to a working breakfast during his state visit, against the wishes of the government. these are only apparent appearances. because in totalitarian conditions, even a breakfast or a suppressed student demonstration can, under certain circumstances, set history in motion. our collective identity is made up of what makes us unique as individuals, as well as different layers of what we call our shared identity. to a greater or lesser extent, each of us is also shaped by our family, community, region, company, church, political party or association, our people, our cultural circle and, finally, the people of this planet. all of this shows wherever we see our home, whether it's geographically, ideologically, linguistically, ethnically or in any other way that we all share. the european union is a great example of the kind of europe we want to see, a europe which is not only a europe of the people, but also a europe of the people. in short, the world is colorful, and so is humanity and each of us. the commission has already taken a number of initiatives in this area. on all levels of our identity, we also have a certain degree of sovereignty, but on no level do we have complete sovereignty, nor can they. what is important is that these sovereignties complement each other and, if possible, do not contradict each other. you can probably guess why i am raising this point now: the debates on the european constitution or the treaty of lisbon are largely concerned with the question of the relationship between state sovereignty and european sovereignty. the answer is clear: they should complement each other. because if i feel european, it doesn't mean i stop being czech. on the contrary, as a czech i am also european. i often say, in a rather poetic way, that europe is the home of our countries. i am convinced that european sovereignty will gradually increase in the future. i do not know how fast or slow this will happen, or what twists and turns this path will bring, but i do know that the process of integration must continue. because in the end, this is in the existential interest not only of europeans, but of all of us. the reasons for this are obvious: we all live in the space of a single global civilization, where it really does not matter whether the owner of a greenlandic fishing company lives in taiwan and owns shares in a brazilian bank, or whether the owner of a czech mining company runs its operations from iceland via computer. in such a space, various transnational, supranational or continental communities play an increasingly important role now and in the future. this does not mean the end of nation states now or in the future, but only that these states are coming together and acting together in many things. the technical and economic development alone will make this necessary. on the other hand, at a time when the world is moving towards an unfortunate unification, the formation of several smaller communities of states or peoples, which are similar in some respects, can be one of the means of better defending their national or regional identity. the gradual and unforced integration of states naturally also promotes peaceful coexistence. or were not the wars of past centuries mostly wars of nation states? what better way to tame forms of national madness than by the objective cooperation of peoples? the principle of multi-layered sovereignty can only be accepted if there is a civil and political identification with it. i have noticed that in our country and certainly in many other countries, people often speak of 'us' - in my case, the czechs - and of 'them', meaning any evil foreigners in brussels, as if we were not in brussels ourselves. this contrast between 'us', who are a priori good, and the 'other', who are evil and who want to harm us at any cost, reveals above all one thing: an inadequate understanding of the integration process itself. again, you have to be patient. we are in the same boat, and that boat is on the right track; and it will remain on the right track if all its passengers share responsibility and do not just play their own game and pursue their own goal. we do not gain a prominent or distinguished position in an existing community by whining about unspecified national interests, which merely conceals a lack of inner self-confidence, but only by meaningful cooperation and participation in the common work. europe has been the main centre of civilization on this planet for centuries, or at least it believed it was. it therefore felt entitled to export its culture, religion and inventions to the whole world, regardless of whether anyone wanted them. moreover, these exports of value were often accompanied by violence. it can even be said that the whole of modern civilization has its origins in europe - not only the splendor but also, to an equal extent, the short-sightedness of today. europe should learn from all this and build on it in a new way. and it's done so that it no longer imposes on the world, but only seeks to inspire the world. by setting an example that others can follow but do not have to. it is difficult to find another region on earth what is probably the most stable supranational union in the world today. the european union is not a political union, but a political union, and it is not a political union. it was rather the result supranational or continental organisations on the basis of a certain common moral rather than political minimum. but these relations are only meaningful if they are based on two principles: complete equality between the parties and maximum honesty. a relationship is not a partnership if you put up blinders for practical reasons, for example, because you're afraid that the oil or gas supply will be interrupted, and you close your eyes to the fact that many freedom-loving journalists are being killed, or to many other bad things that you would like to talk about under different circumstances. it is not a partnership, because it is based on falsehood. real partners need to be able to tell each other everything they're thinking, the whole truth, and they need to be able to hear the whole truth. the european integration which has brought peace to the greater part of our continent for so long is indeed a unique attempt to create a democratic union of states. this is not a pure federation, nor will it be anytime soon, nor is it a traditional confederation. it is simply something new. may this experience be instructive to others. but that's not the point. i believe that the the controversial things that have shaped or influenced the whole character of modern civilization. this is a process which may be slowly beginning now. i am referring to the abandonment of the cult of profit at any cost, without regard to the long-term and irreversible consequences, the abandonment of the cult of quantitative growth and ever-increasing growth, the abandonment of the primitive notion that america or china or anyone else must necessarily catch up and overtake, and also the abandonment of the dangerously ill-conceived colonization of the earth and the mindless plundering of the planet without regard to the environment and the interests of future generations. i am referring, of course, to sophisticated energy-saving concepts in which the success of a state is measured not latest findings in cosmology, and he should also think about what will be after his death. it should bow before the mystery of the universe and of existence itself, in short, it should see itself more strongly in the context of eternity and infinity, as it already did in the first stages of european development. we should seriously consider that nothing that has happened can ever be undone, that everything is remembered somewhere - if only in the form of a flying light - and that therefore nothing is forgiven forever. but back to europe as a partner of others: the vast majority of wars in number of members. in this or similar way two things could be solved at once: firstly, it could dispel the impression expressed in many national parliaments that they are excluded from european decisions. secondly, it would ensure that there is a union body which guarantees the absolute equality of all member states. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. such a solution would also make unnecessary the cumbersome composition of the commission by nationality and the complicated counting of votes in the council. i admit that it would be more important for me personally that the commissioners were indeed the best experts in their field than that they were at all costs my countrymen or even party on the tape. the services directive (2006/123/ec) is characterised by the partial liberalisation of the flow of services within the european union. the aim of the directive was to unlock economic potential. this has opened up many opportunities for both consumers and businesses. the single market has become more fully exploitable. the main beneficiaries of the liberalisation of the services market are small and medium-sized enterprises, for which the previously existing barriers were the most burdensome. according to the european commission, in the eu member states, about 70% of gdp is generated in services. the number of employees in the service sector is also similar. the benefits of the services directive include: increased competitiveness in the internal market. the implementation of this directive has been an opportunity for the european economy to grow and has created jobs. it should be added that this is one of the objectives of the lisbon strategy and is aimed at increasing the competitiveness of the european economy. in addition, this has the effect of increasing the range of services offered. the results achieved should provide an incentive to continue work on further liberalising this directive.

the next item on the agenda is the statements by the council and the commission on the preparations for the copenhagen summit on climate change.
acting president of the council. - mr president! - what is it? i would like to thank the commissioner for his reply. the last time i was here in parliament to discuss climate issues was just before i met my colleagues at the october meeting of the environment council. at that meeting we agreed on a strong and united eu mandate for the un climate conference in copenhagen. we agreed, among other things, that by 2050 the eu's emissions must be reduced by between 80% and 95% compared with 1990. we also stated that the eu will reduce emissions by 20% by 2020 under all circumstances, but that we want to reduce by 30% if a sufficiently far-reaching agreement is reached in copenhagen. when comparing emission reductions with those of other countries, we will not least attach importance to the objective of limiting the temperature increase to 2 degrees, as a benchmark also for comparison with emission reductions in other countries. emissions from international transport shall be reduced. we have set ourselves the target of reducing air traffic by 10% and maritime traffic by 20% by 2020 compared with 2005. let me also say clearly that the eu demands that the shipping and aviation levies be used to pay for the efforts of developing countries, especially the poorest and most vulnerable countries. it has to be one of the results in copenhagen. the destruction of rainforests must be halved by 2020 and stopped by 2030. the eu is calling for decisions at the copenhagen summit to stop deforestation, support reforestation and create sustainable forestry. only then can we reduce emissions fast enough to achieve a successful outcome in copenhagen. the eu has gradually clarified and moved its positions forward, and thus has been able to make demands and put pressure on other parties all along the way. this has been done in particular in cooperation with the european parliament, where the climate and energy package has formed the basis of the eu's ambitious positions. now, there's only two weeks left until the copenhagen climate summit. there are many pessimists around us who have been sidelining the riot in the last month. but what really counts is the political will to lead and the eu has that will. to achieve the result we have been working for so long, we must now mobilise all the forces within the european union. the european parliament, in particular, will continue to play an important role. let me therefore first state that the eu's objective for an agreement remains unchanged. it is necessary to reach a far-reaching and comprehensive agreement in copenhagen. earth's climate has waited long enough. the time for a settlement is now. yesterday we held an extraordinary meeting of the environment council to work together to make copenhagen the climate change milestone we wanted. in the eu decision for the copenhagen conference, the heads of state or government stated that the eu's objective is for the copenhagen process to lead to a legally binding agreement for the period from 1 january 2013 building on the kyoto protocol and containing all its essential elements. it requires an agreement in copenhagen that, taken together, will deliver emissions reductions so large that the goal of keeping global temperature rise below 2 degrees is within reach. an agreement with all countries that means that the developed countries commit to emission reductions that cover their total emissions, that means economy-wide target; we assume that every industrialized country appends its commitments to the copenhagen agreement, including the united states. an agreement whereby developing countries commit to action that reduces emissions relative to what would have happened without action, particularly in the major economies, and whereby developed countries provide immediate financial support for necessary actions in developing countries, not least in the poorest countries, in 2010, 2011 and 2012. an agreement establishing a system of long-term support for emission reduction, adaptation, technology cooperation and technology transfer. finally, an agreement must also include a review mechanism so that it can be adapted to what science shows is necessary to cope with the climate. there has been talk of a 'two-step solution'. for the eu, the copenhagen agreement is rather the decisive step. the decision on all matters of climate importance will be taken in copenhagen. the binding agreement will be transposed into a ratifiable text with a clear timetable, which is a more technical matter, as the content will be delivered in a comprehensive agreement. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the use of the term 'competent authority' to cover all the activities of the european union. in fact, such a settlement also enables us to take action more quickly than would otherwise have been the case. it will also be crucial to our achievement of the 2°c target. the eu has been particularly active in providing rapid funding for adaptation and forestry measures. rapid action is needed if we are to be able to turn the earth's emissions curve down fast enough. what's on the table right now is not enough to meet the 2-degree target. the most far-reaching offers at the negotiating table have been put forward by the eu, while we have been pressing for other parties to raise their bids. that's what happened. we have seen that the fact that we have used our 30% target as leverage has also put pressure on other parties. it is gratifying that developed countries such as norway and japan have raised their bids, and recently russia, and that developing countries such as south korea, brazil and indonesia have also recently presented ambitious plans. we're going to keep pushing. our 30 percent will continue to be used as leverage. now we're waiting for the united states and china in particular. we note that president obama has spoken of an agreement which would either contain only certain parts or be merely a political declaration. he also agreed that it should contain all the key elements and also the measures that can be put into effect immediately. a copenhagen agreement must cover all the world's emissions. without bids from the us and china, only half of the deal is covered. let me be very clear. a deal could be put on hold if the us and china put sufficiently ambitious bids on the table. the eu will continue to press for adequate measures to be put forward in the negotiations. two weeks before the final negotiations, we will continue to hold our leadership. i look forward to continuing cooperation with parliament, not least through the cop15 group which will be in copenhagen. i look forward to the dialogue. we will work together to achieve a very successful, ambitious and real agreement in copenhagen.

mr. chairman, please! i am not afraid to say that the stockholm programme is the most ambitious initiative in recent years in the area of justice in the european union. i am all the more pleased that one of the fundamental ideas of this programme is to make life easier for the people of the european union. the successful implementation of the stockholm programme in the area of justice will of course depend on the creation of a truly european judicial culture, changes in the practical approach to the creation of new law, and the proper functioning of the e-justice portal. the principle of mutual recognition, which i call fundamental, requires mutual trust, but also trust in the legal systems of other countries, which is what we've been talking about here today. these values can only be achieved through mutual knowledge and understanding, thus creating a european judicial culture. mutual knowledge and understanding can only be achieved through an active policy of exchange of experience, visits, information sharing, training for judicial staff, especially judges of the first instance, and a thorough modernisation of the university curricula in community universities, which is of the utmost importance. another issue is to emphasise the importance of the multilingual e-justice portal. the portal should have access to legal databases, to judicial and non-judicial electronic redress, to intelligent systems designed to help citizens find ways to solve legal problems and to use extensive registers, lists of judicial staff or simple guides to the legal system of each member state, so i am very pleased that minister and commissioner barrot have spoken about this. i would also like to stress the need to develop european legislation of the highest quality in the field of judicial cooperation in civil matters, based on properly designed impact assessments, in order to provide citizens and businesses with effective instruments to address the various legal problems in the internal market. in an era of growing euroscepticism in many eu member states, the stockholm programme offers us the opportunity to show citizens that the eu institutions are responsive to their current needs.
mr. chairman, please! the stockholm programme is the answer to the important question of ensuring the security of the citizens of the union. but that is not always the answer. we do not need a complete unification of criminal and civil law, but only the harmonization of criminal and civil law, and that only in narrow, clearly defined areas. europe needs above all good cooperation between police and judicial authorities so that judicial decisions are effectively enforced and criminals are effectively prosecuted, regardless of the union's internal borders. the stockholm programme should therefore provide a number of incentives and focus on this. i would like to draw attention to three points in order to coordinate the activities of the member states. first, given the great value of free movement of persons, cooperation is necessary in the exchange of information on criminals who pose a particular threat to public policy. i am thinking in particular of the sexual offenders who are a threat to the weakest and most vulnerable, namely children, as the stockholm document rightly points out. work should be started as soon as possible on the establishment of a european register of sexual offenders, especially those who commit the most aggressive and serious crimes against children, with as wide an access to it as possible for interested persons and organisations. the freedom of movement of persons must be linked to the flow of knowledge and information about possible risks in order to adequately protect the public, including the most vulnerable, in this case children. secondly, the effectiveness of the execution of confiscation orders should be ensured. this is particularly true of the effective fight against organised crime, so that a judgment given in one country allows the proper search for the criminal's hidden assets in another country and their subsequent confiscation. this applies to both the direct and the indirect benefits derived from the offence. thirdly, while accepting that custodial sentences constitute the appropriate criminal response to minor offences, it must not be overlooked that, in certain particularly justified cases, custodial sentences constitute the only real and effective protection of the public against the most serious offences. therefore, it must be borne in mind that such punishment is also a just response to the most cruel crimes. in conclusion, i would like to express my appreciation for the document prepared and to stress that the programme should aim at improving cooperation between member states while preserving the national distinctiveness of their legal systems.

member of the commission. − in response to the first question, from mr tarabella, on energy prices, i can state that with the adoption of the third internal energy market package, the importance of the citizen in the internal energy market has been elevated considerably. the new measures are intended to improve the operation of the retail energy market and provide additional consumer protection. these topics are discussed and followed up at the citizens’ energy forum, established with the aim of improving the functioning of the retail market to the benefit of individual consumers. the forum, involving the representatives of consumers, industry, national energy regulators and national administrations, seeks to improve implementation of energy legislation and may develop elements for codes of conduct with self-regulating and even quasi-binding effects on the industry. in this context, a working group on billing was established at the first meeting of the forum in 2008. the working group’s recommendations are examples of good billing practice and were presented and endorsed at the second meeting of the forum in 2009. energy regulators and industry will report on the implementation of the billing recommendations in the next forum, which is expected to be in the autumn of 2010. the third internal energy market package also brought a new instrument intended to inform consumers – the european energy consumer checklist. the checklist is a tool that will help inform consumers in the member states of their rights – notably on billing – and assist with the implementation and enforcement of energy legislation. it aims to provide consumers with simplified, accurate and practical information on local energy markets. the harmonisation of the competences of energy regulators in relation to consumer protection, which will result in active market monitoring, will further enhance their protection.
member of the commission. − mr tarabella, your question is very much concentrated on why the charter was dropped. the public consultation entitled towards a charter on the european energy consumers was launched in july 2007. the results of the consultation showed that there was little knowledge of existing energy consumer rights. the idea of a charter that would create a single piece of legislation covering consumer rights that are currently included in a number of european directives and numerous national implementation instruments was rejected for legal reasons. the energy consumer rights that are in the existing european legislation are already legally binding. you ask why there cannot be a standard bill for all consumers. our working group on billing, set up by the first citizens’ energy forum, confirmed that industry’s right to self-regulation, promoting innovation in billing, should be preserved. at the same time, greater transparency and comparability of offered prices and services to consumers should be ensured. billing accuracy is closely related to metering frequency. meter-reading frequency is not defined by eu legislation. however, this is indirectly addressed by smart metering. i would like also to stress that during the citizens’ energy forum we endorsed the recommendations for good practice in billing, which aims to provide consumers with simple and clear information on gas and electricity bills. through the consumer market scoreboard, where we investigated different consumer markets, we spotted that the markets from where we had most complaints is the electricity market. the second is financial markets, and the third is local transport. that is why the commission has launched a major study on the retail electricity market and will present the results to the forum in 2010. this is the second layer of implementing the results of the consumer markets scoreboard and i believe that in the future this one will remain as one of the strongest instruments to make our diagnosis on how the retail market is functioning, especially in this case, which is of such an important and basic interest and also very much related to services.
member of the commission. − we are aware that the commission is not a price setter. what we can do and what we are committed to doing is to make prices transparent. in one of the recent directives – the 2007 consumer credit directive – we asked the banks to establish a common methodology to calculate the interest rate, on the basis of which consumers could compare the offers and find the best solution for them. we have several tools to work with; this is about unfair commercial practices and it is precisely the transparency of prices that is core to that directive. we also have another horizontal directive, on unfair commercial terms, which concerns whether the terms relate to undue and unjust enrichment. that is what i believe you hinted at when you asked the question about prices. this matter is in our hands and we also need to do everything possible to ensure that enforcement in all member states across europe is equally well implemented, because all these directives depend very much on how they are implemented. that is why i am proposing to the european commission a communication on enforcement. here we are breaking new ground, because enforcement is normally in the hands of the member states, but we need to compare the results and to have benchmarks, which, by the way – concerning the previous question on metering and on understanding – is why we are strongly encouraging the project on smart metering. this may not be a pan-european initiative, but countries like sweden, which is holding the presidency, are among the pioneers in this area. i can only encourage everyone to look at this example and make maximum use of it. this could also lead on to other questions, such as how to calculate the carbon footprint all of us leave through energy consumption. turning to other areas, the commission has recently been doing much more on labelling in respect of energy efficiency and more price comparison, encouraging the use of consumer indexes, such as has been the case in italy and other countries, because this is also a very good service, provided through the internet, which helps consumers to fight for a better price. however, in order to make this happen we need to have cross-border shopping and availability. cross-border trade via the internet currently stands at only nine per cent in the european union, so we really have a call of point of view of consumers and of businesses – to improve this really very poor level of cross-border trade in europe.
member of the commission. − following the request of member states and stakeholders, the commission proposed the regulation on nutrition and health claims, which was adopted in december 2006 by parliament and the council. the aim of the regulation is precisely to ensure that nutrition and health claims made on foods are truthful, clear and based on generally accepted scientific evidence, so that the consumer is adequately protected. the commission therefore aims to establish lists of permitted health claims as well as to update permitted nutrition claims. the regulation sets authorisation procedures to ensure that only scientifically substantiated health claims are made. these procedures involve firstly the european food safety authority, which assesses the substantiation of health claims; secondly, the commission, which proposes draft measures authorising or rejecting health claims accordingly; and thirdly, the member states, which give their opinion on the measures in the regulatory committee. the commission has so far adopted four regulations authorising or rejecting health claims. similar measures will continue to be adopted according to the evaluation of the health claims from the european food safety authority, thereby ensuring that consumers are not misled.
member of the commission. − i can only agree with the honourable member. this is exactly the reason why we put forward this regulation. i must say we were amazed by the number of applications received. we were expecting a few hundred and we received 44 000 claims. we consolidated this 44 000 into a group of 4 000, which we submitted to the european food safety authority (efsa) for an opinion. that is the reason why efsa is not in a position to complete the examination of all 4 000 claims within the time limit of december 2010. but i think it is very important for the consumers that we finish this process and that they know exactly when they see a claim, and they see some food in the supermarket with a claim, they will know for sure that this is based on science and is not misleading.

in writing. - in today's vote on the eu strategy for the copenhagen climate conference, the european parliament took a radical and unrealistic position. the european parliament is calling for a doubling of co2 emissions reductions in eu countries, challenging the recently hard-won climate package (paragraph 33 calls for a 40% reduction). the european parliament, by calling for €30 billion a year to be spent on clean technologies in developing countries, expects coal-fired countries such as poland to pay twice for co2 emissions: once as a fee for emissions trading and once as a contribution to help developing countries combat climate change (paragraph 18 says that the contribution should be no less than €30 billion a year). in demanding that the member states' contribution to clean technologies in developing countries be calculated on the basis of co2 emissions and gdp, parliament omitted the criterion of the ability to bear these costs. this means a cost of 40 billion euros for poland over the next 10 years! vice-president of the commission. − madam president, i would like to thank the committee on legal affairs for raising these questions. you raised so many big and fundamental questions which definitely need to be discussed in the coming months. this issue is definitely intensive, interesting, exciting and very future-oriented. i will first of all give an overview concerning this concrete question. first of all: the google books project. in essence, it is an initiative aimed at providing a tool to find, search and buy books for a wide audience of users. for rights holders, it may represent an additional channel of trade and so an additional source of revenue. let me add that in europe, the google books project is deployed in collaboration with libraries and concerns only public domain books. in-copyright books are only included in the project by way of the google partner programme addressed to publishers willing to conclude agreements with google. the google books class action settlement concerns the google books project in the united states and aims to conclude a litigation procedure which has been going on for over four years. if approved, it will provide an additional source of revenue for rights holders but also, and most importantly, make the hitherto unavailable out-of-print and orphan works available for online search and access to us users. moreover, its financial incentives may bring rights holders of orphan works out of the shadows. now, when it comes to the google book search project, the commission sees the google initiative as a demonstration that new business models are evolving to provide almost instant access to vast numbers of works to an increasing number of consumers. because the european commission favours the digitisation of books in european libraries and beyond, and because digitisation of books is a task of herculean proportions, where private sector support is needed, the commission favours initiatives such as google’s book search project as long as they respect intellectual property rights and do not lead to the distortion of competition. when it comes to the google books settlement, the commission has been actively engaged in consultations with european publishers and with google. in september 2009, the commission organised a public hearing bringing together european stakeholders and the settlement parties to exchange views and seek clarification on the various elements of the agreement. but meanwhile, important changes have occurred. due to numerous objections raised about the initial settlement by google’s competitors, foreign governments (france and germany) and the us department of justice, the terms of the settlement were revised and these revisions were submitted to the us court on 13 november 2009. first, the revised settlement has been significantly narrowed in scope. now, only books either registered with the us copyright office or published in the united kingdom, australia or canada by 5 january 2009 are covered by the settlement. all other books are outside the scope of the settlement. consequently, only united states, united kingdom, australian and canadian authors and publishers will, in future, be represented on the board of the books rights registry, the body that administers the terms of the settlement. secondly, publishers from countries other than the united states, the united kingdom, australia and canada will now have to negotiate individually to become part of google books services in the united states. the new version of the settlement gives rise to two remarks. first, being outside the settlement is not always an advantage. when you are out, you can no longer control what google does with the copies they have scanned up to now. second, publishers from eu member states – apart from the united kingdom – will now no longer participate in a major transformation of the book market. the google books project in the united states will receive a major thrust forward, with no european publishers any longer a part of it. even though services negotiated under this settlement will only be available to united states users, this absence could be detrimental to cultural diversity. in this regard, the commission has been calling, and will repeatedly call, on member states: firstly, to intensify their digitisation policies; secondly, to explore the possibilities for public-private partnerships for digitisation; and, thirdly, to ensure that all digitised material becomes available through europeana. if member states do that, the google books settlement may turn out to be the catalyst, not a threat, for europe’s initiatives in the area of access to digitised culture. this brings me to your second question. the debate on the google books settlement has shown that europe cannot afford to be left behind on the digital frontier. europe has to act swiftly. to this end, the commission is fully committed to working on a copyright framework that will facilitate large-scale digitisation of european library collections. we believe that copyright rules have to be flexible enough in order not to overly complicate the creation of online libraries.
on behalf of the ppe group. - madam president! - i have to go. i thank you for that statement and the question from the legal affairs committee, mrs niebler's comments, the commissioner's reply. these are extremely important matters, including for the committee on the internal market and consumer protection. the process of digitising books offers us enormous new opportunities, but it must serve - and let us remember this - the interests of the publishing market and the readers, that is, the interests of businesses and consumers in europe. this previous version of the google deal threatened to monopolize the entire literary heritage by one private company, and now that danger is not entirely far away. after all, google has scanned millions of copyrighted titles from all over the world. so far, he's been using these scans illegally, using only the american fair use formula, without asking the authors or publishers for permission. the new agreement continues to flout the basic principle of the berne convention, which states that the copyright holder should be asked for permission before using his work, not just given the opportunity to sign off, i.e. bearing the responsibility, effort and cost. and the agreement covers books from all over the world published in english in countries that are covered by the agreement. google uses out of print and orphan works to scan books. both of these categories are very loosely defined. after all, the authors of orphan works can often be found if they are searched carefully. and out of print is very often a book that the author has abandoned or the publisher has abandoned with full knowledge. is there a danger that google could take away publishers' freedom of publishing policy and authors' potential profits? and the consumer. the book industry could be weakened by google's projects in the long run if rights holders don't get the royalties they're due. publishers, in order to survive in a competitive market, will stop producing valuable, peer-reviewed, expensive books. for the consumer, this means the de facto replacement of high-quality publications by cheap, unverified, unambitious works, and ubiquitous advertising. so i expect the european commission to develop a policy that will allow the further development of digitisation, but at the same time will not negatively affect the development of creativity, the interests of the market and readers in europe.
madam president! the potential benefits and opportunities that the google project offers to consumers, researchers, most publishers and authors for the preservation of cultural heritage are largely beyond dispute. but we cannot ignore the legal consequences, and that is what i would like to focus on as a representative of the legal affairs committee. first of all, the conditions to be met are obvious. it's about respecting copyright and creating a proper system of royalties for authors. unfortunately, google's project is based on the anglo-saxon legal system and north american market realities, which are absolutely inappropriate for the european union's order. so google's activities in our territory are facing legal obstacles, but also ethical obstacles. google assumes that a copyright owner who does not wish to be covered by the settlement is obliged to notify the fact. this is clearly against our law, which requires that you have to get permission from the copyright owner and pay the copyright fee to scan and share a book. another issue is so-called orphan books, i.e. books whose copyright owners have not been identified. in most member states, collecting societies represent the interests of known right holders as well as those not yet identified, inter alia, by securing the proceeds of sales for a certain period in case the right holders are located in the future. i would also like to stress the need to adapt european copyright law to the challenges of the digital age, while fully sharing the view of commissioners reding and mccreevy, and also the words of commissioner kallasa today, that the digitisation of copyrighted works must fully respect the principle of copyright, fair remuneration for authors who can benefit most from the access of the wider european public to their works. and that opportunity, of course, we cannot afford to lose in europe.
madam president! the possibilities of the internet have inspired google to bring out-of-print, forgotten, dust-covered publications back to life in cyberspace. the idea of a modern replica of the famous library of alexandria, however, led to a copyright dispute. the agreement reached two weeks ago has already satisfied the american society of composers and authors and the association of american publishers and some of their european counterparts. the agreement provides for the scanning and sharing of items issued in four countries: the united states, the united kingdom, australia and canada, for a fee. users in these countries will be able to read 20% of the e-book for free (the cost will be covered by the advertiser), while the other 80% will be paid for out of their own pocket. from the point of view of the author and the publisher, this means two benefits. first, a one-time fee from google for the ability to scan a book between 60 and 300 dollars, and second, 63% of the revenue generated by an e-book on google books. in other words, the author makes money by making even one page of his book available online. few people realize that a non-british european google books user, such as a belgian or polish internet user, will not have access to even 20% of the e-books. the service will be available mainly in english, and any european publisher or author wishing to join the programme will have to contact google on their own. europeans will only have free access to the least attractive category of books public goods for which copyright has long since expired, such as the french national library, which has not lent books for 200 years. this will not result in a complete electronic library of european titles. despite some concerns about google's project, such as its monopoly on the production and distribution of e-books and the need to give up part of its revenues from fees and advertising, i believe that the union is doomed to inefficiency without a uniform copyright solution. the legal confusion surrounding google has demonstrated the consequences of the lack of a uniform copyright law in the union, as well as the inability to provide a coherent response to the google books format initiatives. it is clear to the naked eye that the harmonisation of copyright law in the european union has become an urgent necessity.
madam president! first, digitalisation is a huge opportunity to bring cultural heritage, european and global, to as many europeans as possible. it is perfectly in line with the new lisbon strategy. however, it seems that the whole issue of orphan works requires uniformity in the first place, which is why european solutions for the management of the revenue from orphan works should be unified in the first place. member states have different solutions here. secondly, the issue of unrevised works requires special supervision. well, out of print should be standardized in my opinion. there can be no situation where there is no strict regulation of unrepeated works. third, we cannot accept in the european legal system an opt-out method that gives google the ability to digitize collections without the author's consent. i think we should be looking at a broader eu approach in this area. and i think that if we want to compete with google in this positive sense of the word, or if we want to cooperate, we should certainly accelerate the european union and above all, we should accelerate the member states in this area.
vice-president of the commission. − madam president, the commission is doing its utmost to develop the digital field in our society. it seems to me that google – and particularly its books project – has appeared as a great integrating factor for the european union, because, as you know very well, – and this is in all papers – copyright so far has been explicitly in the hands of member states and national legislation. now we need some kind of common approach, for which the commission is very happy to provide proposals. the next commission will definitely take all these issues very seriously and this will be a high priority. we agree that the books need to go online and fast. they will go anyway, whether we want it or not. the most important thing is that authors need to be paid for online books. we are planning a framework directive on these issues – including collective societies, which need to be transparent and accountable to their members. the framework directive will appear somewhere between autumn 2010 and spring 2011. we should not fall behind, and we are proposing simple eu rules on orphan book works and also books which are out of print. the eu proposal will ensure that books are only digitised with prior permission, and there will also be a serious search for orphan works. let us continue this discussion. once again we would thank the committee on legal affairs, and the honourable members mrs niebler and mr lehne, for their initiative in initiating this interesting debate.
in writing. the new google books service offered by google has been the subject of much controversy recently. the project involves making a huge number of scanned books available free of charge, with 4 million books by european authors among the works scanned. this raises questions about the limits of freedom on the internet and the challenges facing policy-makers in the rapidly developing information society. as the european commission rightly points out, the digitisation of copyright-protected works must fully respect the principle of copyright and fairly remunerate the authors who can benefit most from the access of the general european public to their works. at the same time, however, the commission is questioning the adequacy of the european copyright system to the challenges of the digital age: will the current set of rules allow european consumers to access books in digital form? does it guarantee a reward for the authors? the 'google books' project enables a much larger number of readers to access books than would be possible in a traditional library. however, the free distribution of books online is subject to restrictions, as is the sharing of music. the law has not kept pace with the development of digital communications, and it is therefore necessary to create a new legal framework to regulate the changing reality. it is also necessary to find a balance between the benefits of projects such as google books and the authors' right to remuneration.
