of this institute from the german federal budget is under discussion. this may explain why the institute does a lot of publicity work, but apparently does not place much importance on the fact that its findings can be adequately tested by us. however, i think i have been misunderstood: even if we only read about it in the press, we take it as a sign of possible new scientific knowledge, and i have already passed it on to the scientific committee. i do not need the invitation that has been addressed to me here. the moment i get the hint that there might be new scientific knowledge about the safety of toys and the limits we have, that's passed on to the scientific committee. but i have to say again, you cannot ask me, and i cannot ask you, to decide a methodological dispute between scientists. you can't do that! i can't do this, you can't do this. all i can do is say, this question of the methodology for measuring possible limit values has been discussed extensively in this parliament, in the council and in the commission. and the view of this german institute has not been shared by any other scientific institute in europe, by any other! if you think i was obliged to follow the opinion of one institution and not the opinion of all the others, then you can tell me that and then you can blame me for it. i can't take that responsibility. neither can any of you. but i say again, if any new knowledge emerges, the process will be set in motion. unfortunately, mrs weisgerber, you said it would have to go faster, but it can't. we are dealing with very complicated scientific questions here. tests are necessary. there are - you may not know this - extensive animal studies, for example, that are needed to verify such statements. you can't force science to create knowledge in a certain time frame. i'm sorry, but that's not possible. so i'm just going to have to ask you to accept that i'm telling you that the scientific committee has told us that they can deliver substantiated results by the middle of next year. he will. on the basis of these results, the commission will make new proposals without delay if it should turn out that there are indeed new findings. just so we're clear, i'm not going to... mr creutzmann, the principle is that we use the least possible risk. i don't need the federal institute for risk assessment to teach me that. that is why the demands you derived from it have been met. mrs. rühle, you say i should have gone to the press sooner. you'll be surprised to hear that i did. and just as i do not believe that what i have said here in parliament tonight will be taken up by the european media, especially the german media, so my factual and, as i found it, calm explanation of what is important has unfortunately not been taken up by the german media. but i have made the necessary explanation and clarified the facts. i am happy to make the text available to you. mrs. davidson, we have the strictest legislation in the world. we can be proud of that. the commission is the only body in the world which can be expected to take the lead in ensuring that toys are as safe as possible. i can only agree with mrs schaldemose european standardisation organisations have been given the relevant contracts. but standards are no different than other scientific papers. you cannot have them available within a week, a month or a few months. it takes time. but all these standards we have talked about are in the works and will be in place in time and will also allow us to establish a precise comparability between products and to strengthen market surveillance. the last point i want to make is that the car seats that have been mentioned here and which have caused safety problems in america are not toys. they are therefore not covered by the toy directive but by the general product safety directive. we don't have to hide from the americans here. the system we have in europe in terms of general product safety has been improving in recent years. if unsafe products appear on the european market, we can now assume with some certainty that all the other member states and the commission will indeed be informed and that appropriate action will be taken.

i wanted to read the important information first. on 2 december i received a communication from the commission to the european parliament and the council on the consequences of the entry into force of the treaty of lisbon for the ongoing interinstitutional decision-making procedures. under the communication, parliament as such is recognised as the competent institution for all the proposals contained in the communication for which the treaty of lisbon recognises parliament's competence. parliament also notes that the european commission is withdrawing certain proposals on the same grounds. for other legislative proposals pending on 1 december 2009, the date of entry into force of the treaty of lisbon, the chair shall ask the relevant parliamentary committees of that term, in accordance with the minutes, to examine the legal bases and procedural changes proposed by the european commission, as well as any other changes that need to be made in the light of the provisions of the treaty of lisbon, and to decide whether they intend to confirm positions already adopted as a result of the consultation as a first reading of the ordinary legislative procedure or the approval procedure. parliament reserves the right, of course, to ask the european commission to submit new proposals in any event. for proposals on which parliament has not been consulted before the entry into force of the treaty of lisbon, it is for the european commission to submit new proposals under the ordinary legislative procedure or the appropriate procedure. it was a communication on our legislative activities in the near future a communication on the interaction between the european commission and the european parliament in the legislative process. as you know, we are in a transitional period - we are moving from the treaty of nice to the treaty of lisbon, and at the same time we have a new term of office for the european parliament. we don't have a commission approved yet. all this requires a fairly laborious and legal interaction between the commission and parliament, and this is what this communication is about.

mr president, i should like to make four points. firstly let me emphasise the need to use our 2010 budget, and in particular the european cohesion policy financial instruments, with the utmost expediency in order to stimulate economic activity in all of the union’s regions and cities and create the leverage necessary to revitalise member states’ economies. cohesion policy is providing a strong and necessary bridge between recovery from the crisis and long-term structural transformation of the european economy. secondly, it is for this reason that the committee for regional development has encouraged the commission and member states not only to use the financial resources available to invest in what are cohesion policy 2007-2013 priorities – climate change, knowledge and innovation, energy efficiency, renewable energy, broadband, sustainable urban transport and renewal of skills – but also to promote the leverage function of the cohesion policy; which is to efficiently use all the financial engineering tools which the cohesion policy has created in collaboration with the european investment bank in order to assist small and medium-sized companies not only to survive this difficult period but first of all to go the distance, to adapt to the changing face of the global economy which is transforming itself and to rise up to the challenge – and the opportunity – of climate change. thirdly, let me inform members that all payment applications for the european regional development fund and the cohesion fund from the 2009 budget, totalling eur 25.5 billion, have been fully used, thus contributing to recovery, structural change, growth, employment and to climate-change energy efficiency. lastly, in this context, i regret the cuts in support for candidate countries, the ipa regional development and human resources instrument, which addresses areas such as unemployment, social exclusion and education investment – a cut of eur 7 million, which is 0.5% of the available operational credits that go to administration – without regard to the need of ensuring good local administration and without regard to the basic principles of good financial management which is so dear to this house.

ladies and gentlemen! the 2010 budget is a difficult compromise. on the one hand, it's supposed to help mitigate the economic crisis, and at the same time, we're funding climate change, mainly to reduce co2 emissions. that's good, but in the short term, it's a drag on development, which we're still spending too little on. the increase in research and innovation spending is justified. it improves our competitiveness. it seems that we still under-spend on education, including the erasmus exchange programme. it is good that the milk programme has been funded - albeit too little - because the past year has been difficult for european farmers. if we want to revive the economy, reduce unemployment and social exclusion, we need to increase the amount of money available for micro-credit. it is important for development to finance broadband in rural areas, but as i said, this budget is a compromise.
in writing. − on 10 november 2009, the european commission published a proposal for a decision of the european parliament and of the council establishing a european microfinance facility. it is consistent with the commission's 'implementing a european recovery plan' and with the council's priorities of maintaining employment, creating jobs and promoting mobility, upskilling and adapting to labour market needs and increasing access to employment. this microfinance facility is intended to facilitate access to financial services for the unemployed and for groups of entrepreneurs in difficulty. these are those groups of people who do not have the creditworthiness of commercial banks and would like to start their own business. the introduction of such a support instrument from union funds is particularly important in the context of the current decline in the level of lending and the decline in the value of loans granted. the situation in the credit sector shows that the financial and economic crisis is turning into an employment and social crisis. the empl report contains substantial amendments to the european commission's proposal, including an objection to the transfer of the necessary funds to the european microfinance instrument from the progress programme. the rapporteur requests that a separate budget line be created for this purpose and that the amount of the instrument be increased by an additional eur 50 million over the next four years. in view of the above, i support this report.
in writing. − progress was created to help achieve the european union's employment, social affairs and equal opportunities objectives set out in the social agenda. the budgetary resources of this programme are intended to boost the process of transformation and modernisation in five areas, such as employment, social inclusion and social protection, working conditions, combating discrimination and gender equality. the financial and economic crisis is now turning into a social and employment crisis. the unemployed and disadvantaged groups need active support and guidance if they are to become self-employed. it is the progress programme that targets the most vulnerable groups and therefore i believe that the member states and the european union are responsible for its effective implementation. the union should also make every effort to increase targeted financial support for new individual entrepreneurs and micro-entrepreneurs in the form of monitoring, training, including practical training, and skills development. progress is designed to promote micro-enterprise and the social economy. in the current economic and financial environment, which is characterised by a reduced supply of credit, progress will extend the scope of targeted financial assistance to new entrepreneurs. the main responsibility for employment and social policy lies with the member states, and the european union should be the initiator of these changes. real employment opportunities for all must be created, and the quality and productivity of work must be improved.

vice-president of the commission. − mr president, this was a very effective way of softening me up a bit as i now speak for the final time. i could not have chosen a better subject on which to make my last intervention in the european parliament – which it probably is – than on openness and transparency. let me just state some basic facts. the european commission has provided a proposal. it is the only proposal on the table. we did it in the shape of a recast, which means that we think the basic principles in this regulation are sound; they are ok. we can use them but we have to modernise them, upgrade them and make them more effective. this was the whole idea behind the recast. we have some different views on a few things – how to define documents etc. – but these are still the kind of negotiations that we should engage in and make sure that we move things forward. to do that, we need a first reading from parliament. this is the basic message from our side. we also think, on the basis of a new treaty, that we can do it by expanding the scope of this regulation. that is the main difference, as we see it in the commission. it will now cover all the bodies, agencies etc. of the european union. this is where we are today, so we still hope that parliament will now provide, as soon as possible, a first reading. then we can also have the views of the council so that we can enter into proper discussions and negotiations and finally have a decision. regarding a number of very important issues that you have also raised, mr cashman, in your report: i think there are other means that we can use as they are a bit outside the scope of this regulation. but they are still very important initiatives. they have to do with registers, with things we discussed – today, for example – where we can improve openness and transparency, through other methods and not only through the regulation. this is where we will continue. i know you do not like it very much, but i have taken the initiative to make an openness action plan, parts of which we discussed today, where we can join hands and make efforts to continue on openness and transparency and fight for that. on that positive note – i really want it to be a positive note – i would like to thank you all and i also want to use the opportunity to say ‘merry christmas and happy new year’ to all of you.
in writing. mr president, i consider the issue of access to documents of the eu institutions and bodies that we have raised today to be of the utmost importance in the legislative process of the european union. transparency is essential here, as it enables every citizen of the union to have access to documents which, within the meaning of article 15 (3) of the treaty on the functioning of the european union, are not only part of the legal order in force but also constitute draft legal acts. thus, any legal entity established or resident in the eu can directly influence the newly created right, as a form of public control. the current regulation 1049/2001 provides for adequate access to community documents, but the entry into force of the treaty of lisbon on 1 december 2009 has presented us with a unique challenge, where the role and effective participation of european union citizens has been increased. unrestricted access to documents is therefore a key determinant of the future shape and functioning of the eu.

madam president! the european court of human rights in strasbourg rightly ruled that the display of crosses in school classrooms violates the freedom of religion of students and the right of parents to raise their children in accordance with their own beliefs. the judges unanimously ruled that the school's cross violated the european convention for the protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms. the verdict is simple, clear and universally understood. that is why it has aroused such anger and aggression from clergymen and right-wing politicians. they pretend not to understand it and demand an explanation from the commission and an official position from parliament. it's against the law! the eu institutions are not entitled to assess this judgment, nor any other. let us not forget that there is a tripartite power and that the court is an organ of the council of europe, not of the european union. i answer the questions put by the authors, since they have such doubts: the judgment on the cross does not violate the principle of subsidiarity. on the contrary, it helps those european countries to respect the law, which have forgotten that their constitutions contain, if not a clause on the separation of church and state, then at least a clause on the neutrality of worldview. the court's ruling helps church-oriented national authorities and courts to enforce fundamental rights of citizens that have been violated by the clericalisation of society. citizens of religious states are unable to defend their rights before national courts. it's good they can go to court and get justice. the judgment is consistent with respect for the national identities of the member states and should be enforced. it does not prohibit the display of religious symbols in public spaces, but only in a small part of them, such as public schools. no one is demanding that crosses be removed from churches, from public squares, or from flags, as one of the members of parliament has unwisely said. this is not an interference in church-state relations, but only the defense of citizens whose rights are being violated. in my country too, the progressive clericalisation is restricting the basic rights of poles. i cannot imagine that the european parliament and the commission would prevent my countrymen from asserting their legitimate rights before the court in strasbourg. the commission and parliament's negative attitude to this judgment would be an unwarranted interference and would also make us look ridiculous. i warn you against that!

why we must work together to solve the problem. from our side, we can compensate for years of irresponsible behaviour. we can help finance climate action in the developing world. the european union took its responsibility last week. it is not the form that matters in copenhagen but the substance. we can be satisfied if we get a deal on emissions reductions and on financing, and a commitment to start immediate action and, more importantly, we can start fighting climate change. last year we were suddenly faced with the most serious financial crisis since the 1930s. the ground was literally shaking under our feet. suddenly it became clear to us how interlinked the financial markets were and how interdependent we all were in finding a common response. in the course of only a few months, governments in the eu adopted extraordinary support measures. it was a fast and impressive response but it came with a price. our aggregated deficit in public finances now amounts to almost 7% of gdp – over three times more than last year. twenty member states are experiencing excessive deficit procedures. so the follow-up to the economic and financial crisis has, quite naturally, been another main priority throughout this autumn. let me briefly touch on what we have done. at the end of october we agreed on a fiscal exit strategy, and at last week’s european council we agreed on principles for exiting from financial support schemes. in addition, we agreed on a fundamentally new structure for financial supervision in europe. when financial flows are international, supervision can no longer be national. now it is up to the european parliament to agree to the final steps. it was also clear to us that the ‘bonus culture’ could not continue in the way in which people had become used to. i am pleased that the eu managed to convince the g20 to agree on far-reaching changes to this policy. the new rules will reinforce the need for a link between result and reward. the economic and financial crisis hit us hard but we have shown the ability to act and we have strengthened our resistance. once we have secured our recovery, the eu will stand stronger, thanks to the measures we have adopted. the swedish presidency took place during a period of institutional change. when we took over on 1 july, this parliament was newly elected. we had not yet appointed a president of the european commission. the outcome of the then pending irish referendum was uncertain. it was not clear whether the treaty of lisbon would be ratified by all member states. it was not even clear whether it could enter into force during the swedish presidency. then the drama unravelled. in close consultation with this parliament, josé manuel barroso was appointed president of the european commission for a second term. the presidency now had a stable counterpart in the commission to work with. the outcome of the irish referendum was a victory for ireland. it was a victory for european cooperation. it brought us one step closer to the treaty of lisbon. but then the unexpected happened. at a late stage, the czech president came with new conditions before he would sign. we had to handle these requests in a way that did not trigger similar conditions from other member states and we managed to do this at the european council in october. a few days later the czech president signed. immediately after the signature i started to consult my colleagues again. we had to agree on high-ranking positions – on the president of the european council, and to nominate the high representative. i am not exaggerating when i say it was a relief when all preparations were finalised on 1 december. the treaty of lisbon could finally enter into force. now the european union will be more efficient. it will have better tools to fight climate change and influence the global economic agenda. the new president of the european council will ensure continuity. the high representative will assure coordination in our external relations. we will have a more democratic union with the greater involvement of the european parliament and of our national parliaments. a new era for the european union has begun. when i stood here before you on 15 july, we were still in the throes of the financial and economic crisis. there was uncertainty on the transition of the new treaty. we did not know whether we would manage to unite ourselves and encourage others on the not so long – but very winding – road to copenhagen. with the european council meeting last week, the swedish presidency has delivered on all five of its priorities: a strong eu mandate for climate change; follow-up of the economic and financial crisis; the eu baltic sea strategy; the stockholm programme for justice and home affairs; reinforcing the eu as a global actor, including enlargement, and a new external action service. as i said, with the treaty of lisbon in place, a new era has begun in the european union. i would like to end by thanking all of you. the presidency needed the help of the european parliament in tackling the challenges we were facing. thank you for giving us that help. i would also like to thank the commission, and especially josé manuel barroso. i have probably spent more than a healthy amount of time with josé manuel this autumn. he has been a tremendous support to me and to the swedish presidency. finally, i would like to thank the member states for their will to put aside differences and start compromising – with the best for europe at heart – to find solutions that are not only of benefit to them, but to europe as a whole. this unity is our strength.

opportunities for this new, enlarged european union we have today. we have seen the first evidence that decisive action taken to stabilise the european economy in the face of crisis is bearing some the other objectives. we have seen the appointment of the first president of the european council and of the first high representative, the vice-president of the commission, by the european council. in the past few years the european union has developed a consistent and ambitious approach on climate change. i am very proud that the commission has been the initiator of this very ambitious agenda. the impact of reduced emissions may only be felt in several decades’ time, but we are already taking concrete steps, giving our targets the force of law. let us be frank about this. some of our partners are announcing their intentions by press statements; but we have announced our intentions by law, law that is already agreed by all the member states. the developed world must act, but it must also help the developing world to decouple growth and emissions. i think that it is right that the european council last week centred on how we can put this global leadership at the service of an ambitious deal at copenhagen: by promising help to developing countries not in some distant future but already next year; by making clear that the deal must be comprehensive and must have the verification mechanisms to make it stick; by maintaining our readiness to up our targets, but only if others put ambitious commitments on the table as well. i think the european council achieved very important results, namely on two matters. first, on finance, the council was able successfully to put together a fast-start finance package, bigger than expected and, critically, with every member state involved. of course, some have said that this is not enough coming from the european union, but eur 7.2 billion, more than usd 10 billion in the current circumstances, and for three years, is a very serious commitment. i hope the money is now guaranteed, not just an aspiration. it is now for others to match it. the european council also reiterated its commitment for medium-term financing, to ensure it gives the fair contribution that is necessary for 2020. second, action on climate has sometimes been a divisive point for the european council. however, the atmosphere this time was different. there was a strong shared sense that everyone has an interest in the european union pulling its weight. we should now be getting the benefits from the investment we have made as the pioneers in this agenda. what i did find generally encouraging was recognition that the european union has to stand together. let us hope that this determination holds firm under the pressures of the next two or three days. what can we expect over the next few days? prime minister rasmussen of denmark will probably put forward a text today – but with a lot of the key numbers still left blank. the leaders’ task will be to move this forward to a deal. this is why i am going to copenhagen immediately after this debate. together with prime minister reinfeldt, we will do our best for the european union to lead this debate. we know that the atmosphere at the moment is not easy at copenhagen. we also know that this is part of the usual rhythm of a top negotiation. however, the arrival of so many heads of state and government will be a powerful driver to reach a deal. if that deal includes real commitment to cut emissions from both developed and developing countries; a clear commitment on financing to make this happen; and an agreement on how this is to be applied and verified – if this agreement includes the different elements of the bali road map and can be seen to be in the right ball park to respect the 2°c limit, then i think we will say rightly that it will be a major achievement. we are not there yet, but i believe it is possible to reach that agreement. the next few days will show whether the ambitions we have discussed in this parliament so often are going to be realised, but i sense already that there is a compelling need for change and that we need to make this success in copenhagen. there is a huge amount at stake. there is of course a balance to be found, but there is also a sense that today’s generation knows that there is a challenge which cannot be avoided. i believe last week’s european council left the european union ready to meet the challenge. i hope that with european leadership we will achieve success at copenhagen.

in writing. mr president, i would like to thank you for your kind words. the swedish presidency has been a very positive one. its clear success is first and foremost the completion of the ratification process of the lisbon treaty. as a member of the legal affairs committee, i also regard the compromise reached in the council on the eu patent and the unified patent judicial system as a success. the debate on a common patent for the whole union has been going on for a long time. it is high time that concrete steps were taken in this area, as the lack of uniform regulations is a barrier to the development of european companies and makes it difficult for them to compete with, for example, american companies. we have had many opportunities in the past to see how difficult it is to reconcile the interests of all the member states on the eu patent, and i am all the more grateful to the swedish presidency for the compromise that has been reached, at least for now, at political level. the lisbon treaty gives the union a legal basis for the establishment of intellectual property law and provides for the adoption of relevant standards through the codecision procedure. that is why we are going to have a very interesting debate in parliament during the next spanish presidency, on the basis of a compromise which will be worked out in december this year.
in writing. the 2020 strategy will set the direction of the union's operations and its main priorities for the next 10 years. in the context of the expiring lisbon strategy, it is important to continue the current socioeconomic priorities and to find effective measures to counter the effects of the economic crisis. in the context of the ongoing consultation on the future strategy, i would like to draw attention to two aspects: improving the education system in europe and gender equality in the labour market. the education system in europe needs to change. building a modern knowledge-based economy is not possible without a young, well-educated workforce. more financial support should be provided for existing eu programmes (erasmus, erasmus mundus, leonardo da vinci) and new initiatives should be created to help young people to study, gain experience abroad and have the financial and administrative means to use it at home. the union, which puts the needs of its citizens first, should adopt a programme which, in each of these objectives, promotes the principle of gender equality, particularly in the fight against unemployment. the new strategy must focus on increasing the participation of women in employment. indeed, eurostat research shows that women workers are more affected by the crisis than men, partly because they work in more vulnerable jobs. discrimination in the labour market remains a serious problem that the new strategy must tackle.
in writing. − i supported the launch of the european globalisation adjustment fund because the current situation on labour markets requires us to act for workers. previous crises have been characterised by their regional focus and concentration in one place. then all those who had lost their jobs or were struggling financially could emigrate for gain or work several jobs. today, given the global nature of the financial crisis, that is not an option. the current situation in the financial markets requires support for the many millions of people who have lost their jobs over the past year. this is not just about helping people find a job, of course, but also about taking advantage of the labour market's flexibility and retraining workers, organising appropriate training, for example in computer skills or vocational guidance. the bulk of the egf should be dedicated to promoting entrepreneurship and self-employment, as the opportunity to set up a business and earn an income on one's own account is an opportunity to maintain financial stability and growth in the event of job loss. i believe that programmes such as the european globalisation adjustment fund are very necessary because they are a response to a specific situation and directly support those who have been most affected by the crisis.
in writing. - i welcomed the resolution on the wto, because it is a particularly important issue in our time. it is in the interest of all of us to find a quick solution to this crisis, which is global in nature. it seems that one of the most effective ways to contain the crisis is to expand world trade. it is easier to limit economic reforms to regional or national levels, but in the long run this is not a good way of dealing with a crisis which has a global dimension and which requires common instruments of a global nature. the commission has already taken steps to ensure that the community's trade policy is not distorted by the excessive deficit. at the same time, we must adopt reasonable rules of competition. in those rules, product quality standards and production conditions are particularly important, including in the context of climate change mitigation and co2 emissions reduction. a particularly sensible approach is needed for highly sensitive goods such as agricultural and foodstuffs. in the future, it will be necessary to consider whether, in parallel with the liberalisation of trade in agricultural goods at world level under the wto, it is also necessary to introduce the harmonisation of certain elements of the agricultural policy at world level. the specificities of the agricultural sector, its dependence on climatic conditions and quality issues related to food security, as well as production conditions and the problem of world food security, should be taken into account. in the wto negotiations, we need more understanding of others and goodwill!

head of the central electoral commission of the republic of belarus. secondly, we are open to the possibility of visa facilitation and readmission between the eu and belarus. thirdly, there is the do some preparatory work based on these action plans, which were developed in the framework of the neighbourhood policy. in the discussions we took into account that the situation in belarus is better than it was a year and a half ago, although some steps have been taken backwards. the fact that a student was suspended from university after participating in a voluntary meeting within the framework of the eastern partnership is a very serious example of this. the transition from an authoritarian society to democracy - and this is something many members of this house know very well - is gradual. it will take time for belarus and there will be many obstacles along the way. that's why we need your full support. the global financial crisis is indeed creating opportunities for influence. the belarusian economy is on its knees and russia is no longer ready to pay the bill. in the energy sector, low gas prices are a thing of the past. can we then use this situation to encourage a different development in belarus? yes, there is no other way but dialogue. we must help to strengthen the cautious move towards greater openness. we must consider the effectiveness of sanctions policy. last year's decision to suspend visa restrictions after minsk released the last prisoners in august 2008 contributed to some progress in the dialogue. the use of sanctions is an important means of pressure on the european union. at the same time, the commission has taken several steps towards cooperation with belarus, which is part of the eastern partnership. our support for belarus within the international monetary fund has also been a step in a positive development. these are the conditions and now we must proceed in a wise and sensible way. the decision to extend the suspension of the visa ban list was a signal that we are serious about rewarding the positive steps taken. if we continue in this direction, we can take another step forward. at the moment, the discussions are focusing on two possible options. the first is the development of a formal contractual relationship and the second is the possibility of visa facilitation and readmission agreements. the position adopted by the council has laid the foundations for more concrete reflection on these issues. a partnership and cooperation agreement could mean that we formalise the relationship between the eu and belarus in a new way. this is a way of reconciling conditionality with our various means of pressure within the framework of a legally binding agreement. a partnership and cooperation agreement would also allow belarus to participate fully in the bilateral part of the eastern partnership. with regard to the visa facilitation, the idea is that it should be aimed at ordinary people, the general public, rather than at the leadership level. this would provide an important opportunity to promote contacts between civil society and citizens in belarus and in the eu. this could be a decisive factor in opening up and influencing belarusian society. this is in line with the objective of the eastern partnership. there is a link between visa facilitation and readmission. this should not be a major problem, because here belarus has shown that it can cooperate in border control issues. belarus is strategically located on the eu's eastern border. we therefore have an interest in a belarus which is modernising, developing and taking steps towards a democratic and free country. the importance of having democratic neighbours is a cornerstone of our security strategy. we will work to ensure that our values of democracy, market economy and respect for human rights are reflected in belarus. there is a clear parallel here with the way we develop partnerships with various countries in both the east and the south. i would like to conclude by stressing that we must of course continue to set clear conditions in our relations with belarus. the country must continue to move forward. president lukashenko's repressive policies must be replaced by more democracy and more tolerance. the rule of law must be respected. this message is conveyed in all the bilateral contacts we have between the member states and belarus. we need dialogue to make our demands work. that is why we in the council have also welcomed the increased contacts to strengthen democratic change. we will continue to develop our support for the democracy movement and civil society working for reforms and european integration in belarus. we are very grateful for the european parliament's strong support and commitment to this work.
member of the commission. − mr president, dear colleagues, council president, honourable members, it is a pleasure to discuss with you today our very important but also our very challenging relationship with belarus. i think it is important because belarus lies at a crossroads on our continent; and it is challenging because belarus’ own choices for its own future, and for its relationship with the eu, remain unclear. it still remains to be seen what they will be, so we will have to go on working with them. over the last two years, the european union has sought gradually to engage with belarus and to encourage further reforms, to build on the, i have to say, modest measures taken so far. i am convinced that the most productive approach to belarus will be one based on pragmatism. our engagement with that country needs to reflect positive steps by belarus itself, but we also have to show at least some flexibility. we have signalled clearly that we would like to see belarus take its place as a fully fledged participant in the european neighbourhood policy, and that the bilateral track of the eastern partnership can be opened to belarus if it shows through sustained action its wish to make irreversible steps towards democratic reform. in the mean time we have shown our goodwill in a number of important ways. a number of eu high-level visits to belarus this year helped strengthen political exchanges. we launched a dialogue on human rights issues in june 2009. the commission is engaged in a growing number of technical dialogues with belarus on issues of mutual interest. last month, for instance, the external relations council decided to extend existing restrictive measures, notably the visa ban and the assets freeze, till october 2010, given the lack of significant progress on human rights and fundamental freedoms. however, to encourage democratic progress, the council also extended the suspension of the restrictive measures. and the council also took two further decisions to encourage belarus to stay on the path of reforms. i very much welcome that the commission can now start working on the visa facilitation issue, and on a shadow enp action plan, the ‘joint interim plan’. these steps provide an incentive for moves towards democracy in belarus, which i am confident will be well understood on the one hand by the government, but on the other hand particularly by the people. the joint interim plan will be developed with both the authorities and civil society in belarus, and i hope it will open the door to deeper dialogue with belarus, including on delicate political issues. my services are preparing recommendations with a view to negotiating directives on visa facilitation and readmission agreements. visa facilitation is a priority for the belarusian people, and i would like to see more belarusians visiting the european union, travelling freely, studying and doing business. but naturally the final decision on the negotiation directives will lie with the council. in addition, the commission is prepared to increase the allocations of financial assistance to belarus for the period of 2010-2013. we have proposed a mandate. i really hope this will go further. however, if belarus wishes to come closer to the eu, it is clear it must show this through its actions. there must be an end to political prisoners and politically motivated prosecutions. reform of the electoral legislation in line with osce/odihr recommendations is sorely needed. the liberty of the press, freedom of speech and of assembly should be permitted and become the norm. the european union also encourages belarus to abolish or declare a moratorium on the death penalty. we call for improved conditions for ngos, civil society and human rights activists. all these steps could play their part in accelerating the development of a closer partnership between belarus and the european union. in conclusion, therefore, our offer to belarus is clear. the european union is ready to work closely with minsk and support its political and economic development. but we would welcome significant positive steps from the belarus leadership which would allow us to develop our relationship in the same way as we do with other eastern partners if they play their part.

in writing. in the debate on human rights in belarus and on the decision by member states to extend until october 2010 the sanctions against certain representatives of the belarusian regime, it should be noted that the situation in belarus is gradually changing. the council conclusions of 17 november 2009 stated that new opportunities for dialogue and deeper cooperation between the european union and belarus have emerged. in order to encourage the reform of the belarusian authorities, member states agreed to the temporary lifting of the sanctions on the freedom of movement of senior representatives of the belarusian authorities. the european commission is preparing directives to facilitate the acquisition of eu visas by belarusians and a readmission agreement. nevertheless, it must not be forgotten that human rights in belarus continue to be violated and the hopeful positive steps taken since october 2008, such as the release of most political prisoners and the authorization of the distribution of two independent newspapers, remain insufficient. the use of the death penalty remains a flagrant violation of human rights: belarus is the only european country still to use the death penalty, and in recent months there have been a number of death sentences. we therefore address our demands to the belarusian decision-makers to at least respect human rights, including a moratorium on the death penalty, the renewal of the electoral law and the guarantee of freedom of expression and the media.

author. − mr president, three years ago a major reform of european cohesion policy was introduced taking into account the unprecedented enlargement of the union and new emerging challenges. it was not by chance that, back in 2005 and 2006, the top priorities for european cohesion policy were: the lisbon strategy, innovation and competiveness, climate change, energy security and efficiency, water efficiency, investment in new skills, attractiveness of territories for young people, and quality of life. it is because we have understood that the mission of cohesion policy is to anticipate change, not to follow it, that we have put on the cohesion policy agenda for 2007-2013 all those priorities which we see today in the commission’s europe 2020 agenda. that is why, more than two years ago, the regions 2020 analytical report was published. the purpose was to know what the cohesion policy priorities should be after 2013. today we are well prepared to face the future. a year ago the policy put all its assets at the disposal of the european recovery package, thereby also providing the essential link between the exit strategy from a real economic crisis on the one hand and long-term sustainable growth and structural transformation on the other. but our oral question is about the future. in years to come the europe we live in will be in need of strong collective action to respond to the expectations of its citizens, who are today informed citizens, fully aware of how much depends on choices made by policymakers. those expectations are confirmed by public opinion polls. jacques delors once said that the european single market is about competition that stimulates, about cooperation that makes us stronger and about solidarity that makes us united. european cohesion that makes the single market work is delivered by the european regional policy, which is today based exactly on this triple foundation: competitiveness, cooperation and solidarity. for years we have talked about the need to unlock, to mobilise, the development potential of all european regions and cities. experience and logic clearly show that this mobilisation turns out to be most effective and efficient if pursued through the direct engagement of subnational levels of european governments. the european regional policy has already passed the subsidiarity test. subsidiarity works for europe. the 2006 reform of cohesion policy has made it a modern place-based policy founded on a balance between equity and efficiency, between bottom-up and top-down approaches, between common strategic european objectives and local flexibility. there is a need to move further on those issues, to continue the reform of policy governance, but certain principles should not be abandoned. the new treaty has cemented the new understanding of european subsidiarity already deeply rooted in the cohesion policy, that is subsidiarity extended to local and regional level of governance. we can do more on it, especially with regard to the local level. those who suggest that cohesion policy can be limited to brussels and national level either do not know the european reality, or do not understand that excluding local and regional europe from the pursuit of common european objectives is economically at best unwise and politically dangerous. cohesion is a notion that excludes exclusion. for political, economic, social and legitimacy reasons, cohesion policy must not be divisive: it should be a policy for all, as the internal market is, as the common currency is. all elements of this integration triangle – common market, common currency, cohesion – are mutually strengthening and interdependent. they are our common european public good. we policymakers have raised the stakes by promising to deliver. the challenges are well known; the eu 2020 strategy has been opened to public consultations. development policy with clear targets and tools is needed. cohesion policy is a policy for development that engages all levels of european governance working in concert for european citizens. to conclude, europe needs new energy to take care of its future, to renew itself in an assertive way. it is legitimate to ask where this energy could and should come from. for me the answer is clear. today this energy should come from below. today this energy can be released through the direct engagement of local and regional levels of european governance in the pursuit of common european objectives.
mr. chairman, please! today, cohesion policy is helping to develop road and rail infrastructure, especially in the new member states. this policy has created and will probably create many new jobs in the coming years. investments in environmental protection are also very important. when assessing the policy and its effectiveness, the key question is: what happens after 2013? the european parliament should make it clear that it does not agree to rationalizing cohesion policy. after 2013, cohesion policy should, in addition to these traditional actions and mechanisms, support research, science, development, innovation, the creation of modern jobs and the fight against climate change. cohesion policy should also extend its coverage to rural areas. it is important that it be implemented on a regional and macro-regional basis.
mr. chairman, please! the podkarpatie region, which i represent, is a wonderful, ambitious, hardworking people, a place where many vibrant companies operate, where modern centres such as the air force valley are being built, and at the same time it is one of the least developed areas of the european union. our problems are not due to a lack of will, but to structural and infrastructural constraints that we are trying to eliminate through various programmes. i would like to emphasize that as part of our activities we do not ask for charity, but for support of our initiatives. we also want to make europe's economy more competitive and to find solutions to help protect our climate. however, we want the shift in funding priorities to be gradual rather than drastic, as this would leave the weaker regions to their own devices. it is very important that the regions implement cohesion policy, because this is the best way to achieve results. i would also like to point out that cohesion policy has a very important message for citizens. it shows that europe is united and that it is worthwhile to participate in this unique project.
mr. chairman, please! cohesion policy is a pillar of development policy. it is this policy that most strengthens the subjectivity of regions and local communities. in my opinion, we fall into two extremes. some would like to put too much into this policy, others too little. the most important objective of this policy is sustainable development in various areas. cohesion policy must be one, covering both urban and rural areas. let us remember that the union is very diverse after such a great enlargement. balancing the development opportunities is an important task. the challenges we face today are the economic crisis, the demographic challenge and, finally, climate change. one thing is certain: cohesion policy needs to be continued and adapted to the challenges of the present.
in writing. i am afraid that the provisions proposed by the commission - especially those concerning the abolition of objective 2 and the shift from the regional dimension of cohesion policy to a sectoral approach - could mean a return to the concept of a 'two-speed europe' and a widening of the economic and civilizational distance between 'old' and 'new' europe. such a model would be a departure from the integration of the whole of the 27 member states and from the idea of solidarity enshrined in article 3 of the lisbon treaty. this idea is at the heart of the whole cohesion policy, which is intended to lead to equal opportunities and to eliminate disparities between regions. the commission's proposal to increase the emphasis on research and development of new technologies is to be welcomed. this is the course europe needs. however, it is important to take into account the regions and countries for which the main concern is to achieve a level of employment that is in line with the eu average. keep in mind that there is more than an 11-fold difference in wealth between the richest and poorest areas of the eu. the main objective of the eu's cohesion policy must be to close these gaps. a new version of the document is currently being developed. i hope that the commission will take into account the votes cast in today's debate and those from across the european union and at different levels: local authorities, governments, associations and ngos. a good regional policy can only be pursued in close cooperation with the regions.

acting president of the council. - mr president! - what is it? the council notes with satisfaction that parliament has confirmed the agreement reached at the conciliation meeting on 18 november earlier this year. together with the outcome of the council's second reading, we consider that parliament's second reading can be considered as a joint text of the two arms of the budgetary authority, in accordance with the new article 314 of the lisbon treaty. the council accepts this joint text and the president of the european parliament can therefore declare the budget finally adopted. i would point out, however, that the council considers that this budget should be signed by both parties as soon as you, mr president, declare it finally adopted, since the new treaty stipulates that both the council and parliament are responsible for this. the council regrets that this position has not been taken into account. that said, we do not in any way question what we have agreed. we hope, however, that by next year's budgetary procedure there will have been enough time to sort out these matters. i would also like to take this opportunity to thank once again the chairman of the committee on budgets, mr alain lamassoure, and the three rapporteurs, mr lászlo surján, mr vladimir maňka and mr jutta haug, for their constructive attitude throughout the budgetary procedure, which also shows the very good cooperation we have had in this work. i would like to conclude with a personal reflection. being chairman of the board is probably the best thing i'll ever be. it has been a great honour to serve europe in this way and i want to thank you for it. thank you so much. give it up.

from the treaty of nice to the treaty of lisbon. it was a very difficult transition. we started with the treaty of nice and we are ending with the treaty of lisbon, which is why this declaration is necessary. you need to hear this statement. the 2010 budgetary procedure was exceptional. it was initiated in accordance with article 272 of the treaty establishing the european community, but its final stage was carried out after the entry into force of the treaty of lisbon. on 18 november 2009, the european parliament, the council and the european commission therefore decided to continue the budgetary procedure in accordance with the treaty establishing the european community, but also reached an agreement covering the outcome of the budgetary procedure, including the vote by parliament, which took place in full compliance with the multiannual financial framework. the president of the council has just confirmed on behalf of the council that he has approved the budget we have just voted on. this means that parliament and the council have reached agreement on a common text, respecting the principles and objectives of article 314. i note that the budgetary procedure which was initiated in accordance with article 272 of the treaty establishing the european community and continued in accordance with article 314 of the treaty on the functioning of the european union has been completed in accordance with article 314 of the treaty on the functioning of the european union and the multiannual financial framework. the budgetary procedure can therefore be considered closed and in writing. - mr president! - what are you doing? the conciliation procedure resulted in an agreed level of expenditure satisfactory to parliament for the union's key objectives for the coming year. the agreements on the resources for the implementation of the european economic recovery plan, including energy projects, for which eur 1 980 million has been earmarked, are particularly important. eur 420 million will be allocated to broadband internet deployment, which will contribute to the lisbon strategy. the commission's administrative expenditure was substantially revised at the last minute following the entry into force of the treaty of lisbon. the establishment of the european council as an institution of the union, the establishment of the office of the president of the european council and the establishment of an external service have implications for the budget of the union. the costs of the european council and the presidency, estimated at eur 23.5 million, will be covered by the 2009 savings, while the costs of the creation of the external service may exceed the eur 72 million currently in the 2010 budget reserve. the debate on 2010 spending will not end today. the funds in the reserve may prove insufficient and a budgetary adjustment will be necessary. it is therefore necessary to call on the member states to show responsibility and to allocate the necessary resources to enable the union to fulfil the new obligations arising from the treaty of lisbon.
